196:
## 4. Meghiya Vagga
## 1. Commentary on the Meghiya Sutta
In the first sutta of the Meghiya Vagga, 'Cālikāyaṃ' means in the city named Cālikā. It is said that, except for the area of the gate, there is shifting mud all around that city. Because it is situated depending on that shifting mud, it appears to be moving to those who look at it. Therefore, it is called 'Cālikā'. 'Cālike Pabbate' means there is a mountain not far from that city. Because that mountain is also entirely white, it appears to be moving to those who look at it during the Uposatha days of the dark fortnight. Therefore, it has come to be known as 'Cālika Mountain'. There, they built a great monastery for the Blessed One. At that time, the Blessed One made that city his resort for alms and stayed in that Cālika Mountain Great Monastery. Therefore, it is said: 'He was staying at Cālika on Cālika Mountain.' 'Meghiya' is the name of that Elder. 'Upaṭṭhāko hoti' means he was an attendant. Indeed, during the first period after the Enlightenment (Paṭhama-bodhi), the Blessed One did not have permanent attendants. Sometimes it was the Elder Nāgasamāla, sometimes the Elder Nāgita, sometimes the Elder Upavāna, sometimes the Elder Sunakkhatta. At that time, it was the Elder Meghiya who was the attendant. Therefore, it is said: 'At that time, the Venerable Meghiya was the Blessed One's attendant.'

'Jantugāmaṃ' is the name of another alms village for that same monastery. There is also a reading 'Jattugāmaṃ'. 'Kimikāḷāya' means in the river named 'Kimikāḷā' because of the abundance of black worms. 'Jaṅghavihāraṃ' means walking about to dispel the fatigue that has arisen in the calves due to sitting for a long time. 'Pāsādikaṃ' means inspiring confidence (pāsāda) in those who see it because the trees are not sparse and the leaves are smooth and glossy. It is 'Manuñña' (delightful) because of the pleasant shade and the beauty of the ground. It is called 'Ramaṇīya' (charming) because it delights the mind by generating joy and happiness in those who enter. 'Alaṃ' means sufficient; it also has the meaning of 'yutta' (suitable). 'Padānatthikassa' is for one who desires meditation (bhāvanā). 'Padhānāya' is for the purpose of practicing the ascetic Dhamma (samaṇadhamma). 'Āgaccheyyāhaṃ' means 'I would like to come.' It is said that in the past, that place had been a garden enjoyed by the Elder when he was a king for five hundred successive births. Therefore, just by seeing it, his mind inclined towards staying there. Wait a moment—
197:
The Teacher, having heard the Elder's words and considering them, knew that 'his wisdom has not yet reached maturity.' Thus, while refusing him for the time being, he spoke in this way. As for the words 'Ekakamhi tāva' (While I am alone), he said this to generate gentleness of mind, thinking: 'Even if this monk goes and his task is not accomplished, he will return again without doubt out of affection.' 'Yāva aññopi koci bhikkhu āgacchati' means 'Wait until some other monk besides yourself comes to my presence.' There is also a reading 'koci bhikkhu dissati'. Some also read it as 'āgacchatu', and similarly as 'dissatu'.

'Natthi kiñci uttari karaṇīyaṃ' (There is nothing further to be done) means that because the sixteen tasks such as full understanding (pariññā) regarding the Four Noble Truths have been completed by the four paths, or because Omniscience has been attained, there is no further task to be done beyond that. 'Natthi katassa vā paticayo' means that for one who has already attained the paths and fruits, there is no further repetition or development. A path that has been developed is not developed again, nor is there a task to be done by abandoning again the defilements that have already been abandoned. 'Atthi katassa paticayo' means (from Meghiya's perspective): 'Although there are virtues such as morality (sīla) that have been fulfilled in my continuity, because the Noble Path has not yet been attained, there is still the repetition known as further development for the sake of that path; it is desired.' 'Dear Meghiya, what else can we say to you who are saying, "I will practice the Dhamma of a recluse"?'—this is the meaning.

'Divāvihāraṃ nisīdi' means he sat down for the day-abiding. He sat on that very same auspicious stone slab where he had previously sat for five hundred successive births as a king, enjoying the royal garden surrounded by various groups of dancers. From the moment he sat down, his state as a monk seemed to vanish; he felt as if he had taken on the appearance of a king, surrounded by dancers, sitting on a costly throne under a white parasol. Then, as he was relishing that prosperity, sensual thoughts (kāma-vitakka) arose in the Elder Meghiya. At that very moment, he saw as if two thieves caught with their stolen goods were brought and placed before him. Among those thieves, a thought of ill-will (byāpāda-vitakka) arose through the power of ordering the execution of one; a thought of cruelty (vihiṃsā-vitakka) arose through the power of ordering the binding of the other. In this way, the Elder was surrounded and overwhelmed by unwholesome thoughts, like a tree entwined by a net of creepers or like a honey-gatherer surrounded by bees. Referring to this state of being surrounded by unwholesome thoughts, the words beginning with 'Atha kho āyasmato meghiyassa' were spoken in the Pali text.
198:
How wonderful indeed! Just as the Venerable Ānanda, seeing the wrinkled body of the Blessed One, said, "It is wonderful, Bhante; it is marvelous, Bhante" (Saṃ. Ni. 5.511), so too is it wonderful that unwholesome thoughts surrounded this Elder Meghiya. Other teachers, however, say: "At that time, sensual thought (kāma-vitakka) arose through attachment to the flowers, fruits, and foliage; thought of ill-will (byāpāda-vitakka) arose upon hearing the sounds of birds with harsh voices; thought of harmfulness (vihiṃsā-vitakka) arose with the intention to ward off those birds with clods of earth and such; sensual thought arose through the longing for that garden, thinking 'Let me dwell only here'; thought of ill-will arose through a corrupted mind upon seeing hunters here and there; and thought of harmfulness arose with the intention to harass them." In whatever way it may be, the very arising of wrong thoughts in that Elder is the cause for wonder. "Anvāsattā" means closely attached or intermingled. Even when referring to oneself or to a person worthy of respect in the singular, the plural form is sometimes seen. There is also a variant reading "anusanto".

"Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami" means that, being thus surrounded by wrong thoughts and unable to practice the suitability for meditation (kammaṭṭhāna-sappāya), he reflected: "The Blessed One, who sees far, saw this matter and forbade me. I shall report this matter to the Possessor of Ten Powers." He then rose from his seat and approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he reported his experience, beginning with: "Bhante, here to me..."

In that passage, "yebuyyena" means frequently or constantly. "Pāpakā" means evil. "Akusalā" means those arising from lack of skill, or they are called "pāpaka" because they lead to miserable destinations (duggati), and "akusala" because they are the opposite of the wholesome. "Vitakka" is the state that applies the mind towards an object. Thought accompanied by sensuality is sensual thought (kāma-vitakka); it means thought associated with defilement-sensuality (kilesa-kāma) taking objective-sensuality (vatthu-kāma) as its object. Thought accompanied by ill-will is thought of ill-will (byāpāda-vitakka). Thought accompanied by harmfulness is thought of harmfulness (vihiṃsā-vitakka). Among them, sensual thought, which proceeds by way of excessive delight in sensual pleasures, is the opposite of renunciation (nekkhamma). Thought of ill-will, which proceeds by way of corruption towards beings, thinking "Let these beings be killed, or perish, or not exist," is the opposite of loving-kindness (mettā). Thought of harmfulness, which proceeds by way of the desire to harass beings with hands, clods, sticks, and so forth, is the opposite of compassion (karuṇā).

Why, then, did the Blessed One permit him to go there? "Even if not permitted, this one will surely leave me and go. If a thought were to arise in him in another way, thinking 'I suppose the Blessed One does not permit me to go because he desires an attendant,' that thought would lead to his lack of welfare for a long time..."
199:
"...'The Blessed One does not permit me to go because he desires me as an attendant'—such a thought occurring in another way might arise in the Elder Meghiya. Such a thought occurring in another way would lead to the Elder Meghiya's lack of welfare and suffering for a long time. (Reflecting thus), he gave permission.

Thus, while the Elder Meghiya was sitting there after reporting his experience, the Blessed One, desiring to teach him the suitable Dhamma, spoke the teaching beginning with: 'Meghiya, for the deliverance of mind that is not yet mature...' (aparipakkāya cetovimuttiyā). In that text, 'aparipakkāya' means not yet having reached maturity. 'Cetovimuttiyā' refers to the mind's liberation from defilements. Indeed, in the preliminary stage, the mind's liberation from defilements occurs through substitution (tadaṅga) and suppression (vikkhambhana). In the later stage, it occurs through eradication (samuccheda) and tranquillization (paṭipassaddhi). Since this liberation has been explained in detail below (in the Meghiya Vagga), it should be understood according to the method stated there. In this context, when the inclination (āsaya) is matured and awakened by the states that bring the path and fruit of Arahantship to maturity, and when the deliverance of mind reaches maturity by taking hold of the 'womb of the path' (maggagabbha) through insight, it is called 'mature.' If it does not reach such maturity, it is called 'unripe.'

What are the states that bring the path and fruit of Arahantship to maturity? They should be understood as fifteen states by way of purifying the faculty of faith and so forth. Thus it was said:

'By these three modes, the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) is purified: by avoiding persons without faith, by associating with, following, and attending upon persons with faith, and by reflecting on discourses that inspire confidence.

By these three modes, the faculty of energy (viriyindriya) is purified: by avoiding lazy persons, by associating with, following, and attending upon persons who have aroused energy, and by reflecting on the right efforts (sammappadhāna).

By these three modes, the faculty of mindfulness (satindriya) is purified: by avoiding persons of muddled mindfulness, by associating with, following, and attending upon persons of established mindfulness, and by reflecting on the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna).

By these three modes, the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya) is purified: by avoiding unconcentrated persons, by associating with, following, and attending upon concentrated persons, and by reflecting on the jhānas and liberations (vimokkha).

By these three modes, the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya) is purified: by avoiding unwise persons, by associating with, following, and attending upon wise persons, and by reflecting on the practice of profound knowledge.'
200:
“In this way, by these fifteen modes—avoiding these five persons, associating with, serving, and attending to these five persons, and reflecting on these five Suttantas—these five faculties are purified” (as stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga).

There are another fifteen things that lead to the maturity of liberation (the fruit of the path to Arahantship). They are: the five faculties beginning with faith; the five perceptions conducive to penetration, namely, the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering, the perception of non-self, the perception of abandoning, and the perception of dispassion; and good friendship (kalyāṇamittatā), restraint of virtue (sīlasaṃvara), austerity (abhisallekhatā), arousal of energy (vīriyārambha), and penetrative wisdom (nibbedhikā paññā). Among these, the Teacher, who is skilled in disciplining those who should be disciplined, wishing to show the things that lead to the maturity of liberation such as good friendship to the Elder Meghiya according to his inclination, said: “Five things lead to maturity (of the fruit of the path to Arahantship),” and to explain them in detail, he said: “Here, Meghiya, a monk has good friends,” and so on.

In that context, ‘kalyāṇamitta’ means one who has a good, auspicious, and excellent friend. One who has a friend endowed with qualities such as virtue, who is “a destroyer of evil and a provider of welfare,” and who is helpful in every way, is indeed a kalyāṇamitta. Because one exists together with such good persons in all postures and does not exist without them, one is called ‘kalyāṇasahāya’ (good companion). Because one is inclined, leaned, and sloped toward good persons by way of mind and body, one is called ‘kalyāṇasampavaṅka’ (good associate). By these three terms, he inspires respect for association with good friends.

In that context, this is the characteristic of a good friend—In this Dispensation, a good friend is endowed with faith, endowed with virtue, endowed with learning, endowed with generosity, endowed with energy, endowed with mindfulness, endowed with concentration, and endowed with wisdom. Among these, through the attainment of faith, he believes in the Enlightenment of the Tathāgata and the law of kamma and its result. Because of that faith, he does not abandon his desire for the welfare of beings, which is the cause of Perfect Enlightenment. Through the attainment of virtue, he is dear and pleasing to his fellow practitioners, respected and revered, an admonisher, a censurer of evil, a speaker, and one patient in speech. Through the attainment of learning, he is a speaker of profound talk connected with the Four Noble Truths, Dependent Origination, and so on. Through the attainment of generosity, he has few wishes, is contented, secluded, and not entangled with people. Through the attainment of energy, he is one who has aroused energy for the welfare of beings. Through the attainment of mindfulness, he is one with established mindfulness. Through the attainment of concentration...
201:
...being endowed with concentration, he is undistracted and has a well-concentrated mind. Through the attainment of wisdom, he knows things without distortion. Seeking the course of wholesome states with mindfulness, knowing the welfare and harm of beings as they really are with wisdom, becoming one-pointed in mind regarding that welfare with concentration, and restraining beings from harm and engaging them in welfare with energy. Therefore, it is said:

“Dear, respected, and revered,
A speaker and patient listener,
A speaker of profound talk,
And one who does not urge one to what is improper.”

This first factor leads to maturity (of the path and fruit). This factor called good friendship is mentioned first among these five factors because it is the beginning of the living of the holy life and because it is the most helpful and primary for all wholesome states; thus, it is the first blameless factor that leads to the maturity of liberation of mind (the fruit of Arahantship) by way of purifying faith and so on which are not yet purified. In this context, the great helpfulness and primacy of a good friend should be understood through such Sutta passages as: “Venerable sir, this good friendship is half of the holy life,” said the Treasurer of the Dhamma, the Elder Ānanda. The Buddha prohibited him twice, saying, “Do not say so, Ānanda,” and then said, “Ānanda, this good friendship, this good companionship, is the entire holy life.”

Furthermore, there is another set of factors. In the word “sīlavā” (virtuous), in what sense is it “sīla” (virtue)? It is virtue in the sense of composing (sīlana). What is this “sīlana”? It means composing, the non-scatteredness of bodily actions and so on by way of good character. Alternatively, it means supporting (upadhāraṇa), in the sense of being a foundation for wholesome states such as jhāna. Therefore, it is called virtue because it supports (wholesome states) or because it composes (bodily actions, etc.). This is the meaning of virtue according to the method of linguistic characteristics. Other teachers, however, explain the meaning according to the method of nirutti (etymology) as: “the sense of the head (sira), the sense of coolness (sītala), the sense of composing (sīla), and the sense of restraint (saṃvara).” One who possesses that virtue either in its completeness or in its excellence is “sīlavā” (virtuous), meaning one endowed with virtue.

To show how one is virtuous and endowed with virtue, he said “restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha” and so on. Therein, “Pātimokkha” refers to the virtue of the training rules. For it is called Pātimokkha because it protects (pāti) the one who guards it and frees (mokkheti) him from sufferings such as those of the states of deprivation. Restraint (saṃvara) means guarding, the non-transgression by way of body and speech.
202:
The Pātimokkha itself is the restraint, thus it is called the Pātimokkha restraint (pātimokkhasamvara). Because he is restrained by that Pātimokkha restraint and has the doors of body and speech closed, he is called 'restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint' (pātimokkhasamvarasamvuto). This term illustrates the monk's established state in that virtue (sīla). The term 'viharati' (dwells) illustrates the state of being one who habitually dwells in a manner consistent with that virtue. The term 'ācāragocarasampanno' (endowed with proper conduct and resort) illustrates the qualities that are helpful for the Pātimokkha restraint below and for the application to higher special qualities above. The term 'anumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvī' (seeing danger in the slightest faults) illustrates the nature of not deviating from the Pātimokkha virtue. The term 'samādāya' (having undertaken) illustrates the taking up of the training rules without exception. The term 'sikkhati' (he trains) illustrates the state of being endowed with the training. The term 'sikkhāpadesu' (in the training rules) illustrates the things that should be trained in.

Alternatively—because of the strength of defilements, the ease of doing evil, and the difficulty of doing good, one has the nature of falling frequently into the states of deprivation (apāya); thus he is called 'pātī', referring to an ordinary person (puthujjana). Or, because of impermanence, being cast by the force of kamma into existences and so on, one has the nature of wandering and revolving without stability like a potter's wheel; thus he is called 'pātī'. Or, by the power of death, the individual form (attabhāva) has the nature of falling into various groups of beings; thus he is called 'pātī', referring to the continuity of beings or the mind itself. Because it liberates that 'pātī' (being) from the suffering of saṃsāra, it is called 'Pātimokkham'. Through the liberation of the mind, a being is said to be 'vimutto' (liberated). For it is said: 'Beings are purified through the purification of the mind,' and 'The mind is liberated from the taints (āsavas) without clinging.'

Alternatively, because of causes such as ignorance (avijjā), one falls, goes, or exists in saṃsāra; thus he is called 'pātī'. Is it not said: 'For beings hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, who run on and wander [in saṃsāra]...'? For that 'pātī' (being), liberation from the three types of defilements (saṅkilesa) such as craving occurs through this virtue; therefore it is called 'Pātimokkho'. The formation of the compound as in 'kaṇṭhekālo' and so on should be understood.

Alternatively, because it causes one to fall or perish through sufferings, it is called 'pātī', referring to the mind. It is said: 'The world is led by the mind, pulled around by the mind.' Liberation of that 'pātī' (mind) occurs through this virtue; therefore it is called 'Pātimokkho'. Or, one falls into the suffering of the states of deprivation and the suffering of saṃsāra because of this; thus it is called 'pātī', referring to defilements such as craving. It is said: 'Craving gives birth to a man,' 'A man with craving as his companion,' and so on. Liberation from that 'pātī' (cause of falling) occurs; therefore it is called 'Pātimokkho'.
203: Alternatively, those in which [beings] fall are called 'pātī'; they are the six internal and six external bases (āyatana). It is also said: 'The world has arisen in the six; it makes intimacy in the six' (Sutta Nipāta). Because it is liberation from the 'pātī' known as the six internal and external bases, it is called 'Pātimokkha'. Alternatively, that in which there is falling (vinipāta) is called 'pātī', referring to saṃsāra. Because it is liberation from that saṃsāra, it is called 'Pātimokkha'. Alternatively, because He is the overlord of the entire world, the Blessed One, the Lord of Dhamma, is called 'Pati' (Lord); that by which one is liberated is 'mokkha'. Because it is the means of liberation prescribed by that 'Pati' (Lord), it is called 'Patimokkha'; Patimokkha is the same as Pātimokkha. Or, because it is the root of all virtues, it is called 'Pati' in the sense of being supreme; and since it is 'mokkha' in the sense already mentioned, it is 'Patimokkha'; Patimokkha is the same as Pātimokkha. Thus it is said in detail: 'The Pātimokkha is the beginning, it is the face (entrance)...' and so on. Alternatively, the syllable 'pa' is in the sense of variety (pakāra), and 'ati' is a particle in the sense of absolute (accanta); therefore, because it liberates absolutely through various ways, it is called 'Pātimokkha'. This virtue liberates absolutely—by itself through the power of substitution of opposites (tadaṅga), and together with concentration and wisdom through the power of suppression (vikkhambhana) and eradication (samuccheda); thus it is called 'Pātimokkha'. Or, because it is liberation from each respective fault of transgression, it is 'Patimokkha'; liberation from each respective fault of transgression is the meaning here. Patimokkha is the same as Pātimokkha. Or, 'mokkha' means Nibbāna; because it is the image (reflection) of that Nibbāna, it is called 'Patimokkha'. For the restraint of virtue is the precursor of Nibbāna, like the dawn before sunrise, and it resembles Nibbāna because it extinguishes defilements accordingly. Patimokkha is the same as Pātimokkha. Or, because it occurs in liberation (mokkha), it is called 'Patimokkha'; Patimokkha is the same as Pātimokkha. In this way, the meaning of the word 'Pātimokkha' should be understood here. That by which one restrains or closes [unwholesome states] is 'samvara' (restraint); Pātimokkha itself is restraint, thus it is 'Pātimokkhasamvara'. In terms of meaning, however, it refers to the abstinences (virati) and volitions (cetanā) from the various transgressions that should be avoided. Because one is endowed with that Pātimokkha restraint, he is called 'Pātimokkhasamvarasamvuta'. This is said in the Vibhaṅga: 'He is endowed with this Pātimokkha restraint, well-endowed, approached, possessed, attained; therefore he is called pātimokkhasamvarasamvuto.' 'Viharati' means he dwells or exists by way of the postures (iriyāpatha). 'Ācārasampanno' means not committing all kinds of improper conduct (anācāra), such as wrong livelihood like giving bamboo and so on, or foolishness of body and so on...
204:
The restraint of the Pātimokkha (Pātimokkhasamvara) is indeed the virtue of restraint which cools the defilements and is a substitute for Nibbāna. Alternatively, it is called Pātimokkha because it arises in liberation (mokkha). In this context, the meaning of the word Pātimokkha should be understood thus: it is called restraint (samvara) because it protects through that collection of training rules. Since the virtue of the Pātimokkha itself is the means of protection, it is called Pātimokkhasamvara. In terms of meaning, it refers to the three mental factors of abstinence (virati) and the mental factor of volition (cetanā), because they abstain from various transgressions. One who is endowed with, fully endowed with, has approached, has attained, has arisen, has well arisen, and has reached fulfillment in this Pātimokkhasamvara is said to be 'restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha' (Vibhaṅga 511).

'Dwells' (viharati) means living, occurring, and moving by way of the postures.

'Endowed with conduct and resort' (ācāragocarasampanno) is so called because, by not practicing wrong livelihood such as giving bamboo and by not committing physical misconduct and so forth, one avoids all improper conduct and is endowed with the accomplishment of conduct suitable for monks, described as 'non-transgression by body, non-transgression by speech, and non-transgression by both body and speech'; and because one is endowed with resort (gocara), which means avoiding unsuitable places such as the houses of prostitutes and instead visiting places suitable for seeking alms and so forth.

Alternatively, a monk who is respectful and deferential toward the Teacher, respectful and deferential toward his fellow practitioners, endowed with moral shame and moral dread (hiri-ottappa), well-clothed and well-robed, endowed with graceful postures in advancing, retreating, looking ahead, looking aside, bending, and stretching, who has the doors of his senses guarded, is moderate in eating, devoted to wakefulness, endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña), has few wishes, is easily satisfied, secluded, not socialising with people, who acts respectfully in the minor duties (abhisamācārika-sīla), and dwells with much reverence and esteem—this monk is called 'endowed with conduct' (ācārasampanna).

Resort (gocara) is of three kinds: resort of support (upanissayagocara), resort of protection (ārakkhagocara), and resort of binding (upanibandhagocara). Among these three, the resort of support is a good friend (kalyāṇamitta) who is endowed with the ten subjects of talk (kathāvatthu) and possesses the previously mentioned characteristics; depending on whom one hears what has not been heard, purifies what has been heard, overcomes doubt, straightens one's view, and gains confidence of mind; and by following whose example, one grows in faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom. This good friend is called the 'resort of support'.

When a monk enters a village or reaches a street, he walks with downcast eyes, looking only a yoke's length ahead, and proceeds with the eye-faculty guarded; he walks without looking at elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, women, or men, and without looking up, down, or all around the various directions. This monk is called 'resort of protection'.
205:
The resort of binding (upanibandhagocara) refers to the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). In these foundations of mindfulness, a monk binds his own mind. For this was said by the Blessed One: 'Bhikkhus, what is a monk's resort, his own paternal domain? It is these four foundations of mindfulness.' Among those three kinds of resort, since the resort of support was mentioned previously, resort in this context should be understood by way of the remaining two. Thus, because he is endowed with the aforementioned accomplishment of conduct and this accomplishment of resort, he is called 'endowed with conduct and resort' (ācāragocarasampanno).

'Seeing danger in the slightest faults' (anumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvī) means having the habit of seeing danger in faults of very small or minute proportions. This refers to seeing danger even in minor faults such as Sekhiya offenses and the arising of unwholesome thoughts committed unintentionally through lack of mindfulness. A monk who sees a fault as small as a subtle atom as being as heavy as the king of mountains, Sineru, which is 168,000 yojanas in height; or who sees even a very light offense of wrong speech (dubbhāsita) as being as heavy as a Pārājika offense—such a monk is called 'one who sees danger in the slightest faults'.

'Trains by undertaking the training rules' (samādāya sikkhati sikkhāpadesu) means that whatever training is to be practiced among the training rules, he takes it up well, entirely, in every way, and without remainder, and then practices, carries it out, and fulfills it.

'Effacing' (abhisallekhikā) means having the nature of greatly thinning out the defilements, being suitable for their reduction and abandonment.

'Conducive to opening the mind' (cetovivaraṇasappāyā) means being suitable for serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), which are called the 'opening of the mind' because they remove the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) that cover the mind. Or, it is called cetovivaraṇasappāyā because it is helpful for making the mind of serenity and insight clear and manifest.

Now, in order to show the reason why this talk is called 'effacing' and 'conducive to opening the mind' because it brings about disenchantment (nibbidā) and so forth, the phrase 'for absolute disenchantment' (ekantanibbidāya) and so on is stated. In that passage, 'for absolute disenchantment' means for the sake of becoming disenchanted with the suffering of the round of existence (vaṭṭadukkha). 'For dispassion, for cessation' (virāga, nirodha) means for the sake of the fading away of lust and the cessation of that same suffering. 'For peace' (upasama) means for the calming of all defilements. 'For higher knowledge' (abhiññā) means for knowing all things that should be known with direct knowledge. 'For enlightenment' (sambodha) means for knowing with the four path-knowledges (magga-ñāṇa). 'For Nibbāna' means for the sake of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna). Among these terms, insight (vipassanā) is expressed by the first three terms, the path (magga) by the next two, and Nibbāna by the last two. Serenity and insight...
206:
It is shown that all these superhuman states (uttari-manussa-dhamma), beginning with tranquility and insight and ending with Nibbāna, are accomplished for one who attains the ten subjects of talk (katha-vatthu).

Now, wishing to explain that teaching in detail, he said "Talk on fewness of wishes" (appiccha-kathā) and so on. In that context, appiccha means having no wishes; talk concerning that absence of wishes is appiccha-kathā. Or, talk associated with the state of having few wishes is appiccha-kathā. In this regard, there are four types of persons according to their wishes: the excessively greedy (atriccha), the evil-minded (pāpiccha), the greatly ambitious (mahiccha), and the one of few wishes (appiccha). Among these four, one who is dissatisfied with what he has obtained and desires more and more is called atriccha. Referring to such an atriccha person:

"From four goddesses he reached eight,
from eight to sixteen,
from sixteen to thirty-two;
the excessively greedy Mittavindaka has reached the razor-wheel;
the wheel revolves on the head of the man struck by desire."

And also: "He is called atriccha because of excessive desire, excessive greed, and the intoxication of excessive greed."

One who, desiring gain, honor, and fame, wishes to be praised for qualities he does not possess is called pāpiccha. Referring to such a pāpiccha person: "Therein, what is scheming (kuhanā)? It is the posturing of the posture, or the talk near [the requisites], or the rejection of requisites, by one of evil wishes (pāpiccha) who is obsessed with gain, honor, and fame, and overcome by desire," and so on.

One who wishes to be praised for the qualities he does possess, and who knows no moderation in receiving [requisites], is called mahiccha. Referring to such a mahiccha person: "Here, someone who is faithful wishes, 'Let people know me as faithful'; being virtuous, he wishes, 'Let people know me as virtuous,'" and so on.

Because of the insatiability of such a mahiccha person, even his own biological mother cannot satisfy his mind. Therefore, it is said:

"A great mass of fire, the ocean,
and a person of great ambition (mahiccha);
even if these three are given requisites by the cartload,
these three remain insatiable."
207:
Avoiding those faults such as excessive greed (atricchatā) and so on, the desire to conceal the qualities one possesses and knowing moderation in receiving [requisites] is called appiccha (fewness of wishes). Such a person of few wishes, because of the desire to conceal the qualities clearly present in himself, does not wish, "Let people know me as faithful," even though he is faithful. Even if he is virtuous, learned, secluded, energetic, mindful, concentrated, or wise, he does not wish, "Let people know me as wise."

That fewness of wishes is of four kinds: fewness of wishes regarding requisites (paccaya-appiccha), regarding ascetic practices (dhutaṅga-appiccha), regarding learning (pariyatti-appiccha), and regarding attainment (adhigama-appiccha). Among these four, one who has few wishes regarding the four requisites considers the donor, the gift, and his own capacity before receiving. If the gift is abundant but the donor wishes to give only a little, he takes only a little according to the donor's wish. If the gift is small but the donor wishes to give much, he takes only a little according to the measure of the gift. If the gift is abundant and the donor also wishes to give much, he knows his own capacity and takes only a moderate amount. Such a monk brings about gain that has not yet arisen, makes firm the gain that has arisen, and pleases the minds of the donors. A monk who practices asceticism and does not want others to know that he possesses the merit of ascetic practices is called dhutaṅga-appiccha. One who does not wish to make known his great learning is called pariyatti-appiccha. One who, though being a stream-enterer (sotāpanna) or the like, does not wish to make known his state of stream-entry to his fellow practitioners is called adhigama-appiccha. Talk that proceeds by way of demonstrating the various benefits of fewness of wishes of such persons, and by way of demonstrating the danger of the opposite, namely, the various forms of desire such as excessive greed, is called appiccha-kathā.

As for "talk on contentment" (santuṭṭhi-kathā), contentment (santuṭṭhi) means being satisfied with what one has obtained. Or, it is contentment that is even, having abandoned uneven desire for requisites. Or, it is satisfaction with what is present. It is also said:
"Not grieving over the past,
not longing for the future,
sustaining oneself with what is present,
one is called 'contented' (santuṭṭha)."
Or, it is satisfaction with the four requisites in the manner permitted by the Blessed One according to the right method. In essence, it is contentment with whatever requisites are obtained, and it is of twelve kinds.
208:
How? Just as there are three kinds of contentment regarding robes—contentment with whatever is obtained (yathālābhasantoṣa), contentment according to strength (yathābalasantoṣa), and contentment according to what is appropriate (yathāsāruppasantoṣa)—so there are three kinds each regarding alms-food and so on.

To explain these divisions: In this Dispensation, a monk receives a robe, whether it be of good quality or poor. He is satisfied with that very robe; he does not long for another, and even if he receives another, he does not take it. This is his contentment with whatever is obtained (yathālābhasantoṣa) regarding robes. Furthermore, a monk may be naturally weak or oppressed by illness and old age; if he wears a heavy robe, he becomes fatigued. If that monk, having exchanged his robe with a compatible monk, is satisfied with a light robe, he is still considered content. This is his contentment according to strength (yathābalasantoṣa) regarding robes. Another monk, having received a costly robe such as one made of silk, reflects: "This is suitable for elders of long standing, for those of great learning, for the sick and weak, or for those who receive little." Having given it to them, he himself collects rags from dust heaps and the like to make a double-layered robe (saṅghāṭi), or he takes and wears their old robes, yet he remains content. This is his contentment according to what is appropriate (yathāsāruppasantoṣa) regarding robes.

In this Dispensation, a monk receives alms-food, whether it be coarse or fine. He is satisfied with that very food he has received; he does not long for another, and even if he receives more, he does not take it. This is his contentment with whatever is obtained (yathālābhasantoṣa) regarding alms-food. Furthermore, a monk may be ill; if he eats coarse food that is contrary to his natural health or his illness, he suffers severe pain and disease. If that monk gives that food to a compatible monk and, having eaten suitable food from him, practices the ascetic Dhamma, he is still considered content. This is his contentment according to strength (yathābalasantoṣa) regarding alms-food. Another monk receives fine alms-food. Just as with the robe, he reflects: "This food is suitable for elders of long standing," and gives it to them. Whether he takes their food or goes on his own alms-round and eats whatever mixed food he receives, he remains content. This is his contentment according to what is appropriate (yathāsāruppasantoṣa) regarding alms-food.

In this Dispensation, a monk receives a lodging, whether it be pleasing or unpleasing, even if it is only a grass hut or a grass mat. He is satisfied with that very place. Even if he later receives a better place, he does not take it. This is his contentment with whatever is obtained (yathālābhasantoṣa) regarding lodgings. Furthermore, a monk may be ill or weak; he receives a lodging that is contrary to his illness or natural health, where his stay is uncomfortable. If he gives that place to a compatible monk and, staying in a suitable lodging belonging to that monk, practices the ascetic Dhamma, he is still considered content.
209:
This is his contentment according to strength (yathābalasantoṣa) regarding lodgings. Another monk, even if he receives a fine lodging, does not accept it, thinking, "A fine lodging is a ground for negligence." Or, due to great merit, he might receive fine lodgings such as caves, pavilions, or gabled houses. Just as with the robes, he gives those lodgings to elders of long standing and, while living anywhere at all, remains content. This is his contentment according to what is appropriate (yathāsāruppasantoṣa) regarding lodgings.

In this Dispensation, a monk receives medicine, whether it be coarse or fine. He is satisfied with that very medicine; he does not long for another, and even if he receives more, he does not take it. This is his contentment with whatever is obtained (yathālābhasantoṣa) regarding medicinal requisites. Furthermore, a monk who needs oil receives molasses; he gives that molasses to a compatible monk and, taking oil from him, prepares his medicine and practices the ascetic Dhamma, yet he remains content. This is his contentment according to strength (yathābalasantoṣa) regarding medicinal requisites. Another monk of great merit receives many fine medicinal requisites such as oil, honey, and molasses. Just as with the robes, he gives them to elders of long standing and, using whatever medicine they bring to him, remains content. Moreover, if a monk is presented with yellow myrobalan steeped in cow's urine in one vessel and the "four sweet foods" (catumadhura) in another, and is told, "Venerable sir, take whichever you desire," and if his illness could be cured by either, he rejects the four sweet foods. Remembering the words, "Yellow myrobalan steeped in urine is praised by the Buddhas and others; the going forth has fermented urine as its support, and in that, you should strive for the rest of your life," he treats his illness with the myrobalan in urine and remains supremely content. This is his contentment according to what is appropriate (yathāsāruppasantoṣa) regarding medicinal requisites.

All such divisions of contentment are called 'santuṭṭhi'. Therefore, in essence, it is called 'contentment with whatever requisites are available' (itarītarappaccayasantoṣa). A talk that proceeds by illustrating the benefits of contentment with whatever is available, and by illustrating the danger of the opposite—evil desires such as excessive greed—is called 'talk on contentment' (santuṭṭhikathā). In the talks that follow, the same method applies; I shall mention only the special distinctions.

In the phrase 'talk on seclusion' (pavivekakathā), there are three kinds of seclusion: physical seclusion (kāyaviveka), mental seclusion (cittaviveka), and seclusion from acquisitions (upadhiviveka). Among these, one who possesses physical seclusion goes alone, stands alone, sits alone, lies down alone, and enters the village for alms alone.
210:
One retreats alone, one advances alone, one undertakes walking meditation alone, one wanders alone, one dwells alone. Thus, in all postures and in all activities, abandoning the company of a group and living in solitude is called physical seclusion (kāya-viveka). The eight attainments are called mental seclusion (citta-viveka). Nibbāna is called seclusion from acquisitions (upadhi-viveka).

It has also been stated thus: "Physical seclusion is for those with secluded bodies who delight in renunciation; mental seclusion is for those with purified minds who have reached supreme purity; and seclusion from acquisitions is for those persons free from acquisitions who have reached the unconditioned (visankhāra)." (Mahāniddesa, 57).

Seclusion itself is called paviveka; talk connected with paviveka is called talk on seclusion (paviveka-kathā).

In this context of talk on non-association (asaṃsagga-kathā), there are five types of association (saṃsagga): association through hearing (savana), association through seeing (dassana), association through conversing (samullapana), association through enjoying together (sambhoga), and physical association (kāya).

Among these five, in this Dispensation, a certain monk hears: "In such-and-such a village or town, there is a woman who is beautiful, attractive, pleasant to behold, and possessed of the most excellent beauty of complexion." Having heard this, he becomes depressed and sinks down; he is unable to maintain the holy life, gives up the training, and returns to the lower life. This entanglement of defilements arising from hearing a disagreeable object (visabhāga-ārammaṇa) is called association through hearing (savana-saṃsagga).

It is not merely that the monk hears, but he himself sees the woman who is beautiful, attractive, pleasant to behold, and possessed of the most excellent beauty of complexion. Having seen her, he becomes depressed and sinks down; he is unable to maintain the holy life, gives up the training, and returns to the lower life. This entanglement of defilements arising from seeing a disagreeable object is called association through seeing (dassana-saṃsagga). The entanglement of defilements arising from mutual conversation after seeing is called association through conversing (samullapana-saṃsagga). Laughing together and so forth are also included in this term. The entanglement of defilements arising from the use of things like leaves or flowers given by a woman, whether one has given something of one's own to her or not, is called association through enjoying together (sambhoga-saṃsagga). The entanglement of defilements arising from acts such as holding a woman's hand is called physical association (kāya-saṃsagga).

Furthermore, regarding one who: "Dwells associated with laypeople in an unsuitable association, sharing their sorrows and sharing their joys, being happy when they are happy, and being sorrowful when they are...
211:
...sorrowful, and personally exerting oneself when their duties and business arise" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.3, Mahāniddesa 164) — such unsuitable association with laypeople as stated, and any association even with fellow practitioners that is a cause for the arising of defilements, having abandoned all that, one establishes a firm sense of urgency (saṃvega) regarding saṃsāra, a strong perception of danger in formations (saṅkhāra), a perception of loathsomeness in the body, shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri-ottappa) preceded by disgust for all unwholesome states, and mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña) in all activities. Being unattached to everything like a drop of water on a lotus leaf, this state of being the opposite of all association is called non-association (asaṃsagga). Talk connected with that non-association is called talk on non-association (asaṃsagga-kathā).

In the term 'talk on the arousal of energy' (vīriyārambha-kathā), energy (vīriya) refers to the state or the action of a heroic person (vīra). Alternatively, it is called vīriya because it should be stirred up or carried out systematically. The arousal of that energy for the sake of abandoning unwholesome states and for the fulfillment of wholesome states is called the arousal of energy (vīriyārambha). This arousal is twofold: bodily and mental. It is threefold: the element of arousal (ārambha-dhātu), the element of endeavor (nikkama-dhātu), and the element of exertion (parakkama-dhātu). It is fourfold by way of the right efforts (sammappadhāna).

All that energy should be understood through the power of a monk who has thus aroused energy: he does not allow a defilement that has arisen while walking to reach the posture of standing; he does not allow a defilement that has arisen while standing to reach the posture of sitting; he does not allow a defilement that has arisen while sitting to reach the posture of lying down. In each of those postures, he suppresses it with the power of energy, not allowing it to raise its head, just as one might catch a cobra by pinning it down with a goat-foot-shaped stick, or as one might strike an enemy's neck with a sharp sword. Talk connected with that energy is called talk on the arousal of energy (vīriyārambha-kathā).

In the talk on virtue (sīla-kathā) and so forth, virtue is of two kinds: mundane (lokiya) and supramundane (lokuttara). Therein, the fourfold purification virtue (catupārisuddhi-sīla), such as the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha, is called mundane virtue. The virtue of the path (magga) and the virtue of the fruit (phala) are called supramundane virtue. Similarly, the eight attainments (samāpatti) together with access concentration (upacāra), which serve as the basis for insight (vipassanā), are mundane concentration (lokiya-samādhi). Concentration associated with the path is called supramundane concentration (lokuttara-samādhi). Similarly, wisdom is also mundane, consisting of wisdom based on learning (sutamaya), wisdom based on reflection (cintāmaya), wisdom associated with jhāna, and insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa). Specifically, in this context, insight wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) is to be taken. Path wisdom and fruit wisdom are supramundane wisdom. Liberation (vimutti) is the liberation of the noble fruit (ariya-phala) and Nibbāna. Other teachers, however, explain the meaning here also by way of liberation by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga), liberation by suppression (vikkhambhana), and liberation by eradication (samuccheda). Knowledge and vision of liberation (vimutti-ñāṇadassana) is the nineteenfold reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa). Thus, of these [talks on] virtue and so forth...
212:
Talk on virtue (sīlakathā), etc., refers to talk that occurs by way of illustrating the benefits mixed with various aspects through the method of properly demonstrating virtue and so forth, or by way of illustrating the disadvantages of the opposites such as immorality (dussīlya), etc.; or it is talk associated with those virtues.

In this context, according to such teachings as "He is himself one of few wishes and speaks to others on talk concerning fewness of wishes" and "He is content with whatever robes he receives and speaks in praise of contentment with whatever robes one receives," it should be understood that talk of such a nature—spoken by one who is himself endowed with qualities such as fewness of wishes and with a beneficial intention for the sake of others—is specifically called "talk on fewness of wishes" (appicchatā-kathā), etc., being described here as "effacing" (abhisallekhika).

Only the talk of a practitioner (kāraka-puggala) particularly accomplishes the desired goal. Indeed, it will be said later: "Meghiya, for a monk who has a noble friend, this is to be expected... he obtains without difficulty."

"Evarūpāya" means talk of such a nature as described. "Nikāmalābhī" means one who obtains what is desired, one who has what is liked; obtaining at will the opportunity to hear and contemplate these ten talks at all times. "Akicchalābhī" means obtaining without pain or difficulty. "Akasiralābhī" means obtaining abundantly.

"Āraddhavīriyo" means one with aroused energy. "Akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya" means for the sake of abandoning unwholesome, evil states, in the sense of them arising from lack of skill. "Kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ" refers to the states of the Path and Fruit along with insight (vipassanā), which are called "wholesome" (kusala) in the sense of shaking off the loathsome unwholesome states and in the sense of being blameless. "Upasampadāya" means for the sake of fulfillment, for the sake of producing them within one's own continuity. "Thāmavā" means endowed with the strength of energy known as persistence (ussōḷhi). "Daḷhaparakkamo" means one with firm effort, with non-lax energy. "Anikkhittadhuro" means one who has not laid down the burden, with non-retreating energy.

"Paññavā" means wise through insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā). "Udayatthagāminiyā" means for the sake of penetrating the arising and passing away of the five aggregates. "Ariyāya" means the faultless wisdom that stands far from defilements by way of suppression (vikkhambhana). "Nibbedhikāya" means wisdom that leads to penetration. "Sammā dukkhakkhayagāminiyā" means wisdom that leads rightly, by way of cause and method, to the Noble Path called "the destruction of suffering" because it exhausts the suffering of the round (vaṭṭa-dukkha).

Among these five factors, virtue, energy, and wisdom are the internal factors of the yogi. The other two are external factors. Nevertheless, only through properly relying on a noble friend...
213:
...can the remaining four factors be fulfilled. Wishing to show the great helpfulness of the noble friend in this matter, the Teacher expands the teaching starting with: "Meghiya, for a monk who has a noble friend, this is to be expected," and so forth. In that text, "pāṭikaṅkhaṃ" means what is certainly to be desired, what will inevitably happen. The word "yaṃ" refers to the action. The meaning is this: in the phrase "he will be virtuous," the state of being virtuous and endowed with virtue of a monk who has a noble friend arises. Because that monk is constantly engaged in the fulfillment of virtue, that fulfillment of virtue is a benefit that will certainly and inevitably come to that monk. The same method should be understood for the phrases "he will dwell restrained by the restraint of the Pāṭimokkha," and so forth.

Thus, the Blessed One, having shown the fulfillment of the entire Dispensation through noble friendship and so forth to the Venerable Meghiya—who, without taking the advice of the Blessed One (the supreme noble friend in the world including the devas), entered that forest grove and fell into such a state of distress—now wishes to reveal the method of meditation to the Elder Meghiya, who has developed a desire to practice in that forest. This is because his meditation was not successful previously due to being oppressed by thoughts of sensual desire (kāma-vitakka), etc., and because [the following meditations] are the direct opposites of those thoughts. Furthermore, wishing to teach the meditation for the sake of the highest path, the Fruit of Arahantship, He said: "Meghiya, a monk, established in these five factors, should further develop four [other] factors," and so forth. In that statement, "tena" refers to that monk who, by relying on a noble friend, is endowed with the qualities of virtue and so forth as mentioned. Therefore, He said: "established in these five factors." "Uttari" means that if dangers such as lust (rāga) arise for a person who has begun tender insight (taruṇa-vipassanā), then for the sake of clearing those dangers, four factors should be developed, produced, and increased beyond that.

"Asubhā" refers to the meditation on foulness in any appropriate one among the eleven subjects of foulness. "Rāgassa pahānāya" means for the sake of abandoning sensual lust (kāma-rāga). This meaning should be illustrated by the simile of the rice reaper: A man takes a sharp sickle and reaps the rice in a rice field starting from the edge. Then, cows break through the fence and enter. That man puts down the sickle, takes a stick, drives the cows out by the same path they entered, repairs the fence as it was before, and then takes the sickle again to reap the rice. In this simile, the rice field should be seen as the Buddha's Dispensation. The rice reaper is like the practitioner (yogāvacara). The sickle is like wisdom. The time of reaping is like the time of performing the work of insight (vipassanā). The stick is like the meditation on foulness (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna). The fence is like restraint (saṃvara). The entry of cows by breaking the fence is like the arising of lust due to negligence without reflection. Putting down the sickle, taking the stick to drive out the cows, repairing the fence, and then re-establishing oneself in insight is like the time of performing the work of insight meditation after clearing away lust with the meditation on foulness, just like the time of reaping rice. This comparison should be noted. Wishing to show such a method of meditation, He said: "The meditation on foulness should be developed for the abandoning of lust." "Mettā" refers to [the abandoning] of ill-will...
214:
The analogy here is as follows: the arising of lust (rāga) due to negligence, without reflection or consideration, is like cattle entering after breaking a fence. Putting down the sickle, taking up a staff, driving the cattle out by the same path they entered, repairing the fence to its original state, and then resuming the reaping of sali rice from where one left off—this is like removing lust through the meditation on foulness (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna) and then returning to the work of insight (vipassanā). Referring to this method of meditation, it was said: "The meditation on foulness should be developed for the abandoning of lust."

'Mettā' refers to the meditation on loving-kindness. "For the abandoning of ill-will (byāpāda)" means for the purpose of abandoning arisen anger, following the same method already mentioned. 'Mindfulness of breathing' (ānāpānasati) refers to the mindfulness of breathing consisting of sixteen bases. "For the cutting off of thoughts (vitakka)" means for the purpose of cutting off arisen thoughts, following the same method already mentioned. "For the uprooting of the conceit 'I am' (asmimāna)" means for the purpose of completely cutting off the ninefold conceit that arises as "I am."

'Anicca-saññino' (those with the perception of impermanence) refers to those who perceive things as impermanent through the power of the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā), which proceeds as "All conditioned things are impermanent," because they do not exist after having come to be, because they possess rise and fall, because they are subject to breaking up, because they are temporary, and because they are the opposite of permanence.

"The perception of non-self (anatta-saññā) will be established" means that the perception of non-self, known as the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā), which proceeds as "All phenomena are non-self," is established in the mind and stands very firmly because of the absence of core essence, because of being beyond control, because of being alien, because of being empty, because of being hollow, and because of being void. Indeed, when the characteristic of impermanence is seen, the characteristic of non-self is also seen. For among the three characteristics, when one is seen, the other two are also seen. Therefore, it was said: "Meghiya, for one who has the perception of impermanence, the perception of non-self is established."

When the characteristic of non-self is seen, the conceit that arises as "I am" is easily abandoned; thus it was said: "One with the perception of non-self reaches the uprooting of the conceit 'I am'." "Nibbāna in this very life" means reaching the Parinibbāna without fuel in this very existence, in this very selfhood, within the phenomena already seen. This is the summary here. For the detailed explanation, the method of meditating on foulness and so forth should be taken as stated in the Visuddhimagga.

"Having known this matter" means having known this matter concerning the Venerable Meghiya, which is the cutting off and destruction of the treasure of merit by the thieves of wrong thoughts. "This inspired utterance" refers to the inspired utterance that illuminates the danger and the benefit in not abandoning and in abandoning sensual thoughts and so forth.
215:
In that verse, 'khudda' has the meaning of lowly or contemptible. 'Vitakkā' refers to the three evil thoughts such as sensual thought (kāma-vitakka) and so forth. Because they are more loathsome than all other thoughts, they are called 'khudda' (lowly thoughts) here, as in the teachings beginning with "Na ca khuddamācare" (One should not practice even a slight wrong).

'Sukhuma' (subtle) is intended to mean thoughts of relatives (ñāti-vitakka) and so forth. These include thoughts of relatives, thoughts of the country (janapada-vitakka), thoughts of immortality (amarā-vitakka), thoughts connected with sympathy for others, thoughts connected with gain, honor, and fame, and thoughts connected with not being despised by others. Because these thoughts are not as harsh or coarse as sensual thoughts and the like, they are called 'sukhuma' (subtle thoughts) due to their non-gross nature.

'Anugata' means following along with the mind. When a thought arises, the mind follows that thought because it directs the mind toward that object. There is also a Pali reading 'anuggatā', which means established by following the object. 'Manaso uppilāvā' means those that cause the mind to be uplifted, puffed up, or agitated.

"Ete avidvā manaso vitakke" (Not knowing these thoughts of the mind) refers to one who does not know these mental thoughts, such as sensual thoughts, as they really are through the full understanding of the known (ñāta-pariññā), full understanding by investigation (tīraṇa-pariññā), and full understanding as abandoning (pahāna-pariññā), in terms of their gratification (assāda), danger (ādīnava), and escape (nissaraṇa).

"Hurā huraṃ dhāvati bhantacitto" (With a wandering mind, one runs from here to there) means that because wrong thoughts have not yet been abandoned, one has an unsteady mind and runs or wanders back and forth among various objects through the power of gratification, thinking "sometimes of forms, sometimes of sounds," and so forth. Alternatively, "Hurā huraṃ dhāvati bhantacitto" means that because thoughts have not been fully understood, one has a mind that wanders through the power of ignorance and craving which are rooted in those thoughts, running and transmigrating back and forth from this world to the next world through the taking up and laying down of the aggregates.

"Ete ca vidvā manaso vitakke" (And knowing these thoughts of the mind) refers to one who knows these mental thoughts, such as sensual thoughts of the various types mentioned, as they really are in terms of gratification and so forth. 'Ātāpiyo' means one who is energetic. 'Saṃvarati' means one closes or restrains. 'Satimā' means one who is endowed with mindfulness. 'Anuggate' means those that have not arisen because they are difficult to obtain.

This is what is meant: Knowing well these aforementioned mental thoughts, such as sensual thoughts, as the cause of the mind's agitation through the Path-knowledge (magga-paññā) accompanied by insight-knowledge (vipassanā-paññā), and being ardent (ātāpī) and mindful (satimā) due to the presence of right effort and right mindfulness which are the associates of that Path-knowledge, that person, through the development of the Noble Path, restrains those thoughts that should not arise in the future and have not yet arisen, closing them off at the moment of the Path through the power of restraint by knowledge (ñāṇa-saṃvara).
216:
...cuts off the path of coming. An Ariya-sāvaka (Noble Disciple) who has become thus is a 'Buddha' through the awakening to the Four Noble Truths, and by attaining Arahatship, abandons these sensual thoughts (kāma-vitakka) and so forth completely, without remainder, cutting them off at the root. In this context, some also read 'anugate'. Its meaning should be understood as previously stated below.

## The Commentary on the First Sutta is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Uddhata Sutta

In the second sutta, 'Kusinārāyaṃ' means in the city of the Malla kings named Kusinārā. 'Upavattane mallānaṃ sālavane' means that just as the Thūpārāma Cetiya is in Anurādhapura, that Sāla grove is in the southwest of the city of Kusinārā. Just as the road entering the city from the south gate of Thūpārāma goes facing east and turns north, similarly, the row of Sāla trees from the garden goes facing east and turns north. Therefore, it is called 'Upavattana' (the turn). It is in the Sāla grove of the Malla kings at that turn. 'Araññakuṭikāyaṃ' refers to a small hut built in a place covered with trees and bushes not far from the row of Sāla trees, hence it is said 'he dwells in a forest hut'. Those monks were devoid of reflection, had abandoned effort, and lived heedlessly. Therefore, it is said 'Uddhatā' (restless) and so forth.

Among those terms, they are called 'Uddhata' because they have much restlessness and an unpeaceful mind. There is conceit (māna) which is like a reed in its hollowness. Because they have conceit like a reed that has grown upwards, they are called 'Unnaḷa'. It means those who have empty conceit that has risen high. They are called 'Capala' (fickle) because they are endowed with or frequently engage in the frivolity of decorating their bowls and robes. They are called 'Mukhara' (talkative) because they have harsh speech and are foul-mouthed. They are called 'Vikiṇṇavāca' (scatter-brained in speech) because they have disorganized or confused speech due to much 'animal talk' (tiracchāna-kathā). They are called 'Muṭṭhassatī' (forgetful) because their mindfulness is confused or lost. It means they are devoid of mindfulness and live heedlessly. They are called 'Asampajāna' (uncomprehending) because they are entirely devoid of clear comprehension. They are called 'Asamāhita' (unconcentrated) because they lack mental concentration even for the duration of a finger-snap (or milking a cow). They are 'Vibbhantacitta' (agitated in mind) because they have a fickle nature and a mind that trembles in various ways, like a deer frightened by danger. They are 'Pākatindriya' (unrestrained in faculties) because they do not guard the sense faculties, of which the mind is the sixth.
217:
“Knowing this meaning” means knowing the heedless living of those monks through restlessness and so forth. “This inspired utterance (Udāna)” means he uttered this Udāna which clearly explains the disadvantages and advantages of living heedlessly and living heedfully, respectively.

In those verses, “unprotected” means insecure because of the absence of the protection of mindfulness. “By the body” means the group of six consciousnesses. Indeed, having seen a form with eye-consciousness, because of the occurrence of covetousness (abhijjhā) and so forth through the grasping of signs (nimitta) and features (anubyañjana) in that form, the door of consciousness cannot be protected by mindfulness. The same method applies to ear-consciousness and so forth. Thus, referring to the lack of protection of the group of six consciousnesses, it is said “with an unprotected body.” Some teachers, however, say the meaning is “by the body” (physical). In their view too, if the meaning is applied according to the method already stated, it would be appropriate. Others read “with an unprotected mind.” In their view also, the meaning is just as stated. “Oppressed by wrong view” means defiled by the adherence to wrong views such as eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi). “Overcome by sloth and torpor” means overcome by sloth (thīna), which has the characteristic of mental sluggishness, and torpor (middha), which has the characteristic of physical sluggishness. It should be connected as “by that body or mind.” “Goes into the power of Mara” means falling into the state where one can be dealt with according to the will of all Maras, such as the Mara of defilements (kilesa-māra). It means not being able to transcend the domain of those Maras.

Indeed, with this first verse, the Blessed One showed the 'vatta' (round of suffering) by way of censuring the heedless living of those monks, saying that those who do not protect the entire mind because of the lack of protection by mindfulness, who have perverted grasps such as “it is permanent” due to improper reflection caused by the absence of wisdom, and who therefore cannot raise their heads from the round of saṃsāra because they are overcome by laziness due to the lack of effort in performing wholesome deeds. Now, to show 'vivatta' (the cessation of the round), he spoke the second verse: “Therefore, one with a protected mind...”

In that verse, “Therefore, one with a protected mind” means because one with an unprotected mind becomes one who can be dealt with according to Mara’s will and remains only in saṃsāra, therefore, one should be one with a protected mind by guarding and closing the sense faculties, of which the mind is the sixth, through the restraint of mindfulness. Indeed, when the mind is protected, the faculties such as the eye are also protected. “One whose range is right intention” means because one whose range is wrong intention, by reflecting improperly in various ways and grasping various wrong views, is oppressed by wrong view...
218:
Since the mind is prone to being manipulated by Māra as he wishes, one who acts with wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) should have the range of right intention (sammā-saṅkappa), such as the thought of renunciation (nekkhamma-saṅkappa). One should make right intention associated with jhāna, etc., the dwelling place of one's mind.

"Sammā-diṭṭhi-purekkhāro" means that one who has right intention as their range and has discarded wrong view first places right view—characterized by the knowledge of the ownership of kamma (kammassakatā) and then by the knowledge of things as they really are (yathābhūta-ñāṇa)—at the forefront. As previously mentioned, being engaged in virtue (sīla) and concentration (samādhi), one undertakes insight (vipassanā), contemplating and reflecting on formations (saṅkhāra). Knowing their arising and passing away, and distinguishing arising and cessation through fifty modes in the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha), one attains the knowledge of arising and passing away (udayabbaya-ñāṇa). Thereafter, through the power of the contemplation of dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā), etc., one exerts effort in insight, gradually attaining the noble path (ariya-magga). The monk who overcomes sloth and torpor (thina-middha) through the highest path (arahatta-magga) abandons all miserable states of existence (duggati). In this way, because that monk has already abandoned the defilements to be discarded by the lower paths, he completely cuts off sloth and torpor arising in consciousness accompanied by greed and dissociated from view (diṭṭhi-vippayutta lobha-sahagata) using the attained path of arahantship. Because conceit (māna), etc., which are abandoned along with sloth and torpor, are also discarded, the monk whose defilements are destroyed and who is an Arahant (khīṇāsava) abandons all destinations (gati) known as miserable states due to their association with the three types of suffering (dukkhatā), as the root of existence is severed. The meaning is that he would stand in Nibbāna thereafter.

## The Commentary on the Second Sutta is Finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Gopālaka Sutta

In the third sutta, "Koseleasu" refers to the princes of the country named Kosala. A single district where these princes reside is also called "Kosala." In that Kosala district, "cārikaṃ carati" means traveling through the countryside at an unhurried pace. "Mahatā" means great due to virtues and also great in number because the count is indefinite. "With the Saṅgha of monks" (bhikkhu-saṅghena) means with the group of recluses united by commonality in view and virtue, "saddhiṃ" means together. "Maggā okkamma" means moving away from the road, and "aññataraṃ rukkhamūlaṃ" means (arriving) near a large tree endowed with thick leaves and branches, providing cool shade.

"Aññataro gopālako" refers to a certain guardian of a herd of cows, named Nanda by name. That Nanda was wealthy, with great riches and great possessions. Like whom...
219:
Just as the ascetic Keniya (lived with possessions) in his monk-like state, so too Nanda the cattle-herd protected the cattle of Anāthapiṇḍika the merchant, and while acting as a cattle-herd, he warded off royal oppression and protected his own wealth. From time to time, that Nanda would take the five products of the cow (pañca-gorasa), go to the great merchant to hand them over, and then visit the Teacher. He would see the Teacher, listen to the Dhamma, and invite the Teacher to visit his place of residence. The Teacher, waiting for the maturation of his knowledge, did not go immediately. Later, while wandering through the countryside surrounded by a large Saṅgha of monks, knowing "Now the knowledge of this cattle-herd is mature," he left the road not far from the cattle-herd's residence and sat at the foot of a tree, waiting for his arrival.

Nanda the cattle-herd, hearing "The Teacher is coming this way while wandering through the countryside," was very joyful and went quickly. He approached the Teacher, paid homage, exchanged greetings, and sat to one side. Then the Blessed One preached the Dhamma to him. He was established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala), invited the Blessed One, and offered milk-rice (pāyāsa) for seven days. On the seventh day, the Blessed One gave the blessing (anumodanā) and departed. Therefore, it is said in the Pali: "The Blessed One instructed the cattle-herd sitting to one side with a Dhamma talk... (pe) ...rose from his seat and departed."

In that Pali text, "sandassesi" means showing clearly the wholesome and unwholesome states, kamma and its result, this world and the next, and at the end of the progressive talk (anupubbī-kathā), clearly showing the Four Noble Truths. "Samādapesi" means making him firmly grasp and establish himself in virtues like sīla, saying "To realize the Truths, these states should be produced in one's own continuity." "Samuttejesi" means that when those undertaken states are gradually developed, they become part of penetration (nibbedha-bhāgiya), becoming sharp and clear so they can quickly bring about the noble path; thus he properly sharpened and brightened them. "Sampahaṃsesi" means he thoroughly gladdened him by making the mind joyful through showing the distinction between the earlier and later stages of meditation (bhāvanā).

Alternatively, in this context: showing by dispelling confusion regarding blameworthy and blameless states and the Truth of Suffering, etc., is "sandassana." Encouraging by dispelling negligence in right practice is "samādapana." Enthusing by dispelling the mind's laziness is "samuttejena." Gladdening due to the accomplishment of right practice is known as "sampahaṃsana." Thus, Nanda the cattle-herd was established in the fruit of stream-entry by the Blessed One's spontaneous Dhamma teaching.
220:
“He accepted” means that Nanda the cowherd, who had seen the Four Noble Truths, having invited [the Buddha] saying, “Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept my [alms-food together with the Saṅgha],” the Buddha accepted (consented) by mind alone, without moving his limbs or speech. Therefore, it is said, “by silence [he accepted].”

“Milk-rice without water” means milk-rice that is not mixed with water. “Having prepared” means having arranged or made ready. “And fresh clarified butter” means having taken butter and, at that very moment, having prepared the melted clear ghee. “With his own hands” means serving with his own hands out of respect. “He satisfied” means he fed the prepared food. “He refused” means he caused [the Buddha] to decline by saying, “Enough, enough.” “Who had eaten” means one who has finished the meal. “Who had removed his hand from the bowl” means one who has taken his hand away from the bowl. There is also a variant reading “one with a washed bowl and hands,” which means one whose bowl and hands are washed.

“Low” means taking a seat that is not high; sitting only on such a seat is the custom of those living in the regions of the Noble Ones (Ariyas). That Nanda the cowherd also sat near a wooden plank seat that was prepared in the vicinity of the Teacher. “With a talk connected with the Dhamma,” etc., is said in reference to the Anumodanā (thanksgiving) given on the seventh day. It is heard that Nanda caused the Buddha and the Saṅgha of monks to stay there for seven days and performed a great offering. On the seventh day, however, he offered milk-rice without water. The Teacher, knowing that Nanda’s wisdom was not yet mature enough for the attainment of the higher paths in that existence, performed only the Anumodanā and departed.

“At the boundary of the village” means the area between the villages. It is said that the villagers once had a quarrel with Nanda over a pond. Nanda defeated the villagers and took the pond. Because of that, a man who bore a grudge followed Nanda, who was carrying the Teacher’s bowl to a distance. When the Buddha said, “Lay follower, return,” Nanda paid homage to the Blessed One, performed a circumambulation, and also raised his hands in salutation to the Saṅgha of monks. He returned with his hands raised to his head, shining with the light of his ten fingernails, until he passed out of sight. While returning, he was shot with an arrow and killed while traveling alone in the forest area between the two villages. Therefore, it is said, “Soon after he had departed... he was killed.” The monks who were following behind, having been delayed by some business, saw Nanda dead in that manner and reported the matter to the Blessed One. In reference to that report, it is said, “Then many monks,” and so on.

“Knowing this matter” means that the man who killed Nanda, an Ariya disciple who had seen the Four Truths, had accumulated much demerit similar to an ānantariya karma. Therefore, knowing this meaning—that a wrongly directed mind does an act even more terrifying than what thieves or enemies might do to these beings—he uttered this Udāna that illustrates that meaning.

In that Udāna verse, “Diso disaṃ” means a destroyer [seeing] a destroyer, or a thief seeing a thief; the rest of the words [such as “seeing”] should be added to complete the sense. Whatever ruin he might do, whatever harm he might do to that person. In the second line, the meaning should be understood in the same way. One enemy, being a betrayer of a friend, might wrong another in terms of his children, wife, fields, property, cattle, buffaloes, and so on; seeing the thief who has wronged him in the same way, or an enemy seeing an enemy with whom he has a grudge for some reason, might, out of his own harshness and cruelty, do whatever ruin to him, or might oppress his children and wife, or destroy his fields and so on, or deprive him of life. A mind wrongly set in the ten unwholesome courses of action makes that person more evil than that [enemy]. For an enemy or a foe of the kind mentioned can only cause suffering or the end of life in this very existence. But this mind wrongly set in the unwholesome courses of action...
221:
In that Udāna verse, “Diso disaṃ” means a destroyer [seeing] one to be destroyed, or a thief [seeing] a thief; the word “seeing” is the remainder of the speech to be added. “Yaṃ taṃ kayirā” means whatever harm or ruin he might do to him; in the second line also, this is the method. This is what is meant: A thief who is a betrayer of a friend, committing offenses against another’s children, wife, fields, property, cattle, buffaloes, and so on, seeing the thief who has likewise wronged him; or an enemy seeing an enemy with whom he has a grudge for some reason, might, out of his own harshness and cruelty, do whatever ruin to him, or might oppress his children and wife, or destroy his fields and so on, or deprive him of life. A mind wrongly set because of being wrongly established in the ten unwholesome courses of action makes that person more evil than that [enemy]. For an enemy or a foe of the kind mentioned can only cause suffering or the end of life in this very existence. But this mind wrongly set in the unwholesome courses of action does not only lead to ruin in the present life; it casts one into the four woeful states for even a hundred thousand existences and does not allow one to raise one’s head.

## The Commentary on the Third Sutta is finished.

## 4. Yakkhapahāra Sutta Commentary

In the fourth sutta, “Kapotakandarāyaṃ” means in the monastery of this name. It is said that in former times, many pigeons (kapota) lived in that mountain grotto (kandara); therefore, that mountain grotto was called “Kapotakandara.” In later times, the monastery built there was also known as “Kapotakandara.” Therefore, it is said, “In the monastery of this name, Kapotakandara.” “Juṇhāya rattiyā” means on a night of the bright fortnight (waxing moon). “Navavaropitehi kesehi” means with hair recently shaved; here, the instrumental case [kesehi] is used in the sense of a characteristic mark (itthambhūtalakkhaṇa). “Abbhokāse” means in an open space where there is no roof or enclosure above.

Among those two Great Elders, the Venerable Sāriputta had a golden hue, and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna had the hue of a blue lotus. Both of those Great Elders were born of the high Brahmin caste, were endowed with the fulfillment of aspirations (abhinīhāra) for one incalculable (asaṅkheyya) and a hundred thousand aeons, had attained the six supernormal powers and the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), were great Arahants (khīṇāsava), and were attainers of meditative absorptions (samāpatti).
222:
