Those two Great Elders, who had reached the pinnacle of the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa), graced the Kapotakandara monastery, shining brilliantly like two lions entering a golden cave, like two leopards descending to a playground, like two Chaddanta elephant kings entering a blooming sal forest, like two Garuda kings entering a silk-cotton forest, like two Vessavaṇa deities riding the Naravāhana vehicle, like two Sakkas seated upon the Paṇḍukambala stone seat, like two Mahābrahmās residing within a single celestial mansion, and like two moons or two suns stationed in the firmament.

Among those two Elders, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna sat in silence, while the Venerable Sāriputta entered into a certain meditative attainment. With reference to this attainment, it is said: 'having entered into a certain concentration.' In that text, 'a certain concentration' refers to the attainment of the sublime abode of equanimity (upekkhā-brahmavihāra-samāpatti). Some teachers say it is the 'attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling' (saññāvedayitanirodha-samāpatti), while others say it is the 'attainment of the fruition of Arahantship' (arahattaphala-samāpatti). Indeed, only these three attainments are capable of protecting the physical body. Among these three, although it was mentioned earlier that the attainment of cessation can be called by the name 'concentration' (samādhi), the teachers specifically praise and explain the last one, the attainment of fruition.

'They were going from the north to the south' means that after attending a gathering of Yakkhas in the northern direction, they were traveling toward the south to return to their own abodes. 'It occurs to me' means it appears in my mind. The word 'maṃ' (me) is used in the accusative case with the sense of possession because of its association with the word 'pati'. The meaning is: 'The thought arises in my mind to strike this venerable one on the head.' That Yakkha, it is said, had harbored a grudge against the Elders in a previous life. Therefore, upon seeing the Elder, such a thought arose with a corrupt mind. The other Yakkha, however, was of a wise nature; thus, he forbade him, saying, 'Enough, friend,' and so on. In that passage, 'Do not strike' (mā āsādesī) means do not assault, do not give a blow. 'Great' (uḷāra) refers to being endowed with noble and supreme virtues such as morality (sīla).

'Disregarding' (anādiyitvā) means not showing respect, not listening to his words. Since not listening to his words is indeed disregarding him, it is said: 'disregarding that Yakkha.' 'Struck him on the head' means that, exerting all his strength and while still stationed in the air, he gave a heavy blow with his fist on the head; the meaning is he made a fist-strike on the crown. 'So great' means the blow was so powerful because of his immense strength. 'With that blow' means by that striking which was the instrumental cause. 'Seven cubits' refers to seven cubits by the measurement of a man of medium height. 'A great elephant' (nāga) refers to an elephant king. 'Would cause to sink' means it would cause it to sink or submerge into the earth.
223:
There is also the reading 'osāreyya', which means he would crush it to powder. 'Seven and a half cubits' (aḍḍhaṭṭhamaratana) means the measurement of seven cubits and a half of the eighth cubit. 'A great mountain peak' means a vast mountain peak the size of Mount Kelāsa. 'Would split' (padāleyya) means he would break it into pieces like shards of a pot. The connection should be understood as 'he would even cause it to sink, he would even split it.'

At that very moment, a great feverish heat arose in the body of that Yakkha. Afflicted by pain and unable to remain in the air, he fell to the ground. At the very moment he fell to the ground, the great earth—which is two hundred and forty thousand leagues thick and capable of supporting even the king of mountains, Sineru, which is one hundred and sixty-eight thousand leagues high—gave way, as if unable to bear that evil being. Flames arising from the Avīci hell seized him even as he was screaming; thus screaming and lamenting, he fell into Avīci. For that reason, it is said: 'Then that Yakkha, crying out "I am burning, I am burning," fell into the great hell right there.' In that passage, 'apatāsi' means he fell.

How is it? Did that Yakkha go to hell in that very Yakkha-form? He did not. Due to the power of the evil kamma to be felt in the present life (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya), he experienced great suffering in his Yakkha-form. However, due to the heinous kamma (ānantariya kamma) to be felt in the next life (upapajjavedanīya), he was reborn in hell immediately after his death-consciousness (cuti). As for the Great Elder, because his body was supported by the power of the meditative attainment, there was no deformity or change. The Yakkha struck him only at the moment he was emerging from the attainment. Seeing him being struck thus with his divine eye, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna approached the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta), and at the very moment of his approach, the General of the Dhamma emerged from his attainment. Then, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna inquired about his bodily well-being, and the other replied to him. Therefore, it is said: 'The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna saw... my head hurts a little.'

In that passage, 'hurts a little' (thokaṃ dukkhaṃ) means my head is pained or has reached a state of suffering only slightly, as if being stung by a bee. The head, which is the site of the pain, is called 'pain' (dukkha). There is also a variant reading 'sīse thokaṃ dukkhaṃ'. Why did the Elder's head hurt even a little, despite his body being supported by the power of the attainment? It was because he had only recently emerged from it.
224:
Although the suffering based on the body is not apparent during the attainment, just as the suffering caused by the biting of mosquitoes and so forth to a person who is asleep becomes slightly apparent when he wakes up, the slight suffering in the head (where he was struck) became apparent when he emerged from the attainment.

"Even though a Yakkha of great strength struck the body with all his might, there was no such thing as a change (disfigurement) in the body," said Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, with a mind full of wonder and amazement. When he made clear the great power of the General of the Dhamma by saying, "Friend Sāriputta, it is wonderful," etc., that Venerable Sāriputta also said, "Friend Moggallāna, it is wonderful," etc. By way of expressing the greatness of [Moggallāna's] psychic power, he showed that his own stains of envy, stinginess, and ego (issā, macchariya, ahaṅkāra) were well-abandoned. "I do not even see a mud-sprite (paṃsupisācaka)" means he did not even see a minor peta wandering in rubbish heaps and such. Thus the Great Elder, the foremost among those desiring the higher attainment, spoke referring to his not seeing those petas at that time because of not directing his attention (anāvajjana). Therefore, he said, "at this time."

The Blessed One, while staying at Veḷuvana, heard this conversation of the two chief disciples with his divine ear. Therefore it was said, "The Blessed One heard," etc.; the meaning is as already stated.

"Knowing this matter" means knowing the greatness of the psychic power of Venerable Sāriputta who had reached the strength of attainment. "This inspired utterance" refers to this Udāna which illustrates his attainment of the state of 'tādi' (steadfastness).

In that Udāna verse, "Whose mind is like a rock, steady and unmoving" means the mind of an Arahant is like a solid stone mountain; because of the absence of all agitation, it remains steady until reaching mastery (vasībhāva), and is not shaken or moved by any of the worldly conditions (lokadhamma). Now, to show the manner of that person's unshakeability along with the reason, "virattaṃ" (dispassionate) etc. was said. In those words, "dispassionate towards things that incite lust" means dispassionate towards all things of the three planes (tebhūmaka-dhamma) which are the cause for the arising of lust, by means of the Noble Path called 'virāga' (dispassion); the meaning is that lust is completely eradicated in all ways regarding those things. "In things that incite anger" means he does not get angry, does not bear ill-will, and does not undergo any change in the face of all objects of resentment (āghātavatthu). "Whose mind is thus developed" means the mind of such a Noble Person is developed in the manner stated, leading to the state of 'tādi'. "How can suffering come to him?" means how can suffering caused by beings or formations (saṅkhāra) approach such a supreme person? The meaning is that for such a person, suffering no longer exists.

## The Commentary on the Fourth Sutta is finished.
225:
## 5. Commentary on the Nāga Sutta

In the commentary on the fifth sutta (Nāga Sutta): "At Kosambī" means in the city named Kosambī because it was established at the place where the hermit named Kusumba lived. "At Ghositārāma" means in the monastery built and donated by the merchant Ghosita. "The Blessed One was living crowded [by people]" means the Blessed One was living in a state of being constrained. If asked whether the Blessed One has congestion or mixing with people, the answer is no. Because no one can approach the Blessed One without his wish. The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are difficult to approach because they are unstained in all things. However, out of compassion desiring the welfare of beings, and in accordance with the promise "Being freed, I shall free others," he tolerates the periodic approach of the eight assemblies who wish to cross the four floods (ogha). He himself, urged by great compassion and knowing the right time, goes to those assemblies. This is the habit of all Buddhas, and here "living crowded" (ākiṇṇavihāra) is intended in this sense.

To the monks in Kosambī who were quarreling in this Dispensation, the Teacher brought the story of King Dīghīti of Kosala and gave advice with the verse beginning: "Hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world," etc. On that day, while those monks were still quarreling, the night turned into dawn. On the second day too, the Blessed One told the same story, but while they were still quarreling, the night turned into dawn again. On the third day too, the Blessed One told the same story. Then a certain monk said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One be unconcerned and live devoted to a pleasant dwelling in this very life. We shall be known by this strife, quarrel, contention, and dispute." The Teacher thought: "The minds of these hollow men (mogha-purisa) are completely overwhelmed; it is no longer possible to make them understand, and there is no reason to try to make them understand here. What if I were to live a solitary life? Only then will these monks desist from quarreling." Thus, because it was no longer appropriate to live in the same monastery with those quarreling monks, and because of the frequent visits from lay followers and others, it was said: "At that time the Blessed One was living crowded," etc.

In that Pali, "dukkhaṃ" means not pleasant, undesirable because the mind is not at ease. Therefore he said, "I live uncomfortably." "Vūpakaṭṭho" means being far away because of staying in seclusion. Having thought thus, the Blessed One attended to his bodily needs early in the morning and [went] to Kosambī...
226:
Thinking, 'By this quarreling and by speaking such opposing words, we shall become famous,' [the monks spoke thus]. The Blessed One [thought], 'Indeed, these men are empty of the Path and Fruit, and their minds are exhausted. At this time, it is not possible to make them understand; there is no means to make them understand here. It would be good if I were to live a life of solitary practice. By living in this way, these monks will refrain from quarreling.' He contemplated thus. Because it was not proper to stay in the same monastery with those monks who were thus quarreling, and because he had to live in a crowded manner (ākiṇṇavihāra) due to the visits of lay followers and others, the Pali text beginning with 'At that time, the Blessed One lived in a crowd' was taught. In that Pali, 'dukkhaṃ' means the absence of happiness and the presence of what is undesirable, due to having a displeased mind. Therefore, it is said, 'he lived uncomfortably.' 'Vūpakaṭṭho' means established in seclusion, thus being remote. Having contemplated thus, the Blessed One, having performed his morning duties, wandered for alms in Kosambī. Without informing anyone, he departed alone without a companion and stayed at the foot of a beautiful Sāla tree in the Pālileyyaka forest in the Kosala country. Therefore, it is taught [in the Pali], 'Then the Blessed One, in the morning... at the foot of the Bhaddasāla tree.' In that Pali, 'sāmaṃ' means by oneself. 'Saṃsāmetvā' means having put away. In the phrase 'pattacīvaramādāya' (taking bowl and robes), the word 'sāmaṃ' should also be applied. 'Upaṭṭhāke' refers to not calling the attendants such as the merchant Ghosita who lived in Kosambī, nor the chief attendant, the Venerable Ānanda, in the monastery.

When the Blessed One had thus departed, five hundred monks said to the Venerable Ānanda, 'Friend Ānanda, the Blessed One has gone alone; we shall follow him.' The Venerable Ānanda restrained them, saying, 'Friends, when the Blessed One himself puts away his lodgings, takes his bowl and robes, and departs without calling or informing his attendants and without a companion from the Saṅgha of monks, at that time, it is the Blessed One's intention to live in solitude. A disciple should act according to the teacher's intention. Therefore, the Blessed One should not be followed during these days.' He himself did not follow. 'Anupubbena' means in due order. While wandering on tour through villages and market towns, thinking, 'I shall first see the monk who is accustomed to living alone,' he went to the village of Bālakaloṇakāra. There, he spoke to the Elder Bhagu about the benefits of living alone throughout the period after the meal and throughout the three watches of the night. On the following day, after wandering for alms with the Elder Bhagu as his attendant monk, he had the Elder remain there and, thinking, 'I shall see the three clansmen who are living in harmony,' he went to the Pācinavaṃsamigadāya forest. To those monks also, he spoke about the benefits of living in harmony throughout the night. Having had those monks also remain there, he reached the village of Pālileyyaka alone. The inhabitants of Pālileyyaka came out to meet him and gave offerings to the Blessed One. In the forest named Rakkhita, not far from the village of Pālileyyaka, they built a leaf hut for the Blessed One and, requesting, 'May the Blessed One stay here,' they settled him there. 'Bhaddasālo' refers to a pleasant and beautiful Sāla tree in that forest. The Blessed One, depending on that village, stayed at the foot of that Sāla tree near the leaf hut in the forest. Therefore, it is said, 'He stays in the Pālileyyaka forest, in the Rakkhita forest, at the foot of the Bhaddasāla tree.' 'Hatthināgo' refers to a great elephant, the leader of the herd. 'Hatthikalabhehi' means with young elephants. 'Hatthicchāpehi' means with very young elephants who are still dependent on milk. Those young elephants...
227:
...are also called 'bhiṅkā'. 'Chinnaggāni' means eating the branches resembling stumps that are left over after the tips have been broken and eaten by the elephants going ahead. 'Obhaggobhaggaṃ' refers to what has been repeatedly broken and brought down from high places by that noble elephant. 'Assa sākhābhaṅgaṃ' means those young elephants eat the branches and twigs belonging to that noble elephant. 'Āvilāni' means having to drink drinking water that is turbid and mixed with mud because those [other] elephants went down and drank first. 'Ogāhā' means from the watering place. There is also a Pali reading 'ogāhaṃ'. 'Assa' means of that noble elephant. 'Upanighaṃsantiyo' means they bump and rub against him. Even when being thus bumped and rubbed, he does not get angry because of his noble nature; therefore, those female elephants simply rub against that noble elephant. 'Yūthā' means the herds of elephants.

'Approached where the Blessed One was' means that noble elephant, being weary of living with the herd, entered that forest. Seeing the Blessed One there, he became as cool as if his fever had been extinguished by a thousand jars of water. With a confident mind, he stood near the Blessed One. From then on, being established in the forefront of service, he cleared the area around the beautiful Sāla tree and the leaf hut so that there was no grass, fresh leaves, or rubbish, and swept with branches. He provided the Blessed One with water for washing the face, brought water for bathing, and gave tooth-sticks. He brought sweet fruits from the forest and offered them to the Teacher. The Teacher consumed those fruits. Therefore, it is said, 'In that forest, that noble elephant clears the place where the Blessed One stays of grass, fresh leaves, and rubbish; with his trunk, he places water for drinking and for use nearby for the Blessed One.' Having brought firewood with his trunk and rubbed them together to start a fire, he made the wood burn. He heated pieces of stone in that fire, rolled those stones with sticks, and dropped them into a pit [of water]. Knowing the water had become hot, he approached and stood near the Blessed One. The Blessed One, knowing 'The noble elephant desires my bathing,' went to that place and performed the act of bathing. The same method applies to drinking water. Because it happened when it was cold on that day, it is said with reference to that approach: 'With his trunk, he places water for drinking and for use nearby for the Blessed One.'

'Atha kho bhagavato rahogatassa' and the following words show the reflection on the bliss of seclusion (viveka-sukha) by the two great 'nāgas' (the Buddha and the noble elephant), and its meaning is as already stated. 'Knowing his own seclusion' means knowing the physical seclusion (kāya-viveka) obtained by not being crowded with anyone. As for the other types of seclusion, they are always present for the Blessed One.
228:
"This inspired utterance" refers to the utterance of this Udāna which explains the similarity in the desire for and great delight in solitude (viveka) between himself and the elephant king.

The summary of the meaning in that Udāna verse is as follows: The mind of this elephant king, whose tusks are like the poles of a chariot, matches and compares with the mind of the Buddha-elephant. How does it match? Just as the Buddha-elephant, thinking, "In the past, I lived crowded [with people]," felt disgust for that previous crowded living and, developing solitude, now delights and finds great pleasure in the forest alone without a companion; so too, this elephant king, having felt disgust for living crowded with his herd of elephants in the past and developing solitude, now delights and finds great pleasure in the great forest alone without a companion. Therefore, considering that his mind matches the mind of the Buddha-elephant, it means that they are identical in their desire for the delight of being alone.

## The Commentary on the Fifth Sutta is finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Piṇḍola Sutta

In the sixth sutta, "Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja" means "Piṇḍola" because he went forth as a monk while seeking (ulati) alms-food (piṇḍa). It is said that he was a brahmin whose wealth had been exhausted and, seeing the great gains and honor arising for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he left home and went forth for the sake of alms-food. That Piṇḍola used to wander around taking a large shard (pottery fragment) as a "bowl"; he would drink a bowlful of gruel, eat rice, and chew cakes and snacks. Then, they reported his gluttonous nature to the Blessed One. The Blessed One did not allow him a bowl-bag; therefore, he had to place the bowl upside down under the couch. Even when placing it, he would tilt and place it while rubbing it [against the floor], and when taking it, he would pull it out while rubbing it. As time went by, due to frequent rubbing, the bowl became thin and worn out, reaching a state where it could only hold about one measure (nāḷika) of rice. Then, they reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One allowed him a bowl-bag. Later, by developing the faculties (indriyabhāvanā), that elder was established in the fruit of Arahantship (Arahattaphala), the highest goal. Thus, he is called "Piṇḍola" because he formerly sought alms-food in a special way, and "Bhāradvāja" by clan; combining both, he is called "Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja."
229:
"Āraññaka" (forest-dweller) means one who dwells in the forest because of rejecting dwellings near a village. This is the name of one who undertakes and practices the forest-dweller's ascetic practice (āraññaka-dhutaṅga). Similarly, "piṇḍapāta" (alms-food) means the falling of morsels of material food known as alms; it means the falling of alms and food given by others into the bowl. "Piṇḍapātika" means one who seeks alms-food by approaching various houses. Or, "piṇḍapātī" means one who has the habit of wandering for the sake of alms; "piṇḍapātī" is the same as "piṇḍapātika." "Paṃsukūla" (rag-robe) is so called because it is like a rag-robe in the sense of being discarded on top of dust in refuse heaps, etc., or in the sense of being raised up. Or, it is called "paṃsukūla" because it reaches a state of being loathsome like dust. The wearing of rag-robes is called "paṃsukūla"; one who has the habit of wearing them is called "paṃsukūlika." The three robes known as the outer robe (saṅghāṭi), the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga), and the inner robe (antaravāsaka) are called "ticīvara" (triple robe). The carrying of these three robes is called "ticīvara"; one who has the habit of carrying them is called "tecīvarika." The meanings of terms such as "appiccha" (fewness of wishes) have already been stated previously.

"Dhutavāda" (proponent of ascetic practices) means: "dhuta" refers either to a person who has shaken off defilements or to the Dhamma that shakes off defilements. In this regard, it should be understood that there are four types of persons: (1) one who is himself an observer of ascetic practices but does not speak to others about them; (2) one who is not himself an observer but speaks to others about them; (3) one who is neither an observer nor speaks to others; and (4) one who is both an observer himself and speaks to others about them. Among these four, if a person himself undertakes and practices the ascetic qualities but does not urge or establish others for that purpose, this is the first person. If a person does not himself undertake and practice the ascetic qualities but only urges others to undertake them, this is the second person. If a person is devoid of both, this is the third person. If a person is endowed with both, this is the fourth person. The Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja was this fourth type of person. Therefore, he is called a "dhutavāda." This designation is made by way of a part representing the whole (ekadesa-sarūpeka-sesa), just as in the term "nāmarūpa" (name-and-form).

In the term "adhicittamanuyutta" (devoted to the higher mind), the state of the higher mind should be understood as being due to association with the eight attainments or association with the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship. However, in this context, they say it is the "mind of the fruit of Arahantship" (arahattaphalacitta). In those various attainments, concentration (samādhi) itself is the higher mind; but here, it should be understood as the concentration of the fruit of Arahantship. Some teachers, however, say: "Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind should from time to time give attention to three signs," as found in the Adhicitta Sutta (A. iii, 103), where the mind of tranquillity and insight (samatha-vipassanā) is intended as the higher mind. That statement is not good. Only the former meaning should be accepted.
230:
“Having understood this matter” (Etam-atthaṃ viditvā) means having understood in every aspect that matter which is the attainment of resolution and perfection of requisites of the Venerable Piṇḍolabhāradvāja, known as devotion to the higher mind (adhicittānuyoga). Thus, wishing to show that “devotion to the higher mind is the practice of my teaching,” he uttered this inspired utterance.

In that verse, “anūpavādo” means not reviling anyone at all by speech. “Anūpaghāto” means not performing any harm to anyone by body. “Pātimokkhe”: here, the meaning of the word Pātimokkha has been stated below in various ways; it is the restraint (saṃvara) characterized by the non-transgression of the seven groups of offenses in that Pātimokkha. “Mattaññutā” means knowing the measure in receiving and consuming. “Pantañca sayanāsanaṃ” means a remote lodging that is secluded and free from disturbance. “Adhicitte ca āyogo” means the repeated practice of meditation for the attainment of the eight attainments (samāpatti).

Alternatively— “anūpavādo” means not speaking any words of opposition to anyone. By this, all verbal virtue (vācasika-sīla) is included. “Anūpaghāto” means not performing any harm or harassment to others by body. By this, all bodily virtue (kāyika-sīla) is included. To show how both of these are included within the teaching of the Buddhas, it is said: “Pātimokkhe ca saṃvaro.” The word “ca” is merely a particle. “Pātimokkhe ca saṃvaro” means non-reviling and non-harming which constitute the restraint of the Pātimokkha.

Or else, “Pātimokkhe” is the locative case in the sense of basis (adhikaraṇa). It means restraint in the Pātimokkha which is the support. What is that restraint? It is non-reviling and non-harming. For, at the time of full ordination, the Pātimokkha virtue is undertaken generally without distinction; for one established in that Pātimokkha, the restraint by way of not performing reviling or harming thereafter is called non-reviling and non-harming.

Or else, “Pātimokkhe” is the locative case in the sense of what is to be accomplished (nipphādetabba), just as it is said: “Unsettledness of mind has unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) as its proximate cause.” It means non-reviling and non-harming to be accomplished by that Pātimokkha, or simply non-reviling and non-harming included within the Pātimokkha restraint. By this word “saṃvaro”...
231:
...the taking of these four restraints, namely: restraint by mindfulness (sati-saṃvara), restraint by knowledge (ñāṇa-saṃvara), restraint by patience (khanti-saṃvara), and restraint by energy (vīriya-saṃvara), is the group of four restraints that accomplishes the Pātimokkha.

“Moderation in food” means knowing the measure in food by way of seeking, receiving, consuming, and disposing. “Remote lodging” means secluded dwellings such as forests and the foot of trees that are conducive to meditation. “Devotion to higher mind” means the effort by way of Samatha and Vipassanā meditation for the purpose of producing the Fruition of Arahantship (arahattaphala-citta), which is called higher mind (adhicitta) because it is superior and excellent among all minds. “This is the teaching of the Buddhas” means that non-reviling of others, non-harming, Pātimokkha restraint, moderation in seeking, receiving, etc., living in seclusion, and the aforementioned devotion to the higher mind are the instruction and advice of the Buddhas. Thus, it should be understood that the three trainings (sikkhā) are taught by this verse.

## The Commentary on the Sixth Sutta is finished.

## 7. Sāriputtasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, there is nothing new to be commented upon. In the verse, “adhicetaso” means for one who has the higher mind, one endowed with the Fruition of Arahantship which is superior to all minds. “Appamazzato” means for one who is not negligent, one endowed with constant practice in blameless states through diligence (appamāda). “Munino” means for the sage; as it is said: “He who knows both worlds, therefore he is called a sage,” thus by knowing both worlds, knowledge is called sagacity (mona); or because he is endowed with that knowledge known as the knowledge of the Fruition of Arahantship, the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) is called a sage (muni); for that sage. “Monapathesu sikkhato” means for one training in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) which are the paths to sagacity known as the knowledge of Arahantship, or in the three trainings. This is said by taking the preliminary practice (pubbabhāga-paṭipadā). Since an Arahant is one who has completed the training, it should be understood here as: for the sage who has reached the state of a sage by training in this way. And because of this, the meaning of these three terms is indeed appropriate: “adhicetaso” by way of the lower path and fruit minds, “appamazzato” by way of diligence in the practice to realize the Four Noble Truths, and “munino” by way of being endowed with the path knowledge. Or else, “appamazzato”...
232:
The meaning of the words 'Sikkhato' should be understood as having a causal sense. It means for the person endowed with the mind of Arahatship (Adhicetaso) because of the cause of non-negligence and because of the cause of training. 'Sorrows do not occur for such a one (tādino)' means that within such an Arahant sage (khīṇāsava-muni), sorrows and mental distress caused by separation from loved ones and so forth do not occur. Alternatively, 'tādino' means for a sage of such a nature who is endowed with the characteristic of 'tādi' (steadfastness); sorrows do not occur for him—this is the meaning here. 'Upasantassa' means for one who is peaceful through the absolute subsiding of lust and so forth. 'Sadā satīmato' means for one who is never without mindfulness because of reaching the fullness of mindfulness.

In this sutta, by 'Adhicetaso', the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā) is shown; by 'appamazzato', the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā) is shown; and by 'munino monapathesu sikkhato', the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā) is shown. Or, by 'munino', the training in higher wisdom is shown; by 'monapathesu sikkhato', the preliminary practice of those supramundane trainings is shown; and by 'sokā na bhavanti' etc., the benefits of fulfilling the trainings are shown. The rest is just as previously stated.

## The Commentary on the Seventh Sutta is finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Sundarī Sutta

In the eighth sutta, the meaning of the words 'sakkato' and so forth has already been explained below. 'Asahamānā' means not being able to endure, the meaning is 'being envious'. It should be connected as: 'being unable to endure the honor and offerings to the Saṅgha of monks.'

'Sundarī' is the name of that female wanderer. It is said that at that time, among all the female wanderers, she was the most beautiful, lovely to behold, inspiring, and endowed with the highest beauty of complexion; therefore, she was known as 'Sundarī'. That female wanderer had not yet passed her youth and was of unrestrained conduct; therefore, those heretics urged the female wanderer Sundarī to do an evil deed. Those heretics of other sects, having lost their own gains and honor since the appearance of the Buddha, saw the grand and immeasurable gains and honor flowing to the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks, in the manner mentioned below in the commentary on the Akkosasutta. Being overcome by envy, they gathered together and consulted: "Since the time the ascetic Gotama appeared, we have been ruined and have lost our gains and honor. To us..."
233:
"...no one even knows of our existence anymore. Based on what reason is the world so devoted to the ascetic Gotama and offers him such grand honor and respect?" they consulted. Among them, one said, "It is because he is of high birth, born from the unbroken lineage of Mahāsammata." Another said, "It is because many wonders appeared at his conception." Another said, "It is because when he was brought to pay homage to the hermit Kāladevila, his feet turned up and rested on the hermit's matted hair." Another said, "It is because at the time of the Ploughing Festival, when he was laid to sleep under the shade of a rose-apple tree, the shadow of the tree remained stationary without shifting even after midday." Another said, "It is because he is handsome, lovely to behold, and pleasing due to his physical perfection." Another said, "It is because he saw the omens of the old, the sick, the dead, and the monk, became stirred with spiritual urgency (saṃvega), and renounced the future glory of a Universal Monarch to become a monk."

Thus, not knowing the Blessed One's accumulation of merit and wisdom gathered over an immeasurable time, his perfections (pāramīs) that have reached the pinnacle, his incomparable practice of effacement (sallekha), and the Buddha-power such as the peerless attainment of knowledge and abandonment, they praised only those various reasons for the Blessed One's popularity that they themselves had seen or heard. When they searched for a reason for him not to be respected but saw none, they consulted: "By what means can we create ill-repute for the ascetic Gotama and destroy his gains and honor?" Among them, one wise man, sharp in counsel, said: "Friends, in this world of beings, there is no being who is not attached to the pleasure of women. This ascetic Gotama is also handsome, like a god, and young. If he finds a woman of equal beauty to himself, he might become attached. Even if he does not, the people will have doubts. Come, let us incite the female wanderer Sundarī in such a way that the ill-repute of the ascetic Gotama spreads across the earth."

Hearing these words, the others said, "This plan of yours is well-conceived. If we do this, the ascetic Gotama, oppressed by ill-repute, will be unable to lift his head and will flee to wherever he can." Being of one mind, they went to Sundarī to incite her. Seeing them, she asked, "Why have you all come together?" The titthiyas, without speaking, sat in a secluded place at the edge of the park. She went there and spoke to them repeatedly, but receiving no answer, she asked, "How have I offended you? Why do you not give me an answer?" "Even though it is so, you remain indifferent while we are being harassed," they said.
234:
“Who is harassing you?” they asked. “Do you not see the ascetic Gotama harassing us and wandering about after making us lose our gains and honor?” they replied. When she asked, “What should I do in this matter?” they said, “In that case, you should go near the Jetavana monastery frequently and say such and such to the great multitude.” Sundarī accepted, saying, “Very well.” Referring to this, it is said, “The sectarians of other faiths, being unable to endure the honor shown to the Blessed One,” and so forth.

In that Pali, “ussahasi” means “you are able.” “Atthaṃ” means benefit or a task. “Kyāhaṃ” should be resolved as “kiṃ ahaṃ” (What [should] I [do]?). Although those sectarians were not related to Sundarī, they wished to support her simply because of their common life as wanderers, and acting like relatives, they said, “Sister, are you able to work for the benefit of your relatives?” Therefore, Sundarī, like a vine or a deer clinging to a foot, said, “I have already sacrificed my life for the sake of my relatives.”

“In that case” means: “You say, ‘I have sacrificed my life for your benefit’; you are also in the first stage of life, beautiful and possessed of grace. Therefore, act in such a way that, depending on you, disgrace will arise for the ascetic Gotama.” Having said this, they sent her off, saying, “Go to Jetavana frequently.” That foolish woman, like one wishing to play the game of flower-garlands with a row of saw-teeth, or like one touching a fierce elephant in rut by its trunk, or like one inviting death with her forehead, accepted the words of the sectarians. Taking flowers, perfumes, ointments, betel, and mouth-fresheners, she went towards Jetavana at the time when the great multitude, having heard the Dhamma from the Teacher, were entering the city. When asked, “Where are you going?” she replied, “I am going to the presence of the ascetic Gotama; I live with him in the same Gandhakuṭi.” After sleeping in a certain park of the sectarians, she came down to the Jetavana road early in the morning and headed towards the city. When asked, “Sundarī, where have you come from?” she said, “After sleeping with the ascetic Gotama in the same Gandhakuṭi and delighting him with sensual pleasure, I have come back.” Referring to this, it is said, “Saying, ‘Very well, sirs,’ the female wanderer Sundarī, having agreed to the words of those sectarians of other faiths, went to Jetavana frequently.”

After a few days had passed, the sectarians gave money to some thugs and said, “Go, kill Sundarī and leave her in the heap of flower-refuse not far from the ascetic Gotama’s Gandhakuṭi, then come back.” Those thugs did accordingly. Then the sectarians made a great commotion, saying, “We do not see Sundarī,” and went to the King...
235:
After reporting to the King, when asked by him, “Where did you search?” they replied, “During these days she has been staying at Jetavana; we do not know what happened to her there.” The King granted permission, saying, “In that case, go and search for her there.” Taking their attendants, they went to Jetavana and, pretending to search, uncovered the flower-refuse heap. Placing her body on a small litter, they brought it into the city and reported to the King, “The disciples of the ascetic Gotama, in order to conceal the evil deed committed by their teacher, killed Sundarī and left her in the flower-refuse heap.” The King, without investigating, said, “In that case, go and parade through the city.” They wandered through the city streets saying, “See the deed of the Sakyaputta ascetics!” and so forth, and then returned to the palace gate. The King had Sundarī’s body placed on a platform in the charnel ground where corpses are discarded and had it guarded. The citizens of Sāvatthī, for the most part excluding the noble disciples, wandered about abusing the monks inside and outside the city, saying, “See the deed of the Sakyaputta ascetics!” and so forth. Therefore, it was said, “Yadā te aññiṃsu titthiyā paribbājakā vodiṭṭhā kho sundarī” and so forth.

In that Pali, “aññiṃsu” means they knew. “Vodiṭṭhā” means clearly seen, specifically seen coming and going to Jetavana, or seen many times. “Parikhākūpe” means in the moat. “Yā sā mahārāja sundarī” means, “Great King, there is that wanderer who is well-known as ‘Sundarī’ in this city because of her beauty.” “Sā no na dissati” means, “That wanderer was dear to us like our eyes or our life; now she is not seen.” “Yathānikkhittaṃ” means just as it was placed by themselves after ordering men to put it in the flower-refuse heap. There is also a variant reading “yathānikhātaṃ,” which means in the manner of being buried in the earth. “Rathiyāya rathiyaṃ” means from one main road to another. “Vīthi” refers to a thoroughfare that passes through. “Siṅghāṭakaṃ” is a three-way junction. “Alajjino” means those who are shameless, who lack revulsion for evil. “Dussīlā” means those without virtue. “Pāpadhammā” means those of low nature and inferior conduct. “Musāvādino” means liars, because while being immoral, they falsely claim, “We are virtuous.” “Abrahmacārino” is said in reproach, meaning, “These are indeed of unnoble conduct because of practicing sexual intercourse.” “Dhammacārino” means those who practice wholesome states. “Samacārino” means those who practice evenly through bodily actions and so forth.
236:
"Kalyāṇadhammā" means those of good nature; it should be connected with the phrase "they will profess." In this context, because of the association with the word "nāma," the future tense "paṭijānissanti" is used. "Sāmañña" refers to the state of a recluse (samaṇa) which stills evil. "Brahmañña" refers to the state of a noble person who has warded off evil. "Kuto" means for what reason. "Apagatā" means they are far removed or departed from all sides. "Purisakicca" (human business) is said in reference to engaging in sexual intercourse.

Then the monks reported that matter to the Blessed One. The Teacher said, "Monks, if that is so, you too should counter those people with this verse," and he spoke the verse beginning with "Abhūtavādī." In reference to that verse of counter-accusation, it is stated in the Pali: "Then many... [pe] ...men of base deeds in the next world." In that verse, the Teacher spoke the words, "Monks, this sound (accusation) will not last long," knowing through his omniscience that the loss of reputation (defamation) would end within seven days, in order to reassure the monks.

In the verse, "Abhūtavādī" refers to one who, without seeing another's fault, tells a lie and accuses another with what is untrue and false. "Yo vāpi katvā" means whoever, having committed an evil deed, says, "I did not do this." "Pecca samā bhavanti" means both of these persons, when they go from this life to the next world, become equal in their destination by going to hell. For them, only the destination (gati) is determined, but the lifespan (the duration of suffering) is not fixed. This is because if one commits much evil, one suffers in hell for a long time, and if one commits a little evil, one suffers for only a short time. Since the deeds of both are base, it is said: "Nihīnakammā manujā parattha" (Men of base deeds are equal in the next world). The word "parattha" should be connected with the preceding word "pecca." The meaning is that when they die and go from this life, those of base deeds become equal in the next world.

"Pariyāpuṇitvā" means having learned. "Akārakā" means those who do not commit the offense. The thought occurred to the townspeople: "These monks do not commit this act." Indeed, these monks, the sons of the Sakyan (Sakyaputtiya), certainly did not commit that evil deed which other sectarians (titthiyas) have been proclaiming while wandering throughout the entire city. This is because, even though we accuse them with such improper and harsh words, these monks do not show any sign of agitation and do not abandon their patience and delight in good conduct. They are merely "cursing" (speaking the truth) by saying the Dhamma: "The speaker of untruth goes to hell." These Sakyaputtian monks are like those who make an oath while cursing those who accuse them without investigation..."
237:
...they say. Alternatively, they "curse" by saying, "Whoever does (evil) and says 'I did not do it'." The meaning is: "These monks are making an oath to us to let us know their innocence."

Immediately after hearing the verse spoken by the Blessed One, those people, through the power of the Buddha, were struck with apprehension and a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) arose. They thought, "We did not see this matter with our own eyes; what is heard as news may be true or may be false. These other sectarians only desire the harm and ill-will of these monks. Therefore, we should not speak these words out of mere belief; recluses are indeed difficult to know." From then on, they ceased their reviling.

King Kosala also ordered his men to find those who murdered Sundarī. Then those scoundrels, while drinking liquor with the money (given by the sectarians), quarreled with one another. Among them, one said to the other, "You killed Sundarī with a single blow, threw her into the flower-refuse heap, and now you are drinking liquor with the money obtained from that. So be it, so be it!" The king's men, hearing these words, arrested the scoundrels and presented them to the King. The King asked the scoundrels, "Did you kill Sundarī?" They replied, "Yes, your Majesty." When asked, "Who made you kill her?" they replied, "The other sectarians made us kill her, your Majesty." The King summoned the sectarians, made them confess the matter, and ordered them to wander through the city saying, "This Sundarī was caused to be killed by us, who wished to bring disrepute to the recluse Gotama. There is no fault in the recluse Gotama, nor in the disciples of Gotama; the fault is only ours."

They did as they were told. The great multitude believed the truth and reviled the sectarians. The sectarians received the appropriate royal punishment for murder. From then on, the offerings, honor, and respect toward the Buddha and the Saṅgha became even greater. The monks, filled with a sense of wonder and amazement, paid homage to the Blessed One and joyfully reported the matter. Therefore, it is said (in the Pali): "Then many monks... 'Venerable Sir, that sound (of accusation) has disappeared'."

Why did the Blessed One not inform the monks that "this act is the work of the sectarians"? There is no benefit in telling the Noble Ones (ariyas). Among worldlings (puthujjanas), however, if there were those who did not believe, that lack of belief would lead to their harm and suffering for a long time; thus he did not speak. Furthermore, it is not the habit of the Buddhas to predict such future events. The Blessed One makes manifest the side of defilement only by referring to others. Considering that it is impossible to prevent the ripening of kamma that has already found its opportunity, the Blessed One remained silent, disregarding the cause of the accusation.

Not in the sky, nor in the middle of the ocean,
Nor by entering a mountain cleft,
Is there a place found on earth
Where one staying might be free from evil kamma.

Knowing this matter, the Blessed One endured the harsh words spoken by the fools through the restraint of patience (khantisaṃvara) alone. For the Blessed One, who is endowed with the power of patience and established in the supramundane Dhamma, there is no suffering (caused by those words).
238:
He clarified the nature of defilement. Knowing that kamma, and kamma that has found its opportunity, cannot be averted, the Blessed One remained silent, ignoring the accusation and the cause of that accusation. Thus it was also said:

“Not in the sky, nor in the middle of the ocean,
Nor by entering a mountain cleft;
There is no place on earth where one can stay
And be escaped from evil kamma.”

Knowing this meaning—knowing in every aspect that for a wise person endowed with the power of patience (khantibala), there is no such thing as being unable to endure harsh words spoken by foolish people with the intent of striking at the vitals—he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) which clarifies the power of patient endurance.

In that inspired verse, “Unrestrained people stab with words, like an elephant gone to battle is struck by arrows” means that foolish people, who are unrefined and unrestrained because they lack any restraint in bodily conduct and so forth, stab or pierce with the weapons of speech, just as enemies strike a noble elephant that has entered the battlefield with arrows; this is their nature. “Having heard harsh words spoken, a monk should endure them with an uncorrupted mind” means that a monk, who is in the habit of seeing the danger in saṃsāra, should remain established in patient endurance and tolerate the harsh words spoken by those foolish people intended to wound the heart, refuting the false as false and the true as true, while recollecting my “Simile of the Saw” (Kakacūpama) instruction, without even a slight corruption of mind, thinking, “This is the nature of saṃsāra.”

Here, a question may be asked: For what kamma did the Blessed One, who possesses a vast store of merit accumulated with great respect over an immeasurable time, encounter such a terrible and false accusation? The answer is: In a past life, while he was a Bodhisatta, he was a scoundrel named Munāḷi. He associated with wicked people and wandered about with much improper attention (ayoniso manasikāra). One day, he saw a Paccekabuddha named Surabhi putting on his robes to enter the city for alms. At that time, a certain woman was passing not far from that Paccekabuddha. The scoundrel accused him, saying, “This monk is unchaste (abrahmacārī).” Due to that kamma, he suffered in hell for many hundreds of thousands of years. By the remaining result (vipāka) of that kamma, even now as a Buddha, he was falsely accused because of the woman Sundarī.
239:
Why did the Blessed One, the Teacher of gods and humans, who possesses a great store of merit accumulated with respect over an immeasurable time, encounter such harsh and false accusations? The answer is: In a past life, while he was a Bodhisatta, he was a scoundrel named Munāḷi. He associated with wicked people and wandered about with much improper attention. One day, he saw the Paccekabuddha named Surabhi robing himself to enter the city for alms. At that time, a woman was walking not far from the Paccekabuddha. The scoundrel accused him, saying, “This monk practices unchaste sexual conduct.” Because of that kamma, the Bodhisatta suffered in hell for many hundreds of thousands of years. By the remaining result of that kamma, even now as a Buddha, he faced false accusations because of Sundarī.

Just as this happened, other sufferings like the accusations by Ciñcamāṇavikā and other deviant women occurred. All these are the remaining results of past kamma, which are called “shreds of kamma” (kammapilotika). This was said in the Apadāna text as follows:

“On a delightful stone slab, beautiful with the light of various gems, amidst various fragrant forests, in the vicinity of Lake Anotatta.

The World Leader, surrounded by a large Saṅgha of monks, sat there and explained his own past kammas.

‘Listen, O monks, to the kamma performed by me. Even in Buddhahood, the shreds of kamma (kammapilotika) bear fruit. Listen to that kamma.’

‘In a previous life, I was a scoundrel named Munāḷi. I accused the innocent Paccekabuddha Surabhi.’

‘By the result of that kamma, I wandered in hell for a long time, experiencing painful feelings for many hundreds of thousands of years.’

‘By the remainder of that kamma, in this final birth, I have received accusations because of Sundarī.’

‘I accused a disciple named Nanda of a Buddha who had conquered all; because of that, I wandered in hell for a long time.’

‘I wandered in hell for ten thousand years. Having obtained human status, I received many accusations.’

‘By the remainder of that kamma, Ciñcamāṇavikā falsely accused me in the presence of the multitude.’

‘In the past, I was a learned Brahmin, respected and honored. In the Mahāvana forest, I taught the Vedas to five hundred youths.’”
240:
“Then a fierce hermit named Bhīma, possessed of the five higher powers (abhiññā) and great psychic power, arrived there. Seeing that innocent hermit arrive, I falsely accused him.

Then I said to my students, ‘This hermit is a consumer of sensual pleasures.’ The youths also rejoiced in my words.

Then all the youths, as they went for alms from house to house, told the people, ‘This hermit is a consumer of sensual pleasures.’

By the result of that kamma, all these five hundred monks have received accusations because of the female wanderer Sundarī.

In a past life, for the sake of wealth, I killed my half-brother. I threw him into a mountain cleft and crushed him with a stone.

By the result of that kamma, Devadatta threw a stone, and a splinter of that stone crushed my big toe.

In the past, when I was a boy playing on the main road, I saw a Paccekabuddha and threw a potsherd at him on the path.

By the result of that kamma, in this final birth, Devadatta dispatched assassins to kill me.

In the past, I was an elephant trainer. I offended and threatened a noble Paccekabuddha who was wandering for alms with an elephant.

By the result of that kamma, the fierce elephant Nāḷāgiri came towards me in the noble city of Giribbaja.

In the past, I was a king, a ruler of the land, and I killed a man with a spear. By the result of that kamma, I suffered intensely in hell.

By the remainder of that kamma, now a splinter of stone has pierced the skin of my foot. Kamma never disappears.”
241:
“I was once a fisherman’s son in a fishing village. Seeing fish being killed, I felt a sense of joy.

Due to the result of that unwholesome kamma, I suffered from headaches. When King Viṭaṭūbha slaughtered the Sakyans, all the Sakyans were killed.

In the dispensation of the Buddha Phussa, I insulted the disciples, saying: ‘Eat barley! Do not eat rice!’

Due to the result of that kamma, while I was residing in the city of Verañjā at the invitation of a brahmin, I had to eat barley for three months.

When a wrestling match was taking place, I mistreated the son of a wrestler. Due to the result of that kamma, I suffered from back pain.

I was once a physician and caused the son of a merchant to have diarrhea. Due to the result of that kamma, I suffered from dysentery.

At that time, as the youth Jotipāla, I said to the Buddha Kassapa: ‘Where could there be enlightenment for this shaveling? Enlightenment is extremely difficult to attain.’

Due to the result of that unwholesome kamma, I practiced many severe austerities (dukkharacariyā) for six years in the Uruvelā forest. Only after that did I attain enlightenment.

Obstructed by my past kamma, I could not reach the supreme enlightenment through the right path, but had to seek it through the wrong path.

Having exhausted both merit and demerit, free from all feverish distress, without sorrow, without exhaustion, and free from taints (āsavas), I shall attain Nibbāna.”

Thus the Victorious Buddha, who has attained all supernormal powers and strengths, and who is the foremost among the assembly of monks, explained this at the great Lake Anotatta.

## The Commentary on the Eighth Sutta Ends.
242:
## 9. Commentary on the Upasena Sutta

In the ninth sutta, the Upasena Sutta, “Upasenassa” refers to the name of that Elder. Because he was the son of the Brahmin Vanganta, they also called him “Vangantaputta.”

This Elder was the younger brother of the Venerable Sāriputta. Having ordained in the Dispensation and attained higher ordination (upasampadā) before the training rules were fully established, he became a preceptor (upajjhāya) when he had only two years of seniority (vassa). He gave higher ordination to a certain monk and went with that monk to pay respects to the Blessed One. When the Blessed One asked about that monk’s status as his co-resident (saddhivihārika), He rebuked him as recorded in the Khandhaka: “Vain man (mogha purisa), you have turned too quickly to abundance, that is, to forming a group.” At that time, like a thoroughbred horse struck by a whip, his mind was filled with urgency (saṃvega), and he thought: “If I am now rebuked by the Blessed One because of my followers, it would be well if I were praised by the Blessed One precisely because of my followers.” With such zeal, he undertook all the ascetic practices (dhutanga) and began practicing insight meditation (vipassanā). Before long, he became a great Arahant endowed with the six supernormal powers (abhiññā) and the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). He then trained his own disciples to be dhutanga-practitioners as well. When he approached the Blessed One with those disciples, as recorded in the Santhata training rule, he received praise from the Blessed One regarding his followers: “Upasena, this following of yours is truly pleasing.” He was placed in the foremost position (etadagga) among those who are “pleasing in every way” (samantapāsādika) and was included among the eighty Great Disciples.

One day, after returning from the alms round and finishing his meal, when his pupils had gone to their respective places for the day’s rest, he took water from a water pot, washed his feet, cooled his body, spread out a piece of leather, and sat down for the day’s abiding at his resting place, reflecting on his own virtues. Then, hundreds and thousands of his virtues appeared to him in succession. He thought: “If such virtues are evident even in me, a disciple, what must the virtues of my Teacher, the Blessed One, be like?” He then directed his attention toward the virtues of the Blessed One. According to the power of his knowledge, many billions of virtues appeared to him. He reflected on the Teacher’s virtues as: “My Teacher is of such virtue (sīla), such concentration (samādhi), such wisdom (paññā), such liberation (vimutti),” and “Thus indeed is the Blessed One: an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened one,” and so on. Then he reflected on the virtues of the Dhamma as “well-expounded” (svākkhāto) and the virtues of the Noble Saṅgha as “practicing well” (suppaṭipanno). Thus, as the virtues of the Triple Gem appeared to the Venerable Upasena in various ways, he remained in a state of great joy and happiness. To show this matter, the words beginning with “To the Venerable Upasena Vangantaputta, who had gone into seclusion...” were spoken in the Pali text. In those words, “rahogatassa” means one who is staying in a secluded place, being alone. “Evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi” means that a reflection arose in his mind in the manner just described. “Aho vata me” means “Oh, how wonderful it is for me to have obtained this human life and these gains.”
243:
Having reflected on the virtues of the Blessed One, he then reflected on the virtues of the Dhamma, beginning with 'Svākkhāto' (Well-expounded), and the virtues of the Noble Saṅgha, beginning with 'Suppaṭipanno' (Of good conduct). Thus, as the manifold virtues of the Triple Gem became manifest, the Great Elder sat experiencing sublime rapture and joy, with a mind full of delight. To illustrate this matter, the words beginning with 'Āyasmato Upasenassa Vaṅgantaputtassa rahogatassa' (To the Venerable Upasena, son of Vaṅganta, who had gone into seclusion) were spoken.

In that passage, 'rahogatassa' means gone into a secluded place, being alone. 'Evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi' means a reflection arose in his mind in the manner now to be described. 'Lābhā vata me' (What a gain for me!) means 'Indeed, these benefits such as obtaining human birth, the arising of a Buddha, and the attainment of faith are mine; oh, what a gain these are for me!' 'Suladdhaṃ vata me' (What a good fortune for me!) means 'That which I have obtained—the going forth (pabbajjā), the higher ordination (upasampadā), and the opportunity to serve the Triple Gem in the Dispensation of the Blessed One—is indeed a great fortune for me.' The reason for this is shown by the words beginning with 'Satthā ca me' (And the Teacher is mine).

In that context, he is called 'Satthā' (Teacher) because he instructs beings according to their needs regarding the welfare of the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal. He is called 'Bhagavā' (Blessed One) due to reasons such as possessing the six glories. He is 'Arahaṃ' (Worthy One) because he is remote from defilements, has slain the enemies that are defilements, has destroyed the spokes of the wheel of Saṃsāra, is worthy of requisites and offerings, and because of the absence of doing evil even in secret. He is 'Sammāsambuddha' (Perfectly Enlightened One) because he has rightly and by himself awakened to all phenomena. This is a summary here; the detailed explanation should be taken from the 'Description of the Recollection of the Buddha' in the Visuddhimagga.

'Svākkhāta' means well-expounded, spoken in a way that definitely leads out of suffering. 'Dhamma-vinaya' refers to the Dispensation (Pāvacana). It is called 'Dhamma-vinaya' because it upholds those who practice according to the instructions from falling into the suffering of Saṃsāra, and because it disciplines defilements such as lust. 'Sabrahmacārino' (Fellow-celibates) refers to those who practice together the Noble Path, which is the Dispensation of the Blessed One, called 'Brahma' in the sense of being excellent. 'Sīlavanto' (Virtuous) refers to those who possess virtue by way of the Path and Fruit. 'Kalyāṇadhammā' (Those of good qualities) refers to those who possess beautiful and excellent qualities such as concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. By this, the 'Suppaṭipanna' (good conduct) of the Saṅgha is shown. 'Sīlesu camhi paripūrakārī' (And I am one who fulfills the virtues) means 'After I ordained, I did not live as one who speaks "animal talk" (lowly talk) or as one preoccupied with bodily strength; rather, I fulfilled the fourfold virtue, such as the restraint of the Pātimokkha, making it unbroken, flawless, unspotted, and unblemished, [leading] towards the Noble Path...'
244:
Indeed, the Dhamma-Vinaya, which is taught as having the quality of leading out from the suffering of Saṃsāra, is called Dhamma-Vinaya because it protects all beings who practice according to the instructions in the Buddha's words from falling into the suffering of the round of rebirths, and because it disciplines defilements such as greed. 'Fellow practitioners' (sabrahmacārī) are so called because they practice together the Noble Path (Ariya Magga), which is the Buddha's Dispensation, called 'Brahma' due to its noble meaning. 'Virtuous' (sīlavanta) means they possess virtue through the power of the virtue of the Path and Fruition. 'Of good nature' (kalyāṇadhamma) means they are so called because these good qualities such as concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation exist in those fellow practitioners of mine. By these words, the quality of 'practicing well' (suppaṭipanna) of the Saṅgha is shown.

'I too am a fulfiller of virtues' means that after ordaining, I did not live as one who habitually engages in 'animal talk' (tiracchānakathā) or as one who is preoccupied with strengthening the physical body. Indeed, I fulfilled the fourfold virtue, such as the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha (pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla), making it unbroken, untorn, unspotted, and unspeckled, praised by the wise, and untouched by craving and views, and I have reached the Noble Path itself. By these words, he shows his attainment of the lower two fruits. In truth, Stream-enterers and Once-returners are fulfillers of virtues.

'I am one with a well-concentrated mind' means that through the divisions of access concentration (upacāra) and absorption concentration (appanā), I am concentrated in every way and possess an undistracted mind. By this statement of being a fulfiller of concentration, he shows his attainment of the third fruit (the fruit of Non-returning). Indeed, Non-returners are fulfillers of concentration.

'I am an Arahant, one whose taints are destroyed' means that because taints such as the taint of sensual desire are entirely destroyed, he is called 'one whose taints are destroyed' (khīṇāsava). Because those taints are destroyed, he has the fetters of existence cut off, and being worthy of the highest offerings in the world including the devas, he is an Arahant. By these words, he shows the completion of what had to be done (katakaraṇīya).

'I have great psychic power and great majesty' means that because he is endowed with great mastery over psychic powers such as the power of determination (adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi) and the power of transformation (vikubbanā-iddhi), he is 'of great psychic power' (mahiddhika). Because he is endowed with the attainment of extensive majesty of merit and majesty of attributes, he is 'of great majesty' (mahānubhāva). By these words, he shows his possession of mundane super-knowledges (abhiññā) and the successive meditative attainments (samāpatti). Because of their mastery over the super-knowledges, the Noble Ones are of great psychic power as they can accomplish whatever they wish; and because their continuums are purified by the attainment of various meditative attainments and the perfection of prior requisites, they are of great majesty.

'My life is good' means that as long as this body of mine, which is endowed with such qualities as virtue, lasts, the welfare and happiness of beings will only increase. Because I am a good field of merit for sowing the seeds of wholesome deeds, my life is also good and excellent. 'Death is good' means that if these five aggregates were to be extinguished today or at this very moment, like a fire without fuel, that death, which is called Parinibbāna without further rebirth, is also good for me. Thus, he shows the quality of steadfastness (tādi) in both life and death. In this way, because the Great Elder had an overflowing habit of unabandoned joy (somanassa), he reflected with extensive joy, with great respect for the Dhamma, and by experiencing the rapture of the Dhamma (dhamma-pīti).

The Teacher, while seated in the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), knew this with his Omniscient Knowledge and uttered this inspired utterance (Udāna) which clarifies the Elder's quality of steadfastness in both life and death. Therefore, it is said: 'Then the Blessed One... (pe)... uttered this inspired utterance.'

In that text, 'The life that does not burn' means that the life of a person whose taints are destroyed does not burn or afflict him because there is no future occurrence of the aggregates at all. Even the life that is currently occurring...
245:
Alternatively, because life is a conditioned phenomenon (saṅkhata-dhamma) in every respect, and because of the attainment of abundance in mindfulness and wisdom, and being well-endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña) in all matters, it [life] cannot oppress (that person). If a foolish worldling (andha-puthujjana) who associates with wicked people, is frequent in improper attention (ayoniso manasikāra), does not perform wholesome deeds, and does not perform merit, he suffers with remorse, thinking, "Alas, I have not done what is good," and so on; thus, his life is said to burn him. Other than him, the virtuous worldlings (kalyāṇa-puthujjana) and the seven types of trainees (sekha) who have not done evil but have performed merit, do not suffer later because they avoid things that cause burning and are endowed with things that do not cause burning; thus, their life does not burn them. Regarding the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), there is nothing even to be said (about burning); thus, the explanation is made by way of the suffering of the process of existence (pavatti-dukkha).

"Maraṇante na socati" means he does not grieve at the end known as death, or at the time near death, because grief (soka) has been eradicated at its root by the path of non-returning (anāgāmi-magga) alone. "Sa ve diṭṭhapado dhīro, sokamajjhe na socati" means that person is called "diṭṭhapada" because he has seen the four groups of dhammas such as non-covetousness, or because he has seen Nibbāna itself. The Arahant, called "dhīra" (the wise) because of being endowed with fortitude, does not grieve even when standing in the midst of beings who have not yet abandoned lust and are thus called "soka" (grief) due to their nature of grieving, or in the midst of worldly conditions (lokadhamma) which are the causes of grief.

Now, to show that for this Arahant there are no causes of grief in any respect, the words beginning with "ucchinnabhavataṇhassa" are spoken. In that context, one for whom craving for existence (bhavataṇhā) has been completely cut off by the path of arahantship (arahatta-magga) is called "ucchinnabhavataṇha." For that Arahant monk whose mind is peaceful because the remaining defilements have subsided without remainder (there is no more grief). "Vikkhiṇo jātisamsāro" means that saṃsāra, which has the previously mentioned characteristics—the succession of the aggregates (khandha), and the uninterrupted occurrence of the elements (dhātu) and sense bases (āyatana) beginning with birth—is especially exhausted. Therefore, for him, there is no further renewed existence; because there is no further renewed existence in the future for such a noble person (ariya-puggala), his cycle of birth (jātisamsāra) is exhausted. Why is there no further renewed existence for him? It should be stated by reversing the logic: because his craving for existence is cut off and his mind is peaceful. Alternatively, the meaning should be connected as: the cycle of birth is exhausted, and for that very reason, there is no further renewed existence for him.

## The Commentary on the Ninth Sutta is finished.
246:
## 10. Sāriputtaupasamasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the tenth sutta, "attano upasamaṃ" refers to [reflecting on] the complete subsiding of one's own defilements through the highest path (arahatta-magga), which is the cause for reaching the pinnacle of the disciples' perfection (sāvaka-pāramī).

Indeed, the Venerable Sāriputta saw directly the suffering of heat, oppression, and distress born of defilements like lust (rāga) in beings whose defilements have not yet subsided, as well as the suffering of birth, aging, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, etc., which have the formations of defilements (kilesa-abhisaṅkhāra) as their cause. Having weighed the suffering rooted in the round of existence (vaṭṭa) of those beings in the past and future, and being moved by compassion, he also recollected the considerable suffering caused by defilements that he himself experienced during his time as a worldling, and repeatedly reflected on the subsiding of his own defilements, thinking: "The defilements that were the cause of such great suffering have now been well-abandoned by me." While reflecting, he also reflected on the state of the defilements having subsided specifically through the respective path-knowledges: "This many defilements were subsided by the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga), this many by the path of once-returning (sakadāgāmi-magga), this many by the path of non-returning (anāgāmi-magga), and this many by the path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga)." Therefore, it is said: "reflecting on his own peace (calm)."

Other teachers, however, say: "The Elder, having entered the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala-samāpatti) and having reflected on that attainment, repeatedly reflected on the peace, thinking: 'Indeed, this peaceful and sublime state of this attainment of the fruit of Arahantship exists because of having the absolutely peaceful unconditioned element (Nibbāna) as its object, and because of the complete subsiding of defilements by itself.'" Others say: "The fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala) alone, which arises at the end of the subsiding of all defilements without remainder, is called 'upasama' (peace/calm) here; he sat reflecting on that fruit."

"Etamatthaṃ viditvā" means: the abandonment of defilements or the fruit of Arahantship, which is caused by the state of being a great wise one, etc., of the Venerable Sāriputta, and which is not shared with others among the disciples, is spoken of by the term "upasama" (peace/calm). Having known the meaning, characterized as the reflection on that abandonment of defilements, in all its aspects, he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) which demonstrates the power of that reflection.

In that inspired verse, "upasanta-santacittassa" is grammatically analyzed as: of one whose mind is peaceful, having become truly calmed. Indeed, a mind whose defilements are calmed by the suppression (vikkham-bhana) of an attainment is not called "upasanta-santa" (truly calmed and peaceful) in every respect, because that calming is not permanent. It is not so with the calming by the highest path (arahatta-magga). Because the defilements are absolutely cut off by that highest path, the mind of the Arahant is called "upasanta-santa" because it no longer needs to have defilements calmed again, and because it is peaceful, having had the defilements calmed by serenity (samatha), insight (vipassanā), and the lower paths.
247:
Because of the state of being truly tranquil, he is called "upasanta-santa." Therefore, it is said: "One who has become truly tranquil and has a peaceful mind is called one with a tranquil and peaceful mind (upasanta-santa-citta)." Alternatively, since "upasanta" refers to the subsiding (of defilements), "upasanta-santa-cittassa" means for one whose mind is peaceful due to the absolute subsiding of defilements.

In another way, although all Arahants have the subsiding of defilements without remainder, the Teacher spoke by qualifying it with the word "upasanta" as "upasanta-santa-cittassa" to show the subsiding of defilements of the General of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati), which is the cause of reaching the summit of the disciple's perfection of knowledge (sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa), and which is unique and superior among disciples.

In this context, the meaning is: "upasanta" means intensely or firmly tranquil; one who is tranquil by being truly tranquil through that firm tranquility is "upasanta-santa"; for one who has such a mind—all this is the same as the previous method. For it was in this way that the Blessed One praised and extolled him in various ways, saying: "Monks, Sāriputta is of great wisdom, of wide wisdom, of joyous wisdom, of swift wisdom, of sharp wisdom, of penetrating wisdom" (M. Ni. 3.93). "Netticchinnassa" means craving for existence (bhavataṇhā) is called "netti" (the lead/conduit) because it leads to saṃsāra; because that cord of craving for existence has been cut, he is called "netticchinna." It means for one whose craving has been thus abandoned. "Mutto so mārabandhanā" means such a person whose fetters of existence (bhava-saṃyojana) are exhausted is released from all bonds of Māra; for him, there is no further task to be done for the sake of release from Māra's bonds; therefore, the General of the Dhamma reviews his own tranquility. The rest is exactly as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Tenth Sutta is finished.

## The Commentary on the Meghiya Chapter is also finished.
248:
## 5. Soṇa Vagga

## 1. Commentary on the Piyatara Sutta

In the first sutta of the Mahā Vagga, "Mallikāya deviyā saddhiṃ" means together with his own chief queen named Mallikā. "Uparipāsādavaragato" means having gone to the upper part of the excellent palace. "Kocañño attanā piyataro" means is there any other person who is dearer than oneself. "Atthi nu kho te" means "Is there for you?"—thus he asks the queen.

Why does he ask? This Mallikā was the daughter of a poor flower-garland maker in Sāvatthī. One day, while taking a cake from the market and going to the flower garden thinking "I will eat it," she saw the Blessed One entering for alms, surrounded by the community of monks. With a devoted heart, she offered that cake to the Blessed One. The Teacher showed a sign of sitting in a suitable place to consume it, and the Venerable Ānanda spread a robe for him. The Blessed One sat there, consumed the cake, rinsed his mouth, and smiled. The Venerable Ānanda asked, "Venerable Sir, what will be the result of this woman's gift?" The Blessed One replied, "Ānanda, this woman has today given the first meal to the Tathāgata; this very day she will become the beloved and pleasing chief queen of the King of Kosala."

On that very day, the King, having fought with his nephew King Ajātasattu in Kāsīgāma and being defeated, fled and entered the city. Thinking "I will wait until the army arrives," he entered that flower garden. When Mallikā saw the King approaching, she performed services for him. The King, pleased with her service, had her father summoned, gave him great authority, and having her brought to the inner palace, established her in the position of chief queen. Then one day, the King thought: "I have given great authority to this Mallikā. What if I ask her, 'Who is dear to you?' She will say, 'You, Great King, are dear to me,' and then she will ask me back. Then I will tell her, 'You too are dear to me.'" Thus, he asked her while speaking pleasantly to create mutual intimacy.

However, Queen Mallikā, being wise and a supporter of the Buddha and the Saṅgha, thought, "This question should not be answered by looking at the King's face (to please him)," and speaking the truth, she replied, "Great King, there is no one else dearer to me than myself."
249:
Queen Mallikā, wishing to make the meaning she had answered clear to the King by means of an analogy, asked the King just as she herself had been asked by the King: “Great King, is there anyone dearer to you than yourself?” The King, unable to deny it because of the truth of the Queen’s statement, replied just as the Queen had answered, speaking according to the truth: “For me too, there is no one dearer than myself.”

After answering thus, the King, being of limited wisdom, thought: “I am a king, a lord of the earth, who lives having conquered the great circle of the earth; it is fitting for me to say, ‘I see no other dearer than myself.’ But this low-born woman, though placed in a high position by me, does not love me, her lord, in that way, but says in my presence, ‘Only myself is dearer.’ How harsh she is!” Being displeased, he challenged her: “Are not the Three Jewels (Ratanattaya) dearer to you than yourself?” The Queen replied: “Great King, I love the Three Jewels only because I desire for myself the bliss of heaven and the bliss of liberation (mokkha); therefore, only myself is dearer to me.” All this world loves others only for the sake of one’s own benefit. One who desires a son desires him thinking, “This son will support me in my old age.” One desires a daughter thinking, “My lineage will increase.” One desires a wife thinking, “She will serve at my feet.” Others, such as relatives and friends, are also loved according to their respective functions. Thus, the world loves others only by seeing its own benefit; this was the Queen’s intention.

Then the King thought: “This Mallikā is clever, wise, and subtle. She says, ‘Only myself is dearer to me.’ It now appears to me also that only myself is dearer to me. Indeed, I shall report this matter to the Blessed One, and I shall remember it as the Teacher explains it to me.” Having thought thus, he approached the Teacher and reported that matter. Therefore, it was said (in the Pali): “Then King Pasenadi of Kosala... (pe) ...is dearer.”

“Having known this meaning” means having fully understood the meaning stated by the King that “In the world, for all beings, oneself is the most dear to oneself,” he uttered this inspired utterance (Udāna) to clarify that meaning.

In that Udāna verse, “Having traversed all directions with the mind” means having followed with the mind by way of searching through all the ten directions without exception. “One found no one dearer than oneself anywhere” means that any man, even searching with all his effort, [could not find] another more dearly beloved than himself...
250:
Even if one searches in all directions with various efforts, one will not find or see anyone dearer than oneself anywhere. It is only because one cannot find anyone dearer than oneself that the self is the dearest to each of those various beings. Therefore, one who loves oneself, reflecting that all beings love themselves, desire their own happiness, and loathe suffering, should not harm or kill another being, even down to an ant or a small insect, if one desires one's own welfare. One should not oppress them with the palm of the hand, clods of earth, sticks, and so forth. For the suffering caused by oneself to another appears back in oneself at a later time, as if it had migrated from the other to oneself. This is the nature of kamma.

## The commentary on the first sutta is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Appāyuka Sutta
