In the second sutta, the phrase "It is wonderful, Bhante" should be understood as an expression of wonder regarding something blameworthy, just as in the Meghiya Sutta. "Yāva appāyukā" means those who are short-lived, having a very brief life. "Sattāhajāte" means on the seventh day after birth. "Tusitaṃ kāyaṃ upapajjī" means he was reborn in the Tusita deva realm by way of taking rebirth.

It is said that one day, after his meal, the Elder Ānanda was sitting in his daytime resting place. Reflecting on the glory of the Buddha's physical body (rūpakāya), which was adorned with the 32 major marks and 80 minor marks, exceedingly beautiful and an unsurpassed sight, he experienced great joy and rapture, thinking: "How wonderful is the perfection of the physical body of the Buddhas! It is delightful to behold, inspiring from all sides, and captivating to the heart." Then he thought: "To a mother who has given birth, even an ugly son is as dear as if he were handsome. If the Buddha's mother, Queen Mahāmāyā, were still alive, what great joy and rapture would arise in her upon seeing the Buddha's beauty? It is a great loss for my maternal aunt, the Queen, who passed away seven days after the Blessed One was born." Having thought thus, he approached the Blessed One and, reporting his reflection, spoke the words "It is wonderful, Bhante," and so on, as if to lament her early death.
251:
Some teachers, however, say: "Although Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī requested the Blessed One for ordination with great effort, she was refused. I (Venerable Ānanda), however, having requested through a skillful means, the Blessed One permitted her the going-forth and the full ordination by way of her accepting the Eight Heavy Rules (garudhamma). Having accepted those rules and obtained the going-forth and full ordination, the foster-mother brought about the second assembly of the Blessed One and became the cause for the fourth assembly. If the Blessed One's mother, Mahāmāyā Devī, were still alive, both of these Khattiya sisters together would have graced this Sāsana. Also, the Blessed One, out of great reverence for his mother, would have easily permitted the going-forth and full ordination for women in the Sāsana. However, because of the mother's short lifespan, this ordination was accomplished with difficulty." With this intention, the Elder spoke the words beginning with "It is wonderful, Bhante," in the presence of the Blessed One. That is not the reason. For when the Blessed One permits the going-forth in his Sāsana for his mother or any other woman, he permits it only after making it a serious matter (by imposing the heavy rules), not lightly, because of his desire for the long endurance of the Sāsana.

Other teachers, however, say: "The Elder, reflecting on the infinite and immeasurable qualities of the Buddha, such as the Ten Powers (dasabala) and the Four Kinds of Self-Confidence (caturvesārajja), which are not shared by others, thought: 'It is inappropriate that this Buddha-mother, who carried in her womb for ten months the Teacher, the supreme person in the world of such great majesty, should become the attendant of anyone else. Why? Because it is fitting for the qualities of the Teacher that his mother should pass away seven days after the Blessed One was born and, having passed away, be reborn in the Tusita heaven.' Thus, having a sense of wonder and amazement, and wishing to inform the Blessed One of the thought that had arisen in him, he spoke the words beginning with 'It is wonderful, Bhante.'"

The Teacher, however, because the passing away of a Bodhisatta's mother seven days after the birth of a Bodhisatta is established as a natural law (dhammatā), spoke the words beginning with "So it is, Ānanda," wishing to clarify that natural law. As for that natural law: just as all Bodhisattas, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs), are reborn in the city of Tusita, stay there for the full extent of their lifespan, and at the end of their life, being requested by the deities of the ten thousand world-systems to take rebirth in the human world to attain Enlightenment, they observe the time, the continent, the region, and the family; in the same way, they also observe the lifespan of the mother before taking rebirth. This Blessed One also, while still a Bodhisatta staying in the city of Tusita, while making the Five Great Observations (pañca mahāvilokanāni)...
252:
...having discerned that the lifespan of the mother was ten months and seven days, and knowing, 'This is the time for me to take rebirth; it is now proper to be born,' he took rebirth. Therefore, this should be understood as the habitual practice of all Bodhisattas. That is why the Blessed One said, "Ānanda, the mothers of Bodhisattas are short-lived," and so on.

In that passage, "they pass away (kālaṃ karonti)" means they pass away solely due to the exhaustion of their lifespan as mentioned, not because of the birth itself. The place where Bodhisattas in their final existence have resided is like a shrine-room (cetiyaghara); it is not fit to be used by others. Nor is it possible to remove the mother of a Bodhisatta and place another in the position of Chief Queen (aggamahesī). Therefore, the lifespan of a Bodhisatta's mother is only ten months and seven days. That is why they pass away at that time. It is with this meaning in mind that the Great Bodhisattas make the fifth great observation.

At what age do they pass away? They pass away in middle age (majjhimavaya). In the first stage of life, beings have strong desire and lust (chandarāga) for their own bodies. Therefore, women who become pregnant at that age are generally unable to protect the womb well. Even if they could carry the pregnancy, that fetus would be prone to many illnesses. However, after passing through two parts of middle age and reaching the third part, the base (vatthu/womb) is clear and pure. Children born from a pure base are free from disease. Therefore, the mothers of Bodhisattas enjoy prosperity in the first stage of life and then, having given birth in the third part of middle age, they pass away.

"Having known this matter" means having known that for the mother of a Bodhisatta and all other beings, life in an individual existence (attabhāva) ends in death; and by way of illustrating that meaning, he uttered this inspired solemn utterance (Udāna) which encourages effort in the faultless practice.

In that Udāna, "whoever (ye keci)" is an indefinite designation. "Those who have come to be (bhūtā)" means those who have been born. "Those who will be (bhavissanti)" means those who will be born in the future. The word "vā" (or) expresses a variation in thought, and the word "api" (also) expresses inclusion. By this, it also includes those who are currently being born. By this much, all beings included in the three periods of time, such as the past, are included without remainder. Alternatively, womb-born (gabbhaseyyaka) beings are called "bhūtā" from the time they emerge from the mother's womb; before that, they are called "bhavissanti." For the moisture-born (saṃsedaja) and the spontaneously born (upapātika), after the moment of the rebirth-linking consciousness...
253:
"Beings who have come to be" (bhūta) refers to those who will come to be by virtue of the existence that is to arise before that. Alternatively, all beings are called "beings who have come to be" by virtue of their present existence, and "those who will come to be" (bhavissanti) by virtue of the existence that will arise again in the future. Arahants are called "beings who have come to be." Indeed, they have only come to be and will not come to be again; those other than the Arahants are called "those who will come to be."

"All beings will go, leaving the body" means that all beings, divided into various kinds by virtue of existence (bhava), mode of birth (yoni), destination (gati), station of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti), and abode of beings (sattāvāsa), will leave and cast off their own bodies and go to the next world; however, Arahants will go to Nibbāna. Herein, it is shown that there is no one who is of a nature not to die. "The wise one, knowing this total loss" means that a wise person, being of a prudent nature, knows the arising, decline, and death of all beings, or the destruction and fragility of all beings, through the power of mindfulness of death (maraṇānussati) or through the power of contemplating impermanence (aniccatā). "Ardent, one should lead the holy life" means that while performing the work of insight (vipassanā), being endowed with the energy called ardency (ātāpiya), a person who has aroused energy through the four right efforts (sammappadhāna) should practice the holy life of the Path (magga-brahmacariya), which is the means to transcend death without remainder; this is the meaning.

## The Commentary on the Second Sutta is finished.

## 3. Suppabuddha-kuṭṭhi Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, "In Rājagaha, there was a leper named Suppabuddha" means there was a man named Suppabuddha in the city of Rājagaha. He was a leper, his body severely ravaged by leprosy. "The poorest of men" means he was the most destitute among all the people in Rājagaha. He lived by sewing together rags discarded by people at rubbish heaps, roadsides, and so on, to wear; holding a potsherd, he went from house to house, subsisting on the rice-water and leftover scraps he received. Even that food he did not obtain as much as he desired due to his past kamma. Therefore, he is called "the poorest of men." "A pitiable man" means he had reached the state of being most pitiable among men. "A wretched man" means he was extremely lowly because of being reviled and despised by people. "In a great assembly" means in a great assembly of monks and lay followers.
254:
One day, it is said, the Blessed One, surrounded by a large community of monks, entered Rājagaha for alms. Having ensured that the monks could easily obtain alms-food, he departed from the alms-round after the meal, surrounded by a few monks. Waiting for the arrival of those lay followers (upāsakas) who had given alms and the remaining monks, he stayed at a certain pleasant spot within the city itself. At that very moment, monks came from various places and surrounded the Blessed One. The lay followers also approached the Blessed One, thinking, "We will return after listening to the discourse of appreciation (anumodanā) and paying homage," and a great assembly was formed. The Blessed One indicated his intention to sit. At that very moment, they prepared a seat worthy of a Buddha. Then the Blessed One, resplendent with the thirty-two marks of a great man and adorned with the eighty minor marks, shining with a fathom-wide aura, emitting the six-colored Buddha-rays of blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and brilliant, illuminating the entire area with the incomparable glory of his physical body, sat upon the prepared noble Buddha-seat like the full moon surrounded by a host of stars. Surrounded by the host of monks, he preached the Dhamma with a Brahma-voice as sweet as the song of the Karavīka bird, roaring a lion's roar like a maned lion on a flat slab of realgar.

The monks, too, being of few desires, contented, secluded, unassociated, energetic, resolute, rebukers of evil, blamers of sin, speakers of advice, patient in receiving instruction, and endowed with virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, wore their cloud-colored rag-robes (paṃsukūla) and surrounded the Blessed One like well-tamed scent-elephants, listening to the Dhamma with attentive ears. The lay followers, too, wearing clean clothes and with clean upper robes placed on their shoulders, having given great gifts in the morning, honored the Blessed One with perfumes, flowers, and so on. After paying homage and showing deep respect to the community of monks, they surrounded the Blessed One and the community of monks with restrained hands and feet, listening to the Dhamma respectfully with attentive ears. Therefore, it is said, "At that time, the Blessed One was seated, surrounded by a great assembly, preaching the Dhamma." 

Suppabuddha, however, overcome by the weakness of hunger and wandering in search of food, entered the middle of the street. Seeing that great gathering of people from afar, he thought, "Why is this great crowd of people assembled? Surely, I think food is being given here. Perhaps if I go there, I might be able to get some food or snacks." With this desire arising, he went there and saw the inspiring Blessed One...
255:
He saw the Blessed One, who is inspiring, causing confidence, tamed by the noble taming, attained to tranquility and composure, tamed, guarded, with peaceful faculties, and endowed with well-established concentration, preaching the Dhamma while surrounded by that assembly. Urged by the maturity of his past merits (upanissaya) accumulated in previous lives, he thought, "It would indeed be good if I too could listen to the Dhamma," and sat down at the edge of the assembly. Referring to his sitting at the edge of the assembly, it is stated in the Pali: "Suppabuddha the leper saw... he sat down right there at one side, thinking, 'I too will listen to the Dhamma.'"

'Sabbāvantaṃ' means including all persons, such as the low and so on, without leaving out anyone in that assembly. It is also read as 'Sabbavantaṃ'. 'Cetasā' means with a mind associated with the Buddha-eye (Buddha-cakkhu). Since knowledge is indicated by using the mind as the head, it means with the knowledge of the inclinations and underlying tendencies (āsayānusaya-ñāṇa) and the knowledge of the degrees of the faculties (indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa). 'Ceto paricca manasākāsi' means he discerned the minds of that assembly individually and took them to heart; he surveyed them. 'Bhabbo dhammaṃ viññātuṃ' means capable of attaining the Path and Fruit, endowed with the necessary support (upanissaya). 'Etadahosi' refers to the thought that occurred to the Blessed One: "Although this Suppabuddha reached such a state because of an offense against the Paccekabuddha named Tagarasikhī, the support (upanissaya) for the Path and Fruit within his heart is shining like a pure gold nugget (nikkha) covered by dust; therefore, he is one who can easily understand." Thus, He said, "This person here is capable of understanding the Dhamma."

'Anupubbī kathaṃ' (Gradual Discourse) refers to the discourse given in order: virtue (sīla) immediately after giving (dāna), heaven (sagga) immediately after virtue, and the Path (magga) immediately after heaven. The Blessed One first shows the gratification along with the cause, and then, in order to make beings detached from sensual pleasures, he reveals the danger through various methods. To those whose hearts are moved by hearing the danger, he shows the state beyond the round (vivaṭṭa) by way of explaining the benefits of renunciation (nekkhamma).

'Dānakathaṃ' (Talk on Giving): This giving is the cause of happiness, the root of attainments, the basis of wealth, the protection, shelter, destination, and refuge for those on a rough path. In this world and the world beyond, there is no support, basis, object, protection, shelter, destination, or refuge equal to giving. This giving is like a jeweled throne in the sense of being a support, like the great earth in the sense of being a basis, like a rope in the sense of being an object to hold, like a boat in the sense of crossing over suffering, like a brave general in the sense of providing relief, like a city surrounded by a moat in the sense of protecting from danger, like a lotus in the sense of being unstained by the impurities of stinginess and so on, like fire in the sense of burning up [unwholesome states], like a cobra in the sense of being difficult to approach [by enemies], and like a lion in the sense of being fearless.
256:
It is like an elephant in the sense of strength, like a white bull considered auspicious in the sense of supreme blessing, and like the Valāhaka horse king in the sense of leading safely to a secure land. Giving grants the glory of sovereignty in the world, the attainment of a universal monarch, the attainment of Sakka, the attainment of Māra, the attainment of Brahmā, the knowledge of a disciple's perfection, the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha, and the knowledge of a Supreme Buddha—thus is the talk connected with the virtues of giving.

Because one who gives is able to undertake virtue, he gave the talk on virtue (sīlakathā) immediately after the talk on giving. 'Sīlakathā' means this virtue is the support, basis, object, protection, shelter, destination, and refuge of beings. For the attainments and happiness of this life and the next, there is no support, basis, object, protection, shelter, destination, or refuge equal to virtue. There is no ornament like the ornament of virtue, no flower like the flower of virtue, and no scent like the scent of virtue. The world including the devas, when looking at a person adorned with the ornament of virtue, wearing the flower of virtue, and anointed with the scent of virtue, can never be satisfied—thus is the talk connected with the virtues of virtue.

In order to show that this heaven can be obtained by depending on this virtue, he gave the talk on heaven (saggakathā) immediately after virtue. 'Saggakathā' means heaven is a place that is desirable, lovely, and delightful; constant play and constant success are obtained there. The Cātumahārājikā devas enjoy divine happiness and divine success for nine million years; the Tāvatiṃsa devas enjoy it for thirty-six million years—thus is the talk connected with the virtues of heaven. Even the mouths of the Buddhas are not enough to describe the success of heaven. It has also been said: "Monks, I could speak about heaven in many ways," and so on.

After thus enticing them with the talk on heaven, just like decorating an elephant and then cutting off its trunk, he gave a talk on the danger (ādīnava), degradation (okāra), and defilement (saṃkilesa) of sensual pleasures in order to show: "This heaven is also impermanent and unstable; one should not form desire and lust for it," by the method: "Sensual pleasures provide little gratification, much suffering, and much despair; the danger in them is even greater." In that context, 'ādīnava' means fault. 'Okāra' means a low nature, a base nature that should be practiced by the ignoble and not by the noble. 'Saṃkilesa' means the defilement of beings in Saṃsāra because of those sensual pleasures. Therefore, he said: "Alas, sirs, beings are defiled!"
257:
In this way, by threatening with the dangers of sensual pleasures, He showed the benefits of renunciation (nekkhamma). He also illustrated and praised the virtues of monkhood and the meditative absorptions (jhānas), etc.

In the passage beginning with "kallacitta," "kallacitta" means a mind that is ready for work (kammaññacitta). Because the faults of the mind, such as lack of faith, have been removed by the preceding teaching, the mind becomes a suitable vessel for the teaching to follow, meaning it is ready for the work of insight (vipassanā). "Kammakkhamacitta" has the same meaning. It should be understood that the Buddha knew when he had a "soft mind" (muducitta) because it is free from the defilements of wrong view and conceit; a "mind free from hindrances" (vinīvaraṇacitta) because it is free from sensual desire and so on; an "uplifted mind" (udaggacitta) because it is joined with abundant rapture and joy in the right practice; and among those, a "confident mind" (pasannacitta) because it is endowed with the perfection of faith.

Alternatively, "kallacitta" means a mind free from the disease of sensuality. "Muducitta" means a mind that is not harsh due to the power of loving-kindness, being free from ill-will. "Vinīvaraṇacitta" means a mind that is not obstructed because it is not distracted, being free from restlessness and remorse. "Udaggacitta" means a mind that is not dejected due to the power of proper exertion, being free from sloth and torpor. "Pasannacitta" means a mind that is committed to the right practice, being free from doubt.

"Atha" means afterwards. "Sāmukkaṃsikā" means discovered by Himself, taken up by Himself, seen by Himself through His self-evolved knowledge (sayambhū-ñāṇa), and not shared with others (asādhāraṇa). What is that teaching? It is the teaching of the Noble Truths. Therefore, He said, "Suffering, Origin, Cessation, and the Path." Since this is the presentation of the essence of the Truths, the Noble Truths should be preached here. These should be understood in detail in all their aspects according to the method stated in the Visuddhimagga.

By the simile beginning with "seyyathāpi," He shows Suppabuddha’s abandonment of defilements and the arising of the Noble Path. "Apagatakāḷakaṃ" means free from black spots or impurities. "Sammadeva" means very well. "Rajanaṃ" means dye such as blue, yellow, red, or madder. "Paṭiggaṇheyya" means it would take the dye firmly or become bright. "Tasmiṃyeva āsane" means right in that sitting place. By this, Suppabuddha’s quick insight, sharp wisdom, and "pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge" (sukhāpaṭipadā khippābhiññā) are shown.

"Virajaṃ vītamalaṃ" means "stainless" (virajaṃ) because of the absence of the dust of lust, etc., which leads to the lower realms, and "faultless" (vītamalaṃ) because of the removal of the impurities of wrong view and doubt without remainder. Alternatively, "stainless" because of the absence of the dust of defilements to be abandoned by the first path (Sotāpatti-magga), and "faultless" because of the removal of the five types of immoral impurities. "Dhamma-cakkhu" refers to the Path of Stream-entry. To show the manner of its arising, He said: "Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease." Indeed, that Path arises while penetrating conditioned phenomena by way of its function, taking Cessation (Nibbāna) as its object.
258:
In this matter, this comparison should be noted: the mind should be seen as the cloth. The state of the mind being defiled by impurities such as lust should be seen as the cloth being soiled by external stains. The progressive discourse (anupubbīkathā) should be seen as the washing board. Faith should be seen as water. The exertion of energy in purifying the mind through the procedure of faith, etc.—by moistening it with the cool water of faith and making the faults of defilements loose through mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—should be seen as the effort of washing the cloth by moistening it with water and thoroughly rubbing out the stains with cow-dung ash and soap. The suppression of defilements through the exertion of energy should be seen as the removal of stains from the cloth through that effort. The Noble Path should be seen as the dye. The mind, from which defilements have been suppressed, becoming exceedingly pure and bright through the Path should be seen as the pure cloth becoming radiant with that dye.

Thus, Suppabuddha, sitting at the edge of the assembly, heard the Dhamma teaching and reached the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Wishing to report the virtue he had attained to the Blessed One, but not daring to push through the middle of the assembly, he followed the Blessed One when the people had paid homage and were returning, and when the Blessed One went to the monastery, he himself also went to the monastery.

At that moment, Sakka, the king of devas, knowing that "This Suppabuddha the leper wishes to make known the virtue he has attained in the Teacher's Dispensation," thought, "I will test him." He went and stood in the air and said this: "Suppabuddha, you are a poor man, a wretched man, a miserable, lowly man. I will give you immeasurable wealth. Say: 'The Buddha is not the Buddha, the Dhamma is not the Dhamma, the Saṅgha is not the Saṅgha. I have had enough of the Buddha, I have had enough of the Dhamma, I have had enough of the Saṅgha.'"

Then Suppabuddha asked him, "Who are you?" When he said, "I am Sakka, the king of devas," Suppabuddha said, "You blind fool, shameless one! You are not a fit person to speak with me, you who say such unspeakable things. Furthermore, why do you call me a poor, wretched, and miserable man? Am I not the true-born son of the Lord of the World? I am neither poor, nor wretched, nor miserable. On the contrary, I am one who has attained great happiness, and I am a man of great wealth." Having said this, he spoke:

"The treasure of faith, the treasure of virtue, the treasure of shame (hiri) and fear of wrongdoing (ottappa),
The treasure of learning (suta) and generosity (cāga), and wisdom is indeed the seventh treasure.
If any woman or man possesses these treasures,
They say of that person, 'He is not poor,' and his life is not in vain."
259:
“I possess these seven noble wealths. Those who possess these wealths are not called ‘poor’ by the Buddhas or the Paccekabuddhas.”

Sakka, having heard Suppabuddha's words, left him on the way and went to the Blessed One to report the entire conversation. Then the Blessed One said to Sakka, “Sakka, even a hundred or a thousand Sakkas like you would not be able to make Suppabuddha the leper say, ‘The Buddha is not the Buddha, the Dhamma is not the Dhamma, the Saṅgha is not the Saṅgha.’” Suppabuddha the leper also went to the Blessed One, and after being welcomed by the Teacher, he reported the spiritual qualities he had attained. Referring to this, it is said: “Then Suppabuddha the leper, having seen the Dhamma,” and so on.

In that passage, ‘diṭṭhadhamma’ means one who has seen the Dhamma of the Noble Truths. The same method applies to the remaining terms. In the term ‘diṭṭhadhamma’, the word ‘dhamma’ is used in a general sense. Since ‘seeing’ (dassana) can also refer to seeing with the physical eye other than the vision of knowledge, the term ‘pattadhamma’ (one who has reached the Dhamma) is used to exclude such types of seeing. Since ‘reaching’ (patti) can also occur in ways other than reaching through knowledge, the term ‘viditadhamma’ (one who has known the Dhamma) is used to distinguish it. Since such knowledge of the Dhamma can also occur partially, the term ‘pariyogāḷhadhamma’ (one who has plunged into the Dhamma) is used to show knowledge without remainder. By saying this, it illustrates Suppabuddha's penetration of the aforementioned Four Noble Truths. Path knowledge, by the power of a single realization, accomplishes the function of full understanding (pariññā) and so on, and is said to have plunged completely into the things to be fully understood without remainder; no other knowledge besides this Path knowledge can do so. Therefore, it is said: “Because this person has seen the Dhamma of the Noble Truths, he is called diṭṭhadhamma.” For that reason, it is said: “one who has crossed over doubt,” and so on.

In that passage, he is called ‘tiṇṇavicikiccho’ because he has crossed over the sixteen types of doubt and the eight types of doubt, which are like a fearful wilderness. Because of that crossing, the indecision (kathaṃkathā) that arises in the form of “Is it thus? Is it not thus?” regarding the process of existence and so on has vanished and been eradicated; thus he is ‘vigatakathaṃkathō’. Because he has abandoned the evil states that cause fear and is well-established in the qualities of virtue and so on which are the opposites of those states, he has attained confidence, proficiency, and clarity; thus he is ‘vesārajjappatto’. In this Suppabuddha, there is no longer a need to depend on the faith of others regarding the Triple Gem; thus he is ‘aparappaccayo’. Where? It says, “in the Teacher's Dispensation.”
260:
In the words beginning with “abhikkantaṃ,” although this word “abhikkanta” is found in many senses such as exhaustion, excellence, extreme beauty, and great delight, here it should be understood in the sense of great delight (abbhanumodana). Therefore, Suppabuddha said “Abhikkantaṃ, bhante” twice, out of both devotion and praise. It means, “Excellent, venerable sir! Excellent!” Alternatively, “abhikkantaṃ” means extremely surpassing, extremely desirable, extremely pleasing, and extremely good. Of these two mentions of the word “abhikkanta,” with one he praises the Blessed One's teaching, and with the other, he praises his own devotion.

The meaning here is: “Venerable sir, this Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One is extremely delightful. Venerable sir, my devotion that has arisen based on the Blessed One's Dhamma teaching is also extremely delightful.” Or, he spoke the two words wishing to praise the Blessed One's words through various ways, such as: because they destroy anger, because they lead to the attainment of supramundane qualities, likewise because they increase faith, because they generate wisdom, because they are meaningful, because they are well-phrased, because the meaning of the words is clear, because they have deep meaning, because they are pleasant to the ear, because they go to the heart, because they do not involve self-exaltation, because they do not involve disparaging others, because they are cool with compassion, because they are pure with wisdom, because they are delightful when they appear, because they can withstand scrutiny, because they are pleasant to listen to, and because they bring welfare and happiness whenever they are reflected upon.

After that, he praises the teaching itself with four metaphors. Among those metaphors, “nikkujjitaṃ” means an object placed face down or turned downwards. “ukkujjeyya” means to set it face upwards. “paṭicchannaṃ” means covered with grass, leaves, etc. “vivareyya” means to open or uncover. “mūဠှဿ” means to one who is confused about the directions. “maggaṃ ācikkheyya” means to point out the way by taking one's hand and saying, “This is the way.” “andhakāre” means in the darkness characterized by four factors. This is the word-by-word meaning.

The explanation of the meaning (atthayojanā) is as follows: Just as someone might set upright what was overturned, even so, the Blessed One has raised me up from wrong teachings, I who had turned my back on the true Dhamma and was established in wrong teachings. Just as one might reveal what was hidden, even so, the Blessed One has revealed the Dispensation which had been covered by the thicket of wrong views since the disappearance of the Dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa. Just as one might point out the way to one who is lost, even so, the Blessed One has made clear the path to heaven and liberation to me who had reached a wrong path and a base path. Just as one might hold up an oil lamp in the darkness, even so, the Blessed One has lit the lamp of the teaching which destroys the darkness of delusion for me who was submerged in the darkness of delusion and could not see the qualities of the Jewels such as the Buddha. Thus, the Dhamma has been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways and through various methods.
261:
Having praised the teaching in this way, with a mind full of faith in the Triple Gem due to that teaching, and performing an act of devotion, he spoke the words beginning with "Esāhaṃ."

In the phrase "Esāhaṃ," it should be analyzed as "Eso ahaṃ" (This I). "Bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi" means "The Blessed One is my refuge, my resort, the destroyer of my suffering, and the provider of my welfare." With this intention, it means "I approach the Blessed One, I associate with Him," or "I know and understand Him in this way." For those roots that have the meaning of "going" also have the meaning of "knowing."

"Dhamma" is so called because it supports those who practice according to the instruction, who have attained the Path, and who have realized Cessation, preventing them from falling into the four lower realms. In essence, that Dhamma is the Noble Path and Nibbāna. It has been said:
"Monks, among conditioned things, the Noble Eightfold Path is said to be the foremost."
And: "Monks, among all things, whether conditioned or unconditioned, detachment (Nibbāna) is said to be the foremost."

Not only the Noble Path and Nibbāna, but also the four Noble Fruits along with the Scriptural Teaching (Pariyatti) are called Dhamma. It has also been said:
"The Dhamma that is the fading of lust, the fourfold Path;
The Dhamma that is free from craving and sorrow, the fourfold Fruit;
The Dhamma that is unconditioned, Nibbāna;
This Dhamma that is not repulsive, sweet, proficient, and well-analyzed, the Scriptural Teaching;
Go to this Dhamma for refuge."

In this verse, "rāgaviraāga" refers to the Path. "Aneja-masoka" refers to the Fruit. "Asaṅkhata" refers to Nibbāna. "Appaṭikūlaṃ madhuram-imaṃ paguṇaṃ suvibhattaṃ" refers to the Scriptural Teaching.

"Bhikkhusaṅgha" refers to the group of eight noble persons united by the similarity of view and virtue. With these words, Suppabuddha declared his realization of the Three Refuges.

In the words, "May the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts," "ajjatagge" means starting from today. There is also the reading "ajjadagge," where the letter "d" is inserted for euphonic combination (sandhi). "Ajja agge" means starting from today. "Pāṇupetaṃ" means as long as life continues (until the end of life). It means, "May the Blessed One recognize and know me as a lay follower (upāsaka) or an attendant (kappiyakāraka) who performs duties for the Triple Gem, having gone for refuge through the three refuges without seeking any other teacher." Although Suppabuddha's establishment in the refuges was accomplished through the attainment of the Noble Path, he spoke thus to make his intention clear.
262:
Rejoicing and appreciating the Blessed One's words means rejoicing in the Blessed One's speech with the mind and expressing that appreciation through words in the manner described to make that joy evident. Having paid homage to the Blessed One and circumambulated Him, he departed means that having bowed to the Blessed One with the fivefold prostration and circumambulated Him three times, with a mind inclined toward the Teacher's virtues, he departed while looking only at the Blessed One and keeping his hands in prayerful salutation until He was out of sight.

Suppabuddha, who had thus departed, was a man afflicted by leprosy, with fingers and toes severed, his entire body cracked and painful, with blood and pus oozing from all sides, tormented by itching and flies, foul-smelling like excrement, extremely loathsome, and in a state deserving of the utmost pity. As if thinking, "This body is no longer fit to be the support for this extremely peaceful and most sublime Noble Dhamma," although his merit capable of leading to heaven provided an opportunity, he was urged by a destructive unwholesome kamma accumulated in the past that leads to a short life. Consequently, a cow with a young calf ran at him and gored him to death. Therefore, it is stated in the Pali: "Then, not long after Suppabuddha the leper had departed, a cow with a young calf gored him and took his life."

The reason heard is that in a past life, Suppabuddha was the son of a wealthy merchant. While playing with three other merchant sons, they took a courtesan, who was the beauty of the city, to a garden and enjoyed themselves all day. At sunset, he said to his companions, "This woman has a thousand coins, much gold, and expensive ornaments in her hands. There is no one else in this forest but us, and night has fallen. Come, let us kill her, take all the wealth, and go." Those four men, being of one mind, attempted to kill her. While being killed, the courtesan made a wish: "These shameless and heartless men, after having been intimate with me, are killing me, who am innocent, purely out of greed for wealth. Let them kill me this once, but may I become an ogress and be able to kill them many times." Having made this wish, she died. Among those four, one became the clansman Pukkusāti, one became Bāhiya Dārucīriya, one became Tambadāṭhika the executioner, and one became Suppabuddha the leper. For hundreds of lifetimes of these four people, she was reborn in the womb of an ogress and took their lives in the form of a cow. Due to the result of that evil kamma, they had to die in the middle of their journey.
263:
In those various lives, they met their death in the interim. Thus, death occurred instantly for Suppabuddha the leper; therefore, it was said: "Then, not long after [the Blessed One] had departed... [the cow] deprived [Suppabuddha] of life." Then, many monks informed the Blessed One of his death and asked about his future state. The Blessed One explained it. Therefore, it was said: "Then, many monks," and so forth.

In that text, "because of the destruction of the three fetters" means because of the total eradication and abandonment of these three bonds of existence: personality belief (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), skeptical doubt (vicikicchā), and attachment to rules and rituals (sīlabbataparāmāsa). "Sotāpanna" means one who has first reached the Noble Path known as the "Stream" (sota). Indeed, it was said: "Friend Sāriputta, it is said, 'The stream, the stream.' Friend Sāriputta, what is the stream? It is just this Noble Eightfold Path," and so forth.

"Avinipātadhamma" means one who does not have the nature of falling (vinipāta), one who by nature does not fall into the four woeful states by way of rebirth. "Niyata" means assured by the law of Dhamma (dhamma-niyāma), by the law of rightness (sammatta-niyāma). "Sambodhiparāyaṇa" means one for whom enlightenment (sambodhi), consisting of the three higher paths, is the ultimate destination, resort, and refuge, which must inevitably be reached. By this term "sambodhiparāyaṇa," in response to the question "What is his destination? What is his future state?", it is shown that Suppabuddha's destination was only good, not evil. However, the King of Dhamma, the Blessed One, did not directly show the destination reached by Suppabuddha, but spoke only this much, wishing to reveal it through the sequence of the question. 

For the Blessed One saw: "When I have spoken this much, a certain monk in this very assembly, skilled in the sequence of discourse, will ask about the cause of Suppabuddha's leprosy, poverty, and wretchedness; then, I shall conclude the teaching by revealing that cause through the sequence of that question." Therefore, it was said: "When this was said, a certain monk," and so forth. In that text, "hetu" is the specific cause, while "paccaya" is the general condition; this is the distinction between the two. "Yena" means by which cause (hetu) and by which condition (paccaya).

"Bhūtapubbaṃ" means it happened before. To show what occurred in the past, he said "Suppabuddha," and so forth. When did it happen? It is said that in the past, before the appearance of a Buddha, in a certain place near the city of Bārāṇasī, a young man...
264:
In the past, before the appearance of the Tathāgata, in a village near the city of Bārāṇasī, a young woman was guarding a field. Seeing a Paccekabuddha and having a heart full of faith, she offered him a Paduma lotus flower along with five hundred parched rice flowers and made a wish to have five hundred sons. At that very moment, five hundred hunters offered sweet meat to the Paccekabuddha and made a wish: "May we be the sons of this woman, and may we attain the special Dhamma attained by you, venerable sirs." That woman lived out her life and was reborn in the deva world. Passing away from the deva world, she was reborn in the womb of a Paduma lotus in a certain lake. A hermit saw the girl and cared for her. As she walked here and there, with every step she took, Paduma lotus flowers sprang up from the ground. A forest hunter saw this and informed the King of Bārāṇasī. The King brought the girl and made her his chief queen. A pregnancy was established in the queen's womb. Prince Mahāpaduma resided in her womb, and the remaining five hundred princes were born depending on the impurities of the womb. When those princes reached maturity, while playing in the Paduma lotus lake in the garden, they sat on individual lotus flowers; having mature wisdom, they contemplated the destruction and decay of conditioned things and attained Paccekabodhi-knowledge. The verse clarifying their enlightenment was as follows:

Knowing the impermanence, the destruction and decay,
Of the lotus born from the water, with its petals,
Beautifully bloomed and frequented by swarms of bees,
One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.

Thus, when those five hundred Paccekabuddhas had penetrated and realized Paccekabodhi-knowledge, among those five hundred Paccekabuddhas, a Paccekabuddha named Tagarasikhī entered the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) for seven days in the Nandamūla cave on Mount Gandhamādana. After seven days, having emerged from the attainment of cessation, he came through the air and descended on Mount Isigili. In the morning, having adjusted his lower robe and taking his bowl and robes, he entered the city of Rājagaha for alms. At that time, in the city of Rājagaha, a son of a wealthy merchant was leaving the city with a large retinue to play in the garden. Seeing the Paccekabuddha Tagarasikhī, he thought: "Who is this man wearing dye-stained clothes? He must be a leper; that is why he goes about covering his body with a leper's robe." Thinking thus, he spat, turned his left side toward him, and departed. Referring to that act of departing, it was said: "Suppabuddha the leper, in this very city of Rājagaha... departed."
265:
In that Pali, 'kvāyaṃ' means 'who is this?'. It is spoken with the intent to revile. There is also a Pali reading 'kovāyaṃ'. Regarding the term 'kuṭṭhī' (leper), the merchant's son spoke this as an insult, attributing the disease of leprosy to that venerable one who was not actually a leper. 'Kuṭṭhicīvarena' means with the robe of a leper. Generally, lepers take any old rags to cover their sores and protect themselves from gadflies, mosquitoes, snakes, and scorpions; this is intended to show that he was like that. Alternatively, because he wore rag-robes (paṃsukūla), the many colored patches made him look like a body afflicted with leprosy, and thus he said 'kuṭṭhicīvarena' out of contempt.

'Niṭṭhubhitvā' means having spat. 'Apasavyato karitvā' means that while wise people, upon seeing such a Paccekabuddha, would pay homage and circumambulate him to the right (padakkhiṇa), this man, out of ignorance and disrespect, left him on his left side (making a left-handed turn) and departed. There is also a reading 'apasavyāmato'. 'Tassa kammassa' refers to the result of the evil deed committed by reviling Tagarasikhī Paccekabuddha with the words 'Where is this leper?', spitting, and passing him on the left. 'Niraye paccittha' means he was cooked (burned) by the fires of hell. Some read 'paccitvā nirayagginā'.

'Tasseva kammassa vipākāvasesena' means the karma by which he took rebirth in hell does not give its result in the human world. However, there was that specific intention (cetanā) that arose from his misconduct toward the Paccekabuddha, which became karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (aparāpariyavedanīya). That very intention, through its nature as aparāpariyavedanīya karma, caused him to experience leprosy, poverty, and extreme misery during the course of his life (pavattikāla), even when he had obtained a triple-rooted rebirth (tihetu-paṭisandhi) among humans due to other meritorious deeds. With reference to that similarity in the nature of karma, it is said 'due to the remainder of the result of that karma'. Such usage is seen in the world for similar things, as in the example: 'That very partridge, those very medicines'.

Having thus answered the question asked by that monk, 'Venerable Sir, what is the cause?', the Buddha now speaks the words beginning with 'so tathāgata-ppaveditaṃ' to answer the question previously asked by the monks, 'What is his destination? What is his future state?'. Therein, 'tathāgata-ppaveditaṃ' means the Dhamma taught, declared, and made manifest by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata. 'Āgammā' means having reached or having known by depending on. There is also a reading 'tathāgata-ppavedite dhammavinaye'. 'Saddhaṃ samādiyi' means he firmly took up the two kinds of faith—the preliminary faith based on the Triple Gem and the supramundane faith—thinking, 'The Blessed One is the Fully Enlightened One; the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One; the Saṅgha has practiced well'.
266:
Thinking 'The Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples has practiced well', he firmly took up both kinds of faith: the preliminary faith depending on the Triple Gem and the supramundane faith. He took it up in such a way that it would not need to be taken up again, holding it until the end of existence, and producing it within his own mental continuum. The same method applies to the terms beginning with 'took up virtue' (sīlaṃ samādiyi). 'Sīla' (virtue) refers to the path-virtue and fruition-virtue along with the preliminary virtue. 'Suta' (learning) refers to the two kinds of learning: learning of the scriptures (pariyatti-bāhusacca) and learning of penetration (paṭivedha-bāhusacca). Indeed, even the scriptural teachings were heard, mastered, reflected upon by the mind, and well-penetrated by vision by the disciples for the sake of penetrating the truths at the time of hearing the Dhamma. 'Cāga' (generosity) refers to the relinquishment of the defilements and formations to be abandoned by the first path. Because of that generosity, the noble disciples are liberal in giving, open-handed, and delight in relinquishing. 'Paññā' (wisdom) refers to the path-wisdom and fruition-wisdom along with insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā).

'Kāyassa bhedā' (with the breaking up of the body) means due to the discarding of the clung-to aggregates (upādinnak-khandha). 'Paraṃ maraṇā' (after death) means due to the taking up of new aggregates immediately after that passing away. Alternatively, 'kāyassa bhedā' means the cutting off of the life-faculty. 'Paraṃ maraṇā' means after the death-consciousness (cuti). By the three terms 'sugatiṃ' (happy destination), 'saggaṃ' (heaven), and 'lokaṃ' (world), only the celestial realm is meant. Indeed, that realm is a 'happy destination' (sugati) because it is beautiful with its attainments. It is 'heaven' (sagga) because it is exceedingly excellent with its forms and so on. It is called 'world' (loka) because only happiness is experienced there at all times, or because it is subject to crumbling. 'Upapanno' means he arrived there by way of taking rebirth-linking. 'Sahabyataṃ' means the state of being together. The derivative meaning is: one who exists or dwells together is 'sahabya', meaning one who stands together or lives together. The state of such a one is 'sahabyatā'. 'Atirocati' means he shines and glows, surpassing and outshining others. 'Vaṇṇena' means by the perfection of his appearance. 'Yasasā' means by his retinue. Indeed, just as a man might throw away a broken clay pot smeared with filth and take up a pure gold vessel made of Jambunada gold, adorned with various jewels and entwined with nets of radiant light, so Suppabuddha discarded the aforementioned 'foul corpse' here and, in a single mind-moment, obtained the aforementioned divine state together with a great retinue.

'Knowing this significance' means having known in every aspect the danger in not avoiding evil and the benefit in avoiding it, he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) to clarify that meaning.

The summary of the meaning of that inspired utterance is: Just as a man with sight, possessing physical energy and carrying his body, would avoid uneven places such as precipices, or avoid groups of fierce elephants, horses, snakes, dogs, and bulls...
267:
In this way, in this world of living beings, which is the world of sentient beings, a wise man, knowing his own welfare through his wisdom, should avoid evil and unwholesome misconduct. If he does not avoid it, he would meet with great ruin and destruction, just as this Suppabuddha met with great ruin because he did not avoid evil toward the Paccekabuddha named Tagarasikhī. Alternatively, just as the leper Suppabuddha, having relied on the Dhamma teaching of the Buddha, has now reached a state of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), avoided evil, and attained a noble distinction, so too should another person who desires to attain noble distinction avoid evil.

## The Commentary on the Third Sutta is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Kumāraka Sutta

In the fourth sutta, 'kumārakā' refers to young and youthful persons. In this sutta, 'kumārakā' is intended to mean boys who understand the meaning of what is well-spoken and ill-spoken. These beings are called 'kumārakā' or 'bālā' (children) from the day of their birth until they are fifteen years old. After that, until they are twenty years old, they are called 'yuvāno' (youths).

'Macchake bādhenti' means that in a pond near the road during the summer when the water has dried up, they scoop out the remaining water from the hollows and catch, torment, and kill small fish, thinking, 'We shall cook and eat them.' 'Tenupasaṅkami' means he approached the pond which was a little distance from the road. Why did he approach? He approached to create a sense of familiarity and trust in those boys. In the phrase 'bāyatha vo', the word 'vo' is merely a particle. 'Dukkhassa' is a genitive case used in the sense of the ablative 'dukkhasmā' (from suffering). 'Appiyaṃ vo dukkhaṃ' means he asks, 'Is not the suffering that will arise in your bodies unpleasant and undesirable to you?'

'Etamatthaṃ viditvā' means that having known in every aspect the matter that although these beings do not desire suffering for themselves, by practicing the causes of suffering, they are effectively desiring that suffering. 'Imaṃ udānaṃ' means he uttered this inspired utterance, which has the benefit of prohibiting evil deeds and making clear their faults.

The meaning of that inspired utterance is: O boys, if you do not love or delight in all the suffering that will occur in the realms of woe, or the various kinds of suffering such as short life in the happy realms or misery in the human realm; if you fear that suffering, do not perform evil such as killing living beings, whether openly by not concealing it from others through body or speech, or secretly in private by concealing it and performing unwholesome mental kamma such as covetousness (abhijjhā) at the mind-door, even as small as a grain of dust. If you perform that evil kamma now or in the future, there is no escape for you from that suffering, even if you run away intentionally with the thought, 'The suffering which is the result of that kamma will not follow us who are fleeing from here to there' in the four realms of woe like hell or in the human realm. He shows that it will surely ripen when there is a conjunction of other causes such as destination (gati) and time (kāla). Some also read 'palāyane'; according to the method mentioned, it means when there is going or departing to any place. This meaning should be understood through this verse: 'Not in the sky, nor in the middle of the ocean... [can one escape] evil deeds' (Dhp 127).
268:
...whether by body or speech, such as killing living beings, or by concealing it in private and performing even a tiny bit of evil, unwholesome states such as covetousness (abhijjhā) only at the mind-door. If you do that evil kamma now, or if you do it in the future, there is no liberation or escape for you from that suffering, even if you run away by moving here and there, thinking, 'The suffering which is the result of that kamma will not follow us as we flee from here to there' in the four realms of woe such as hell, or among humans. He shows that it will surely ripen when there is a conjunction of conditions such as destination (gati) and time (kāla). Some also read 'palāyane'; according to the method mentioned, it means when there is going or departing to any place. This meaning should be understood through this verse: 'Not in the sky, nor in the middle of the ocean... [can one escape] evil deeds.'

## The Commentary on the Fourth Sutta is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Uposatha Sutta

In the fifth sutta, 'tadahu' means on that day. In the word 'uposathe', it is called 'uposatha' because [noble ones] dwell practicing on this day. It means they dwell endowed with virtue (sīla) or by fasting (anasana). This word 'uposatha' appears in the sense of virtue (sīla) in passages such as 'I observe the Uposatha endowed with eight factors.' It appears in the sense of Vinaya acts such as the recitation of the Pātimokkha in passages such as 'The Uposatha or the Pavāraṇā.' It appears in the sense of fasting (upavāsa) in passages such as 'The herdsman's Uposatha, the Nigaṇṭhas' Uposatha.' It appears in the sense of a designation (paññatti) in passages such as 'The Naga king named Uposatha.' It appears in the sense of a day in passages such as 'Today is the fifteenth-day Uposatha.' Here too, it should be understood only in the sense of a day. Therefore, 'tadahu-uposathe' means on that day which was the Uposatha day.

'Nisinno hoti' means he was sitting, surrounded by a great assembly of monks, to recite the Ovāda-pātimokkha. Having sat down, while observing the minds of the monks, he saw an individual of poor virtue (dussīla) and remained silent out of compassion for him, thinking, 'If I recite the Pātimokkha while this person is sitting here, his head will split into seven pieces.'
269:
In this context, even though the Buddha had said, "Dawn has risen," referring to the rising of the sun, the Venerable Ānanda requested the Blessed One to recite the Pātimokkha, saying, "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha to the bhikkhus." This request was made because, at that time, the training rule stating, "Bhikkhus, the Uposatha should not be performed on a non-Uposatha day," had not yet been prescribed. Because the Venerable Ānanda requested the recitation of the Pātimokkha three times, the Blessed One, in explaining the reason for not reciting it, did not directly say, "Such and such a person is impure," but instead said, "Ānanda, the assembly is impure." Why did the Blessed One let the time pass through the three watches of the night in that manner? It was because from that day forward, He no longer wished to recite the Ovādapātimokkha and intended to make the matter of that immoral monk manifest.

Regarding "He saw" (addasa): How did He see? While discerning the minds of the bhikkhus in that assembly with His knowledge of encompassing the minds of others (cetopariyañāṇa), He saw the immoral mind of that worthless person (moghapurisa). Since seeing the mind is equivalent to seeing the person endowed with that mind, it is said, "The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna saw that immoral person," and so forth. Just as one who has attained the knowledge of encompassing the minds of others can know the minds of others that will occur within the next seven days in the future, so too can they know them in the past. "Immoral" (dussīla) means without virtue, devoid of virtue. "Evil-natured" (pāpadhamma) means one who, due to being immoral, has a low disposition and a base nature. "Impure" (asuci) means not pure because of being endowed with impure bodily actions and so forth. "Of suspicious conduct" (saṅkassarassamācāra) refers to one whose conduct is such that others, upon seeing some unseemly act, might suspect, "Could this have been done by him?" Alternatively, it refers to one who, upon seeing bhikkhus consulting together on some matter, suspects within himself, "Are these bhikkhus consulting because they know the deed I have done?" and thus his conduct is to be remembered with suspicion.

"Of concealed actions" (paṭicchannakammanta) refers to one whose deeds are hidden because they are shameful and ought to be concealed. "Not a recluse" (asamaṇa) refers to one who, though wearing the loathsome guise of a recluse, is not a true recluse. "Claiming to be a recluse" (samaṇapaṭiñña) refers to one who falsely claims, "I too am a recluse," when being counted in matters such as the taking of voting tickets (salāka). "Not a celibate" (abrahmacārī) refers to one who does not lead the holy life. Seeing other bhikkhus who lead the holy life, well-dressed, well-covered, and carrying their alms bowls, wandering for alms in villages and towns to make a living, he, though not a celibate, behaves in the same manner and makes himself manifest in the Uposatha and other ceremonies...
270:
...as if giving a pledge, "I too am one who leads the holy life," thus he is called "one claiming to be a celibate" (brahmacāripaṭiñña). "Rotten within" (antopūti) means that the corruption of virtue, which is a rotten deed, has entered inside. "Leaking" (avassuta) means being wet from the oozing of defilements such as lust through the six sense doors. "Like refuse" (kasambujāta) means being like rubbish because of the arising of defilements such as lust, and because he is to be discarded by the virtuous. "Sitting in the midst of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha" (bhikkhusaṅghassa majjhe nisinnaṃ) means sitting in the middle of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha as if he were a member of the Saṅgha. "You are seen" (diṭṭhosi) means that the Blessed One saw that this person was not a monk of natural status (pakatatta). Because he was seen in this way, "There is no communion (saṃvāsa) for you, such as performing communal acts, together with the bhikkhus." Since there is no such communion for you, "Friend, get up"—thus the connection of the words in this context should be understood.

Although it is said many times that "that person remained silent even for the third time," the Elder [Moggallāna] remained silent with the intention, "He will leave on his own out of weariness," or "Now I shall know the practice of these bhikkhus." "Taking by the arm" (bāhāyaṃ gahetvā) means that since the Blessed One and I have seen him as he truly is, and he does not get up even though told "Get up" three times, [the Elder] thought, "Now is the time to expel him; let there not be an obstacle to the Saṅgha's Uposatha," and thus he took him by the arm. "Leading out from the outer gatehouse" (bahidvārakoṭṭhakā nikkhāmetvā) means leading him out from the gatehouse hall. The word "outside" (bahi) indicates the place of exit. Alternatively, it means leading him out from the outer gatehouse and not from the inner gatehouse; in both cases, it means putting him outside the monastery. "Applying the bolt and the crossbar" (sūcighaṭikaṃ datvā) means inserting the small door-pin and the large crossbar, effectively closing the door-leaf well. "Even until being taken by the arm" (yāva bāhāgahaṇāpi nāma) shows that it is a wonder that this worthless person waited until he was taken by the arm, whereas he should have left as soon as he heard the words, "Ananda, the assembly is impure." This should be understood as a wonder that is blameworthy.

Then the Blessed One thought: "Now the Bhikkhu Saṅgha is like a mass of scum (abbudajāta); impure persons come to the Uposatha. Tathāgatas do not perform the Uposatha or recite the Pātimokkha in an impure assembly. If the Pātimokkha is not recited, the Saṅgha's Uposatha will be interrupted. What if, from now on, I allow only the bhikkhus themselves to recite the Pātimokkha?" Having thought thus, He allowed only the bhikkhus themselves to recite the Pātimokkha. Therefore, it is said: "Then the Blessed One... [said]... 'Bhikkhus, you yourselves should recite the Pātimokkha.'"
271:
In that text, "na dānāhaṃ" means "Now I shall no longer perform the Uposatha, I shall no longer recite the Pātimokkha." The letter "na" (not) should be understood as connected to each action individually. There are two types of Pātimokkha: the Āṇāpātimokkha (Pātimokkha of Authority) and the Ovādapātimokkha (Pātimokkha of Exhortation). Among these, the Pātimokkha beginning with "Suṇātu me, bhante" is called the Āṇāpātimokkha. This Āṇāpātimokkha is recited only by the disciples; the Buddhas do not recite it. It is recited once every fortnight. The three verses beginning with "Khantī paramaṃ... Sabba-pāpassa akaraṇaṃ... Anūpavādo anūpaghāto... Etaṃ buddhāna sāsanaṃ" are called the Ovādapātimokkha. This Ovādapātimokkha is recited only by the Buddhas; the disciples do not recite it. They recite it once every six years. During the lifetime of long-lived Buddhas, only this recitation of the Ovādapātimokkha exists. For short-lived Buddhas, however, it exists only during the first period of enlightenment (paṭhamabodhi). After that, the other, the Āṇāpātimokkha, is recited by the bhikkhus; the Buddhas do not recite it. Therefore, our Blessed One also recited the Ovādapātimokkha for about twenty years, and then, seeing this obstacle, he did not recite it thereafter. "Aṭṭhānaṃ" means it is not a cause. "Anavakāso" is a synonym for that same word "aṭṭhānaṃ." Just as a cause is called "ṭhāna" (place/ground) because the effect stands depending on that cause, it is also called "anavakāso."

The word "yaṃ" refers to the action and should be applied according to the method mentioned below.

"Bhikkhus, there are these eight wonderful and marvelous qualities in the Great Ocean"—what is the connection here? The non-recitation of the Pātimokkha in an impure assembly is a wonderful and marvelous thing in this Dispensation. Wishing to explain this wonderful quality along with seven other wonderful and marvelous qualities, the Teacher first spoke the words beginning with "Bhikkhus, there are these eight wonderful and marvelous qualities in the Great Ocean," intending to show the eight wonderful and marvelous qualities in the Great Ocean as a simile.

They are called "Asuras" because they do not shine or look beautiful like the natural devas. Alternatively, they are called "Asuras" because they are the opponents of the devas called Suras. This refers to Vepacitti Asura, Pahārāda Asura, and so on. Their realm is situated at the lower part of Mount Sineru. When they enter or leave that realm, they create pavilions and such at the foot of Mount Sineru and enjoy themselves greatly while playing. Their delight in the Great Ocean is due to seeing these virtues; thus, it is said, "Whenever the Asuras see the Great Ocean, they take delight in it." Here, "abhiramanti" means they find delight and live without weariness.

"Anupubbaninno" and the other terms are all synonyms for the state of being gradually slanting. "Na āyatakeneva papāto" means there is no steep precipice from the very beginning like a great pit with a sheer cliff. In fact, the Great Ocean exists with a gradual slope from the shore, deepening by a finger-breadth, two finger-breadths, a cubit, a fathom, an usabha, and so on.
272:
It is not a steep precipice from the very beginning like a great pit with a sheer cliff. It is shown that the Great Ocean, starting from the shore, becomes gradually deeper—by a finger-breadth, two finger-breadths, a span, a cubit, a yaṭṭhi, an usabha, a half-gāvuta, a gāvuta, a half-yojana, a yojana, and so on—until it reaches a depth of eighty-four thousand yojanas at the base of Mount Sineru.

"Ṭhitadhammo" means having a stable nature, a nature that remains constant. "Na matena kuṇapena saṃvasati" means it does not remain together with the carcass of any animal such as an elephant or a horse. "Tīraṃ vāheti" means it carries [them] to the shore. "Thalaṃ ussāreti" means it casts [them] onto the dry land by the striking of the waves, as if picking them up by hand and throwing them. "Gangā Yamunā" refers to the river that emerges from the southern mouth of Lake Anotatta; where it flows as five streams, it is known by five names such as the Gangā.

In this context, here is the account of the origin of these rivers from the beginning: This Jambudīpa is ten thousand yojanas in extent. Within it, an area of four thousand yojanas is covered by water and is known as the ocean. Humans live in an area of three thousand yojanas. The king of mountains, Himavanta, stands in an area of three thousand yojanas. That mountain is five hundred yojanas in height, adorned with eighty-four thousand peaks, and is made beautiful by five hundred small rivers flowing all around. In that Himavanta mountain, there are seven great lakes: Lake Anotatta, Lake Kaṇṇamuṇḍa, Lake Rathakāra, Lake Chaddanta, Lake Kuṇāla, Lake Mandākinī, and Lake Sīhapapāta, which are fifty yojanas in length, breadth, and depth, and one hundred and fifty yojanas in circumference.

Among those great lakes, Lake Anotatta is surrounded by these five mountain peaks: Sudassana peak, Cittakūṭa peak, Kāḷakūṭa peak, Gandhamādana peak, and Kelāsa peak. Among those mountains, Sudassana peak is made of gold, is three hundred yojanas high, curves inward, and is shaped like a crow's beak. That mountain stands covering Lake Anotatta itself. Cittakūṭa peak is made of the seven kinds of gems. Kāḷakūṭa peak is made of collyrium stone. Gandhamādana peak is made of masāragalla stone and is the color of green gram inside. That mountain is abundant with these ten kinds of fragrances: fragrance of roots, fragrance of heartwood, fragrance of softwood, fragrance of bark, fragrance of peel, fragrance of trunk, fragrance of resin, fragrance of flowers, fragrance of fruits, and fragrance of leaves. It is covered with various kinds of medicinal plants and stands glowing like burning embers on the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight. Kelāsa peak is made of silver. All these mountains also...
273:
All those mountains have the same height and shape as Mount Sudassana, and they stand covering Lake Anotatta. In that Lake Anotatta, rain falls due to the power of the devas and the power of the nāgas, and rivers also flow into it. All those waters enter only Lake Anotatta. When the moon and the sun travel along their southern or northern courses, they cast their light into Lake Anotatta through the mountain passes. When they travel directly above, they cannot cast their light. For that reason, the name 'Anotatta' (The Unheated) became well-known for that lake.

In that Lake Anotatta, there are delightful stairways and stone slabs made of gems. There are clear waters, free from fish, turtles, and the like, resembling crystal and devoid of impurities. There are also bathing places created by the kamma of the beings worthy of using those waters. In that lake, the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, powerful disciples, and sages perform their bathing and other activities. Devas, yakkhas, and others also play in the water.

On the four sides of Lake Anotatta, there are four outlets for the water: the Lion's Mouth, the Elephant's Mouth, the Horse's Mouth, and the Bull's Mouth. From these mouths, four rivers flow. On the banks of the river that issues from the Lion's Mouth, lion kings (kesara-sīha) are very numerous. Similarly, on the banks of the rivers issuing from the Elephant's Mouth and the others, elephants, horses, and bulls are very numerous. The river that issues from the eastern direction circumambulates Lake Anotatta three times to the right and, without approaching the other three rivers, travels through the Eastern Himavanta by a path not frequented by humans and enters the Great Ocean. The rivers issuing from the western and northern directions likewise circumambulate to the right and travel through the Western Himavanta and Northern Himavanta respectively by paths not frequented by humans and enter the Great Ocean.

However, the river that issues from the southern direction circumambulates the lake three times to the right and travels directly southwards on a stone surface for sixty leagues. Then, striking a mountain and rising upwards, it becomes a water column three gāvutas in circumference, travels through the sky for sixty leagues, and falls onto a stone slab named Tiyaggala. That stone slab is broken by the force of the water column. At that place of falling, a lake named Tiyaggala, fifty leagues in size, is formed. Breaking the bank of that lake, the water enters the stone and travels for sixty leagues. From there, it breaks through the solid earth and travels through a tunnel for sixty leagues. Then, striking the transverse mountain named Viñjha, it splits into five streams, like the five fingers on a palm, and flows forth.

In the place where that river travels circumambulating Lake Anotatta three times, it is called the 'Āvaṭṭagaṅgā'. In the place where it travels directly on the stone surface for sixty leagues, it is called the 'Kaṇhagaṅgā'.
274:
In the place where it travels through the sky for sixty leagues, it is called the 'Ākāsagaṅgā'. The river that stays in the fifty-league expanse at the Tiyaggala stone slab is called the 'Tiyaggaḷapokkharaṇī'. In the place where it breaks the bank, enters the stone, and travels for sixty leagues, it is called the 'Bahalagaṅgā'. In the place where it travels through the tunnel for sixty leagues, it is called the 'Umangagaṅgā'. In the place where it strikes the transverse mountain named Viñjha and flows as five streams, it is known by five names: Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Aciravatī, Sarabhū, and Mahī. Thus, it should be understood that these five great rivers flow from the Himavanta.

In this context, words such as 'Nadī' and 'Ninnagā' refer to the lineage (gotta) of those rivers. Words such as 'Gaṅgā' and 'Yamunā' refer to their names (nāma). 'Savantiyo' refers to all rivers, large or small, that flow along. 'Appentī' means they cling to or descend into. 'Dhārā' refers to the streams of rainwater. 'Pūrattaṃ' means the state of being full. It is the nature of the Great Ocean that one cannot say, 'At this time, the rain is scarce, so we shall catch fish and turtles with nets,' or 'At this time, the rain is very heavy, so we can no longer find a place to stretch our backs (to rest).' This is because, since the beginning of the aeon, the water that stands touching the girdle of Mount Sineru after raining does not recede downwards even by a finger's breadth, nor does it increase upwards.

'Ekaraso' means having a single taste unmixed with other tastes. 'Muttā' refers to various kinds of pearls, categorized by small, large, round, long, and so on. 'Maṇī' refers to various kinds of gems, categorized by red, blue, and so on. 'Veḷuriyo' refers to various kinds of beryl (cat's eye) categorized by shapes such as the color of ripe bamboo or the color of the sirīsa flower. 'Saṅkho' refers to various kinds of conch shells, such as those that spiral to the right, those with red bellies, and those used for blowing. 'Silā' refers to various kinds of stones, categorized by colors such as white, black, or the color of green gram. 'Pavāဠံ' refers to various kinds of coral, categorized by small, large, light red, deep red, and so on. 'Lohitaṅgo' refers to various kinds of rubies, such as the padumarāga. 'Masāragallaṃ' refers to a variegated gem (kabaramaṇi). It is also called 'Cittaphalika'.

'Mahataṃ bhūtānaṃ' means of beings with large bodies. There are three types of fish: Timi, Timingala, and others. A fish capable of swallowing a Timi fish is called a 'Timingala'. A fish capable of swallowing both the Timi and the Timingala is called a 'Timitimingala'. 'Nāgā' refers to the nāgas living on the surface of the waves as well as the celestial nāgas living in mansions.
275:
"Evameva kho" means: Although the Teacher is able to analyze and show sixteen, thirty-two, or even more wonderful and marvelous things in this Dispensation, at that time, wishing to analyze and show only eight things to be compared in accordance with the eight things taken as similes, He said: "Monks, just so, there are eight wonderful and marvelous things in this Dhamma-Vinaya," and so forth.

In that text, by "gradual training" (anupubbasikkhā), the three trainings are included. By "gradual action" (anupubbakiriyā), the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) are included. By "gradual practice" (anupubpapaṭipadā), the seven contemplations (anupassanā), the eighteen great insights (mahāvipassanā), the thirty-eight classifications of objects (ārammaṇavibhatti), and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma) are included. "There is no penetration of final knowledge all at once" (na āyatakeneva aññāpaṭivedho) means that there is no such thing as the penetration of Arahantship without first fulfilling virtue and so forth, like a frog jumping; rather, the attainment of Arahantship occurs only after fulfilling virtue, concentration, and wisdom in due order.

"My disciples" (mama sāvakā) is said with reference to the Noble Ones, such as stream-enterers and so forth. "Does not dwell with" (na saṃvasati) means not performing communal acts such as the Uposatha and so forth together. "Expelled" (ukkhipati) means removed. "Only in a distant place" (ārakāva) means in a very far-off place.

"For that reason, there is no depletion or fullness of the Nibbāna element" means that even during the incalculable aeons when Buddhas do not arise and not a single being can attain Parinibbāna, it cannot be said at that time that "the Nibbāna element is empty." On the other hand, during the time of a Buddha, when incalculable beings realize the Deathless in a single assembly, it cannot be said then that "the Nibbāna element has become full."

"Taste of liberation" (vimuttirasa) is the taste of being liberated from defilements. Indeed, the entire fulfillment of the Dispensation is for the sake of the mind's liberation from the taints (āsava) through non-clinging.

"Jewels" (ratanāni) are called jewels in the sense of producing delight (rati). When things such as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) are developed, they produce no small amount of rapture and joy even in the preliminary stage, let alone in the later stage.

For it is said:
"Whenever one contemplates the rise and fall of the aggregates,
One gains rapture and joy; for those who know, that is the Deathless."

The rapture and joy based on worldly jewels is not worth even a sixteenth part of the rapture and joy produced by these factors of enlightenment; this meaning has been shown below. Furthermore—
276:
"It is called a 'jewel' (ratana) because it is respected, of great value, incomparable, rare to see, and the requisite of beings of superior merit."

If something is called a jewel because of being respected and so on, then the nature of a jewel truly exists only in the factors of enlightenment such as the foundations of mindfulness. Indeed, it is through the power of these factors of enlightenment that disciples attain the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvakapāramī-ñāṇa), Paccekabuddhas attain the knowledge of private enlightenment (paccekabodhi-ñāṇa), and Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas attain Supreme Enlightenment (sammāsambodhi); thus, they are the proximate cause (āsannakāraṇa). Supporting conditions (upanissaya) such as giving (dāna) and so on are merely remote causes (paramparakāraṇa). Thus, the nature of being a jewel is most excellent in the factors of enlightenment, both in the sense of producing delight and in the sense of being respected and so on. Therefore, it was said: "Among them, these are the jewels, namely, the four foundations of mindfulness," and so forth.

In the term "satipaṭṭhāna," "paṭṭhāna" means establishing by plunging into the object. Mindfulness itself is the establishing; thus, it is "satipaṭṭhāna." Because the object is fourfold as body and so on, it is said "the four foundations of mindfulness." Indeed, they are analyzed as contemplation of the body and so on because they abandon the perceptions of beauty, happiness, permanence, and self in the body, feelings, mind, and mental objects, and instead grasp the nature of foulness, suffering, impermanence, and non-self.

They strive well by means of this [energy], or it itself strives well; or because it is a praised and excellent striving, it is called "sammappadhāna" (right exertion). Or, because it makes the state of striving right for a person, it is "sammappadhāna." This is a designation for energy (vīriya). That [energy] is said to be "the four right exertions" by performing four tasks: the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states, the abandoning of arisen unwholesome states, the arising of unarisen wholesome states, and the development of arisen wholesome states.

It is called "iddhi" because it succeeds (ijjhati); the meaning is that it is accomplished or produced. Or, beings succeed, prosper, and reach excellence by means of this; thus, it is "iddhi." According to the first meaning, the "iddhi" itself is the base (pāda); thus, "iddhipāda" means a constituent of success. According to the second meaning, it is the base, foundation, or means of attainment for success; thus, it is "iddhipāda." Indeed, by means of this, they reach and attain the success known as higher and higher distinction. Since this "iddhipāda" is brought into existence by making the four predominant factors such as desire (chanda) and so on the leaders and chiefs, it is said "the four bases of power."

"The five faculties" (pañcindriyāni) are the five faculties such as faith and so on. Among them, the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) is so called because it overcomes lack of faith and exercises lordship in the characteristic of decision (adhimokkha). The faculty of energy (vīriyindriya) overcomes laziness and...
277:
(The energy faculty) overcomes laziness and is characterized by exertion (paggaha); (the mindfulness faculty) overcomes forgetfulness and is characterized by presence (upaṭṭhāna); (the concentration faculty) overcomes distraction and is characterized by non-distraction (avikkhepa); (the wisdom faculty) overcomes ignorance and is characterized by seeing (dassana). It is called the wisdom faculty (paññindriya) because it exercises dominance.

These five (faculties) themselves are to be known as "powers (bala)" in the sense of being unshakable by faithlessness and so on, and in the sense of being firm in the associated mental states.

"Seven factors of enlightenment (sattabojjhaṅga)" means they are factors of enlightenment (bodhi, i.e., the knowledge of the path of Arahantship), or they are factors of the one who has enlightenment. That harmony of states (dhamma-sāmaggī) known as mindfulness, investigation of states, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity, which arises at the moment of the supramundane path, is the opposite of many dangers such as sluggishness, agitation, non-exertion, indulgence in sensual pleasures, self-mortification, the view of annihilation, and the view of eternalism. Through this harmony of states, the noble disciple wakes up from the sleep of defilements, or penetrates the Four Noble Truths, or realizes Nibbāna itself; therefore, it is called "enlightenment (bodhi)." Because they are factors of that enlightenment consisting of the harmony of states, they are "factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga)," like the factors of jhāna or the factors of the path. Alternatively, the noble disciple is called "enlightenment (bodhi)" because he knows through the aforementioned harmony of states; because they are factors of that (noble disciple who is) enlightenment, they are "factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga)," like the parts of an army or the parts of a chariot. Thus the ancient teachers said: "The factors of the person who knows (the Four Noble Truths) are the factors of enlightenment." The meaning of the factors of enlightenment should also be understood in the sense that "they lead to enlightenment."
