"The Noble Eightfold Path" is "noble (ariya)" because it is far from the defilements to be abandoned by each respective path, because it makes one noble, and because it causes the attainment of the noble fruit. It is "eightfold (aṭṭhaṅgika)" because it has eight factors such as right view, or because it is a collection of eight factors. It is called "path (magga)" because it goes along killing the defilements, because it is sought by those desiring Nibbāna, or because it seeks Nibbāna itself. In this way, the detailed explanation of the meanings of the foundations of mindfulness and so on should be understood.

"Stream-enterer (sotāpanna)" means one who has reached and stands in the stream (sota) known as the path; the meaning is one who stands in the fruit of stream-entry. "One practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry" means one standing in the first path who is practicing to personally realize the fruit of stream-entry; he is also called "the eighth person (aṭṭhamaka)." "Once-returner (sakadāgāmī)" is a person standing in the second fruit who has the nature of coming to this human world only once more by way of rebirth. "Non-returner (anāgāmī)" is one who has the nature of not returning to the sense world by way of rebirth...
278:
He is a person established in the third fruit (Anāgāmiphala). The classification of noble persons (ariya-puggala) such as faith-followers (saddhānusārī), Dhamma-followers (dhammānusārī), and one-seeders (ekabījī) is simply a division of these same noble persons. The rest is as previously explained. "Having known this matter" means having known the fact that in his Dispensation (Sāsana), there is no living together with an immoral person who is like a rotting corpse. "This inspired utterance" refers to the inspired utterance (udāna) that explains the reason for distinguishing between those who are unfit to live with and those who are fit to live with.

In that inspired utterance, "Rain pours down heavily on what is covered" means that a monk who conceals an offense (āpatti) he has committed will commit another new offense; thereafter, the rain of offenses and the rain of defilements (kilesa) pour down excessively. "Rain does not pour down on what is open" means that a monk who has committed an offense and does not conceal it, but opens it up, reveals it to his fellow practitioners, and atones for it, confesses it, and rises from it according to the Dhamma and Vinaya, does not commit another new offense. Because of that opening up, the rain of further offenses and the rain of defilements do not pour down on him. Since this is so, one should open up and reveal a concealed offense. "When this is done, it does not rain excessively" means that when the offense is thus revealed, the rain of defilements does not pour down on or drench the individual self of the person who committed the offense. In this way, that person, undrenched by defilements, becomes one of pure virtue and concentrated mind. By undertaking and contemplating insight (vipassanā), he gradually reaches Nibbāna. This is the meaning.

## The commentary on the fifth sutta is finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Soṇa Sutta

In the sixth sutta, "among the Avantis" means in the Avanti country. "In the city of Kuraraghara" means in the city of that name. "On Mount Pavatta" means on the mountain named Pavatta. Some also read it as "Mount Papāta." "The lay follower Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa" means he was named Soṇa by name; he was a lay follower (upāsaka) because he declared his status as a lay follower through the three refuges; he was known as "Kuṭikaṇṇa" although he should have been called "Koṭikaṇṇa" because he wore an ear-ornament worth ten million (koṭi). The meaning is that he was not Sukhumāla Soṇa.
279:
## Adhippāyo (Explanation)
This Soṇa Upāsaka, having heard the Dhamma from the Venerable Mahākaccāyana Thera, became very confident in the Dispensation (Sāsana) and established himself in the Three Refuges and the Precepts. He built a monastery at a place endowed with shade and water on Mount Pavatta, invited the Thera to reside there, and served him with the four requisites. Therefore, it is stated in the Pali text: "He was an attendant of the Venerable Mahākaccāyana."

That lay devotee used to go to pay respects to the Thera from time to time. The Thera also preached the Dhamma to him. Having heard that Dhamma, he lived with great spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and made an effort in the practice of the Dhamma. Once, while traveling to the city of Ujjenī with a caravan for trade, the caravan halted in a forest along the way. During the night, fearing the crowd of people, he moved to a suitable place and fell asleep. The caravan departed at dawn, and no one woke Soṇa; they all dispersed and left. When he woke up at daybreak and saw no one, he followed the caravan's tracks quickly and reached a banyan tree.

There, he saw a man with a huge body and a terrifying appearance, eating his own flesh that was falling off from his bones. He asked, "Who are you?" The man replied, "Venerable sir, I am a hungry ghost (peta)." When asked, "Why are you doing this?", he said, "It is because of my own past evil deeds." When asked again, "What deed was that?", he replied, "In a past life, I was a dishonest merchant living in the city of Bhārukaccha. I cheated others of their property and consumed it. When monks came for alms, I insulted them, saying, 'Eat your own flesh!' Because of that deed, I am now experiencing this suffering." Hearing those words, Soṇa felt extreme shock and spiritual urgency (saṃvega).

Continuing from there, he saw two young petas with dark blood flowing from their mouths and asked them in the same way. They also told him about their deeds. It is said that when they were young and making a living through the perfume trade in the city of Bhārukaccha, their mother invited Arahants and offered them food. They went home and insulted her, saying, "Why do you give our property to the monks? May dark blood flow from the mouths of the monks who eat the food given by you!" Because of that deed, they suffered in hell, and due to the remaining result (vipāka) of that deed, they were reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts and are now experiencing such suffering. Hearing those words, Soṇa also felt great spiritual urgency (saṃvega).
280:
That Soṇa went to the city of Ujjenī, completed his business, and returned to the city of Kururaghara. He approached the Venerable Mahākaccāyana Thera, exchanged pleasantries, and then informed the Thera about the matter of those hungry ghosts. The Thera also preached the Dhamma to him, clarifying the disadvantages of the round of rebirth (saṃsāra) and the benefits of liberation from it. Soṇa paid homage to the Thera, returned home, ate his evening meal, and went to bed. After sleeping for only a short while, he woke up and sat on his bed, beginning to reflect on the Dhamma as he had heard it. As he reflected on that Dhamma and remembered the state of those hungry ghosts, the suffering of saṃsāra appeared to him as extremely terrifying, and his mind inclined toward ordination. When the night turned to dawn, Soṇa performed his bodily hygiene, approached the Thera, informed him of his intention, and requested ordination. Therefore, it is said (in the Pali text): "Then the lay devotee Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa, having gone into seclusion... 'Venerable Mahākaccāyana, may the venerable one please ordain me.'"

In that Pali text, the brief meaning of the words beginning with "yathā yathā" is as follows: In whatever way the Venerable Mahākaccāyana Thera preaches, teaches, prescribes, establishes, reveals, analyzes, clarifies, and demonstrates the Dhamma—to me, who investigates and reflects in those various ways, this thought occurs: "There is this holy life (brahmacariya) consisting of the three trainings (sikkhā); one should practice this holy life perfectly and completely until the final consciousness, without breaking or breaching it even for a single day. One should practice it purely from all sides until the final consciousness, without staining it with the defilement of kileas even for a single day." "Sankhalikhitaṃ" means it should be practiced purely, like a polished conch shell. For me, living in the midst of people, it is not easy to practice this holy life perfectly and completely... It would be good if I were to shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron-dyed robes, leave the household life, and enter the state of homelessness. The work of those living in a house, such as farming and trading, is called "agāriya" (household life). Since that work does not exist in the state of a monk, ordination is called "anagāriya" (homelessness). The meaning is: "I shall enter, approach, and properly practice that state of homelessness (anagāriya)."

Thus, Soṇa Upāsaka informed the Thera of what he had contemplated in seclusion and, desiring to practice that holy life, said, "Venerable Mahākaccāyana, may the venerable one please ordain me." The Thera, however, considering whether Soṇa's wisdom was mature or not, and waiting for the maturity of his wisdom, first discouraged his desire for ordination with the words "Dukkaraṃ kho" (It is difficult), and so on. In that Pali text, "kataṃ kataṃ" means eating only one meal a day, living in seclusion, being free from defilements, and practicing the holy life. Thus, with the timely meal (kālabhojana) and...
281:
Mahākaccāyana Thera, having examined the maturity of Soṇa's wisdom and waiting for the right time, initially discouraged his desire to go forth, saying, "It is very difficult," and so on.

In that context, "eating one meal" refers to the abstinence from eating at the wrong time (vikālabhojana-virati), as taught in the words: "He becomes one who eats one meal, abstaining at night, abstaining from eating at the wrong time." "Sleeping alone" means sleeping without a companion. Here, using "sleeping" as the primary example, it is intended to show physical seclusion (kāyaviveka) in the four postures as taught in the method: "He stands alone, he walks alone, he sits alone," and so on; it does not mean merely sleeping alone. "Holy life" (brahmacariya) refers to the holy life of abstaining from sexual intercourse, or the holy life of the Dispensation known as the practice of the three trainings (sikkhāttaya). The word "Ingha" is an indeclinable used in the sense of urging. "Right there" means only at home. "Devote yourself to the teaching of the Buddhas" means to practice the five, eight, or ten precepts, categorized as permanent virtue (niccasīla), observance virtue (uposathasīla), etc., and the corresponding development of concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (paññā). This is indeed what is called the Buddha's Dispensation that a lay follower (upāsaka) should practice in the preliminary stage. Therefore, he said: "Eating one meal at the appropriate time, sleeping alone, and practicing the holy life."

In that context, "at the appropriate time" (kālayutta) means associated with the times known as the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days, and the extraordinary fortnight (pāṭihāriyapakkha); or it means a time that is suitable, possible, and appropriate for you to practice during the aforementioned times; it does not mean going forth at all times. All these words were spoken because Soṇa's wisdom was not yet mature and because of the difficulty of abandoning sensual pleasures, wishing him to become fit for right practice, not because of a genuine desire to prevent his wish to go forth. "Preparation for going forth" (pabbajjābhisaṅkhāra) means the beginning and effort to go forth. "It subsided" means it calmed down because the faculties were not yet mature and the sense of urgency (saṃvega) was not yet intense. Although his desire to go forth subsided, he followed the procedure instructed by the Thera, approaching and attending on the Thera from time to time to listen to the Dhamma. For that Soṇa, the desire to go forth arose a second time in the same manner, and he informed the Thera. The Thera rejected it a second time as well. But on the third occasion, knowing the maturity of his wisdom, the Thera considered, "Now it is time to ordain him," and gave him the going forth (pabbajjā). After three years had passed since his going forth, the Thera searched for and gathered a group [of monks] and gave him the higher ordination (upasampadā). Referring to this, it was said: "A second time Soṇa... (pe) ...gave him higher ordination."

In that Pali, "having few monks" means there were only a few monks. At that time, it is said that monks mostly lived only in the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa). Therefore, in that region, only a few [monks]...
282:
...existed, and they lived separately, such as one in one town and two in another. "Kicchena" means with difficulty. "Kasirena" means with hardship (through great effort). "Tato tato" means from those various villages and towns.

Indeed, when the Thera brought a few monks and was bringing others, those who had arrived first departed due to some business. After waiting for some time, when those monks were brought back again, the others departed. Thus, because of the repeated bringing of monks, it took a long time for the assembly of the Saṅgha to be formed. At that time, Mahākaccāyana Thera lived alone.

"Having assembled a group of ten monks" means that at that time, the Blessed One had authorized higher ordination (upasampadā) even in the border regions (paccantadesa) only with a group of ten monks. It was because of this reason that, requested by the Thera, the Blessed One later authorized higher ordination in the border regions with a group of five monks. Therefore, it is stated in the Pali: "For three years... (pe) ...having assembled."

"One who has spent the Rains" (vassaṃvuṭṭhassa) refers to one who, after receiving higher ordination, has entered and completed the first Rains Retreat. "Such and such" (īdiso ca īdiso ca) means of such a nature and of such a nature; it means "I have heard of that Blessed One as being endowed with such perfection of the form-body (rūpakāya) and such perfection of the Dhamma-body (dhammakāya)." "I have not seen that Blessed One face to face" – by these words, it is shown that the Venerable Soṇa had a desire to see the Blessed One with the faith of a worldling (puthujjana).

Later, however, while staying in the same Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi) with the Teacher, being requested by the Teacher at dawn, he respectfully took to heart the sixteen Aṭṭhakavaggas in the presence of the Teacher, and having well-applied his mind to the whole, he recited them as one who experiences the meaning and the Dhamma. While reciting, based on the joy (pāmojja) associated with the Dhamma and with a concentrated mind, at the conclusion of the melodic recitation (sarabhañña), he established insight (vipassanā), and by contemplating conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra), he gradually reached Arahantship. It is said that for the sake of this Arahantship, the Blessed One himself commanded him to stay in the same Fragrant Chamber.

Some teachers, however, say: "I have not seen that Blessed One face to face" refers only to seeing the physical body (rūpakāya). In truth, the Venerable Soṇa, right after going forth, took a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) from the Thera and, while striving and exerting himself, became a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) while still a novice. After receiving higher ordination, he thought, "Even lay followers can be Stream-enterers; I too am a Stream-enterer; what is special about this?" and developed insight for the higher paths. Within that very Rains Retreat, he became an Arahant endowed with the six supernormal knowledges (chaḷabhiññā) and performed the invitation (pavāraṇā) with pure invitation. By seeing the Noble Truths, one is said to see the Dhamma-body of the Blessed One.
283:
He performed the Pavāraṇā with a pure Pavāraṇā. Indeed, by seeing the Noble Truths, one is said to have seen the Dhamma-body (Dhammakāya) of the Blessed One. For it has been said: "Vakkali, he who sees the Dhamma sees me; he who sees me sees the Dhamma" (Saṃ. Ni. 3.87). Therefore, for that elder, the seeing of the Dhamma-body had already been accomplished previously. However, it is said that after performing the Pavāraṇā, he had a desire to see the form-body (Rūpakāya).

There is also a reading: "Sace maṃ upajjhāyo anujānāti" (If my preceptor permits me). However, they write "Bhante" (Venerable Sir). Likewise, there is a reading: "Sādhu sādhu, āvuso Soṇa, gaccha tvaṃ, āvuso Soṇā" (Excellent, excellent, friend Soṇa, you may go, friend Soṇa). The word "Āvuso" (friend) is not present in some palm-leaf manuscripts. Similarly, there is a reading: "Evamāvuso'ti kho āyasmā Soṇo". Indeed, during the lifetime of the Blessed One, it was the custom for monks to address one another as "Āvuso". The meaning of the words beginning with "Bhagavantaṃ pāsādikaṃ" has already been explained below.

"Kacci bhikkhu khamanīyaṃ" means: Monk, is this body-machine of yours, with its four wheels and nine openings, bearable? Is it possible to endure, to bear, and to maintain it? Does the burden of suffering not overwhelm you? "Kacci yāpanīyaṃ" means: Is it possible to keep going and move about in various duties? This shows the absence of any obstacles. "Kacci'si appakilamathena" means: Have you come this long distance without fatigue?

"Etadahosi" refers to the thought that occurred to the Venerable Ānanda, who was recollecting the custom of the Buddhas, which will now be mentioned starting with "Yassa kho maṃ Bhagavā". "Ekavihāre" means in a single fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭi). Indeed, here the fragrant chamber is intended by the word "vihāra". "Vatthuṃ" means to dwell.

Regarding the words "Nisajjāya vītināmetvā": Since the Blessed One, wishing to extend a friendly welcome to the Venerable Soṇa by entering meditative attainments, entered all the attainments common to disciples in direct and reverse order, and entered the dwelling after much of the night had passed... (pe)... the Venerable Soṇa also, knowing the Blessed One's intention, entered all those attainments in accordance with that and entered the dwelling after much of the night had passed... (pe)... so say some teachers. And after entering...
284:
Having been permitted by the Blessed One, he made a screen with his robe and spent the night sitting at the feet of the Blessed One. "Ajjhesi" means he commanded (or requested). "Paṭibhātu taṃ bhikkhu dhammo bhāsituṃ" means: "Monk, may the Dhamma to be spoken occur to you (may it appear before your eye of wisdom); speak the Dhamma as you have heard it, as you have mastered it."

"Soḷasa aṭṭhakavaggikāni" refers to the sixteen discourses belonging to the Aṭṭhakavagga, such as the Kāmasutta. "Sarena abhaṇi" means he spoke with the sound of reciting the suttas; the meaning is that he spoke by way of melodic recitation (sarabhañña). "Sarabhaññapariyosāne" means at the conclusion of the recitation. "Suggahitāni" means they were well-learned. "Sumanasikatāni" means they were well-attended to in the mind. Some people, even if they learn well at the time of learning, later, when attending to it by way of recitation and so on, misplace the consonants or cause the words to be reversed; this elder did not do so. This elder attended to them well, exactly as they were learned. Therefore, it is said: "Sumanasikatāni means well-attended to in the mind." "Sūpadhāritāni" means they were well-retained even in terms of meaning. Only when the meaning is well-retained can the Pali text be recited correctly.

"Kalyāṇiyāsi vācāya samannāgato" means he was endowed with gracious speech, like that of urbanites, which is complete in words and consonants and rounded by speaking according to the rules of soft and hard sounds (sithila and dhanita). "Vissaṭṭhāya" means with distinct speech. By this, his fluency in recitation is shown. "Anelagaḷāya" means "elā" refers to a fault; because it does not flow with that fault, it is "anelagaḷā". The meaning is with such faultless speech. Alternatively, "anelagaḷāya" means being faultless and fluent, having words and consonants that are faultless and not slurred, and having words and consonants that are not deficient. This is true. That is why the Blessed One placed that elder in the foremost position (etadagga), saying: "Monks, among my monk disciples who are speakers of beautiful words, Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa is the foremost" (A. Ni. 1.206). "Atthassa viññāpaniyā" means capable of making the intended meaning known.

"Kativasso" (How many years/vassa): It is said that he was in the third stage of middle age and, being endowed with a dignified appearance, he appeared to others as if he had been ordained for a very long time. Some teachers say the Blessed One asked with reference to that appearance, but that is not the reason. In reality, the Teacher asked "How many years (vassa) do you have?" to inquire: "Since you are like this (appearing like a senior elder), you are fit to enjoy the bliss of concentration; why have you been negligent for so long?" That is why he said: "Monk, why did you wait so long (before ordaining)?"
285:
In that context, 'kissa' means for what reason. 'evaṃ ciraṃ akāsi' means why did he take so long, for what reason did he live in the midst of laypeople for such a long time without approaching the monkhood. 'ciraṃ diṭṭho me' means I see you after a long time. 'kāmesu' refers to both sensual defilements (kilesa-kāma) and sensual objects (vatthu-kāma). 'ādīnavo' means fault or danger. 'api ca' means even though the danger in sensual pleasures was seen in some way, I was not able to leave the household life for that long. Why? Household life is narrow, and the state of a householder is crowded with various duties and obligations. Therefore, (Venerable Soṇa) said, "There are many duties, many things to be done."

'etamatthaṃ viditvā' means knowing this meaning in every aspect: that the mind of one who sees the danger in sensual pleasures as it truly is does not settle (in household life) even after a long time, but rather turns away like a drop of water on a lotus leaf. 'imaṃ udānaṃ' means knowing well the process of arising (saṃsāra) and the cessation (from saṃsāra), and never delighting in that arising or its causes, he uttered this inspired utterance which explains this meaning.

In that inspired verse, 'disvā ādīnavaṃ loke' means seeing with wisdom the fault or danger in the entire world of formations (saṅkhāra-loka) as "impermanent, suffering, and subject to change," etc. By this phrase, the section on insight (vipassanā-vāra) is spoken. 'ñatvā dhammaṃ nirupadhiṃ' means knowing truly the Dhamma of Nibbāna, which is without acquisitions (nirupadhi) because of the relinquishing of all acquisitions (upadhi), and penetrating it with Path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) as the nature of escape, seclusion, the unconditioned, and the deathless. The meaning of the words 'disvā' (having seen) and 'ñatvā' (having known) should be understood as having a causal sense, as in "having drunk ghee, there is strength," "having seen a lion, there is fear," and "having seen with wisdom, the taints (āsavas) are exhausted."

'ariyo na ramatī pāpe' means because of being far from defilements, the Noble virtuous person does not delight even in a slight evil. Why? 'pāpe na ramatī suci' means because of having very pure conduct of body, etc., the pure person does not delight or rejoice in evil things that are defiling, just as a royal swan does not delight in a place of excrement. There is also a variant reading: 'pāpo na ramatī suciṃ'. Its meaning is: an evil person does not delight in the pure, blameless Dhamma of purification; rather, just as village pigs, etc., delight in an impure place of excrement, he delights only in the impure, defiling unwholesome states. Thus, the teaching is presented in reverse by way of opposition.

When the Blessed One had uttered this inspired utterance, the Venerable Soṇa rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and by the words of his preceptor, in the border regions...
286:
Venerable Soṇa requested five things, such as higher ordination by a group of five monks. The Blessed One also permitted those five things. All of this should be understood according to the method mentioned in the Vinaya Mahāvagga Khandhaka.

## The Commentary on the Sixth Sutta is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Kaṅkhārevata Sutta

In the seventh sutta, 'Kaṅkhārevata' is the name of that elder. Having gone forth in the Dispensation and attained higher ordination, he lived as one possessed of virtue and good conduct. However, he was full of doubts (kukkuccha) regarding the Vinaya, such as 'Mung beans are not allowable; mung beans are not allowable to be consumed; molasses is not allowable,' and so forth. Because of this, he was known as Kaṅkhārevata. Later, having taken a meditation subject from the Teacher and striving with effort, he realized the six superknowledges (abhiññā) and spent his time in the bliss of jhāna and the bliss of fruition. Mostly, however, he reflected with esteem on the Noble Path (ariya-magga) he had attained. Therefore, it is said: 'reflecting on his own purification by overcoming doubt.' For the wisdom of the Path overcomes all doubts without remainder—not only the sixteen types of doubt such as 'Was I in the past?' but also the eight types of doubt stated as 'He doubts the Buddha... he doubts the things arisen through dependent origination'—and because it is completely purified from other defilements that he had to abandon, it is intended here as 'Purification by Overcoming Doubt' (kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi). Indeed, because this venerable one had been plagued by doubt for a long time, he sat reflecting with esteem, 'By attaining this Dhamma of the Path, these doubts of mine have been abandoned without remainder.' He did not sit reflecting thus because seeing mind-and-matter with its causes is not the end of overcoming doubt.

'Knowing this matter' means knowing that matter called the overcoming of doubt without remainder by the Noble Path, he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) explaining that matter.

In that inspired utterance, 'whatever doubt there is in this world or the next' refers to doubts arising in this present individual existence (attabhāva) such as 'Am I? Am I not?' or in other past or future individual existences such as 'Was I in the past?' and so forth. 'One's own or another's' means in that same way...
287:
In the manner already mentioned, there is doubt or uncertainty (vicikicchā) that arises within one's own person (attabhāva) through the power of the object, known by oneself; or that which arises in another's person, such as "Is he the Buddha or not?"; or that which arises in others regarding the principal and supreme [Buddha], known by others.

"Those meditators (jhāyino) who abandon them, living the holy life ardently..." refers to those who are meditators through meditation on an object (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna) or meditation on characteristics (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna). Having exerted effort in insight (vipassanā) and fulfilling the four right efforts (sammappadhāna), they are ardent. Living and attaining the holy life of the Path, they are individuals established in the first Path, such as those who follow by faith (saddhānusārī). They abandon all those doubts; they cut them off completely at the moment of the Path (maggakkhaṇe). After that moment, those doubts are said to be abandoned. Therefore, there is no permanent abandonment of those doubts other than through this moment of the Path.

Thus, the Blessed One, placing meditation (jhāna) at the forefront, praised the attainment of the Noble Path by the Venerable Kaṅkhārevata through the excellence of his meditation, and inspired by this praise, he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna). For this very reason, he placed that Elder in the foremost position (etadagga), saying: "Monks, among my monk disciples who are meditators, Kaṅkhārevata is the foremost."

## The Commentary on the Seventh Sutta is Finished.

## 8. Saṅghabheda Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the eighth sutta, "he said this to the Venerable Ānanda" means that Devadatta, having failed to harm the Blessed One by sending assassins, releasing the elephant Nāḷāgiri, or rolling down a great rock, intended to "split the Saṅgha and break the wheel of authority." With this intention, he spoke the words beginning with "From this day forth" (ajjatagge). "Apart from the Blessed One" (aññatreva bhagavatā) means excluding the Blessed One, without acknowledging him as the Teacher. "Apart from the Order of Monks" (aññatra bhikkhusaṅghā) means excluding the Order of Monks. "I will perform the Uposatha and Saṅgha-kamma" means that having separated the Order of Monks who follow the Blessed One's advice, he would perform the Uposatha and Saṅgha-kamma separately with those monks who followed him. "Devadatta will split the Saṅgha" means that since Devadatta had prepared all those who would cause the split, it was certain that Devadatta...
288:
Today Devadatta will split the Saṅgha; he will divide it into two. Since Devadatta had prepared all those who would cause the split, it is said, "Today Devadatta will split the Saṅgha." By pointing out any one of the eighteen grounds for a split, such as "declaring what is not-Dhamma as Dhamma," and by convincing them with various reasons, saying "Accept this, approve of this," and having them take the voting tickets (salāka), when a separate Saṅgha-kamma is performed, the Saṅgha is split.

The Blessed One has taught this: "Upāli, the Saṅgha is split by five means: by a formal act (kamma), by the recitation (uddesa), by communication (voharantā), by proclamation (anussāvana), and by the taking of voting tickets (salākaggāha)" (Parivāra, 458).

Among those five, "by a formal act" means by any one of the four types of Saṅgha-kamma, such as the act of proposal (apalokana-kamma). "By the recitation" means by any one of the five recitations of the Pātimokkha. "By communication" means pointing out the eighteen grounds for a split, such as "declaring what is not-Dhamma as Dhamma," through various occurrences. "By proclamation" means speaking into the ear and reciting the formal statement (kammavācā) in this manner: "Do you not know that I am one who has gone forth from a high family and am very learned? Would someone like me have you accept what is not-Dhamma or not-Vinaya? Is it even proper for such a thought to arise in your minds? Would I live without fear of the states of misery?" "By the taking of voting tickets" means having spoken thus to strengthen their minds and make them unwavering, he says, "Take this voting ticket," and has them take it.

In this context, the formal act or the recitation is the standard (pamāṇa), while communication, proclamation, and the taking of voting tickets are preliminary stages. This is because even if one communicates by pointing out the eighteen grounds, proclaims to gain their favor, and has them take the voting tickets, the Saṅgha is not yet split. Only when four or more monks take the voting tickets and perform a separate recitation or formal act is the Saṅgha considered split. Devadatta, having completed all the preliminary stages of splitting the Saṅgha, thought, "Today I will certainly perform a separate Uposatha and Saṅgha-kamma," and spoke the words beginning with "From this day forth." Therefore, they reported, "Venerable Sir, today Devadatta will split the Saṅgha."

"Having understood this matter" (etam-atthaṃ viditvā) means having fully understood in every aspect this act of splitting the Saṅgha being performed by Devadatta—an act that leads to rebirth in the Great Hell of Avīci, lasts for an aeon (kappa), and is incurable. Wishing to clearly show the blameless practice of the virtuous and the nature of their unwholesome and wholesome deeds in due order, he uttered this inspired utterance in the verse beginning with "Good is easy for the good to do" (sukaraṃ sādhunā sādhu).
289:
The Blessed One, having known in every way that act of causing a schism in the Saṅgha committed by Devadatta—which leads to the great Avīci hell, lasts for an aeon, and is incurable by the Buddhas—inspired by the power of the similar and dissimilar practices of the virtuous and the non-virtuous regarding wholesome and unwholesome states in due order, uttered this inspired utterance that clarifies this meaning.

In that verse of inspired utterance, "Sukaraṃ sādhunā sādhu" means that which is called "sādhu" because it accomplishes the welfare of oneself and others; those who practice rightly, such as the disciple Sāriputta and others, Paccekabuddhas, the Fully Enlightened Buddha, or other worldly virtuous people, can easily perform good deeds that are noble, proper, and bring welfare and happiness to oneself and others. "Sādhu pāpena dukkaraṃ" means that good deeds of the aforementioned nature are difficult for a wicked person like Devadatta and others to perform; it means such a wicked person is unable to do that good deed. "Pāpaṃ pāpena sukaraṃ" means that unwholesome states which are ignoble and bring harm to oneself and others can be easily performed by the aforementioned wicked person. "Pāpamariyehi dukkaraṃ" means that Noble Ones (Ariyas) like the Buddha and others find such evil difficult to do; it is of a nature that is extremely difficult to perform. The Teacher shows that this is because such unwholesome states have been completely eradicated by those Noble Ones through the Path of Arahatship.

## End of the Commentary on the Eighth Sutta.

## 9. Commentary on the Sadhāyamāna Sutta

In the ninth sutta, "māṇavakā" refers to young brahmin youths who are in the first stage of life; they are intended in this sutta.

"Sadhāyamānarūpā" is said with reference to speech of a mocking nature. It means those who have the habit of speaking jokingly with the desire to mock others. The grammatical derivation of that word is: mocking speech is called "sadha"; because they speak that word, they should be called "sadhayamānā," but with the vowel lengthened, it is said as "sadhāyamānā." Alternatively, they are called "sadhāyamānā" because they especially speak and act like fools. Because they are of such nature, they are called "sadhāyamānarūpā." There is also a variant reading "saddāyamānarūpā," meaning those making loud and great noises. They passed by not far from the Blessed One, saying various offensive and teasing things within his hearing range. (The Blessed One, knowing this matter,) uttered this inspired utterance by the power of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) that clarifies the meaning of those words regarding wholesome and unwholesome states.

In that verse of inspired utterance, "parittaṃ" means: who among those who, being young, pretend to be wise can know the words spoken by the wise? In this context, they pretend to be wise by making it seem as if they know, saying "We also know." "Vācāgocarabhāṇino" means those who speak only with words as their range. This is because they speak only about the matter of the words and cannot distinguish the meaning. Or, those who speak what is not the range of the Noble Ones' speech, not the range of the Noble Ones' talk...
290:
"Having known this matter" means having known their lack of restraint in speech, he uttered this inspired utterance by the power of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) that clarifies that meaning.

In that verse, "parimuṭṭhā" means those who are dull and forgetful. "Paṇḍitābhāsā" means those who pretend to be wise by acting and speaking as if they alone know in various matters, saying "Who else knows? We alone know this." "Vācāgocarabhāṇino" means those for whom speech alone is the range (gocara) or object; they are called "vācāgocarabhāṇino" because they speak only the mere substance of words without knowing the distinction of the meaning. Alternatively, they are called "vācāgocarabhāṇino" because they speak falsehood (musāvāda), which is not the range of speech, not the range of the Noble Ones' talk. Alternatively, in the word "gocarabhāṇino," the long 'ā' is made short. They do not have mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) etc. as their range, but range only in speech and speak. How do they speak? As much as they wish to stretch their mouths, they stretch them and speak. It means they do not contract their mouths out of respect for others or because it is not their subject. Alternatively, they speak while ranging only in words; it means they are speakers who rely on others' beliefs without knowing themselves. Therefore, without considering the words by which they should be heard, they only wish to stretch their mouths as much as they want. "Yena nītā na taṃ vidū" means they do not know that by which they are led—such as forgetfulness—into shamelessness and the conceit of being wise, thinking "We speak thus." They do not know the reason for their speaking so; it means the ignorant and the foolish do not know.

## End of the Commentary on the Ninth Sutta.

## 10. Commentary on the Cūḷapanthaka Sutta

In the tenth sutta, "Cūḷapanthaka" is so called because he was the younger brother of the Elder Mahāpanthaka and because he was born on the road (pantha); he was known by the name he received in his youth as "Cūḷapanthaka" even in later times. In terms of special qualities, however, he was one with the six direct knowledges (abhiññā) and had attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). [The Buddha said:] "Monks, among my monk disciples..."
291:
Among the monks who are able to create a mind-made body, and among those who are skilled in mental transformation (or the liberation of the mind), this Cūḷapanthaka is the most excellent; thus, he was appointed by the Blessed One to the preeminent position (etadagga) in two categories, being included among the eighty Great Disciples.

One day, after finishing his meal and returning from the alms round, that elder stayed in his daytime retreat, spending the part of the day in meditative attainments. In the evening, even before the lay devotees arrived to listen to the Dhamma, he entered the middle of the monastery. While the Blessed One was residing in the Gandhakuṭī (Fragrant Chamber), the elder thought, "It is not yet the proper time to approach and attend upon the Blessed One," and sat down cross-legged in a suitable place on the floor in front of the Gandhakuṭī. For that reason, it is stated in the Pāḷi: "At that time, the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka was sitting not far from the Blessed One, having sat down cross-legged, keeping his body erect, and establishing mindfulness directed towards the meditation subject." In truth, at that time, that elder sat down having determined a time limit and entered into a meditative attainment.

"Having known this matter" means having known that matter which is the state of the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka's body and mind being well-directed. "This inspired utterance (udāna)" means that if another monk also has a tranquil body, possesses established mindfulness in all postures, and is concentrated and calm, the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance to explain the manifestation of the attainment of the special distinction for that monk, which culminates in Parinibbāna without clinging.

In that verse, "with a steady body" means with the moving body well-placed by abandoning and not performing non-restraint in the bodily door; likewise, with the five-door body well-placed by making the faculties such as the eye free from flightiness; and with the physical body (karajakāya) standing without trembling because of the absence of fidgeting of hands and feet due to being restrained in hands and feet. In brief, it means with the entire body standing in a motionless state, which is called the state of being without distortion. By this term, the monk's purity of virtue (sīlapārisuddhi) is shown. This instrumental case is used in the sense of a characteristic quality (itthambhūtalakkhaṇa). "With a steady mind" shows the accomplishment of concentration (samādhi) by illustrating the steadiness of the mind. Indeed, the steadiness of the mind is called concentration. Therefore, whether by the power of tranquility (samatha) or by the power of insight (vipassanā), when there is steadiness, the mind is said to be "steady" by reaching the state of singleness (ekodibhāva) on the object, and not otherwise. Wishing to show that this well-placing and concentrating of the body and mind as mentioned should be desired at all times and in all postures, he said, "Whether standing, sitting, or..."
292:
In the word "sayāno" (lying down), the word "vā" (or) expresses an indefinite sense. Because it expresses an indefinite sense, it indicates the meaning: "whether standing, or sitting, or lying down, or in any other posture (such as walking)." Therefore, walking meditation (caṅkamana) should also be understood as included here.

"A monk establishing this mindfulness" means that a monk who has pure conduct from the beginning, by calming the coarse defilements of body and mind, makes the body and mind unperturbed. Having obtained blameless happiness, and by the power of tranquility of body and mind (kāyapassaddhi and cittapassaddhi), he makes the mind light, soft, and wieldy, thereby developing the meditation subject and bringing it to the summit. Establishing that mindfulness, which is of great benefit at the beginning, middle, and end of the practice of meditation, means that the monk continues to establish it in each stage, starting from the purification of virtue until the attainment of the special distinction. "He would obtain the distinction of before and after" means that as the monk develops, increases, and expands the meditation subject with a mind guarded by mindfulness in this way, he would obtain the distinction of before and after, which occurs in successive stages and is characterized by increasingly lofty and sublime qualities of tranquility and insight.

In that context, the distinction of before and after is twofold: by the power of tranquility (samatha) and by the power of insight (vipassanā). Among them, by the power of tranquility, the special distinction of development that occurs from the arising of the sign (nimitta) until the mastery (vasībhāva) in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is called the distinction of before and after. By the power of insight, for one who applies himself by taking materiality (rūpa) as the starting point, it begins from the comprehension of material phenomena; for the other, it begins from the comprehension of mental phenomena (nāma), and the special distinction of development that occurs until the attainment of Arahantship is called the distinction of before and after. And only this power of insight is intended here.

"Having obtained the distinction of before and after" means having obtained Arahantship, which is the distinction of before and after that has reached the perfection of excellence. "He would go to where the King of Death sees him not" means that because he has completely transcended the three realms of existence, which are the domain of death known as the King of Death—who oppresses all beings by cutting off the life-faculty—he would reach Nibbāna, which is invisible and not within the range of the King of Death. Whatever has not been mentioned in this chapter should be understood according to the method already mentioned below.

## The Commentary on the Tenth Discourse is finished.

## The Commentary on the Great Chapter (Mahāvagga) is also finished.
293:
## 6. Jaccandha Vagga
## 1. Āyusaṅkhārossajjana Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the first sutta of the Jaccandha Vagga, the word "Vesāliyaṃ" and so forth are to be understood exactly as explained previously. Regarding the phrase "entered Vesālī for alms," at what time did he enter? He entered at the time when he departed from Ukkācela and proceeded to Vesālī. To explain in detail: after the Blessed One had spent the rains retreat at the village of Veḷuvagāmaka, he departed from that village and in due course arrived at Sāvatthī, where he stayed at the Jetavana monastery. At that time, the General of the Dhamma, the Venerable Sāriputta, reflected on his own life-principle (āyusaṅkhāra) and, realizing that "only seven days remain," he asked permission from the Blessed One and went to the village of Nālaka. There, having established his mother in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala), he attained Parinibbāna. The Teacher, having received the relics of the Venerable Sāriputta brought by the Venerable Cunda, had a relic stupa (dhātu-cetiya) built, and then, surrounded by a great assembly of bhikkhus, he went to the city of Rājagaha.

When he arrived at Rājagaha, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna attained Parinibbāna. The Blessed One also took the relics of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, had a cetiya built, and then departed from Rājagaha, proceeding in due course to the city of Ukkācela. There, on the bank of the Ganges, sitting surrounded by the assembly of bhikkhus, he preached the Dhamma concerning the Parinibbāna of the two Chief Disciples. After that, he departed from Ukkācela and went to Vesālī. It is meant that the Blessed One, having thus arrived, dressed in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Vesālī for alms. Therefore, it is stated in the Pali as "at the time when he departed from Ukkācela and proceeded to Vesālī."

In this sutta, "nisīdana" refers to a piece of skin (a sitting cloth). "Cāpāla Cetiya" was formerly the residence of a yakkha named Cāpāla and was thus well-known as the Cāpāla Cetiya. The monastery built there for the Blessed One was also called "Cāpāla Cetiya" by that old name. The same method should be applied to Udena Cetiya and others. "Sattamba" refers to the place where the seven daughters of King Kiki of Kāsi, moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega), left the palace and practiced meditation; that place is called "Sattamba Cetiya." "Bahuputta" refers to a large banyan tree with many hanging roots; because many people used to pray for children from the deity residing in that tree, the place became known as "Bahuputta Cetiya." "Sārandada" was the residence of a yakkha named Sārandada. Thus, all these places were referred to as "cetiyas" because they were occupied by deities even before the appearance of the Buddha.
294:
Even after the Blessed One had made them his residence, they continued to be known and recognized by those same ancient names. In the word "ramaṇီyā," the delightfulness of Vesālī should be understood through the excellence of its ground, the excellence of its people, and the ease of obtaining the four requisites. The delightfulness of the monasteries should be seen in their being neither too far from nor too near the city, their convenience for coming and going, their being locations not crowded with people, their abundance of shade and water, and their suitability for seclusion (viveka).

In the phrase "cattāro iddhipādā," the meaning of the term 'iddhipāda' (bases of power) has already been stated below. "Bhāvitā" means developed. "Bahulီkatā" means practiced repeatedly. "Yānီkatā" means made like a well-yoked vehicle. "Vatthukatā" means made like a foundation or a field for planting seeds, in the sense of being a basis. "Anuṭṭhitā" means firmly established. "Paricitā" means accumulated from all sides, well-developed. "Susamāraddhā" means well-undertaken, or very well-accomplished.

To show specifically after speaking generally, he said the words beginning with "tathāgatassa kho." In this Pali, "kappaṃ" refers to the life-span (āyu-kappa). "Tiṭṭheyya" means that he would stay and remain for the full duration of the human life-span of that particular time. "Kappāvasesaṃ vā" means more than a hundred years, as stated in the phrase "a little or more."

However, the Elder Mahāsီva said: "There is no such thing as an idle boast for the Buddhas. Just as he warded off the death-pangs that arose at the village of Veḷuvagāmaka for ten months, so too, by repeatedly entering that attainment and warding them off, he could remain for this entire Bhadda-kappa (Auspicious Aeon)." Why did he not remain? The physical body (upādinnaka-rūpa) is oppressed by broken teeth, grey hair, and so forth. The Buddhas, before reaching the state of broken teeth and grey hair, attain Parinibbāna in the fifth portion of their life, at a time when they are still beloved and pleasing to the manyfolk. When the Chief Disciples and Great Disciples who followed the Buddha have attained Parinibbāna, he would have to remain alone without a retinue, or surrounded only by young bhikkhus and novices. Then, people might disparage them, saying, "Oh, look at the assembly of the Buddhas!" Therefore, it is said that he did not remain. Although this is said, that statement is not preferred; the Commentary settles only on the meaning of "āyu-kappa" (life-span).

"Obhāsanimittaṃ" means that when a coarse perception is produced, one makes clear to another person, by showing the reason through the "four bases of power" and so forth, the fact that one is able to remain for a full life-aeon by the power of one's development of the four bases of power. Making this ability to remain clear is the act of producing the perception for the request: "May the Blessed One remain for the entire life-aeon." "Obhāsa" (hint/sign) occurs when it is made clear through explicit words; such speech, setting aside figurative language, directly makes one's wish clear.
295:
‘Oḷārike nimitte’ means causing a gross perception. To request the Blessed One to remain for an entire aeon, saying, “Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One remain for an aeon,” the Buddha gave a hint by saying, “Ānanda, whoever has developed the four bases of psychic power...” showing his ability to remain for an aeon through the power of his development of the four bases of psychic power. This is what is meant by causing a gross perception. ‘Obhāse’ means manifest speech. Speech that directly reveals one's intention without using indirect methods is called manifest speech.

‘Bahujanahitāya’ means for the welfare of the multitude. ‘Bahujanasukhāya’ means for the happiness of the multitude. ‘Lokānukampāya’ means out of compassion for the world of beings. What kind of world of beings is meant? It refers to the world of beings who, having heard the Buddha's teaching, penetrate it and drink the nectar of the deathless. During the preaching of the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, eighteen crores of Brahmas, led by Aññā Koṇḍañña, penetrated the Dhamma. Thus, until the conversion of the wandering ascetic Subhadda, the number of beings who penetrated the Dhamma is immeasurable. During the preaching of these four suttas—the Mahāsamaya Sutta, the Maṅgala Sutta, the Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta, and the Samacitta Sutta—there is no limit to the number of beings who attained the realization of the Four Noble Truths. Out of compassion for this immeasurable world of beings, the Buddha's staying occurred. He spoke with the intention that it would be the same in the future. ‘Devamanussānaṃ’ means not only for gods and humans but also for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of other beings such as Nāgas and Garuḍas. However, this was said to show persons with triple-rooted rebirth (sahaituka-paṭisandhi) who are capable of realizing the paths and fruits. Therefore, it means “Let the Blessed One remain for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of other beings as well.” Therein, ‘atthāya’ is for the benefit of worldly prosperity in the present life. ‘Hitāya’ is for the welfare that is the cause of prosperity in the future life. ‘Sukhāya’ is for the happiness of the element of Nibbāna. The previous mention of welfare and happiness should be understood as applying generally to all beings.

In the phrase ‘Yathā taṃ mārena pariyuṭṭhitacitto,’ the word ‘taṃ’ is merely a particle. It means that just as any other worldling whose mind is possessed and overwhelmed by Mara would not be able to penetrate the meaning, so too Venerable Ānanda was unable to penetrate it. Mara can only possess the mind of one whose perversions (vipallāsa) have not been abandoned. For one who has completely abandoned all twelve perversions, there is nothing to be said. As for the Elder Ānanda, he had not yet abandoned four perversions, and thus Mara was able to possess his mind. When Mara possesses the mind, what does he do? He shows a terrifying visual object or makes a terrifying sound heard. Then beings...
296:
...seeing or hearing that, lose their mindfulness and remain with their mouths open. Mara then puts his hand into their mouths and squeezes their hearts, causing them to remain in a state of unconsciousness. But how could Mara be able to put his hand into the mouth of the Elder? He could only show a terrifying object. Having seen that terrifying object, the Elder did not penetrate the hint and sign given by the Blessed One. Why did the Blessed One, though knowing this, speak to him up to three times? It was to reduce the Elder's grief later on by placing the blame on him, saying, “Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One remain for an aeon,” and the Buddha replying, “This is your own wrongdoing, this is your own fault.” The Blessed One saw: “This Ānanda has a very tender heart toward me. Later, when he hears of the relinquishing of the life-principle (āyusaṅkhārossajjana) and the cause of the earthquake, he will request me to remain for a long time. Then I will place the blame on him, asking, ‘Why did you not request earlier?’ Beings do not suffer as much when they realize it is their own fault. By knowing it is his own fault, the Elder's grief will be lessened.”

“Ānanda, you go” means “Ānanda, since you came here for the day-rest (divāvihāra), go to whatever place you wish for the day-rest.” Therefore, he said, “Now you know the time for whatever you intend to do.” In the phrase ‘Māro pāpimā,’ he is called Mara because he kills beings by inciting them to harm. ‘Pāpimā’ (the Evil One) is a synonym for Mara. He is called ‘Pāpimā’ because he is endowed with evil states. “This was spoken before” refers to when the Blessed One was staying at the Ajapāla Banyan tree after the seven weeks at the Bodhi tree. When Mara's daughters came and left after their desires were frustrated, Mara thought, “There is still this means,” and came to say, “Blessed One, the purpose for which you fulfilled the perfections has been attained; the knowledge of omniscience has been penetrated. What is the use of wandering in the world?” and requested, just as today, “Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One now attain final Nibbāna.” The Blessed One rejected him, saying, “I will not yet attain final Nibbāna,” and so on. Referring to that speech, he now said, “This was spoken before,” and so on.

Therein, ‘viyattā’ means those who are accomplished through the attainment of the Noble Path. ‘Vinītā’ means those who are disciplined through the subduing of defilements. ‘Visāradā’ means those who have attained confidence by abandoning views, doubt, and other things that cause fear. ‘Bahussutā’ means those who are very learned by way of the three Piṭakas. They are called ‘Dhammadharā’ because they bear that very Dhamma. Alternatively, ‘bahussutā’ means having both learning of the scriptures (pariyatti) and learning of realization (paṭivedha). They are called ‘Dhammadharā’ because they bear both the scriptural Dhamma and the realized Dhamma. Thus should the meaning be understood in this context.
297:
In this context, the meaning should be understood. 'Dhammānudhammapaṭipannā' refers to those who practice Vipassanā, which is the conformable Dhamma (anudhamma) of the Noble Dhamma (ariyadhamma). 'Sāmīcipaṭipannā' refers to those who practice the successive path of purification suitable for the purification of knowledge and vision (ñāṇadassana-visuddhi). 'Anudhammacārino' refers to those who habitually practice qualities such as fewness of wishes, which are suitable for that practice that attenuates defilements. 'Sakaṃ ācariyakaṃ' refers to the doctrine of one's own teacher, the Buddha. 'Ācikkhissanti' means they will explain from the beginning; it means they will cause others to learn according to the method they themselves have learned. 'Desessanti' means they will properly teach the Pali. 'Paññapessanti' means they will make it known in various ways, they will make it manifest. 'Paṭṭhapessanti' means they will establish it in various ways. 'Vivarissanti' means they will reveal it. 'Vibhajissanti' means they will analyze it. 'Uttānīkarissanti' means they will make the obscure and profound Pali clear and plain. 'Sahadhammena' means with speech accompanied by reasons. 'Sappāṭihāriyaṃ' means making it a means for deliverance from suffering. 'Dhammaṃ desessanti' means they will make known and manifest the ninefold supramundane Dhamma.

Here, through the six terms beginning with 'paññapessanti', six aspects of meaning are shown. At the beginning, through two terms, six aspects of phrasing (byañjana) are shown. By this arrangement, the Word of the Buddha (buddhavacana), which is the Tipitaka, is shown collectively by way of commentary. This is stated in the Netti: 'Twelve terms constitute a Sutta; all those twelve are both phrasing and meaning.'

'Brahmacariyaṃ' refers to the entire holy life of the Dispensation, which is comprised of the three trainings. 'Iddhaṃ' means prosperous by virtue of the arising of meditative absorptions (jhāna). 'Phītaṃ' means reaching growth and being fully flourishing by virtue of the attainment of direct knowledges (abhiññā). 'Vitthārikaṃ' means widespread by virtue of being established in various directions. 'Bāhujaññaṃ' means known and penetrated by many people by virtue of the realization of the masses. 'Puthubhūtaṃ' means reaching an extensive state in every aspect. How? 'Well proclaimed among gods and men' means that as many wise gods and humans as there are, it has been well understood by all of them.

'Appossukko' means being unconcerned, having relaxed effort. 'Evil Māra, you have been wandering around crying out since the passing of the seven weeks, saying: "Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One now attain Parinibbāna; let the Sugata attain Parinibbāna." From today onwards, be one whose effort has subsided; do not strive for the sake of my Parinibbāna.' Thus he spoke. 'Mindful and clearly comprehending, he relinquished the life-principle' means having established mindfulness well, with knowledge...
298:
...having delimited the life-principle, he relinquished it, he gave it up. In that relinquishing, the Blessed One did not relinquish the life-principle like throwing a stone with his hand; rather, he generated the thought: 'On this day three months from now, I shall enter the meditative attainment, and after that, I shall not enter it again.' With reference to the arising of that thought, it is said: 'ossaji'; there is also a reading 'vossajjī'.

But why did the Blessed One, though capable of staying for an aeon (kappa) or the remainder of an aeon, relinquish the life-principle to attain Parinibbāna because of Māra's request instead of staying for that long? The Blessed One did not relinquish the life-principle because of Māra's request, nor would he have stayed because of the Elder Ānanda's request. Rather, he relinquished the life-principle because after three months, there would be no more convertible beings (veneyya) to be tamed by the Buddha. Indeed, the staying of the Blessed Buddhas is only for the purpose of taming convertible beings; if there are no beings to be tamed, for what reason would they stay? If he were to attain Parinibbāna because of Māra's request, he would have attained it when first requested. Even at the Bodhi tree, Māra had requested it. The giving of the hint (nimittobhāsa) was also for the purpose of lessening the Elder Ānanda's sorrow, as per the meaning already stated. Alternatively, the giving of the hint was for the purpose of demonstrating the power of the Buddha. Thus, the Blessed Buddhas, who possess great majesty, stay only as long as they wish, and they attain Parinibbāna only when they wish.

'Mahābhūmicālo' means a great earthquake. At that time, it is said that the ten-thousandfold world system trembled. 'Bhiṃsanako' means something that causes terror. The celestial drums also sounded, the sky thundered without rain, unseasonable flashes of lightning shot forth, and a momentary rain fell.

'Etam-atthaṃ viditvā' means having known that meaning, which is the distinction between the conditioned (saṅkhāra) and the unconditioned (visaṅkhāra), in every aspect. 'Imaṃ udānaṃ' means having relinquished all conditioned things without remainder, he uttered this inspired utterance that illustrates his own going to Nibbāna, the state free from conditions. Why did he utter it? Someone might say: 'The Blessed One relinquished the life-principle out of fear, being oppressed by Māra who followed him closely, saying: "Venerable Sir, attain Parinibbāna."' To show that 'Let there be no opportunity for such a person; there is no such thing as an inspired utterance for one who is afraid,' he uttered this inspired utterance released by the force of joy (pīti), as stated in the commentaries. From that time on, seeing that the Buddha's work would be completed in just three months, he contemplated the virtue of Parinibbāna, thinking: 'Soon I shall lay down this burden of suffering that I have carried for such a long time'...
299:
An expansive joy and happiness arose; it is fitting to say that He uttered an inspired exclamation with the force of that joy. Indeed, the Teacher, who is inclined toward the Unconditioned (Nibbāna) and whose disposition is Nibbāna, remained in the world for a long time for the benefit of beings, as if compelled by the power of His great compassion. Thus, He daily enjoyed attainments numbering two trillion four hundred billion (2,400,000,000,000). Now, because the task of His great compassion was complete, He experienced immeasurable joy and happiness while facing Nibbāna. For that very reason, on the day of His final passing into the element of Nibbāna without remainder of the aggregates (khandha-parinibbāna), just as on the day of His final passing into the element of Nibbāna without remainder of the defilements (kilesa-parinibbāna), the radiance of His body was especially clear, pure, and brilliant.

In the verse, 'tula' refers to kamma of the sensual sphere (kāmāvacara-kamma) because it is clearly discerned even by dogs, jackals, and so forth. 'Atula' refers to sublime kamma (mahaggata-kamma) because it is not 'tula', or because there is no other mundane kamma equal to it. Alternatively, sensual sphere and fine-material sphere kamma are 'tula', while immaterial sphere kamma is 'atula'. Or, kamma with small results is 'tula', and kamma with great results is 'atula'. 'Sambhava' means kamma that causes rebirth, being the cause of renewed existence. 'Bhava-saṅkhāra' refers to kamma that conditions existence. 'Ossaji' means He relinquished. 'Muni' refers to the Buddha-Sage. 'Ajjhattarato' means delighting in one's own internal states. 'Samāhito' means concentrated through access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi). 'Abhindi kavacamiva' means He destroyed [defilements] as if destroying armor. 'Attasambhava' refers to the defilements arisen within oneself. The meaning is this: "He relinquished the mundane kamma known as 'tula' and 'atula', which is called 'sambhava' because it exists with its results, and 'bhava-saṅkhāra' because it conditions various existences. Just as a great warrior on the battlefield tears and destroys his armor, the Buddha-Sage, delighting in internal states and being concentrated, destroyed the defilements arisen within Himself."

Alternatively, 'tula' means weighing or considering. 'Atula' and 'sambhava' refer to Nibbāna and existence (the bliss of attainment). 'Bhava-saṅkhāra' refers to kamma that leads to existence. The Buddha-Sage, considering in this way: "The five aggregates are impermanent; Nibbāna, the cessation of the five aggregates, is permanent," saw the danger in existence and the benefit in Nibbāna. Thus, He relinquished that kamma of the formations of existence, the root of the aggregates, through the Noble Path that brings about the end of kamma, of which it is said, "it leads to the destruction of kamma." How did He, delighting in the internal and being concentrated, destroy the kamma that is like armor arisen within Himself? That Blessed One, delighting in the internal by the power of insight (vipassanā) and being concentrated by the power of tranquility (samatha), destroyed that web of defilements called 'attasambhava' because it was well-formed within Himself like armor, through the power of tranquility and insight from the preliminary stage onwards. By the absence of defilements, He is said to have relinquished [kamma] through the non-occurrence of rebirth. Thus, by abandoning the round of defilements (kilesa-vaṭṭa), He relinquished the kamma of the round of kamma (kamma-vaṭṭa). The Blessed One, whose formations of existence were already relinquished at the foot of the Bodhi tree, maintained His physical body through attainment (samāpatti) just as one supports an old cart with a prop; even now, He did not yet relinquish the support of attainment for the period beyond three months.
300:
Just as a great warrior destroys armor, He destroyed the entire web of defilements called 'attasambhava' because it arose within Himself and stood enveloping the physical body like armor. Due to the very absence of defilements, kamma no longer leads to rebirth and is thus said to be relinquished; in this way, He abandoned kamma by abandoning defilements. Thus, the Blessed One, whose formations of existence were relinquished even at the foot of the Bodhi tree, while maintaining His physical body through the support of attainment just as one maintains an old cart with a prop (vekhamissaka), relinquished the life-force (āyu-saṅkhāra) by generating the thought: "From today, beyond three months, I shall no longer provide the support of attainment."

## The Commentary on the First Sutta is Finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Satta Jaṭila Sutta

In the second sutta, 'bahidvārakoṭṭhake' means outside the gate-tower of the palace, not outside the gate-tower of the monastery. That palace, it is said, was surrounded by four gate-towers on all sides and enclosed by a wall, like the Brazen Palace (Lohapāsāda). Among those gates, He was seated on the noble Buddha-seat prepared in the shade of the palace outside the eastern gate-tower, looking toward the eastern world-system. 'Jaṭilā' refers to those who bear the appearance of ascetics with matted hair. 'Nigaṇṭhā' refers to those who bear the appearance of Nigaṇṭhas wearing white clothes. 'Ekasāṭakā' refers to those who wander about covering the front part of their bodies with a single piece of worn-out cloth tied to their hands, like the single-garment Nigaṇṭhas. 'Parūḷhakacchanakhaloma' refers to those whose armpit hair, fingernails, toenails, and other hair are long; it means those with long hair in the armpits and so on, and long nails. 'Khārivividhamādāya' means taking various bundles of ascetic requisites such as the shoulder-pole (khāri) and so forth. 'Avidūre atikkamanti' means they enter the city by a path not far from the monastery.

"Venerable Sir, I am King Pasenadi of Kosala; do you know my name, Venerable Sirs?" (he said). Why does the King, while sitting in the presence of the Supreme Person in the world, raise his hands in salutation to such naked and ungraceful people? It was for the sake of winning them over. For this thought occurred to the King: "If I do not do even this much for them, they might think: 'We have abandoned our wives and children and endure poor food and painful beds for the sake of this King, yet this King does not show us even a mere sign of respect.'"
301:
The King paid respect. For when that respect was paid, the people would not take us to be 'spies' but would recognize us as 'renunciants.' Thinking, 'What is the use of telling the truth to this man?' they might conceal what they had seen and heard and not speak; but if done in this way, they would speak without concealing. Furthermore, he did this to know the Buddha's disposition. It is said that even though the King approached the Blessed One, he did not believe in the Supreme Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi) for some time. Thus, he thought: 'If the Blessed One knows everything, when I pay respect to these men and say "These are Arahants," he will not consent. But if he follows my lead and consents, where is his omniscience (Sabbaññutā)?' Thus, the King did so to know the Teacher's disposition. The Blessed One, however, knew: 'If I say directly "These are not recluses, they are spies," even if the King believes, the general public, not knowing the matter, would not believe. They would say, "The recluse Gotama listens to the King's words; therefore, he says whatever comes to his mouth." That would lead to their harm and suffering for a long time. Moreover, another's secret deed would be exposed. The King himself will speak of their status as spies.' Knowing this, he said, 'It is difficult to know, [Great King]...' and so on.

In that Pali, by the word 'kāmabhoginā,' the oppression of lust is shown. By both words, the state of a distracted mind is shown. 'Puttasambhādhasayanam' means those whose beds are crowded and narrow with children. Here, by mentioning children first, the acquisition of a wife is also intended. Because it is prominent regarding children and wives, it shows the impurity of the mind oppressed by sorrow due to household life and such. 'Kāsikacandanam' means fine sandalwood; alternatively, it means cloth and sandalwood from the Kāsī kingdom. 'Mālāgandhavilepanam' refers to one who wears garlands for color and scent, scents for fragrance, and unguents for beautifying the skin. 'Jātarūparajatam' means gold and the remaining wealth. 'Sādiyantena' means one who accepts. By all these words, only the state of being exceedingly greedy for sensual pleasures is revealed.

'Saṃvāsena' means by living together. 'Sīlaṃ veditabbaṃ' means 'Whether this person is virtuous or immoral' is to be known by living together, by residing together in one place. And that virtue is to be known over a long period, not a short one. For it is possible to show a restrained manner and guarded senses for a few days. 'Manasi karotā no amanasi karotā' means [it is known] by one who is attentive, not by one who is inattentive. Thinking, 'I will observe and reflect on this person's virtue'...
302:
...only one who reflects with attention can know, not otherwise. 'Paññavatā' means that very virtue can be known only by a wise person, a pundit. For a fool, even if paying attention, is unable to know. By 'vohāra' is meant by conversation, by speaking.

'Among men, whoever lives by trade, know thus, Vāseṭṭha, he is a merchant, not a brahmin'—in this Pali verse, trade is called 'vohāra.' 'Four noble usages (ariya-vohāra)'—in this Pali, intention (cetanā) is called 'vohāra.' 'Designation, name, concept, usage (vohāra)'—in this Pali, concept (paññatti) is called 'vohāra.' 'He would speak by way of mere usage (vohāra)'—in this Pali, speech is called 'vohāra.' In this context as well, that very speech is intended. The face-to-face speech of some does not agree with their speech behind one's back, and speech behind one's back does not agree with face-to-face speech. Likewise, former speech does not agree with later speech, and later speech with former speech. While he is speaking, it is possible to know: 'This person is impure.' But for one of pure virtue, former speech agrees with later, and later with former; face-to-face speech agrees with speech behind one's back, and speech behind one's back with face-to-face speech. Therefore, wishing to show that the state of purity can be known by speaking, he said: 'By conversation, purity is to be known.'

Strength (thāmo) means the strength of wisdom. One who lacks the strength of wisdom, when calamities arise, does not see what should be taken or what should be done, and behaves like one who has entered a house without a door. Therefore, he said: 'Great King, in times of adversity, strength is to be known.' By discussion (sākacchāya) means by speaking together. For the speech of an unwise person floats like a bubble on water; but when a wise person speaks, his wit (paṭibhāna) is endless. Just as a fish is known to be small or large by the agitation of the water.

Thus, the Blessed One did not say directly to the King, 'These are Arahants,' but revealed the means to know Arahants and those who are not. Hearing this, the King was greatly inspired by the Buddha's omniscience and the beauty of his teaching. Expressing his devotion with 'It is wonderful, Bhante,' and so on, he now wished to inform the Blessed One of the truth about those men, saying: 'Bhante, these men are my spies,' and so forth. In that Pali, 'carā' (spies) means those who are not renunciants but are in the guise of renunciants...
303:
Because they have hidden tasks, those who consume the country's alms-food are called 'carā' (thieves/spies). 'Ocarakā' refers to those who move about in the lower regions. In truth, even though they move about on mountain tops, they are still considered those who move in the lower regions because they perform base deeds. Alternatively, 'ocarakā' refers to spies (carapurisa). 'Ocariitvā' means going to another country to investigate and coming to know the events in various places. 'Osārisāmi' means 'I will investigate' or 'I will act.' 'Rajo-jalla' refers to dust and dirt. 'Pavāhetvā' means removing by washing thoroughly. 'Kappita-kesamassu' means having hair and beard trimmed and groomed by barbers according to the methods stated in the treatises on ornamentation. 'Kāmaguṇehi' means by the strands of sensual pleasure or by the bonds of sensual pleasure. 'Samappitā' means well-attached or fully endowed. 'Samaṅgībhūtā' means being together with. 'Paricāressanti' means they will cause the sense faculties to wander about or they will indulge them.

'Knowing this significance' means knowing the fact that those king's men, for the sake of their own livelihood, were deceiving the world in the guise of monks. 'This Udāna' means He uttered this Udāna which demonstrates the rejection of dependence on others and the deception of others.

In that verse, 'One should not strive in all things' means that a monk should not strive or exert effort in any evil states such as the work of a messenger or a spy, as these king's men do. The meaning is that without striving in any such things, one should strive only in even a small amount of merit. 'One should not be another's man' means that one should not be a servant who attends to another person while in the guise of a monk. Why? Because by performing such service, one might commit evil deeds such as spying. 'One should not live depending on another' means one should not lead a livelihood depending on another, such as a ruler, with the thought, "My happiness and suffering depend on that person." One should be one's own island, one's own refuge, and have no other refuge. Alternatively, because it brings about harm, one should not live depending on other unwholesome kamma known as 'ocaraṇa' (spying). 'One should not trade with the Dhamma' means one should not preach the Dhamma for the sake of wealth and gain. Indeed, one who preaches the Dhamma to others for the sake of wealth is said to be trading with the Dhamma; thus, one should not do so. Alternatively, for the sake of wealth, like the men of King Kosala, performing the work of a spy while adopting the marks of monkhood and performing meritorious deeds so as not to be suspected by others is said to be trading with the Dhamma. Even one who practices the pure holy life in this Dispensation, but does so vowing for [rebirth among] a certain group of devas,

## End of the Commentary on the Second Sutta.

## 4 - Cūḷavagga - 3 - Akiriya Sutta

In that Akiriya Sutta, 'One's many evil unwholesome states have been abandoned' refers to the 800 defilements that have arisen in one's own continuity throughout the beginningless saṃsāra, such as the 13 types of greed, hatred, and delusion, 12 types of improper attention, shamelessness, fearlessness of wrongdoing, anger, enmity, disparaging, rivalry, envy, stinginess, deceit, treachery, stubbornness, impetuosity, pride, excessive pride, intoxication, heedlessness, 13 types of ignorance, 3 unwholesome roots, 3 types of misconduct, defilements, perverted perception, 3 types of proliferation (papañca), 4 perversions (vipallāsa), taints (āsava), floods (ogha), yokes (yoga), ties (gantha), 4 graspings, 5 wildernesses of the heart, fetters, hindrances, delight, 26 roots of contention, the body of craving, 7 underlying tendencies, 8 wrongnesses, 9 groups of craving, 40 unwholesome courses of action, 10 or 12 types of wrong view, 108 varieties of craving, and so on; as well as the 1500 defilements that arise together with those defilements and many evil unwholesome states.
304:
In the Dispensation, even if a person practices the holy life which is pure in every way, but does so by undertaking it for the sake of a certain group of deities, that person is also said to be 'trading in the Dhamma.' The meaning is that one should not practice or engage in such trading in the Dhamma.

## The Commentary on the Second Sutta is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Paccavekkhaṇa Sutta

In the third sutta (Akiriya Sutta), 'having abandoned his many evil unwholesome states' refers to: greed (lobha), hatred (dosa), delusion (moha), perverted attention (viparīta-manasikāra), lack of shame (ahirika), lack of dread (anottappa), anger (kodha), enmity (upanāha), disparaging (makkha), domineering (paḷāsa), envy (issā), stinginess (macchariya), deceit (māyā), treachery (sāṭheyya), obstinacy (thambha), impetuosity (sārambha), conceit (māna), arrogance (atimāna), intoxication (mada), negligence (pamāda), craving (taṇhā), ignorance (avijjā), the three unwholesome roots, the three types of misconduct, the defilements (saṅkilesa), uneven perception (visama-saññā), thought (vitakka), proliferation (papañca), the four perversions (vipallāsa), the taints (āsava), the floods (ogha), the yokes (yoga), the ties (gantha), the wrong courses (agati-gamana), craving, clinging (upādāna), the five wildernesses of the heart (cetokhila), the five shackles of the heart (cetovinibandha), the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), delight (abhinandana), the six roots of contention (vivādamūla), craving, the bodily tie (kāyasatta), the underlying tendencies (anusaya), the eightfold wrongness (micchatta), the nine things rooted in craving, the ten courses of unwholesome action, the sixty-two types of views (diṭṭhigata), the one hundred and eight types of craving's movement, and so forth. The Blessed One sat reflecting on the fifteen hundred defilements that had occurred in his own continuity throughout the beginningless round of rebirths, as well as the many evil, base, unwholesome states—unwholesome in the sense of being born from lack of skill—which were abandoned without remainder along with their residual traces (vāsanā) at the foot of the Bodhi tree, having been eradicated by the Noble Path. He sat reflecting in successive order: 'This defilement of mine has been abandoned; this defilement of mine has been abandoned.'
