'And many wholesome states' refers to: virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), wisdom (paññā), liberation (vimutti), the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimutti-ñāṇadassana), the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), the four right efforts (sammappadhāna), the four bases of power (iddhipāda), the four noble paths (ariya-magga), the four fruits (phala), the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), the four knowledges that distinguish the modes of birth (yoni), the four noble lineages (ariyavaṃsa), the four knowledges of intrepidity (vesārajja-ñāṇa), the five factors of striving (padhāniyaṅga), the fivefold right concentration, the fivefold knowledge of right concentration, the five faculties (indriya), the five powers (bala), the five elements of escape (nissāraṇīya-dhātu), the five knowledges of the bases of liberation (vimuttāyatana-ñāṇa), the five perceptions that ripen liberation (vimuttiparipācanīya-saññā), the six bases of recollection (anussatiṭṭhāna), the six things to be revered (gārava), the six elements of escape, the six constant dwellings (satatavihāra), the six unsurpassed things (anuttariya), the six types of wisdom partaking of penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya-paññā), the six superknowledges (abhiññā), the six uncommon knowledges (asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa), the seven things that prevent decline (aparihāniya-dhamma), the seven noble treasures (ariya-dhana), and the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga).
305:
The seven qualities of a good man (sappurisadhamma), the seven bases for shedding defilements (nijjaravatthu), the seven perceptions (saññā), the seven teachings on persons worthy of offerings (dakkhiṇeyyapuggala), the seven teachings on the powers of the Arahants (khīṇāsavabala), the eight teachings on the causes for obtaining wisdom (paññāpaṭilābahetu), the eight rightnesses (sammatta), the eight transcendences of worldly conditions (lokadhamma), the eight grounds for arousing energy (ārambhavatthu), the eight teachings on inopportune moments (akkhaṇa), the eight thoughts of a great man (mahāpurisavitakka), the eight teachings on the spheres of mastery (abhibhāyatana), the eight liberations (vimokkha), the nine qualities rooted in wise attention (yoniso manasikāra), the nine factors of effort for purification (pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅga), the nine teachings on the abodes of beings (sattāvāsa), the nine removals of resentment (āghātappaṭivinaya), the nine perceptions (saññā), the nine diversities (nānatta), the nine successive abidings (anupubbavihāra), the ten qualities that make for protection (nāthakaraṇa), the ten spheres of Kasina (kasiṇāyatana), the ten courses of meritorious action (kusalakammapatha), the ten rightnesses (sammatta), the ten dwellings of the noble ones (ariyavāsa), the ten qualities of one beyond training (asekkhadhamma), the ten powers of the Tathāgata (tathāgatabala), the eleven benefits of loving-kindness (mettānisaṃsa), the twelve aspects of the Wheel of Dhamma (dhammacakka), the thirteen benefits of ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), the fourteen Buddha-knowledges (buddhañāṇa), the fifteen qualities maturing liberation (vimuttiparipācanīya), the sixteen types of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati), the sixteen qualities that do not cause remorse (aparantapanīya), the eighteen types of great insight (mahāvipassanā), the eighteen Buddha-qualities (buddhadhamma), the nineteen reviewing knowledges (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa), the forty-four bases of knowledge (ñāṇavatthu), the fifty knowledges of rise and fall (udayabbayañāṇa), the meritorious qualities exceeding fifty, the seventy-seven bases of knowledge (ñāṇavatthu), the Great Diamond Knowledge (mahāvajirañāṇa) capable of entering two million four hundred thousand kotis of attainments in succession, the reviewing knowledges for investigating the Universal Patthana (samantapaṭṭhāna) with its infinite methods, and likewise the knowledges that reveal the inclinations (āsaya) and so forth of infinite beings in infinite world systems—these are such qualities.

These and many other such meritorious and faultless qualities of his own reached fulfillment and growth through the cultivation of the perfections (pāramīs) and the cultivation of the path (magga) over an infinite period of time. He sat reviewing them, grouping the Buddha-qualities into clusters and heaps with a sense of appreciation, thinking: 'These faultless qualities exist in me; these faultless qualities exist in me.' Such reviewing, however, was only partial and not exhaustive. Even the Blessed One himself cannot fully review all Buddha-qualities in detail without remainder, because they are infinite and immeasurable.

For it has been said:
'Even if a Buddha were to speak the praise of a Buddha,
And were to speak of nothing else for an entire aeon,
The long and extended aeon would come to an end,
But the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted.'
306:
Another verse was also spoken by the commentators:
'To the Great Sage of great effort, there are infinite names in accordance with his qualities.
If names were derived from his qualities, there could be more than thousands and tens of thousands.'

Indeed, at that time, after the meal, having returned from the alms round, the Blessed One entered the monastery. Standing at the front of the Fragrant Chamber (gandhakuṭi), he showed the proper conduct to the monks. When they had departed, he entered the Great Fragrant Chamber and sat on the prepared noble Buddha-seat, directing his knowledge toward the sphere of his past lives. As he did so, those past masses of suffering appeared to him continuously, one after another, in infinite and immeasurable varieties. The Blessed One, directing the range of his knowledge toward the defilements, thinking, 'These defilements are indeed the root cause of such a great mass of suffering,' reviewed them in succession by way of their abandonment. He then thought, 'These defilements have indeed been well abandoned by me without remainder.' Again, he reviewed the Noble Path—with its aspects, its surroundings, and its manifestation—which brings about the abandonment of those defilements, and he turned his mind toward his own faultless qualities such as virtue (sīla), which are of infinite and immeasurable varieties. Therefore, it is said in the Pali: 'At that time, the Blessed One sat reviewing his many abandoned evil, unwholesome qualities, and his many wholesome qualities that had reached fulfillment through cultivation.'

Having reviewed them in this way, he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna), which is an expression of the joy and happiness (pītisomanassa) that had arisen.

In that inspired utterance, 'Ahu pubbe' (It was before) means: before the arising of the knowledge of the path of Arahantship (arahattamaggañāṇa), this entire mass of defilements such as lust (rāga) existed in my continuity; it is not that any single defilement among this mass of defilements did not exist (all were present). 'Tadā nāhu' (Then it was not) means: at that time, at the moment of the Noble Path, that mass of defilements did not exist; there is no defilement, even as small as an atom, that is not abandoned at the moment of the Path of Arahantship. Some also read 'Tato nāhu,' meaning: after that moment of the Path of Arahantship, it did not exist. 'Nāhu pubbe' (It was not before) means: this immeasurable faultless quality of mine, which is now found to have reached fulfillment through cultivation, also did not exist before the moment of the Noble Path. 'Tadā ahu' (Then it was) means: when the knowledge of the supreme path arose in me, then all faultless qualities arose in me. Indeed, along with the attainment of the supreme path, all the qualities of omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa) come into the hands of the Buddhas.
307:
"It has not been, it will not be, and it does not exist now" refers to the faultless state, the Noble Path (Ariya Magga), which arose at my seat of enlightenment (Bodhimanda) and by which the entire host of defilements was abandoned without remainder. Just as this Noble Path had not been and did not exist for me before the moment of the path, so too, because there are no defilements to be abandoned by it, like those defilements, it will not be in the future—it will not arise—and even now in the present time, it is not found (does not exist) because there is no task to be performed by it. Indeed, the Noble Path does not occur many times. Therefore, it is said: "They do not go to the further shore twice."

Thus, the Blessed One, reflecting on the unwholesome states abandoned without remainder in his own continuity by the Noble Path, and on the immeasurable faultless states reached through the perfection of development (bhāvanā), uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) released by the force of joy that had arisen within him. By the previous discourse, only the first two grounds of self-confidence (vesārajja) were spoken of; the latter two are already revealed by the revelation of Perfect Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi).

## The Commentary on the Third Sutta is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the First Nānātitthiya Sutta

In the fourth sutta, in the phrase "ascetics, brahmins, and wanderers of various sects" (nānātitthiya-samaṇa-brāhmaṇa-paribbājakā): "tittha" (ford) means that by which one crosses the flood of saṃsāra, which is the path to Nibbāna. However, here, "tittha" is intended as the views and visions held by those with wrong views through the power of perverted distortions (vipallāsa). Those who are devoted to those various types of "fords" such as eternalism are "nānātitthiya" (of various sects). Ascetics such as the naked Nigaṇṭhas, brahmins such as the Kaṭhakalāpas, and wanderers such as the Pokkharasātas are "samaṇa-brāhmaṇa-paribbājakā." Because they are both sectarians of various views and also ascetics, brahmins, and wanderers, they are called "nānātitthiya-samaṇa-brāhmaṇa-paribbājakā."

They see by means of this view, or they themselves see, or it is just the act of seeing thus, as "the self and the world are eternal," etc.; therefore it is "diṭṭhi" (view). This is a designation for wrong adherence (micchābhinivesa). Those who have various and manifold views by way of eternalism, etc., are "nānādiṭṭhika" (of various views). Acceptance by way of eternalism, etc., is "khanti" (patience/preference); liking is "ruci" (inclination). In terms of ultimate reality...
308:
...they are the distortions of mind (citta-vipallāsa) and distortions of perception (saññā-vipallāsa) occurring as "the self and the world are eternal," and so on. Likewise, because they have various preferences (khanti), they are "nānākhantika"; because they have various inclinations (ruci), they are "nānāရုစိက" (nānārucikā). For those of wrong views, having first liked and accepted the mind in such and such a way, they later adhere to it, saying, "This alone is the truth, all else is empty."

Alternatively, it is called "diṭṭhi" because of seeing in such and such a way as "the impermanent is permanent," etc.; it is called "khanti" because of accepting it; it is called "ruci" because of liking it. Thus, it should be understood that by all three terms, only "view" (diṭṭhi) is meant. "Nānā-diṭṭhi-nissaya-nissita" means those who rely on, cling to, or resort to the basis, object, or cause of various views by way of imagining eternalism, etc., or who rely on the support consisting of the view itself; it means they stand without relinquishing that view. For those of wrong views, the views themselves are the supports for their modes of adherence.

"Santi" means they are, they exist, they are found. "Eke" means some. "Samaṇa-brāhmaṇa" means those who are ascetics (samaṇa) by having gone forth, and brahmins (brāhmaṇa) by birth, or those who are accepted in the world as "ascetics" and "brahmins." "Evamvādino" means those who habitually speak in the manner to be described. "Evamdiṭṭhino" means those who have views occurring in the manner to be described. Between these two, the second term shows the wrong adherence of those with views, while the first term shows their conventional expression by way of establishing others in that view according to their own adherence.

"The world is eternal; this alone is the truth, all else is empty": here, "world" (loko) means the self (atta). For it is intended as "world" by those with views because merit, evil, and their results are located there, or because it is resorted to by those intent on the state of being an agent (kāraka), etc. The meaning is: "This vision of ours—that this world called 'self' is eternal, deathless, permanent, and stable—this alone is the truth, not perverted; but the vision of others, such as 'it is not eternal,' is empty and false." By this, all four types of eternalism (sassatavāda) are shown.

"Asassato" (not eternal) means not permanent, impermanent, unstable, and subject to passing away. By the very rejection of the state of being eternal with the word "asassato," annihilation (uccheda) is indicated; thus all seven types of annihilationism (ucchedavāda) are indicated.

"Antavā" (finite) means having an end, bounded, of limited measure, and not all-pervading. By this, [the self] having the measure of the body, the measure of a thumb, or the measure of a part...
309:
It points to views such as 'the self has the dimension of an atom.' 'Infinite' means without limit, or all-pervading. By this word 'infinite,' the views of teachers such as Kapila and Kaṇāda are indicated.

'The soul is the same as the body' means that whatever the body is, that itself is the entity called the soul; and whatever the entity called the soul is, that itself is the body. Thus, one regards the soul and the body as one and the same, not as two different things. By this statement, the view 'the self has form,' like that of the Ājīvakas, is indicated. By the statement 'the soul is one thing, the body is another,' the view 'the self is formless (purely mental)' is indicated.

In the phrase 'the Tathāgata exists after death,' 'Tathāgata' refers to a being. For a person with wrong view refers to one who has reached such a state—characterized as a doer, an experiencer, or as something permanent and stable—as a 'Tathāgata.' It means that after death, following the breaking up of this body, that being exists or is found in a higher state of existence. By this statement based on the eternalist grasp, the sixteen doctrines of percipient existence, the eight doctrines of non-percipient existence, and the eight doctrines of neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient existence are indicated. 'Does not exist' means it is no more, it is not found. By this, the doctrine of annihilationism is indicated. 'Both exists and does not exist' means it both is and is not. By this, the doctrines of partial eternalism and the seven doctrines of percipient existence are indicated. By the statement 'neither exists nor does not exist,' it should be understood that the doctrine of eel-wriggling (amarāvikkhepavāda) is indicated.

It is said that these people of various views, having come from different regions and residing in Sāvatthī, once gathered at a debate forum. Upholding their own views and disparaging the views of others, they fell into dispute. Therefore, it was said, 'They became quarrelsome,' and so on.

In that context, 'bhaṇḍana' (quarrelling) is the preliminary stage of strife. 'Bhaṇḍanajātā' means those in whom quarrelling has arisen. 'Kalaha' is simply strife; or it should be understood as 'kalaha' because it involves harming through mockery. Because they spoke opposing views to one another, they are called 'vivādāpannā' (fallen into dispute). Because it strikes at the vital points (mamma), the mouth itself is like a weapon, hence 'mukhasatti' (mouth-spears), which is harsh speech (pharusavācā). Just as by metonymy (kāraṇūpacāra), where the cause is spoken of as the effect, it is said 'the arising of a Buddha is happiness' or 'one experiences evil deeds,' so too harsh speech is called 'mouth-spears.' With those mouth-spears, they lived stabbing and piercing one another. 'The Dhamma is like this' means the nature of reality is exactly like this, as I have said: 'The world is eternal.' 'The Dhamma is not like this' means it is not like what you have said: 'The world is not eternal.' The same method should be applied to the remaining terms.
310:
The nature of reality is like this. Just as you say 'the world is not eternal,' the same method should be applied to the remaining terms. The dispute of those wanderers became well-known throughout the entire city of Sāvatthī. Then, the monks who had entered Sāvatthī for alms heard about it and thought, 'We have this topic of conversation as a gift; what if we report this matter to the Blessed One? Perhaps, depending on that, we might receive a subtle and profound Dhamma teaching from the Teacher.' So, after their meal, at the time of the Dhamma teaching, they reported this matter to the Blessed One. Therefore, it was said: 'Then a number of monks...' and so on.

Upon hearing this, the Blessed One, wishing to reveal the wanderers' lack of understanding of the Dhamma as it really is, said: 'Monks, the wanderers of other sects...' and so on. In that passage, 'andhā' (blind) means they are blind due to the absence of the eye of wisdom. Therefore, he said 'eyeless.' Here, wisdom is intended as the 'eye.' Thus it was said, 'They do not know the benefit,' and so on. In that context, 'they do not know the benefit' means they do not know the benefit of this world and the benefit of the next world; they do not penetrate the growth and prosperity in this world and the next. As for the ultimate benefit, Nibbāna, what need is there to mention it? If they are confused even about the mere process of existence (pavatti), how will they know cessation (nivatti)? 'They do not know the harm' means to the same extent that they do not know the benefit, they also do not know the harm. Because they do not know the Dhamma (the nature of things), they also do not know what is not Dhamma. Because they hold perverted views, they treat the Dhamma, even if it is wholesome, as unwholesome; and they treat what is not Dhamma, even if it is unwholesome, as wholesome. Not only are they confused about Dhamma and non-Dhamma, but they are also confused about their results (vipāka). Thus, they speak of karma as result, and result as karma. Likewise, they do not know the true nature (sabhāva-dhamma), nor do they know what is not the true nature (asabhāva-dhamma). Being so, they proclaim the true nature as not the true nature, and what is not the true nature as the true nature.

Thus, the Blessed One, having shown the blindness of the wanderers due to their lack of the eye of wisdom because of their possession of delusion and wrong views, now said: 'Monks, once in the past...' and so on, to clarify the matter with the simile of those blind from birth (jaccandha). In that passage, 'bhūtapubbaṃ' means what happened before, what occurred in the past. 'There was a certain king' refers to a king who was not well-known in the world by name or clan. 'That king addressed a certain man'—it is said that when the king saw his auspicious, perfectly-formed royal elephant mount coming to attend on him, he thought: 'How excellent, indeed, is this elephant vehicle, how beautiful to behold!' At that time, a man blind from birth was walking through the royal courtyard. Seeing him, the king thought: 'These blind people suffer a great loss; they do not get to see such beautiful sights. I shall [gather] all the people blind from birth in this city of Sāvatthī...'
311:
The King thought: "These blind people suffer a great loss as they do not have the opportunity to see such a sightly form. What if I were to gather all those blind from birth in this city of Sāvatthī, have them touch various parts of an elephant with their hands, and then listen to their words?" The King, who was fond of jesting, commanded a man to gather all the blind-from-birth in Sāvatthī and gave him instructions: "Make it so that each blind person touches only one part of the elephant, such as the head, and forms the perception, 'I have seen the elephant.'" That man did exactly as the King commanded.

Then the King asked each of those blind men: "Friends, what is an elephant like?" Those blind men, taking only the part they had touched to be the elephant, said: "An elephant is like this; an elephant is not like that." They began to quarrel with one another, even coming to blows with their fists, and created a great uproar in the palace courtyard. The King, along with his retinue, seeing their distorted behavior, laughed so heartily that his ribs almost broke. Therefore, it is said in the Pāḷi: "Monks, then that King... was delighted."

In that Pāḷi, 'ambho' is a form of address. 'Yāvatakā' means as many as there are. 'Jaccandhā' means blind from birth, those without sight from the time of conception. 'Ekajjhaṃ' means together. 'Bhaṇe' is a casual form of address. 'Hatthiṃ dassehi' means to show the elephant by making it lie down as described. That elephant, being well-trained, lay down without moving. 'Diṭṭho no hatthī' means they spoke as if they had seen it, taking the touching with their hands to be seeing. Because that man had them touch the head and made them understand, "The elephant is like this," those blind men, perceiving the elephant in that way, said: "Your Majesty, an elephant is like a pot (kumbha)." 'Kumbha' has the same meaning as 'ghaṭa' (pot). 'Khīla' refers to a peg. 'Soṇḍa' refers to the trunk (hand). 'Naṅgalīsā' refers to the plow-pole. 'Koṭṭha' refers to a granary. 'Pāda' refers to the leg or thigh. 'Thūṇa' refers to a pillar. 'Naṅguṭṭha' refers to the upper part of the tail. 'Vāladhī' refers to the tip of the tail. 'Muṭṭhīhi saṃsumbhiṃsu' means they clenched their fists and struck one another; they engaged in a fistfight. 'Attamano ahosi' means that King, being fond of jesting, became delighted and filled with joy because of the quarrel among the blind men.

'Evameva kho' is a phrase used to compare the simile with the subject. Its meaning is: Monks, just as those blind people, being sightless and seeing only one part, did not see the elephant in its entirety, and taking only the part they saw to be the elephant, they did not accept the views of others but quarreled and fought with one another; in the same way, the sectarians (titthiyas) outside the Dispensation take a part of the identity (sakkāya), such as form (rūpa) or feeling (vedanā), and based on their own views, perceive it as "Self" (attā). Attributing permanence (sassata) and so forth to it...
312:
...taking only the part they have seen to be the perception of an elephant, and not accepting what others have seen, they fall into dispute and quarrel with one another. In the same way, these sectarians (titthiyas) outside the Dispensation, perceiving a part of the identity (sakkāya) such as form or feeling according to their own views as "Self," attribute permanence and so forth to it. Clinging to the thought, "This alone is the truth, all else is false," they dispute with one another. In reality, they do not know what is beneficial or harmful, what is Dhamma or non-Dhamma. Therefore, they are like the blind, without sight, resembling those blind from birth.

Knowing this matter—knowing in every aspect the nature of these sectarians who, like the blind men with the elephant, do not know or see the true nature of things but wrongly cling to their perceptions and fall into dispute—the Blessed One uttered this Udāna (inspired utterance) that illuminates this meaning.

In that Udāna verse, "Imesu kira sajjanti eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā" means: In this world, some who are called recluses (samaṇa) merely by having gone forth, and some who are called brahmins (brāhmaṇa) merely by birth, cling to these essence-less wrong views such as "The world is eternal," through the power of delighting in their views. Or else, they cling to these five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandhā), such as form, which are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, through the power of delighting in craving and views, saying "This is mine," and so forth. It shows, "Oh, how great is their delusion!" Here, the word 'kira' indicates disapproval. By that word, it points out that there is no reason to be attached to those views. Not only do they cling, but they also dispute by saying, "You do not understand this Dhamma-Vinaya, I alone understand this Dhamma-Vinaya," and so on, reaching a state of conflict through the practice of contentious talk. The word 'naṃ' here is merely a particle. Alternatively, 'viggayha naṃ' means they dispute by taking up that basis for views, or identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) itself, in a contradictory manner such as permanence, because of their distorted vision. They speak specifically, or they proclaim their own view as superior and unerring, clinging to it. Like what? Like the people who see only one part. Just as the blind people, seeing only one part of the elephant, took whatever part they touched and knew to be the elephant itself and disputed with one another, this is the meaning. It should be understood that the word 'iva' is elided here.

## The Commentary on the Fourth Sutta is finished.
313:
## 5. Commentary on the Second Nānātitthiya Sutta

In the fifth sutta, "The self and the world are eternal" means taking one of the forms, etc., as the self or as the world, and holding that form, etc., to be "eternal and stable," both for oneself and by causing others to hold such a view. As it is said: "They designate the self and the world as eternal, taking form as the self and the world... feeling... perception... formations... consciousness as the self and the world, designating the self and the world as eternal."

Alternatively, "self" refers to the basis of I-making (ahaṅkāra), and "world" refers to the basis of mine-making (mammaṅkāra), which is called "attaniya" (belonging to the self). Or, "self" is oneself, and "world" is others. Or, "self" is one of the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha), and the remaining aggregates are the "world." Or, "self" is the conscious continuity of aggregates, and things without consciousness (such as mountains and forests) are the "world." Thus, having taken various objects as "self" and "world" in two ways according to their views, they speak with strong attachment to both as "permanent, stable, and eternal" (nicca, dhuva, sassata). By this, the four types of Eternalism (sassatavāda) are shown. By the word "not eternal" (asassata), the seven types of Annihilationism (ucchedavāda) are shown. "Both eternal and not eternal" means taking some self and world as eternal and some as not eternal, thus meaning "there is that which is eternal and there is that which is not eternal." Alternatively, that very self and world, like those with the view of self-destiny, are both eternal and not eternal; it means it might be eternal and it might not be eternal. In every way, by this text, Partial-Eternalism (ekaccasassatavāda) is shown. By the words "neither eternal nor not eternal," Eel-wriggling (amarāvikkhepavāda) is shown. For those teachers, seeing faults in both Eternalism and Annihilationism, they argue by using evasive speech, saying, "The self and the world are neither eternal nor not eternal."

"Self-made" (sayaṅkata) means made by oneself. Just as the self of various beings performs its own corresponding duties and experiences pleasure and pain, so too the self itself makes itself and the world—which is the object of its enjoyment and is called an obstacle (palibodha)—it creates them; this is their view, just like the view of self (attaladdhi). "Made by another" (paraṅkata) means made by someone other than oneself, such as a Lord (Issara), a Person (Purisa), a Creator (Pajāpati), Time (Kāla), or Nature (Pakati), that the self and the world...
314:
...are made or created. The creators like the Lord (Issara), etc., when creating the self and the world, do not create them solely by their own will, but only after obtaining the cooperative cause of the merit and demerit (dhamma and adhamma) of various beings. Therefore, the view of some is that the self and the world are both self-made and made by another.

"Neither self-made nor made by another" (asayaṅkāra aparaṅkāra) means "asayaṅkāra" because there is no making by oneself in that view, and "aparaṅkāra" because there is no making by another. The word "aparaṅkāra" is spoken with the addition of the nasal (anunāsika). This person with such a view rejects both after seeing faults in both positions. If it is neither self-made nor made by another, how does it arise? To answer this, it is said: "Arisen by chance" (adhiccasamuppanna). It means arisen by chance, arisen without any cause; thus, the doctrine of fortuitous origin (adhiccasamuppannavāda) is shown. By this doctrine, the doctrine of non-causality (ahetukavāda) is also included.

Now, those individuals with wrong views who, just like the self, speak with attachment to pleasure and pain (sukha-dukkha) as being eternal, etc., as a quality or an object of that self. To show their doctrine, the words beginning with "Sante'ke samaṇabrāhmaṇā" (There are some recluses and brahmins) are spoken. This is just as previously explained.

In the phrase "Etam-atthaṃ viditvā" (Having understood this matter), since the simile of the blind men from birth (jaccandhūpamā) is not included in this sutta, that simile should be omitted and the meaning should be applied according to the method stated below. The same applies to the verse.

In that verse, "They sink in the very middle, without reaching the footing (ogadha)" is the distinction. The meaning of that Pali is as follows: Those with wrong views who are attached to such views and to the supports of views, without reaching or attaining the footing (ogadha)—which is called Nibbāna or the Noble Path (ariya-magga) that leads to Nibbāna, because it is the state of reaching the other shore or because it is a place of standing—in the middle of the four floods such as the flood of sensuality (kāmogha), or in the middle of the great flood of saṃsāra itself, they sink and submerge. They stand by this Noble Path, or they stand in this Noble Path; therefore, the Noble Path and Nibbāna are called "ogādha." In this context, the word "ogādha" is shortened to "ogadha." That "ogadha" is divided as "tam-ogadhaṃ."

## End of the Commentary on the Fifth Sutta.

## 6. Commentary on the Third Nānātitthiya Sutta

In the sixth sutta, everything is just as previously explained. In the phrase "Imaṃ udānaṃ" (this inspired utterance), it refers to one who sees formations (saṅkhāra) as they really are, having seen the danger in views, craving, and conceit and avoiding them from afar; and to one who does not see them as they really are, having wrongly attached to them because of not seeing the danger in those formations...
315:
The meaning should be applied as: He uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) which illustrates the crossing over and not crossing over from the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra) in due order.

In those verses of the inspired utterance, 'ahaṅkārapasutāyaṃ pajā' refers to this mass of beings who are settled in wrong view, obsessed with 'I-making' (ahaṅkāra), which is the view that 'the self and the world are self-made (sayaṅkāra),' and who are repeatedly engaged in such a view. 'Paraṅkārūpasaṃhitā' means being associated with the view of 'causation by another' (paraṅkāra), which is the belief that another, such as a Lord (Issara) or creator, performs everything. 'Etadeke nābbhaññaṃsu' means that some recluses and brahmins, seeing the faults in these two views, did not accept them. How so? If there were the view of self-causation (sayaṅkāra), since beings could act according to their own will, only desirable results should occur, and undesirable results should not occur. In reality, although no one desires suffering for themselves, undesirable suffering does occur; therefore, self-causation (sayaṅkāra) cannot be the case.

The view of causation by another (paraṅkāra) also, if it were due to a Lord (Issara), that Lord would act either for his own benefit or for the benefit of others. Among these two, if he acts for his own benefit, he would be one whose task is unfinished, because he must strive to accomplish what is not yet achieved. If he acts for the benefit of others, he should produce only the welfare and happiness of all beings, and not produce non-welfare and suffering. However, since suffering and distress are seen to occur, causation by another (paraṅkāra) through the power of a Lord is not established. Furthermore, if a single, eternal cause called a Lord, which is independent of anything else, were present for the occurrence of things, there would be no arising due to kamma, and all things would have to arise simultaneously because the cause is ever-present. If, on the other hand, that Lord requires other auxiliary causes, then those causes themselves would be the primary cause; what benefit would there be in a conceived Lord whose capacity is incomplete?

Just as causation by another (paraṅkāra) due to a Lord is not established, so too the views that things arise due to Pajāpati, Purisa, Pakati, Brahmā, Kāla (Time), and so on, are also not established, because those entities are unproven and do not escape the aforementioned faults. Therefore, it was said, 'Etadeke nābbhaññaṃsu.' Those who, while not accepting the aforementioned self-causation and causation by another, proclaim that the self and the world are 'arisen by chance' (adhiccasamuppanna), they too do not see the dart (salla) of that wrong view. Those who hold the view of chance arising do not see it as a 'dart' (salla) because they do not transcend wrong view and do not know things as they really are, and because it causes suffering in various ways and has the nature of piercing.

'Etañca sallaṃ paṭikacca passato' means that a person who has begun insight (vipassanā) repeatedly sees the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandhā) as impermanent, as suffering, and as non-self. Such a person sees beforehand with the wisdom of insight that these three types of perverted vision, all other wrong views, and the five aggregates of clinging which are the basis of those wrong views, are a 'dart' (salla) because they pierce and are difficult to extract.
316:
One sees first with the wisdom of insight (vipassanā-paññā). To one who sees thus, at the moment of the Noble Path (ariyamagga), the thought 'I act' certainly does not occur to him. Just as the state of being an agent does not appear to him as his own, so too the thought 'another acts' does not occur to him; there is merely the occurrence of dependently arisen phenomena (paṭiccasamuppannadhamma) known as impermanent. By this sequence of words, it is shown that for one who practices rightly, there is an absence of wrong view and conceit in every way. By showing this, the complete crossing over from the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra) through the attainment of Arahantship is revealed.

Now, to show that one who is attached to wrong views is unable to raise his head from the cycle of rebirth, the Buddha uttered the verse beginning with 'Mānupetā.' In that verse, 'mānupetā ayaṃ pajā' refers to this mass of beings, known as those following wrong views, who are possessed of conceit. They are possessed of conceit characterized by the exaltation of their own grasp, thinking, 'My view is excellent, my adherence is excellent.' 'Mānagantha mānavinibaddhā' means that just as they do not relinquish that view because of that conceit arising again and again, they are called those who have the knot of conceit and are bound by conceit because of being knotted and firmly bound within their own continuity. 'Diṭṭhīsu sārambhakathā, saṃsāraṃ nātiwattatī' means that because of the obsession with one's own view, thinking 'This alone is the truth, all else is false,' and through the power of self-exaltation and disparagement of others, there is aggressive speech and contradictory speech regarding the views of others. It means they do not transcend or cross over the cycle of rebirth because they cannot abandon ignorance (avijjā) and craving (taṇhā), which lead through saṃsāra.

## The Commentary on the Sixth Sutta is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Subhūti Sutta

In the seventh sutta, 'Subhūti' is the name of that elder. That venerable one had made an aspiration at the feet of the Buddha Padumuttara and had accumulated the requisites of merit for a hundred thousand aeons. In this Buddha-arising, he was born into a householder's family of great wealth. Having heard the Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One, he was moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega), left the home life, and ordained. Because of his previous meritorious deeds, as he strove and exerted himself, he soon became one possessed of the six supernormal knowledges (abhiññā). Due to his reaching the pinnacle of perfection in the development of the divine abidings (brahmavihāra), the Blessed One placed him in the foremost position (etadagga) among those who dwell in non-conflict, saying: 'Monks, among my monk disciples who dwell in non-conflict (araṇavihārī), Subhūti is the foremost' (A.N. 1.201). One day, in the evening, that elder descended from his daytime resting place to the monastery courtyard and, in the midst of the fourfold assembly, to the Blessed One...
317:
Seeing the Blessed One teaching the Dhamma, thinking "I will rise and pay respects only when the teaching is finished," he determined the time, sat down at the foot of a certain tree not far from the Blessed One, and entered fruition attainment (phala-samāpatti). Regarding this, it was said in the Pali: "At that time, the Venerable Subhūti... was dwelling in attainment."

In that Pali text, from the second jhāna onwards, all fine-material sphere concentration (rūpāvacara-samādhi) and all immaterial sphere concentration (arūpāvacara-samādhi) are indeed thoughtless concentration (avitakka-samādhi). However, in this context, the Arahatta Fruition concentration (arahatta-phala-samādhi) based on the fourth jhāna is intended as "thoughtless concentration." Wrong thoughts abandoned by the second jhāna and so on are not yet called "well-abandoned" because they are not abandoned without remainder. However, wrong thoughts abandoned by the Noble Path (ariyamagga) are called "well-abandoned" because there is no further task to abandon them. Therefore, the Arahatta Fruition concentration, which occurs at the end of the Arahatta Path, deserves to be specifically called "thoughtless concentration" because it arises when all wrong thoughts have been completely abandoned; how much more so when it is the Arahatta Fruition concentration based on the fourth jhāna. Therefore, it is said: "In this context, the Arahatta Fruition concentration based on the fourth jhāna is intended as 'thoughtless concentration'."

"Etam-atthaṃ viditvā" means having understood in every aspect that matter, which is the abandonment of all wrong thoughts and all defilements of the Venerable Subhūti, he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) that explains that meaning.

In that inspired verse, "Yassa vitakkā vidhūpitā" means that for which noble person (ariya-puggala) all wrong thoughts such as sensual thoughts (kāma-vitakka) have been fanned away, scorched, and utterly cut off and destroyed by the knowledge of the Noble Path.
"Ajjhattaṃ suvikappitā asesa" means that the wrong thoughts liable to arise in one's own internal continuity have been well-destroyed and cut off without leaving even a slight remainder.
In the phrase "Taṃ saṅgamaticca arūpasaññī," the word "taṃ" is merely a particle. Alternatively, the word "taṃ" has a causal (hetu) meaning. Because wrong thoughts have been cut off without remainder, having transcended the five kinds of bonds (saṅga) such as the bond of lust (rāga-saṅga) or all bonds of defilement (kilesa-saṅga), and because of that transcendence, and because of the absence of the nature of form (rūpa), and because of the absence of the change known as deformation (ruppana) therein, or because of being the cause of changelessness, Nibbāna is called "arūpa" (formless/immaterial). One who possesses the perception of the Path and the perception of Fruition that arise by taking Nibbāna as an object is called "arūpasaññī" (one with the perception of the formless).
"Catuyogātigato" means one who has gone beyond the four yokes (yoga)—namely, the yoke of sensual desire (kāmayoga), the yoke of existence (bhavayoga), the yoke of views (diṭṭhiyoga), and the yoke of ignorance (avijjāyoga)—by means of the four Paths as appropriate.
In the phrase "Na jātu meti," the letter "ma" is inserted for euphonic combination (sandhi). It means that certainly, he does not come to a new existence again; in the future, there is no more rebirth in a new existence for that person. Some also recite it as "Na jāti meti," which should be understood with the same previous meaning. Thus, the Blessed One, inspired by the Venerable Subhūti Thera's dwelling in the attainment of Arahatta Fruition and by the Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna), uttered this inspired utterance with a surge of joy.
The explanation of the seventh sutta is finished.

## 6. Jaccavagga - 8. Gaṇikā Sutta
In the eighth sutta, "Dve pūgā" means two groups or gangs. "Aññatarissā gaṇikāya" means regarding a certain prostitute. "Sattā" means being well-attached and delighted, thus becoming "paṭibaddhacittā" (having hearts bound by defilements). I shall speak further of the details as heard. In the city of Rājagaha, on a certain festival day, many drunkards wandering in groups each brought a prostitute and entered the park to play at the festival. After that, on the second and third days of the festival, they also brought those same prostitutes to play at the festival. On that day...
318:
Some also recite "Na jāti meti"; that word also has the same meaning as stated before. Thus, the Blessed One, referring to the Venerable Subhūti Thera's dwelling in the attainment of Arahatta Fruition and to Nibbāna without remainder, uttered this inspired utterance released with a surge of joy.

## The explanation of the seventh sutta is finished.

## 8. Explanation of the Gaṇikā Sutta

In the eighth sutta, "Dve pūgā" means two groups (gangs). "Aññatarissā gaṇikāya" means regarding a certain city-beauty (prostitute). "Sāratta" means being well-impassioned. "Paṭibaddhacittā" means having hearts bound by the power of defilements. It is heard that in the city of Rājagaha, on a certain festival day, many drunkard men wandering in groups each brought a prostitute and entered the park to play at the festival. After that, on the second and third days of the festival, they also brought those same prostitutes to play. Then, on another festival day, other drunkards also wishing to play at the festival in the same way, while bringing prostitutes, brought one prostitute who had been previously brought by the former drunkards. The others, seeing her, said, "This woman is our possession." Those men also said the same. Thus, increasing the quarrel by saying, "Our possession, our possession," they engaged in fisticuffs and so on. Therefore, the words in the Pali beginning with "Tena kho pana samayena Rājagahe dve pūgā" were spoken. In that Pali, "Upakkammanti" means they strike each other. "Maraṇampi nigacchanti" means they reach death due to violent assaults; others also reach suffering as great as death.

"Having understood this matter" means having understood in every aspect that greed for sensual pleasures is the root of dispute and the root of all misfortune. "This inspired utterance" means he uttered this inspired utterance which clearly demonstrates the danger in the two extremes and the benefit in the middle way (majjhimā paṭipadā).

In that inspired utterance, "Yañca pattaṃ" refers to the group of five strands of sensual pleasure, such as forms and so on, which is currently obtained and being enjoyed, whether placing the view "There is no fault in sensual pleasures" in the forefront or not. "Yañca pattabbaṃ" refers to the group of sensual pleasures to be obtained and enjoyed in the future due to kamma performed without renouncing that view, depending on the wrong view: "Sensual pleasures should be enjoyed, sensual pleasures should be consumed, sensual pleasures should be associated with, sensual pleasures should be indulged in; he who enjoys sensual pleasures increases the world, he who increases the world produces much merit." "Ubhayametaṃ rajānukiṇṇaṃ" means both of these (etaṃ)...
319:
Both the sensual pleasures already reached (present) and those to be reached (future) are mixed with the dust of lust and so forth. Indeed, one who enjoys the objects of sensual pleasure is mixed with the dust of lust. When the results of such a defiled mind manifest in the future, one is again mixed with the dust of hatred due to the arising of distress (domanassa). In both cases, one is also mixed with the dust of delusion. To whom does this mixing with dust occur? It is said: "To the one who is afflicted and who trains by imitation." This refers to one who is afflicted with defilements due to the longing for sensual pleasures, and one who is afflicted with suffering as a result of those defilements; it refers to the one who trains by imitating the effects of defilements with a desire to find a remedy in both cases.

Furthermore, "that which is reached" refers to the self-mortification attained through practices such as the naked ascetic vow (acelakavata) and the like. "That which is to be reached" refers to the result to be reached in the planes of misery (apāya) due to the undertaking of actions based on wrong view. Both of these are overwhelmed by the dust of suffering. "The afflicted" refers to one who is afflicted with the suffering of bodily exhaustion. "One who trains by imitation" refers to one who trains by imitating those who hold wrong views.

"Those who regard training as the essence" refers to those who, having taken the training consisting of virtue (sīla) and vows (vata) as they have been undertaken to be the essence, say, "Through this practice, there is purification from saṃsāra." Therefore, it is stated in the Pāḷi: "Those who regard virtue, vows, livelihood, the holy life, and service as the essence." In this context, the abstaining by saying "I shall not do this" is virtue (sīla). The practice of consuming poison or performing difficult tasks is a vow (vata). Livelihood such as eating only leaves is jīvita. Abstinence from sexual intercourse is the holy life (brahmacariya). The firm adherence to these practices or the serving of deities is service (upaṭṭhāna). Alternatively, the serving of deities such as Khandadeva or Siva through offerings like food balls (bhūtapiṇḍaka) or ceremonial decorations (paribhaṇḍa) is service (upaṭṭhāna). Thus, the recluses and brahmins who remain established in taking these aforementioned virtues and so forth as the essence, believing that purification from saṃsāra comes through them, should be understood as "those who regard training as the essence."

"This is one extreme" refers to the devotion to self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga) characterized by the adherence to rites and rituals (sīlabbataparāmāsa); it is called an "extreme" because it is a wrong path away from the Middle Way (majjhimā paṭipadā) and because it is low. "This is the second extreme" refers to the devotion to sensual pleasure (kāmasukhallikānuyoga), characterized by being immersed in sensual pleasures; it is called the second extreme according to the method already mentioned.

These two extremes, namely devotion to sensual pleasure and devotion to self-mortification, are pursued by those who are afflicted by defilements and suffering, as they cling to sensual pleasures mixed with the dust of defilements and suffering—both those reached in the present and those to be reached in the future—and to practices that cause self-torment...
320:
Because these two extremes are practiced by those afflicted with the suffering of defilements, and because they are low and constitute a wrong path, they are called 'antā' (extremes). 'Kaṭasivaḍḍhana' (increasing the cemetery) refers to the increasing of craving (taṇhā) and ignorance (avijjā), which are called 'kaṭasi' in the sense that they are greatly desired by blind worldlings (andhaputhujjana). These 'kaṭasi' increase various types of wrong views. For one who habitually sees gratification in the objects of sensual pleasure and is unable to abandon them, craving and ignorance find a cooperative cause and lead one to hold the view of non-existence (natthikadiṭṭhi), the view of non-action (akiriyadiṭṭhi), and the view of non-causality (ahetukadiṭṭhi), through such thoughts as "There is no result of giving," and so forth. For one devoted to self-mortification, however, ignorance and craving find a cooperative cause and lead one to hold the view of adherence to rites and rituals (sīlabbataparāmāsa) with a desire for self-purification, through such thoughts as "Purification comes through virtue, purification comes through vows," and so forth. The fact that identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) is the basis for them is quite clear. Thus, it should be understood how craving and ignorance increase wrong views by depending on the two extremes.

Some teachers say, "Kaṭasi is a designation for the five aggregates." According to their view, as long as there is no purification from saṃsāra due to those two extremes, those two extremes increase the aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandhā). Other teachers, however, interpret the term 'kaṭasivaḍḍhana' as "the repeated increasing of the cemetery through decay and death." Although these teachers also primarily mean that the two extremes are not the cause of purification from saṃsāra, they do state the reason why 'kaṭasi' increases wrong views.

"Not having directly known these two extremes" (ete te ubho ante anabhiññāya) means that because of not knowing these two aforementioned extremes, one does not know: "These are the extremes, these extremes are held in this way, practiced in this way, lead to such a destination, and result in such a future state." As in the Pāḷi passages such as "Having seen with wisdom, his taints were exhausted," the word 'anabhiññāya' should be understood here as having a causal sense. "Some shrink back" (olīyanti eke) means some fall into a state of contraction or lagging through devotion to sensual pleasure. "Some overrun" (atidhāvanti eke) means some go to excess through devotion to self-mortification. This is because those devoted to sensual pleasure, by not making an effort, shrink back from the right practice due to laziness; this is called 'olīyanti' (shrinking back). Those devoted to self-mortification, having abandoned laziness but making effort in the wrong way, overrun the right practice; this is called 'atidhāvanti' (overrunning). Both of these occur because of not seeing the danger in those extremes. Therefore, it is said: "Not having directly known the two extremes, some shrink back and some overrun." In this context, it should be understood that they shrink back through delighting in craving, and they overrun through delighting in wrong view.
321:
Alternatively, some shrink back (oliyanti) by way of clinging to the view of eternalism, while others overrun (atidhāvanti) by way of clinging to the view of annihilationism.

For instance, some wrong-viewers who strive in self-mortification by way of ox-duty virtue (go-sīla) and so forth, cling to the eternalist view, thinking: "By this virtue, or practice, or austerity, or holy life, I shall become a god or a certain kind of deity; there I shall be permanent, stable, eternal, of an unchanging nature, and remain just so for eternity." Thus, they are said to shrink back in the round of rebirths (saṃsāra). However, some who are devoted to sensual pleasures, desiring to gratify their senses by any means, like those who follow the Lokāyata texts, cling to the annihilationist view in accordance with those texts. Because they seek the cessation of the round of rebirths through improper means, they are said to overrun. Thus, shrinking back and overrunning should be understood by way of the eternalist and annihilationist views.

"And those who, having known through direct knowledge" (ye ca kho te abhiññāya) means those noble persons (ariya-puggala) who, having known those two aforementioned extremes with superior knowledge—namely, path-wisdom accompanied by insight—thinking: "If these extremes are thus grasped and thus practiced, they lead to such a destination and such a future life," they practice the Middle Way (majjhima paṭipadā) rightly. Through that right practice, (they abandon those extremes). "And they were not there" (tatra ca nāhesuṃ) means they did not fall into those two extremes; the meaning is that they abandoned those two extremes. "And they did not conceive by that" (tena ca nāmaññiṃsu) means that because of abandoning those two extremes, they did not conceive through the power of craving, views, and conceit (maññanā), thinking: "I have this abandonment of the two extremes," "I have abandoned the two extremes," "I am superior because of this abandonment of the two extremes," and so forth. This is because all conceivings have been perfectly abandoned. Here, this teaching is given in the past tense as "they were not there" and "they did not conceive" with reference to noble persons established in the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala). However, if the path-moment (magga-khaṇa) is intended, it should be spoken of in the present tense. "For them, there is no round of rebirths for designation" (vaṭṭaṃ tesaṃ natthi paññāpanāya) means for those supreme persons who have thus abandoned all conceivings and attained parinibbāna without clinging, the three rounds—the round of kamma, the round of result, and the round of defilements—no longer exist for the purpose of designation. The meaning is that after the breakup of the present aggregates, like a fire without fuel, they reach a state that cannot be designated.

## The Commentary on the Eighth Sutta is finished.
322:
## 9. Upātidhāvanti Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the commentary on the ninth sutta, the Upātidhāvanti Sutta: "In the blinding darkness of the night" (rattandhakāratimisāya) means at a time of great darkness during the night. Indeed, a night can be free from darkness, such as a full moon night illuminated by moonlight. Even darkness should not be called "deep darkness" (timisa) when the sky is free from defilements such as clouds and mist. Only great darkness is called "deep darkness." This particular night was a new moon night (amāvasī), and the sky was also covered with layers of clouds. Therefore, "in the blinding darkness of the night" means at a time of great darkness during the night. "In the open air" (abbhokāse) means in an uncovered place, such as the monastery courtyard. "While oil lamps were burning" (telappadīpesu jhāyamānesu) means while oil lamps were lit and shining.

Does not the fathom-wide radiance (byāmappabha) of the Blessed One, which naturally spreads to a distance of one fathom, surpassing the light of the moon and sun and emitting a dense, thick Buddha-light, remain by suppressing the darkness? Also, the radiance of His body, emitting the six-colored Buddha-rays such as blue and yellow, naturally remains illuminating an area of eighty cubits all around. In this way, in the place where the Blessed One sat, which was completely illuminated by the Buddha-light alone, is there not no need for lighting lamps? True, there is no need. Nevertheless, lay devotees who desire merit offer oil lamps daily to honor the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks. Thus, it was said in the Sāmaññaphala Sutta: "In this circular pavilion (maṇḍalamāla), lamps are burning." The phrase "in the blinding darkness of the night" is also said only to describe the nature of that night, not because it was dark in the place where the Blessed One sat. Even then, the lamps were lit by the lay devotees only for the purpose of making an offering.

In fact, on that day, many lay devotees living in Sāvatthī, having performed their morning ablutions, went to the monastery and undertook the Uposatha precepts. Having invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, they entered the city and performed a great almsgiving. After escorting the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks and returning, they went to their respective homes and ate their own meals. Then, wearing pure clothes and putting on pure upper robes, they went to the monastery carrying perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and honored the Blessed One. Some attended upon monks who were inspiring to the mind, while others spent the day practicing wise attention (yoniso manasikāra). In the evening, after listening to the Dhamma from the Blessed One, when the Teacher [left] from the pavilion of the Dhamma assembly...
323:
While the Blessed One was staying on the noble Buddha-seat prepared in the open air near the Gandhakuṭi, the lay followers, having approached and attended upon the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, remained at the monastery instead of returning to the city, desiring to purify their Uposatha virtue and to increase their wise attention (yoniso manasikāra). Then, to pay homage to the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, those lay followers lit many oil lamps. Having approached and paid homage to the Teacher and saluted the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with joined palms, they sat at the edge of the assembly of monks and initiated this conversation: "Venerable Sir, these heretics (titthiyas) adhere to and speak of various types of wrong views. In speaking thus, they do not remain fixed in one view, but sometimes hold to eternalism (sassata), sometimes to non-eternalism (asassata), or annihilationism (uccheda), and so on. Holding firmly to ever-new wrong views, saying 'This alone is the truth, all else is empty,' they remain like madmen. What is the destination (gati) of those who are so obsessed? What is their future state?" At that time, many moths (adipātakā) were flying and falling into those oil lamps. Therefore, it was said: "At that time, many moths..." and so on.

In that Pali text, "adipātakā" refers to moths, which are also called "salabha." They are intended as "adipātaka" because they fall into the flame of the lamp. "Āpātaparippātaṃ" means falling headlong and falling by fluttering; it means falling headlong repeatedly and falling after circling around. Some teachers read it as "āpāthe parippātaṃ," meaning falling repeatedly when one comes into the range of the lamp's light. "Anayaṃ" means suffering (lack of prosperity). "Vyasanaṃ" means ruin. By the first word (anaya), suffering equivalent to death is shown; by the second word (vyasana), the death of those insects is shown. Among the insects falling into that lamp, some died immediately upon falling, while others reached suffering equivalent to death.

"Knowing this matter" (etamatthaṃ viditvā) means: seeing that these moths, not knowing their own benefit, meet with useless ruin due to their own efforts, and wishing to show that those with wrong views, like those moths, meet with misfortune and ruin due to their obsession with views, he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna).

In that Udāna verse, "they overreach, they do not reach the essence" (upātidhāvanti na sāramenti) means they do not reach the essence consisting of virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), wisdom (paññā), liberation (vimutti), and so on; they do not attain it by way of the realization of the Four Noble Truths. Even while standing in that essence which is accompanied by the means, as if they were approaching it with a desire for liberation, they overreach and pass it by due to the perversion of view. Regarding the five aggregates of clinging...
324:
"They take [them] by obsessing: 'It is permanent, beautiful, pleasant, and self.'" This is the meaning. "They increase new bonds": by taking them thus, they increase or expand new bonds consisting of craving (taṇhā) and views (diṭṭhi). "They fall like moths into the flame; some are obsessed with what is seen and heard": being thus bound by the bonds of craving and views, some ascetics and brahmins are obsessed with what is seen by their own eye-consciousness or by the vision of [wrong] views, and with what is heard merely by tradition, thinking "It is exactly like this as it is seen and heard." They are obsessed through the obsession with views such as "eternalism" (sassata) and so on. Not knowing the escape which is the absolute benefit, they fall like these moths into the pit of glowing coals which is the threefold existence, burning with the eleven fires such as lust (rāga). The meaning is that they are unable to raise their heads from that pit of glowing coals of the threefold existence.

## The Commentary on the Ninth Sutta is Finished.

## 10. Uppajjanti Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the tenth sutta, "yāvakīvaṃ" means for as long a time. "Yato" means from which time, or at which time. "It is just so, Ānanda" means: "Ānanda, when the Tathāgata arises, gains, honor, and respect increase greatly for the Tathāgata and for the Tathāgata's disciples. But the heretics become powerless, their radiance is destroyed, and their gains, honor, and respect diminish." What you have said is just so; it cannot be otherwise. Indeed, with the appearance of the Wheel-treasure (cakkaratana) of a Wheel-Turning Monarch (cakkavatti), the world does not give up the Wheel-treasure to perform puja, honor, and respect elsewhere. Instead, the whole world honors, respects, reveres, and pays homage to the Wheel-treasure in every way. Thus, if even the result of mere merit that follows the round (vaṭṭa) has such great power, what need is there to mention the Buddha-gem, the Dhamma-gem, and the Saṅgha-gem, which are supported by the fruit of merit that follows the ending of the round (vivaṭṭa) and are the repository of infinite and immeasurable groups of qualities?

The Blessed One, having attained Supreme Enlightenment and set in motion the noble Wheel of Dhamma, when sixty-one arahants had gradually appeared in the world, sent sixty arahants to wander on a mission through the countryside. Then, having gone to the Uruvela forest and established the thousand matted-hair ascetics led by Uruvela Kassapa in arahantship, he sat in the Laṭṭhivana Grove surrounded by those monks. While staying in Rājagaha, he led twelve nahutas of the inhabitants of Aṅga and Magadha led by King Bimbisāra to enter the Dispensation. From that time onwards, for the Blessed One...
325:
Just as the grand gains and honors for the community of monks (Bhikkhu Saṅgha) increased more and more in every way, in that same manner, the gains and honors of all the sectarians (titthiyas) only declined. Then one day, while the Venerable Ānanda was staying in his day-quarters, he reflected on the right practice of the Blessed One and the Noble Saṅgha, and being filled with joy and gladness, he considered the practice of the sectarians, thinking, "How do the sectarians practice?" Then, the wrong practice of those sectarians in every respect appeared before the Venerable Ānanda. He thought, "While the Blessed One—who possesses such great majesty and has reached the ultimate perfection through the support of merit and the practice of the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma—and the Noble Saṅgha are present, how will these pitiable sectarians of other views, who practice wrongly and have no merit, have gains and honors?" Having felt compassion due to the decline of the sectarians' gains and honors, he reported his reflection to the Blessed One, beginning with, "As long as, Bhante..."

The Blessed One did not say, "Ānanda, you have reflected wrongly," but raising his neck, which was like a small golden drum, and making his noble face—which possessed the splendor of a well-bloomed hundred-petaled lotus—even more serene, he rejoiced, saying, "So it is, Ānanda," and repeated the words of the Venerable Ānanda, beginning with, "As long as..." Therefore, it was said [in the Pali text], "Then the Venerable Ānanda... and the Bhikkhu Saṅgha."

Then, regarding this matter, the Blessed One told the Bāveru Jātaka, saying, "In the past, before I arose, some low-born people received honor and respect, but from the time I arose, they came to the decline of gains and honors."

"Having known this matter" means that for those with wrong views, honor and respect exist only as long as the Perfectly Enlightened Ones do not arise in the world. But from the time those Buddhas arise, they lose their gains and honors, becoming lusterless and without majesty, and they are not freed from suffering due to their wrong practice. Having known this matter in every aspect, he uttered this inspired utterance (Udāna) that explains that meaning.

In that Udāna verse, "The firefly shines only that much" means that the firefly shines and glows only for that long. "As long as the sun, the light-maker, has not yet arisen" means as long as the sun, named "Pabhaṅkara" because it creates light simultaneously in the three great continents, has not yet ascended or arisen. Indeed, before the sun rises, fireflies, having found their opportunity, though they are like thorny fruits as they move about, shine in the darkness. "When that sun has arisen, it loses its light and can no longer shine" means—
326:
When the sun, named Verocana, which has the nature of shining with a thousand rays and dispelling the surrounding darkness, has arisen, that firefly loses its light and becomes powerless and black like a crow; it can no longer shine or glow as it did in the darkness of the night. In this way, just as that firefly can only shine in the period before the sun rises, so too the light shown by the power of their own doctrines by the sectarians called "theorists" (takkikā)—because they hold wrong views merely through reasoning and speculation—remains only as long as the Fully Enlightened Buddhas do not appear in the world.

"Neither the theorists are purified, nor are their disciples"—this means that when the Fully Enlightened Buddhas appear in the world, those who hold wrong views do not shine or glow, nor do their disciples shine; indeed, being devoid of splendor, they become as indistinct as arrows shot in the night. Alternatively, the shining of the theorists through their own doctrines and their deceiving of fools exists only for as long as the Fully Enlightened Buddhas do not appear in the world, but not after that. Why is that? Because neither the theorists nor their disciples are purified. Since they have a Dhamma-Vinaya that is poorly proclaimed, are devoid of right practice, and because their teaching does not lead out [of suffering], they are not purified from the round of rebirths (saṃsāra). Therefore, it is said: "Those of wrong views are not released from suffering." Indeed, because the theorists tend to hold what is not true, they are people of wrong views, those who are established in false beliefs, and those of perverted vision; as long as they do not abandon that view, they will never be released from the suffering of saṃsāra.

## The explanation of the tenth sutta is finished.

## The explanation of the Jaccandha Vagga is also finished.
327:
## 7. Cūḷavagga
## 1. Commentary on the First Lakuṇṭakabhaddiya Sutta

In the commentary on the Lakuṇṭakabhaddiya Sutta, which is the first sutta of the Cūḷavagga, regarding the word 'Lakuṇṭakabhaddiya', 'Bhaddiya' was the name of that venerable one; however, because his body was short, people knew that Elder as 'Lakuṇṭakabhaddiya' (Bhaddiya the Dwarf). In detail, that Elder was a son of a good family living in Sāvatthī, possessing great wealth and many possessions. In appearance, he was not inspiring, unattractive, difficult to look at, and extremely short. One day, while the Teacher was residing in the Jetavana monastery, he went to the monastery along with lay followers and, upon hearing the Dhamma teaching, gained faith and went forth, attaining full ordination. Having taken a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) in the presence of the Teacher and performing the work of insight (vipassanā), he attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). At that time, trainee monks (sekha) mostly approached the Venerable Sāriputta to request meditation subjects for the sake of the higher paths, to request Dhamma teachings, and to ask questions.

The Venerable Sāriputta, fulfilling the wishes of those trainee monks, taught them meditation subjects, preached the Dhamma, and answered their questions. Those trainee monks, through their striving and exertion, attained—some the Fruit of Once-returning (sakadāgāmi-phala), some the Fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmi-phala), some Arahantship (arahatta), some the Three Knowledges (vijjā), some the Six Higher Powers (abhiññā), and some the Four Analytical Knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Seeing this, Lakuṇṭakabhaddiya, being a trainee (sekha) himself, knew the proper time and, having reflected on the health of his own mind and his practice of effacement (sallekha), approached the General of the Dhamma, the Venerable Sāriputta. After exchanging pleasant and friendly greetings, he requested a Dhamma teaching. The Venerable Sāriputta also gave a talk suitable to his disposition. Therefore, it was said: 'At that time, the Venerable Sāriputta was showing the Venerable Lakuṇṭakabhaddiya with a Dhamma talk in many ways,' and so forth.

In that text, 'in many ways' means by many reasons such as 'thus the five aggregates are impermanent, thus they are suffering, thus they are non-self.' 'With a Dhamma talk' means with a Dhamma talk that clarifies the arising and passing away, etc., of the five aggregates of clinging. 'Shows' (sandasseti) means he clearly shows those very characteristics of impermanence, etc., and the arising and passing away, etc., as if pointing them out to the eyes while holding them in his hand. 'Encourages' (samādapeti) means making one properly take up the insight (vipassanā) that has the characteristics as its object. It means making one take it up in such a way that the mental process (vīthi) is well-established and proceeds.
328:
In that text, he properly encourages the insight (vipassanā) that has the characteristics as its object; he makes one take it up so that it proceeds having entered the mental process (vīthi). 'Samuttejeti' (rouses) means that when insight is undertaken and the arising and passing away of formations (saṅkhāra) become manifest, by following the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) through timely exertion, restraint, and equanimity, he brings the meditation into the middle path. He properly rouses the insight-mind by purifying the faculties (indriya) so that the insight-knowledge proceeds bravely and clearly; he purifies it by way of cleansing. 'Sampahaṃseti' (gladdens) means he properly gladdens the mind by the power of the balanced meditation thus proceeding, as well as by the power of the meditation to be attained above; or, he thoroughly pleases it by way of the satisfaction gained. 'The mind was liberated from the taints without clinging' (anupādāya āsavēhi cittaṃ vimucci) means that in whatever way the General of the Dhamma, the Venerable Sāriputta, preached the Dhamma, the Elder, contemplating the true characteristics in those various ways, had his knowledge matured due to the power of the teaching and his own perfection of spiritual prerequisites (upanissaya). When his knowledge followed the sequence of the teaching, without grasping any taint among the taints of sensual desire (kāmāsava), etc., his mind was liberated without remainder through the sequence of the paths (magga); it means he realized the Fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala). 'Knowing this matter' (etam-atthaṃ viditvā) means that having known in every aspect that matter of the Venerable Lakuṇṭakabhaddiya's realization of Arahantship, the Buddha uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) clarifying that meaning.

In that inspired utterance, 'uddhaṃ' (above) refers to the fine-material realm and the immaterial realm. 'Adho' (below) refers to the sense-sphere realm. 'Sabbadhi' (everywhere) refers to the entire collection of formations (saṅkhāra). 'Vippamutto' (fully liberated) means liberated in every way—by liberation through suppression (vikkhambhana-vimutti) in the preceding stage, and by liberation through eradication (samuccheda-vimutti) and liberation through tranquilization (paṭipassaddhi-vimutti) in the subsequent stage. Here, by the words 'uddhaṃ vippamutto', the abandoning of the five higher fetters (uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana) is shown. By the words 'adho vippamutto', the abandoning of the five lower fetters (orambhāgiya-saṃyojana) is shown. By the words 'sabbadhi vippamutto', the abandoning of all remaining unwholesome states is shown. Alternatively, 'uddhaṃ' refers to the taking of the future time. 'Adho' refers to the taking of the past time. By taking those two, the present time is also taken because it is connected with both. By taking the future time, the aggregates, bases, and elements occurring in the future are taken. The same method applies to the remaining terms. 'Sabbadhi' means in all existences (bhava) such as the divisions of the sense-sphere. This is what is meant: he is liberated in all existences encompassed by the three periods of time—future, past, and present.
329:
A person thus liberated from defilements no longer regards form, feeling, and so on, in this way: "This thing is I," through the power of view, conceit, and imagining. This means there is no reason for that person to regard them so. Alternatively, the phrase "one who does not regard as 'I am this'" shows the means of attaining the aforementioned liberation. Without making a basis for the imagining that arises as "This is mine, this I am, this is my self" regarding the conditioned things of the three planes included in the three periods of time, the preliminary insight leading to emergence (pubbabhāgavuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā) that arises as "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self" is the proximate cause for that liberation.

This liberated one has crossed the flood so as not to be reborn in a new existence—this means that the Arahant, who is completely liberated from the ten fetters and all unwholesome states in every way, has crossed the fourfold flood—namely, the flood of sensuality, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance—which he had never crossed before even in a dream before attaining the Noble Path; or rather, he has crossed the great flood of saṃsāra for the sake of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa nibbāna), so that he will not be reborn in a new existence; having crossed over, he stands on the other shore.

## The explanation of the first sutta is finished.

## 2. The explanation of the second Lakuṇṭaka Bhaddiya Sutta

In the second sutta, "thinking him to be a trainee (sekha)" means thinking "this person is a sekha." In this context, the word-definition is: he is a sekha because he trains (sikkhati). What does he train in? He trains in higher virtue (adhisīla), higher mind (adhicitta), and higher wisdom (adhipaññā). Alternatively, training is called sikkhā; because this training is his habit, he is called a sekha. Because his training is not yet completed and because he is inclined toward that training, he is indeed one who has the habit of training. He is not like an asekha (one beyond training) whose training is finished and whose effort therein has subsided, nor is he like the common people who have discarded training and are not inclined toward it. Alternatively, he is called a sekha because he is born into the three trainings through the Noble birth, or because he is established in those three trainings.

"Beyond measure" means exceeding the limit, more than enough. The Venerable Lakuṇṭaka Bhaddiya, following the method and the initial instruction mentioned in the first sutta, reached the destruction of the taints (āsavas) while sitting in that very place. However, the General of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati), not realizing his attainment of Arahantship because he did not reflect upon it, thought, "He is still only a trainee," and when he was requested even a little...
330:
...like a noble man giving a great gift, the General of the Dhamma preached the Dhamma in many ways for the destruction of the taints. The Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya, too, without thinking "I have already done what was to be done, what is the use of this instruction?", listened respectfully just as before, out of reverence for the True Dhamma. Seeing this, the Blessed One, while staying in the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī), through his psychic power, made the General of the Dhamma know the destruction of the taints of that Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya, and then uttered this inspired utterance (udāna). Therefore, it was said: "At that time..." and so on. The explanation for the words therein is the same as what was said in the immediately preceding sutta.

In the verse, "he has cut the cycle" (acchecchi vaṭṭaṃ) means he has completely cut the cycle of defilements (kilesa-vaṭṭa). When the cycle of defilements is cut, the cycle of kamma (kamma-vaṭṭa) is also cut. In "he has reached the desireless" (byagā nirāsaṃ), craving (taṇhā) is called "desire" (āsā). Because there is no craving that yearns in this Nibbāna, it is called "desireless" (nirāsa). Because he has reached that desireless Nibbāna specifically, he is called "byagā." This means that because he has attained the path of Arahantship, he has attained it without any further cause for attainment. Since craving is the origin of suffering (dukkha-samudaya), when that craving is abandoned, there is no defilement that remains unabandoned. Therefore, wishing to show specifically the abandonment of craving by the Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya, he said: "The dried-up river does not flow" (visukkhā saritā na sandati). The meaning is: just as the great rivers dry up when the fourth sun appears, so too the river of craving, which has been completely dried up by the arising of the fourth path-knowledge (arahatta-magga-ñāṇa), does not flow; it does not proceed from this point onward. Craving is called a "river" (saritā). Thus it was said: "To the creature there arise joys that are flowing and moistened by craving," and "The river is the spreader (of craving)." "The cut cycle does not revolve" (chinnā vaṭṭaṃ na vattati) means that the cycle cut by the complete destruction of the cycle of defilements has reached the state of non-arising and the state of not yielding fruit. Thus, the severed cycle of kamma does not revolve, it does not proceed. "This is the end of suffering" (esevanto dukkhassa) means that the non-proceeding of the cycle of kamma due to the total absence of the cycle of defilements is the absolute non-arising of the cycle of results (vipāka-vaṭṭa) in the future. This is the end, the limit, and the state of not revolving again for the entirety of the suffering of saṃsāra.

## The Commentary on the Second Sutta is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the First Satta Sutta

In the third sutta, "in sensual pleasures" (kāmesu) means in the objects of sensual pleasure (vatthu-kāma). "Excessively" (ativelaṃ) means beyond the limit. "Attached" (sattā) means that due to the abundance of improper attention (ayoniso manasikāra), they do not see the faults that are present but see only the attractive features, and thus they are strongly attached and infatuated through the power of attachment.
