"Lustful" (rattā) means they are stained by the lust of desire (chanda-rāga) which defiles the mind, like a cloth stained with dye; they are intensely lustful. "Greedy" (giddhā) means they are covetous with an extremely longing nature, and thus...
331:
It means that beings, without looking at the danger and reflecting only on the gratification, are strongly attached and lustful by the power of clinging. 'Rattā' (lustful) means they are stained by sensual desire (chandarāga) which causes the mind to change, like a cloth dyed with dye; thus they are called 'sārattā' (intensely lustful). 'Giddhā' (greedy) means they are greedy through covetousness (abhijjhā), which has the nature of intense longing, and thus they have fallen into greed (gedha). 'Gadhitā' (clung) means they are bound to those sensual pleasures with a nature that is difficult to release, like one infatuated with lust. 'Mucchitā' (infatuated) means they have reached extreme delusion (moha), having no other concern, like one who has become unconscious by the power of defilements. 'Ajjhopannā' (obsessed) means they remain as if they have swallowed and finished it, acting as if it were not shared with others. 'Sammattakajātā' (intoxicated) means they have reached the fulfillment of sensual pleasures and have reached the end with a small amount of pleasant feeling; thus they have become well-intoxicated. There is also a variant reading 'sammodakajātā', which means they have become joyful and have arisen delight. By all these words, it refers only to their being overwhelmed by craving. Here, saying 'in sensual pleasures' (kāmesu) first and then saying 'in sensual pleasures' (kāmesu) again is intended to show the excessive preoccupation of those beings with those sensual pleasures. Therefore, it shows that they were living at that time being endowed with the strands of sensual pleasure in all postures.

In detail, at that time, excluding the noble disciples (ariyasāvakas), all the inhabitants of Sāvatthī proclaimed a festival and, having prepared drinking grounds according to their wealth, were eating and drinking, enjoying sensual pleasures both openly and in secret, indulging their senses, and had fallen excessively into sensual pleasures. While the monks (bhikkhus) were wandering for alms in Sāvatthī, they saw people in various houses, parks, and gardens celebrating festivals and being inclined towards sensual pleasures, acting in that way. Thinking, "Let us go to the monastery and receive the subtle and profound Dhamma," they reported this matter to the Blessed One. Therefore, it was said (in the Pali): "Then many monks... (pe) ... were living in sensual pleasures."

Knowing this matter (etamatthaṃ viditvā) means knowing in every aspect that those people do not see the danger in sensual pleasures, which, although appearing delightful in the drinking grounds, are associated with great fever and many disadvantages, and have harsh, unbearable, and bitter results. Thus, He uttered this inspired utterance (Udāna) which makes clear the danger of both the objects of sensuality (vatthukāma) and the defilement of sensuality (kilesakāma).

In that verse, 'kāmesu sattā' (attached to sensual pleasures) refers to those who are lustful, intoxicated, attached, intensely attached, clinging, and bound to the objects of sensuality by the defilement of sensuality. 'Kāmasangasattā' (attached to the bond of sensuality) means that because of that very attachment to the defilement of sensuality, they are strongly attached and clinging to the objects of sensuality through the bond of lust, as well as through the bonds of wrong view, conceit, anger, and ignorance. 'Saṃyojane vajjamapassamānā' (not seeing the fault in the fetter) means...
332:
Because they bind the round of kamma with the round of result, or one life with another, or beings with sufferings, they do not see the fault (vajja), the defect (dosa), or the danger (ādinava) such as being the root of the suffering of the round, in the things that are objects of the fetters, because they are accustomed to looking only at the gratification in the collection of defilements like sensual lust, which are called fetters (saṃyojana). Indeed, those who are attached to the bond of the fetters can never cross the vast and great flood (ogha). Thus, because of the absence of seeing the danger, they are attached to the bonds which have the nature of fetters, or to the things of the three planes which are the objects of those bonds called fetters. Because of the vastness of the objects and because of the beginningless length of time, they can never cross the vast, extensive, and great flood of sensuality (kāmogha) and so on, or the flood of saṃsāra itself. It means they certainly cannot reach the other shore of that flood.

## The Commentary on the Third Sutta is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Second Satta Sutta

In the fourth sutta, 'andhīkatā' (blinded) means that sensual pleasures make even a non-blind person blind.

As it is said:
'The greedy person does not know the benefit; the greedy person does not see the Dhamma. When greed overcomes a man, then there is a state of blind darkness.'

Therefore, because they are made blind even if they were not blind by sensuality, they are called 'andhīkatā'. The remaining terms are in the same manner as stated in the immediately preceding sutta. In that preceding sutta, the behavior of the people was seen by the monks and reported to the Blessed One, but in this sutta, the Blessed One saw it Himself; this is the only difference. While the Teacher was leaving Sāvatthī and going to the Jetavana monastery, He saw many fish on the way in the Aciravatī River that had entered a fish-trap (kumina) set by fishermen and were unable to get out. After that, He saw a young milk-drinking calf following its mother out of respect and, being thirsty for milk, stretching its neck and putting its mouth between its mother's thighs. Then the Blessed One entered the monastery, washed His feet, and sat on the prepared noble Buddha-seat. Taking the two latter incidents as similes for the former incident, He uttered this inspired utterance.

In that inspired verse, 'kāmandhā' (blinded by sensuality) refers to those who are without eyes, having been made blind by the defilement of sensuality in the objects of sensuality. 'Jālasañchannā' (covered by a net) means like a net, because it brings harm to the beings who have entered within, by turning back and forth, up and down, in the things that are diverse by the power of the past and so on, in one's own person and the persons of others, in the internal bases and external bases, and in the things dependent on those bases...
333:
In that inspired utterance, 'kāmandhā' refers to those who are made blind and deprived of vision by the defilement of sensual lust (kilesakāma) regarding the objects of sensual pleasure (vatthukāma). 'jālasañchannā' refers to those who are covered, overwhelmed, and enveloped by craving (taṇhā), which is like a net because it brings harm to beings caught within the internal and external bases (āyatana) of oneself and others, and in the states dependent on them, which are divided into many parts by way of the past and so on, and which arise repeatedly from below and above. 'taṇhāchadanachāditā' means covered and obstructed by the roof known as craving, just as water is covered by moss and weeds. By these two terms, he shows the state of the wholesome mind's activity being obstructed by the hindrance of sensual desire (kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa).

'pamattabandhunā baddhā' means bound by the Māra of defilements (Kilesa-māra) and the Māra of the son of a god (Devaputta-māra). For when they are bound by Kilesa-māra in the highest sense, they are also said to be bound by Devaputta-māra in that same sense. For it has been said:
'The snare that wanders in the sky, which is the passion born in the mind;
With that I shall bind you, ascetic, you shall not escape from me.'

Namuci, Kaṇha, and Pamattabandhu are three names for Māra. Even Devaputta-māra is called 'Pamattabandhu' (kinsman of the negligent) because, like Kilesa-māra, he binds negligent beings with harm. Some also read 'pamattā bandhane baddhā'. There, 'bandhane' means in the bond of the cords of sensual pleasure (kāmaguna). 'baddhā' means firmly bound. For example, like fish in the mouth of a trap (kumina). Just as fish that have entered the mouth of a trap set by a fisherman are caught by it and meet their death, even so, these beings, caught in the bond of the cords of sensual pleasure set by Māra, undergo aging and death. Just as a milk-drinking young calf follows its own mother and not another, so too, beings bound by the bonds of Māra, wandering in saṃsāra, only follow after death; they do not reach Nibbāna, which is free from aging and death.

## The Commentary on the Fourth Sutta is finished.
334:
## 5. Commentary on the Second Lakundaka Bhaddiya Sutta

In the fifth sutta, 'behind many monks' (sambahulānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ piṭṭhito piṭṭhito) means that one day, the Venerable Lakundaka Bhaddiya, having wandered for alms through the villages with many monks, finished his meal, cleaned his bowl, put it in its bag, hung it on his shoulder, folded his robes neatly, placed them on his left shoulder, and walked with a graceful manner of advancing, retreating, looking ahead, looking aside, bending, and stretching. With downcast eyes and perfect posture, as if manifesting the abundance of his mindfulness and wisdom, he established clear comprehension (satisampajañña) well and walked, placing step after step with a concentrated mind. While walking, he went behind the monks, not mixing with them. Why? Because he lived in seclusion (asaṃsaṭṭhavihāritā). Furthermore, because the appearance of that venerable one was despised and a cause for contempt, worldlings (puthujjana) would disparage him. The Elder, knowing this, walked behind them, thinking, 'May these people not produce demerit on account of me.' Thus, those monks and the Elder reached Sāvatthī, entered the monastery, and approached the Blessed One. Therefore, it is said: 'At that time, the Venerable Lakundaka Bhaddiya...' and so on.

In that text, 'dubbaṇṇaṃ' means ugly. By this, he shows his lack of beauty in complexion and form. 'duddasikaṃ' means having an uninspiring appearance. By this, he shows his lack of minor characteristics (anubyañjana) and graceful appearance. 'okoṭimakaṃ' means short or dwarfish. By this, he shows his lack of height. 'yebhuyyena bhikkhūnaṃ paribhūtarūpaṃ' means having an appearance that is mostly despised by worldling monks. Some worldling monks, such as the group of six (chabbaggiya), not knowing the virtues of that venerable one, would mock him by grabbing and touching his hands, ears, topknot, and so on. Noble ones (ariya) or virtuous worldlings (kalyāṇa-puthujjana), however, do not do so.

'He addressed the monks' (bhikkhū āmantesi): Why did he address them? He addressed them to reveal the virtues of the Elder. The Blessed One thought: 'These monks do not know the great power (mahānubhāva) of my son, and therefore they despise him. That will lead to their harm and suffering for a long time. Let me reveal the virtues of this monk to the monks and free him from their contempt.' Thus, he spoke to the monks.

'Do you see?' (passatha no) is a question: 'Do you see?' It is not easy to attain any of the attainments (samāpatti) common to disciples, such as the fine-material attainments (rūpa-samāpatti), immaterial attainments (arūpa-samāpatti), the divine abidings (brahmavihāra-samāpatti), the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), or the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti). However, there is no such attainment that the Venerable Lakundaka Bhaddiya has not previously attained.
335:
Those attainments (samāpatti) are not of an easy nature; they are very difficult to obtain. There is no attainment that has not been previously entered into by that monk Lakuṇṭakabhaddiya. By this Pali text, having revealed the state of possessing great psychic power in the statement "He is of great psychic power, of great majesty," the Buddha now spoke the words beginning with "Yassa catthāya" to show the state of possessing great majesty. That statement follows the same method as previously mentioned below. In this passage, the Buddha shows: "Monks, this monk..." and so on, "Monks, this monk is not to be looked down upon merely because he is unattractive, unsightly, very short, and follows behind the monks. On the contrary, he possesses great psychic power and great majesty. Whatever is to be attained by a disciple, all that has been attained by him. Therefore, look upon him with respect as if he were a stone umbrella (pāsāṇacchatta). Such looking will be for your benefit and happiness for a long time."

Regarding "Etam-atthaṃ viditvā" (Having understood this matter): Having known in every aspect the mass of virtues of the Venerable Lakuṇṭakabhaddiya, such as his great psychic power and great majesty, the Buddha uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) which elucidates that meaning.

In that inspired utterance, "Nelaṅgo" (faultless-limbed): a fault is called "ela"; because he has no fault, he is "nela." What is that? It is the most purified virtue (sīla). Here, "nela" is intended in the sense of being faultless. Because that faultless virtue is the primary limb (aṅga), he is called "nelaṅga." This term is to be connected with the word "ratho" (chariot) which will be mentioned later; therefore, it means having the limb of most purified virtue. Here, the virtue associated with the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala-sīla) is intended. Because he has a white covering, he is "Setapaccādo." "Paccādo" refers to the blankets and so on that are spread over a chariot. That covering may be white due to being extremely pure and bright, or it may be one of other colors like red or blue. Here, however, because the liberation of the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala-vimutti) is intended, it is called "Setapaccādo" in reference to its state of extreme purity. It is just as mentioned elsewhere: "The chariot has virtue as its equipment." Because it has only one spoke (ara) called mindfulness (sati), it is "Ekāro." "Vattatī" means it proceeds (rolls). "Ratho" (chariot) is said in reference to the Elder's own body (attabhāva).

"Anīghaṃ" means without suffering, like a vehicle free from agitation; the meaning is that it is free from the agitation of defilements (kilesa). "Āyantaṃ" means coming behind many monks. "Chinnasotaṃ" means having the stream [of craving] cut off. For, in order to make an ordinary chariot roll smoothly...
336:
At the axle-ends and in the hub, there is the flowing, oozing, and trickling of applied ghee, oil, and so forth; because of that flow, an ordinary chariot is called 'one with an unbroken stream' (acchinnasota). However, this chariot, which is the person (attabhāva) of the Venerable Bhaddiya, is called 'one with a broken stream' (chinnasota) because the thirty-six streams of craving have been abandoned without remainder; thus it is one with a broken stream. Because there are no bonds of fetters for him, it is called an 'unbound' chariot (abandhana). In truth, for the body of a chariot, there are many bonds to make it firm and motionless along with the axle; because of such bonds, an ordinary chariot is called 'bound' (sabandhana). But this chariot, which is the person of the Venerable Bhaddiya, is called 'unbound' (abandhana) because all bonds of fetters have been completely exhausted; thus it is unbound. The Blessed One, having reached a state of joy due to the virtues of the Elder, said 'Look' by himself. In this way, the Teacher showed the Venerable Lakundaka Bhaddiya by likening him to a well-equipped thoroughbred chariot: with the Dhamma of the Fruition of Arahatship as its pinnacle, with well-purified spokes; with the liberation that is the Fruition of Arahatship as its well-purified canopy; with well-established mindfulness as its good door; being undisturbed because of the absence of the disturbance of defilements; being unstained because of the absence of the stain of craving; being unbound because of the absence of fetters and so forth; well-fenced and well-yoked.

## The Commentary on the Fifth Sutta is finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Taṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta

In the sixth sutta, regarding the word 'Aññāsi Koṇḍañña', 'Koṇḍañña' is the name derived from that venerable one's clan (gotta). Because he was the very first among the disciples to penetrate the Noble Truths, he became known in the Dispensation (Sāsana) only as 'Aññāsi Koṇḍañña' by virtue of the inspired utterance (udāna) spoken by the Blessed One: 'Friends, Koṇḍañña has indeed understood' (aññāsi vata bho koṇḍañño). In the term 'taṇhāsaṅkhayavimutti', the analysis is as follows: Craving is abandoned in this Nibbāna, therefore that Nibbāna is called the destruction of craving (taṇhāsaṅkhaya). Liberation in that Nibbāna, which is the destruction of craving, is 'taṇhāsaṅkhayavimutti'. Alternatively, craving is abandoned by this Path, therefore that Noble Path is called the destruction of craving (taṇhāsaṅkhaya). Liberation which is the fruit or the culmination of that Path is 'taṇhāsaṅkhayavimutti'; in a direct sense, this refers to the attainment of the fruition of Arahatship (arahattaphalasamāpatti). He was sitting while reviewing that attainment of the fruition of Arahatship. This Venerable Aññāta Koṇḍañña frequently entered the attainment of fruition; therefore, he did so here as well.
337:
“Knowing this matter” means knowing the reflection on the highest fruit (Arahattaphala) of the Elder Aññāsi Koṇḍañña, and having known it, the Buddha uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) that clarifies that meaning.

In that verse, “For whom the root is not in the ground” means: for that Noble One (ariya), ignorance (avijjā), which is the root of the tree of the individual existence (attabhāva), as well as the ground (chamā) or earth, which is the support and cause consisting of the taints (āsava), the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), and unwise attention (ayonisomanasikāra), no longer exist because they have been uprooted by the Path of Arahantship (arahattamagga). “Leaves do not exist, where could the creeper be?” means: if there is no creeper, how could there be leaves? This is how the words should be connected. The creeper, which consists of the branches and sub-branches such as pride (māna) and excessive pride (atimāna), does not exist; so how could there be leaves such as intoxication (mada), heedlessness (pamāda), deceit (māyā), and hypocrisy (sāṭheyya)? This is the meaning.

Alternatively, “Leaves do not exist, where could the creeper be?” is taught by considering that for a growing tree-sprout, leaves appear first, and later the creeper, which consists of branches and sub-branches, appears. The meaning in this context is: for that person, if there were no development of the Noble Path, the tree of existence would be liable to arise in saṃsāra; but because the Noble Path has been developed, the root called ignorance and its support, the taints and so on, do not exist. In this regard, by taking the “root,” the kamma that stands in the place of a seed is also taken, as it is the cause of the root, and its absence is also understood. When the kamma-seed is absent, the sprout of consciousness (viññāṇa) caused by that kamma, and the branches such as name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and the six sense bases (saḷāyatana) caused by the sprout of consciousness, will certainly not arise. Therefore, it was said: “For whom the root is not in the ground, leaves do not exist, where could the creeper be?”

“That steadfast one (dhīra) is released from bonds” means: he is steadfast because he has conquered the five Māras through the application of the fourfold right effort (sammappadhāna-vīriya); and because of that very victory, he is released from the bonds of all defilements (kilesa) and volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra). In the phrase “Who is fit to blame him?”, the word ‘nti’ is merely a particle. Who among the wise is fit to blame or censure such a person who is released from all defilements and endowed with unsurpassed qualities such as virtue (sīla), since the very cause for blame is absent? “Even the gods praise him” means: certainly the gods, such as Sakka, who know the excellence of his qualities, praise him; and by the word ‘api’ (even/also), wise humans such as khattiya-scholars also praise him. Furthermore, he is praised and lauded by the Great Brahma, and by other Brahmas, Nagas, Yakkhas, Gandhabbas, and so on.

## The Commentary on the Sixth Sutta is finished.
338:
## 7. Commentary on the Papañcakhaya Sutta

In the seventh sutta, regarding the term “papañcasaññāsaṅkhāpahānaṃ”: defilements are called “proliferations” (papañca) because they expand (papañcenti) the continuity (santāna) in which they have arisen and make it last for a long time. Specifically, these are greed (rāga), hatred (dosa), delusion (moha), craving (taṇhā), wrong view (diṭṭhi), and conceit (māna). Thus it was said: “Greed is a proliferation, hatred is a proliferation, delusion is a proliferation, craving is a proliferation, wrong view is a proliferation, conceit is a proliferation.”

Furthermore, the sense of defiling and the sense of being like rubbish are the meanings of proliferation. Among those proliferations, the cause of the proliferation of greed is the perception of beauty (subha-saññā); the cause of the proliferation of hatred is the grounds for malice (āghāta-vatthu); the cause of the proliferation of delusion is the taints (āsava); the cause of the proliferation of craving is feeling (vedanā); the cause of the proliferation of wrong view is perception (saññā); and the cause of the proliferation of conceit is thought (vitakka). Perception associated with those proliferations is called “perception of proliferation” (papañca-saññā). The parts, portions, or divisions of the perceptions of proliferation are called “reckonings of perceptions of proliferation” (papañca-saññā-saṅkhā). In terms of meaning, it is the group of defilements belonging to each respective proliferation along with their causes. The inclusion of “perception” (saññā) here is because it is the common cause of them. For has it not been said: “The reckonings of proliferation have perception as their source” (Sn. 880)? The “abandoning” (pahāna) of them means the total eradication of defilements like greed and so on by the respective Paths.

At that time, the Blessed One reflected on the defilements that were the cause of misfortune in his own past lives numbering many hundreds of thousands of crores, which had been abandoned along with their residual traces (savāsana) by the Noble Path at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) in this final birth. Having seen the continuity of beings, which is defiled by defilements such as greed, as something difficult to liberate—like a gourd filled with sour gruel, like a jar filled with buttermilk, or like an oil-soaked cloth—he felt a sense of joy and rapture, thinking: “This cycle of defilements (kilesavaṭṭa), which is so entangled and has existed for an beginningless time, has been abandoned by me without remainder; oh, how well it is abandoned!” and he uttered this inspired utterance. Therefore, it was said: “Then the Blessed One, knowing his own abandoning of the reckonings of perceptions of proliferation, uttered this inspired utterance at that time.”

In that inspired verse, regarding the phrase “For whom there are no proliferations and no staying (ṭhiti)”: because the Blessed One describes himself as if he were another person, it means that for that Supreme Person, the proliferations with the characteristics mentioned above do not exist, nor does the “staying” in saṃsāra caused by those proliferations. In the Nettippakaraṇa, however, it is said: “Staying (ṭhiti) means the underlying tendencies (anusaya).” This is because the underlying tendencies are the root of the continuation of existence. For beings in saṃsāra...
339:
They are called papañca (proliferations) because they expand the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra). There is also a variant reading 'papañcaṭṭhiti'. The meaning of that reading is: the existence of papañca because they have not yet been completely cut off by the Path is called papañcaṭṭhiti. Alternatively, because papañca themselves are the cause for the occurrence of the remaining wholesome, unwholesome, and resultant states, their persistence in saṃsāra is called papañcaṭṭhiti. That papañcaṭṭhiti no longer exists for that Foremost Person (the Buddha).

He has transcended craving and views, which are called 'sandāna' (bonds) because they have the nature of binding and are like tethers. He has also transcended ignorance, called 'paligha' (bar), because it is like a cross-bar that prevents entry into the city of Nibbāna. He has transcended them especially by abandoning them along with habitual tendencies (vāsana). Some teachers say that anger is 'sandāna'; that statement should not be accepted. This is because that anger is called 'parābhisajjanī' (that which clings to others).

He is 'nittaṇha' (craving-less) because he is devoid of craving in every way. He is called a 'muni' (sage) because of his knowledge of both worlds and because of his knowledge of his own benefit and the benefit of others. He lives for the benefit and welfare of all beings through the four postures, through various meditative attainments, and through the practice of knowledge that is not shared with others. The entire world of beings, including devas and Brahmās, who possess wisdom, never looks down upon or oppresses that Buddha. On the contrary, they take delight in showing respect and making offerings, honoring him with the thought, 'This person alone is the highest, the supreme, the most excellent, and the foremost in the world.'

## The commentary on the seventh sutta is finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Kaccāna Sutta

In the eighth sutta, regarding the word 'ajjhatta' (internal): this word 'ajjhatta' occurs in the sense of ajjhattajjhatta (purely internal) in such passages as 'the six internal sense bases' (ajjhattikāyatana). It occurs in the sense of niyakajjhatta (one's own internal) in such passages as 'internal phenomena' (ajjhatta dhammā) or 'contemplating the body in the body internally'. It occurs in the sense of visayajjhatta (internal domain), meaning the place of mastery, in such passages as 'without attending to any signs, he enters and dwells in the internal emptiness (the attainment of the fruition of Arahantship)'. Indeed, the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) is the place of mastery for the Buddhas. It occurs in the sense of gocarajjhatta (internal resort/object) in such passages as 'Ānanda, that bhikkhu should settle his mind internally in that same previous sign of concentration'. In this context as well, only the sense of gocarajjhatta should be understood. Therefore, 'ajjhatta' means in the object of meditation which has become the internal resort. 'Purimaṃ' means facing. 'Supatiṭṭhitā' means in the well-established mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati). In this context, jhāna is referred to by using mindfulness as the head. This means: 'having entered the noble jhāna obtained by the power of the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of the body within one's own continuity'.
340:
It should be understood only as gocarajjhatta (internal resort). Therefore, 'ajjhatta' means in the meditation object which is the internal resort. 'Parimukhaṃ' means in front. 'Supatiṭṭhitā' means in the well-established mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati). In this context, jhāna is referred to by using mindfulness as the head. This means: 'having entered the noble jhāna obtained by the power of the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of the body within one's own continuity'.

While the Blessed One was staying in Sāvatthī, one day this venerable elder, after wandering for alms in Sāvatthī and returning from the alms round after the meal, entered the monastery, performed his duties to the Blessed One, and sat for the day-abiding in a place for day-abiding. Having spent the day-part with various meditative attainments, he descended to the middle of the monastery in the evening. While the Blessed One was staying in the Gandhakuṭi (Fragrant Chamber), the elder thought, 'It is not yet the time to approach the Blessed One,' and having determined a period of time under a certain tree not far from the Gandhakuṭi, he sat down, entering the aforementioned meditative attainment. The Teacher, while staying in the Gandhakuṭi itself, saw the elder sitting in that manner. Therefore, it is said: 'At that time, the venerable Mahākaccāna ... [was sitting with mindfulness] well-established.'

'Having understood this matter' means: having understood in every way the attainment of jhāna by the venerable Mahākaccāna Thera, which was achieved by the power of the development of the foundations of mindfulness, the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) that clarifies that meaning.

In that inspired utterance: 'For whom mindfulness is always present, mindfulness of the body is constantly well-established' means: for that person who has undertaken insight (vipassanā), dividing the day into six parts, at all times, mindfulness should be well-established through the power of constant, continuous, and persistent application in contemplating as impermanent, etc., the five aggregates of clinging which have the body as their object, in the two-fold body by way of the distinction of mind and matter (nāmarūpa).

This venerable elder first produced jhāna by the power of the meditation subject of mindfulness of the body, and making that jhāna the basis, he established insight (vipassanā) headed by the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of the body, and reached Arahantship. Later on, he mostly entered that same jhāna, and after emerging from it, he contemplated in that same way and entered the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). The Teacher, wishing to show the method by which he reached Arahantship, said: 'For whom mindfulness is always present, mindfulness of the body is constantly well-established.' Then, to clarify the manner in which that mindfulness is established, he said: 'If it (past kamma) were not, it (present life) would not be for me; if it (future kamma) will not be, it (future life) will not be for me.'
341:
The meaning of that [Pali] should be understood in two ways: by way of the preliminary stage of contemplation and by way of the time of contemplation. Of these two, first, by way of the preliminary stage, 'No cassa no ca me siyā' (It might not be, and it might not be mine) means: if my kamma of defilements had not existed in the past, this present individuality (attabhāva) would not be for me, it would not have arisen. Because kamma and defilements did exist for me in the past, therefore this present individuality of mine, which has those as its cause, now proceeds. 'Na bhavissati na ca me bhavissati' (It will not be, and it will not be mine) means: because of the attainment of the opposite [the Path] in this individuality, the kamma of defilements will not be for me, it will not arise; and in the future, the round of results (vipākavaṭṭa) will not be for me, it will not proceed. Thus, in the three periods of time, this group of five aggregates called my individuality has the kamma of defilements as its cause; it does not have a Creator (Issara) or such as its cause. Just as it is for me, so it is for all beings—thus the vision of mind-and-matter with its causes is shown.

However, by way of the time of contemplation, 'No cassa no ca me siyā' means: because this group of five aggregates is impermanent (anicca) in the sense of non-existence after having come to be, suffering (dukkha) in the sense of constant oppression, and non-self (anattā) in the sense of not being subject to one's will; thus, if there were no such thing as a self, nor anything else distinct from the five aggregates, then, Venerable Sir, if such did not exist, there would be nothing of mine. 'Na bhavissati' should be understood in terms of self and what belongs to self (attaniya). Just as this mind-and-matter is empty of self and what belongs to self in the present and in the past, so too 'Na bhavissati na me bhavissati' means: in the future also, there will be no such thing as a self distinct from the aggregates, it will not proceed. For that very reason, nothing that is a ground for concern will be for me; in the future also, nothing called 'what belongs to self' associated with me will be for me. By this statement, he shows the absence of anything to be grasped as 'I' and the absence of anything to be grasped as 'mine' in the three periods of time. By showing this, the fourfold emptiness (catukkoṭika suññatā) is revealed.

'Anupubbavihārī tattha so' (There, he is one who dwells in succession) means: thus, the practitioner (yogāvacara) who constantly contemplates the emptiness of self and what belongs to self in those formations (saṅkhāras) throughout the three periods of time, when insight knowledges such as the knowledge of rise and fall (udayabbayañāṇa) arise in sequence, he is one who dwells in successive contemplation by way of the practice of successive insight. 'Kālena taret vīsattikaṃ' (In time, he would cross the entangler) means: that practitioner who stands having brought insight to its peak, at the time of the maturity of the faculties, or at the time associated with the Path of insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā), or at the time of the arising of the Noble Path...
342:
...at the time of its arising, because it [craving] constantly entangles the entirety of the three worlds, he would cross the craving called 'the entangler' (vīsattikā); having crossed it, he would stand on the other shore of that craving—this is the meaning.

Thus, the Blessed One, referring to another person, uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) revealing the attainment of Arahantship by the Venerable Mahākaccāna.

## The Commentary on the Eighth Sutta is finished.

## 9. Udapānasutta-vaṇṇanā (Commentary on the Well Sutta)

In the ninth sutta, 'Mallesu' (among the Mallas) refers to the princes who are inhabitants of the country named Malla. A single country which is the dwelling place of those princes is also traditionally called 'Malla' by way of usage; in that Malla country (is the meaning). Some teachers, however, read it as 'Mālesu'. 'Cāriyaṃ caramāno' (wandering on a journey) means: while wandering on a journey through the great region by way of a leisurely tour. 'Mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena' (with a great community of monks) means: with a large group of recluses endowed with immeasurable virtues. For at that time, the Blessed One had a great retinue of monks. 'Thūṇaṃ nāma mallānaṃ brāhmaṇagāmo' (a brahmin village of the Mallas named Thūṇa) is a village called a brahmin village because of the abundance of brahmins, named Thūṇa, located in the Malla country at the southeastern boundary of the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa). 'Tadavasari' means: he arrived at that village; he reached the road leading to Thūṇa village—this is the meaning. 'Assosuṃ' means: they heard; they came to know by following the sound of the words that reached the door of their ears. The word 'kho' is an indeclinable used either as a verse-filler (padapūraṇa) or for emphasis (avadhāraṇa). In that context, with the sense of emphasis, it means they simply heard; there was no obstacle to their hearing. As a verse-filler, it is merely for the smoothness of the words and syllables. 'Thūṇeyyakā' means the inhabitants of Thūṇa village. In the term 'brāhmaṇagahapatikā', they are called 'brāhmaṇa' because they study the Vedas; the meaning is that they recite and study the mantras. This is the definition for brahmins by birth. However, the Noble Ones (ariyas) are called 'brāhmaṇa' because they have barred (bāhita) evil. 'Gahapatikā' (householders) refers to all those who dwell in a house, excluding the warrior caste (khattiya) and the brahmin caste; specifically, the merchant caste (vessa). Brahmins and householders are 'brāhmaṇagahapatikā'.

Now, to show the matter which they heard, it is said: 'The recluse Gotama, sirs...' and so forth. Therein, he should be known as a 'Samaṇa' (recluse) because he has stilled (samita) evil.
343:
It has also been said: "Evil unwholesome states are calmed for him," and so forth (M. i. 434). The Blessed One has also calmed all evil in every way through the peerless Noble Path. Because he has thus calmed evil, this name "Samaṇa" (Ascetic) is a name acquired through the attainment of qualities as they really are. The word "khalu" is an indeclinable used in the sense of report. The word "bho" is merely a form of address arising from the birth of those of the Brahmin class. It is also said: "He is called a 'Bhovādi' if he is one with defilements" (Dhp. 396). "Gotama" is the proclamation of the Blessed One by way of his clan. Therefore, in the phrase "Samaṇo khalu bho Gotamo," the meaning here is: "The ascetic Gotama, it is said, sirs."

The term "Sakyaputta" (Son of the Sakyans) points to the Blessed One’s high birth. The phrase "Sakyakulā pabbajita" (gone forth from the Sakyan clan) points to the fact of his going forth out of faith. It means he went forth out of faith for the sake of attaining renunciation, having abandoned that clan while it was still undiminished, not being overcome by any loss of wealth. "They filled the well with grass and chaff up to its mouth" means they filled the drinking well with grass and chaff to the level of its opening; the meaning is that they closed the well by throwing in grass and such.

It is said that outside that village of Thūna, on the path by which the Blessed One was coming, there was a single well used by the Brahmins. Apart from that, all other water sources such as wells and tanks there were dry and without water at that time. Then the people of Thūna, having no confidence in the Triple Gem and being overcome by stinginess, heard of the Blessed One’s arrival and thought: "If the ascetic Gotama enters this village with his disciples and stays for two or three days, he will establish all these people in his own teaching; then the Brahmin religion will find no footing." Seeking to prevent the Blessed One from staying there, they consulted together: "There is no water elsewhere in this village; we shall make that well unusable. In this way, the ascetic Gotama will not enter this village with his disciples." Having so consulted, all the villagers took water for seven days, filled their jars and such, and then blocked the well with grass and chaff. Therefore it is said: "They filled the well with grass and chaff up to its mouth, saying, 'Let those shaveling ascetics not drink water.'"

In that passage, "muṇḍakā samaṇakā" (shaveling ascetics): while it would be proper to call those with shaven heads "shaven ones" and ascetics "ascetics," they spoke thus with the intention of reviling and showing contempt. The word "mā" is in the sense of prohibition; "mā apaṃsu" means "let them not drink." From the road...
344:
"Okkamma" means having stepped aside from the road. "Etamhā" (from this) refers to that very well which had been treated in such a way by those Brahmins. Did the Blessed One say, "Bring water from this well," without reflecting on the misconduct of those Brahmins, or did he say it knowing and having reflected? The Blessed One said it while knowing, in order to manifest his own Buddha-power, to tame those Brahmins, and to make them free from the "poison" of conceit; it was not because he desired to drink water. For that very reason, unlike in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta, it is not said here, "I am thirsty." However, the Treasurer of the Dhamma (Ānanda), not knowing the Teacher's intention and wishing to report the misconduct committed by the people of Thūna, said: "Now, Bhante, that well..." and so forth.

In that passage, "idāni" means now, at the very time of our arrival. They also read: "Bhante, this well." Although the Elder refused twice, on the third time he thought, "The Tathāgatas should not be opposed three times; some reason must have been seen by the Long-Sighted One." Then, taking the Blessed One’s bowl—which had been offered by the Four Great Kings—he went to the well. As the Elder approached, the water in the well became full, overflowed, and flowed all around; all the grass and chaff floated up and cleared away by themselves. By that flowing stream of water, which increased more and more, all the water sources in that village such as lotus ponds that had been dry became filled; likewise the moats, pits, pools, and low-lying areas. The entire area of the village was submerged by a great flood, just as in the time of heavy rains. The five kinds of water-born lotuses, such as the white, blue, red, and pink lotuses, sprang up and bloomed here and there, covering the surface of the water. Water birds such as swans, cranes, ruddy sheldrakes, teals, and herons dwelt and wandered here and there. When the people of Thūna saw that great flood overflowing in such a way, turbulent with waves all around, rising from the edges, and with delightful foam and bubbles, they were struck with wonder and amazement at what had never happened before, and they consulted thus: "We strove to cut off the water for the ascetic Gotama, but this great flood has increased in this way since the time of his arrival; undoubtedly this is his psychic power and majesty. Indeed, he is of great psychic power and great majesty. It is possible that this great flood might rise up and even submerge our village. Come, let us approach and attend upon the ascetic Gotama, and having confessed our fault, let us ask for his forgiveness."
345:
All of them, being of one mind, formed a group and left the village to approach the Blessed One. Having approached, some bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, some raised their joined palms in reverence, some exchanged pleasant greetings with the Blessed One, some sat down in silence, and some announced their names and clans.

Having done so, they all sat at a respectful distance and said, "Master Gotama, we have here prevented Master Gotama and the disciples of Master Gotama from obtaining water, and we have thrown grass and chaff into that certain well. Although that well is inanimate, as if it were animate and as if knowing the virtues of Master Gotama, it has spontaneously removed all the grass and chaff and become perfectly pure. All the low-lying areas in this place have also become filled with a great flood of water and have become delightful; the creatures that depend on water are greatly pleased. Although we are human beings, we did not know the virtues of Master Gotama, and thus we acted in this way. May Master Gotama please act so that this great flood does not overwhelm this village. Transgression has overcome us according to our foolishness; may Master Gotama accept our confession of this transgression out of compassion for us."

The Blessed One said, "Indeed, transgression has overcome you according to your foolishness. We accept it for your future restraint." Having accepted their confession and knowing their minds were settled in faith, he taught the Dhamma further in accordance with their dispositions. Having heard the Blessed One's Dhamma teaching, they became settled in faith, established themselves in the refuges and so forth, bowed to the Blessed One, circumambulated him, and departed.

Even before they arrived, the Venerable Ānanda, having seen that miracle and being filled with wonder and amazement, took water in his bowl, offered it to the Blessed One, and reported that matter. Therefore, the words beginning with "Evaṃ, bhante" (Yes, Bhante) were spoken in the Pāḷi text.

In that text, "mukhato ovamitvā" means having discarded all that grass and so forth from the mouth (opening) of the well. "Vissandanto maññe" means that the flood of water, which previously had to be drawn up with a long rope, stood brimful so that a crow could drink, as if it were about to overflow from the mouth of the well when the Elder Ānanda arrived after taking the Blessed One's bowl. This description of the water's behavior refers to the time when the Elder arrived. After that, as mentioned before, all the low-lying areas in that village became filled with water. This miracle was not due to the Buddha's resolve, nor by the power of the devas, but rather...
346:
...by the power of the Blessed One's merit, just as when he traveled from Rājagaha to Vesālī to preach the Ratana Sutta (the water rose). Some teachers, however, say, "It was done by devas who desired the welfare of the people of Thūna, in order to inspire faith in the Blessed One." Others say, "The Naga king living beneath the well did this." All such claims are without grounds, because it is clearly shown that the emergence of water occurred solely through the power of the Blessed One's merit.

"Etamatthaṃ viditvā" means having known in every aspect that meaning, which is the fulfillment of one's own desire without a specific resolve, he uttered this Udāna (inspired utterance) to illuminate that meaning.

In that Udāna verse:
If water were always available everywhere,
If water could be obtained just by wishing,
What would one do with a well? What use would it be?
Having cut craving at the root, why would one go seeking?

Beings who are bound by that craving, having no merit, are afflicted by the suffering of not obtaining what they desire. A Fully Enlightened Buddha like me, who stands having cut the root of that craving (or at the root), for what reason would he go seeking drinking water or any other requisite? Some also read "mūlato chettā," meaning one who cuts the root of craving, or one who cuts craving from the very root. This means: the Fully Enlightened Buddha, who, starting from the Great Resolve (Mahāpaṇidhāna) which is the root of Bodhi, fulfilled the entire immeasurable accumulation of merit for the sake of the world's benefit without regard for himself, has cut craving from the root. Since that Buddha no longer experiences the failure to obtain desires caused by craving, for what reason would he go seeking water? But these Brahmins of Thūna, being extremely foolish, did this (refused water) without knowing this reason.

## The Commentary on the Ninth Sutta is finished.

## 10. Utenasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the tenth sutta, the Utena Sutta, "rañño utenassa" means of the king named Utena, who is also called "Vajjirājā." "Uyyānagatassa" means of the king who went to the park for the sake of sporting in the park. Here, the genitive case (gatassa) is used in the sense of disregard (anādara). Alternatively, it is used in the sense of relation (sambandha) in regard to the word "antepuraṃ." "Kāḷakaṇṇikā" means they died by being burned. Here, regarding the women headed by Sāmāvatī, if there is a question: "Whose daughter is this Sāmāvatī? Why was she burned?", I shall provide the answer. She was the daughter of a treasurer in the city of Bhaddavatī, and was a woman placed in the position of a daughter by the treasurer Ghosita. She had five hundred female attendants and was the chief queen of King Utena. This woman named Sāmāvatī was a noble disciple (Sotāpanna) who frequently practiced loving-kindness (mettā); her story is briefly mentioned in this Udāna commentary. For the full details, the life story of Sāmāvatī should be understood as told in the Dhammapada commentary. Māgaṇḍiyā, the daughter of the Brahmin named Māgaṇḍiya, having seen the Blessed One, her parents (offered her), but the Blessed One said, "I would not touch her even with my foot for the sake of sexual intercourse..."
347:
To the one who has gone (to the garden). Here, the genitive case 'gatassa' is used in the sense of disregard (anādara). Alternatively, this genitive case exists as a connection (sambandha) in relation to the word 'antepuraṃ'. 'Kālaṅkatāni' means they died having been burnt by fire. In the phrase 'Sāmāvatīpamukhāni', if one asks 'Who is this Sāmāvatī and why was she burnt?', it is said: She was the daughter of a treasurer in the city of Bhaddavatī, placed in the position of a daughter by the treasurer Ghosaka, had five hundred women as attendants, was the chief queen of King Utena, frequently dwelled in loving-kindness (mettā), and was a noble disciple (ariyasāvikā) named Sāmāvatī. This is just a summary. For the full account of Sāmāvatī’s life from the beginning, it should be understood as stated in the Dhammapada Commentary (Sāmāvatī-vatthu).

The daughter of a Brahmin named Māgaṇḍiya, having heard this verse spoken by the Blessed One to her parents—
"Even after seeing Taṇhā, Arati, and Rāga,
I had no desire for sexual intercourse.
What is this body, full of urine and excrement?
I would not want to touch it even with my foot"—
bore a grudge against the Teacher. Later, when Māgaṇḍiyā was established in the position of queen by King Utena, she learned that the Blessed One had arrived in Kosambī and that the five hundred women led by Sāmāvatī were lay followers (upāsikā). Thinking, "The ascetic Gotama has arrived in this city; now I will know what to do with him, and I will also know what to do with these attendants of his, led by Sāmāvatī," she tried by various means to cause harm to the Tathāgata and those women, but was unsuccessful. Again, one day, while going to play in the garden with the king, she sent a message to her uncle: "Go to Sāmāvatī’s palace, have the cloth-store and oil-store opened, soak the cloths in oil jars, wrap them around the pillars, gather all those women together, close the door, bolt it from the outside, and after setting the house on fire with torches, come down and leave."

Hearing this, the uncle ascended the palace, opened the stores, soaked the cloths in oil jars, and began wrapping them around the pillars. Then the women led by Sāmāvatī approached him, asking, "Uncle, what is this?" "Dear daughters, the king has ordered these pillars to be wrapped with oil-soaked rags for the purpose of strengthening them."
348:
He continued, "It is difficult to know whether the deeds of kings are well-planned or ill-planned; do not stay near me." Saying this, he put the women who had come into the rooms, closed the doors, bolted them from the outside, and after setting fire starting from the base, he descended. Sāmāvatī gave them this advice: "Dear daughters, for us wandering in this beginningless Saṃsāra, the number of times we have died being burnt by fire in this very way is not easy to determine even by Buddha-knowledge; therefore, be heedful."

Those women had reached the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala) in the presence of the noble disciple Khujjuttarā—who had heard the Dhamma from the Teacher, attained the fruits, understood the Dispensation, and reached the analytical knowledge of a learner (sekkhapaṭisambhidā)—while she was preaching the Dhamma exactly as taught by the Teacher. While the house was burning, they remained diligently engaged in the practice of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna) at intervals, and by contemplating the meditation on the discernment of feelings (vedanāpariggaha-kammaṭṭhāna), some reached the second fruit and some the third fruit before they passed away. Then, while the monks were wandering for alms in Kosambī, they learned of that event and, after their meal, informed the Blessed One and asked about their future destination. The Blessed One told the monks of their attainment of the noble fruits. Therefore, it was said: "At that time, of King Utena... (pe)... they did not die fruitlessly."

In that context, "anipphalā" means not without fruit; they died having indeed attained the fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala). While they were attaining those fruits, Sāmāvatī advised them with these verses:

"Exert yourselves, go forth, apply yourselves to the Buddha's teaching;
Shatter the army of Death, as an elephant shatters a hut of reeds.
Whoever shall dwell heedfully in this Dhamma and Discipline,
Having abandoned the cycle of birth, shall make an end of suffering."

Being thus advised by these verses, they practiced insight by contemplating the meditation on the discernment of feelings and attained the second and third fruits. As for Khujjuttarā, because she had remaining lifespan and because she had not performed such kamma in the past, she was outside that palace. Some say, "She had gone ten leagues away." Then, the monks raised a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, such a death is truly unsuitable for noble disciples." The Teacher came and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you sitting together now?" and when they replied, "For such a discussion..."
349:
The Blessed One said, "Monks, although it was not fitting for these women to die in this way in this existence, they have received a death that is indeed fitting for the karma they performed in the past." Having said this, and being requested by the monks, he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, eight Paccekabuddhas regularly took their meals in the king’s palace. Five hundred women attended to those Paccekabuddhas. Among them, seven went to the Himalayas, while one sat in a grass thicket near the riverbank in meditative attainment (samāpatti). Then one day, after the Paccekabuddhas had departed, the King went to that riverbank wishing to play in the water with those women. After playing in the water for half the day, the women, oppressed by the cold and wishing to warm themselves, surrounded that grass thicket—which was covered with dry grass on top—perceiving it to be a "heap of grass," and set it on fire. When the grass burned away and fell, they saw the Paccekabuddha and thought, "The King’s Paccekabuddha is burning! If the King finds out, he will destroy us. Let us make him burn thoroughly." All the women brought wood and other materials from here and there, piled them on top of the Paccekabuddha, set them ablaze, and left, thinking, "Now he will burn."

Initially, they acted without intention, but now they became bound by their karma. However, even if one were to bring a thousand cartloads of wood and set fire to a Paccekabuddha who is within meditative attainment, one could not cause even a trace of heat to affect him. Therefore, on the seventh day, that Paccekabuddha arose from his attainment and departed at ease. Because those women performed that unwholesome karma, they were cooked in hell for many hundreds of thousands of years. Due to the residual result of that karma, they were burned in house fires in this same manner for a hundred existences. This was their past karma.

However, because they realized the Noble Fruits (ariya-phala) and attended upon the Triple Gem in this existence, those among them who were Non-returners (Anāgāmī) were reborn in the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa). Others were reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa, Yāma, Tusita, Nimmānarati, and Paranimmitavasavattī celestial realms.

King Udena, hearing that "Sāmāvatī’s palace is burning," arrived quickly but reached that place only after those women had already burned to death. Upon arrival, having extinguished the fire and being overcome with great sorrow, he learned through a stratagem that Māgaṇḍiyā had caused it. Prompted by the evil karma committed against the noble disciples (ariya-sāvikā), he inflicted royal punishment upon Māgaṇḍiyā along with her relatives. Thus, Māgaṇḍiyā, together with her retinue, friends, and kinsmen, met with ruin and destruction.
350:
"Knowing this matter" means knowing in every aspect the cause of the ruin and destruction of those women led by Sāmāvatī in the fire, and the cause of the ruin and destruction of Māgaṇḍiyā along with her friends and relatives by the king’s authority. He then uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) explaining that matter.

In that verse, "The world is bound by delusion, it appears as if capable" (mohasambandhano loko, bhabbarūpova dissati) means: although the world of beings here appears as if it were capable or endowed with causes, such a person is also bound by delusion, enveloped by delusion. Not knowing what is for their own benefit or harm, they do not practice what is beneficial, but instead accumulate much demerit that brings harm and suffering. There is also a reading "bhavarūpova dissati." Its meaning is: this world is bound by delusion, enveloped by delusion; therefore, one’s self appears as if it were of an eternal nature (sassata-sabhāva), appearing as if one were ageless and immortal. Because of such a perception, one commits deeds that should not be done, such as taking life.

"The fool is bound by acquisitions, surrounded by darkness. It seems as if eternal" (upadhibandhano bālo, tamasā parivārito; sassatoriva khāyati) means: this blind, foolish world is not only bound by delusion, but is indeed bound by acquisitions (upadhi, such as the acquisitions of defilements, etc.) and is surrounded by the darkness of ignorance (avijjā). The meaning is this: because of the absence of that knowledge by which one could see sense pleasures and the aggregates correctly as "impermanent, suffering, and subject to change," the blind worldling is surrounded and obstructed on all sides by the darkness of ignorance. Therefore, they are bound by acquisitions through the power of these acquisitions—namely, the acquisition of sense pleasures, the acquisition of defilements, and the acquisition of the aggregates. Consequently, to that blind worldling who sees with acquisitions, the self appears as if it were eternal, permanent, and existing for all time. There is also a reading "asassatiriva khāyati." Its meaning is: because of the view that "the self always exists and is found," that acquisition of the world, which is otherwise non-eternal (anicca), appears as if it were a part through the power of wrong attachment (micchābhinivesa); it stands before them. In the word "sassatoriva," the letter "r" is a euphonic conjunction.

"For one who sees, there is nothing" (passato natthi kiñcanaṃ) means: for one who grasps the formations (saṅkhāra) and practices insight (vipassanā) by way of impermanence and so on, for that person who sees, knows, and penetrates things as they really are with the Path-knowledge (magga-paññā) accompanied by insight-wisdom, there is no "something" (kiñcana) such as lust (rāga) and so on, by which they would be bound in Saṃsāra. The implication is that only one who does not see in this way would be bound in Saṃsāra by the bonds of ignorance, craving, wrong view, and so forth.

## The Commentary on the Tenth Sutta is finished.
## The Commentary on the Cūḷavagga is also finished.
351:
## 8. Pāṭaligāmiya Vagga
## 1. Commentary on the First Sutta Related to Nibbāna

In the first sutta of the Pāṭaligāmiya Vagga, the term 'nibbānapaṭisaṃyuttāya' refers to [a discourse] that proceeds by way of making known the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu), which relies on the deathless element (amata-dhātu). 'Dhammiyā kathāyā' means by way of a Dhamma teaching. 'Sandasseti' (shows) means he demonstrates Nibbāna by way of its individual essence (sabhāva-lakkhaṇa) and its own characteristics (salakkhaṇa). 'Samādapeti' (encourages) means he makes those monks take up that very meaning. 'Samuttejeti' (rouses) means he inspires and illuminates them, generating enthusiasm in grasping that meaning. 'Sampahaṃseti' (gladdens) means he pleases them thoroughly in every way through the sublime qualities of Nibbāna.

Alternatively, 'sandasseti' means he clearly demonstrates [Nibbāna] in various ways according to the inclinations of those monks, using such methods as: "This is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation," and so on. 'Samādapeti' means he makes them properly take it up, making the monks lean, slope, and incline toward Nibbāna along with the practice for its attainment, saying: "It should be attained through this Noble Path." 'Samuttejeti' means he rouses them to strive for the attainment of Nibbāna, or purifies their minds therein, saying: "Do not fall into negligence or stop halfway in the right practice, thinking 'This Nibbāna is difficult to do or difficult to achieve.' For one who is possessed of the necessary support (upanissaya) and is energetic, this is not difficult. Therefore, exert yourselves, strive, and make an effort through the practice of purification, starting with the purification of virtue (sīla-visuddhi)." 'Sampahaṃseti' means he gladdens, cheers, delights, and consoles the minds of those monks by revealing the benefits of Nibbāna through many methods, such as: "Nibbāna is the crushing of intoxication, the removal of thirst, the uprooting of attachment," "the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion," "the unconditioned," and "the deathless and the peaceful."

'Te dhā' means 'te idha' (those monks here in this Dispensation). 'Aṭṭhiṃ katvā' means having noted, "This is a benefit we should attain," and thus becoming interested in that teaching, considering it beneficial. 'Manasi katvā' means keeping it in mind, without the mind wandering to other objects, [making] that teaching one's own...
352:
...making it the very object of the mind. "Sabbaṃ cetaso samannāharitvā" (applying the whole mind) means reflecting on the teaching from the beginning to the end with the entire active mind, making the attention directed solely toward that teaching. Alternatively, "sabbaṃ cetaso samannāharitvā" means properly bringing the teaching [into the mind] repeatedly with the whole mind. This is what is meant: without letting the teaching—which arose from the mind of the Exalted One as he taught—go outside, one properly brings it in repeatedly without distortion, bringing it into one's own mental continuum and thoroughly attending to the teaching exactly as it was taught. "Ohitasotā" means having ears inclined, ears well-placed. Or "ohitasotā" means having ears that are not distracted. Indeed, even when it is being perceived, non-distraction in hearing (avikkhepa) can be called "restraint of the ear-faculty" (sotindriya), just like the restraint of the eye-faculty (cakkhundriya) and so on. Here, with all four terms starting from "aṭṭhiṃ katvā," the act of listening respectfully is shown by illustrating the monks' devotion to hearing that Dhamma.

"Having understood this matter" (etam-atthaṃ viditvā) means having understood in every way the respectful manner in which those monks listened to that Dhamma talk related to Nibbāna. "This inspired utterance" (imaṃ udānaṃ) means he uttered this inspired utterance which clarifies the existence of Nibbāna in the ultimate sense (paramattha) by way of teaching the Dhamma that is the opposite of [conditioned] things. 

In that inspired utterance, "atthi" means it exists, it is found in the ultimate sense. "Bhikkhave" is an address to those monks. Is it not true that an inspired utterance (udāna) is a statement prompted by joy and happiness or by religious urgency (dhamma-saṃvega), uttered without regard for an audience? And it appears that way in all these suttas. Why then did the Blessed One address those monks while uttering this inspired utterance? It was for the purpose of informing those monks. After teaching the Dhamma related to Nibbāna to those monks, the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance with joy and happiness that arose from recollecting the qualities of Nibbāna. In this world, all natural phenomena other than Nibbāna are found to be dependent on causes (paccaya); they are not found to be independent of causes. Knowing the thought in the minds of those monks, "By what cause is this Dhamma of Nibbāna obtained?" and wishing to inform them, he said, "Monks, there is that sphere (āyatana)," and so on. It should be understood that he did not speak by making them an audience in an absolute sense. "Tadāyatanaṃ" means that cause (kāraṇa). The letter "da" is a phonetic link (padasandhi).
353:
Nibbāna is called an "āyatana" (sphere/base) in the sense of being a cause, because it serves as an object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) for the knowledge of the Path and Fruit (magga-phala-ñāṇa) and so forth, just as visible forms and so forth are object-conditions for eye-consciousness and so forth. By this much, the Blessed One made known to those monks the existence of the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu) in the ultimate sense.

In this regard, the following is the sequence of the Dhamma (dhammanvaya): Since conditioned things (saṅkhata-dhamma) exist in this world, the unconditioned element, which is the opposite of those conditioned things, must also exist among natural phenomena. Just as when suffering (dukkha) exists, its opposite, happiness (sukha), also exists; and just as when heat exists, cold also exists; and when unwholesome states exist, wholesome states also exist. It has been said:

"Just as when suffering exists, that which is called happiness also exists;
Even so, when existence (bhava) exists, the cessation of existence (vibhava/nibbāna) should also be sought.
Just as when heat exists, there exists another which is cool;
Even so, when the three fires exist, Nibbāna should also be sought.
Just as when evil exists, the good also exists;
Even so, when birth (jāti) exists, the birthless (ajāti) should also be sought."
(and so forth, as stated in the Buddhavamsa).

Furthermore, the investigation into the existence of Nibbāna in the ultimate sense will be clarified later.

Thus, the Blessed One, having directly shown the existence of the unconditioned element in the ultimate sense, now speaks the words beginning with "Where there is neither earth nor water" to show its nature by way of excluding those things that are contrary to it. In that passage, because Nibbāna is of a nature contrary to all conditioned things (saṅkhāra), just as Nibbāna does not exist anywhere within conditioned things, so too all conditioned things do not exist in Nibbāna. Indeed, the coexistence of conditioned and unconditioned things is impossible. In this regard, the following is the explanation of the meaning: In that Nibbāna, in that unconditioned element, there is no earth-element (pathavī-dhātu) characterized by hardness, no water-element (āpo-dhātu) characterized by trickling, no fire-element (tejo-dhātu) characterized by heat, and no air-element (vāyo-dhātu) characterized by supporting. By this statement of the absence of the four great elements (mahābhūta), the absence of all derived matter (upādā-rūpa) is also stated, because it is dependent on them. Thus, without remainder...
354:
The absence of the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava) and the fine-material existence (rūpabhava) in that Nibbāna is stated because those existences do not occur apart from the great elements. For neither the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra-bhava) nor the single-constituent existence (ekavokāra-bhava) can occur without the support of the great elements.

Now, although Nibbāna is of an immaterial nature, in order to show that the states pertaining to the immaterial existence (arūpabhava) do not exist in that Nibbāna, it is said: "Neither the sphere of infinite space... [pe]... nor the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception." In that passage, "neither the sphere of infinite space" means that the three types of consciousness belonging to the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana-cittuppāda)—wholesome, resultant, and functional—along with their objects, do not exist in that Nibbāna. The same method applies to the remaining spheres. Just as the sense-world and so forth do not exist in Nibbāna, so too this world and the next world do not exist there; thus He said: "Neither this world nor the next world." The meaning of that text is: both the world of the aggregates and so forth, which is conventionally called "this state of being, the world seen here and now," and the world of the aggregates and so forth, which is conventionally called "the other, the world beyond," do not exist in that Nibbāna. "Neither both the moon and the sun" means: since darkness would exist if there were matter (rūpa), the moon and the sun would have to circulate to dispel that darkness. But where there is no material form at all, how could there be darkness? Or how could there be the moon and the sun that dispel darkness? Therefore, the meaning is that both the moon and the sun do not exist in that Nibbāna. By this Pali passage, He shows only the luminous nature of Nibbāna.

By this much, for the sake of clarifying to those monks who had not yet realized the four truths, the Nibbāna which is the Deathless (amata)—never before experienced even in a dream in the beginningless saṃsāra, extremely profound, extremely difficult to see, subtle and fine, beyond the sphere of logic, ultimately peaceful, to be known by the wise, and extremely sublime—the King of Dhamma first dispels their ignorance and so forth by stating its existence: "Monks, there is that sphere (āyatana)." Then He clarifies that Nibbāna by excluding other things: "Where there is neither earth... [pe]... nor both the moon and the sun." Therefore, that unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu), which is of a nature free from all conditioned things such as earth and so forth, is shown as Nibbāna. For that very reason, He said: "There, monks, I do not say there is a coming."

In that text, "tatra" means "in that Nibbāna." The word "api" is used in the sense of inclusion. Monks, just as I do not speak of a coming of any state from anywhere in the occurrence of conditioned things (saṅkhāra) because they arise according to conditions, so too I do not speak of any coming in that Nibbāna. Why? Because there is no place to be reached by coming. Nor do I speak of a going. Why? Because there is no place to go to. In truth, in that Nibbāna, apart from being an object of the knowledge of beings, there is no coming or going, nor do passing away (cuti) and rebirth (upapatti) occur. There is also the Pali text: "Nor do I speak of a destination (gati)." The meaning of that text is: to a state other than that Nibbāna...
355:
It is because only phenomena (dhamma) arise. Likewise, in that sphere (āyatana) which is Nibbāna, because there is no place to come from, I do not speak of 'coming' (āgati) from anywhere. Because there is no place to go to, I do not speak of 'going' (gati) to anywhere. Indeed, in that Nibbāna, apart from the making of it an object by the knowledge of beings, there is no coming or going; nor do passing away (cuti) and rebirth (upapatti) occur. There is also a Pali reading "Tadāpahaṃ." The meaning of that text is: that sphere (Nibbāna) is said to have no 'coming' (āgati) because it is not to be come to like going from one village to another. It is said to have no 'going' (gati) because it is not to be gone to. It is said to have no 'staying' (ṭhiti) because it is not a location like the earth or mountains. Alternatively, I do not speak of staying, passing away, or rebirth because there is no arising (uppāda) as it is not connected with conditions, no passing away (cavana) as it has the nature of the Deathless (amata), and no staying (ṭhiti) defined by those two because there is no arising or cessation.

However, in reality, that Nibbāna is called "unestablished" (appatiṭṭha) because it does not stay in anything, both because it has the nature of the formless and because it is not connected with conditions. It is called "non-occurrence" (appavatta) because there is no occurrence (pavatta) in that Nibbāna and because it is the opposite of occurrence. Although it is of a formless nature, Nibbāna is called a "sphere" (āyatana) which is simply non-apprehending of an object, because unlike feelings and so on, it does not take any object and it does not depend on any support. This word "eva" (only/certainly) should be applied to both terms: "certainly unestablished" (appatiṭṭham-eva) and "certainly non-occurring" (appavattam-eva). "This is the end of suffering" (esevanto dukkhassa) means: there exists Nibbāna with the characteristics already mentioned, described and praised by words such as "unestablished" and so on; that Nibbāna alone is the end (pariyosāna) of the entire suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa-dukkha), because when it is attained, all suffering no longer exists. Therefore, He shows that "the end of suffering" is the very nature of that Nibbāna.

## The Commentary on the First Sutta is finished.

## 2. The Commentary on the Second Sutta Connected with Nibbāna

In the second sutta, "this inspired utterance" (imaṃ udānaṃ) means: He uttered this inspired utterance to show the state of Nibbāna being hard to see because of its inherent depth. In that inspired utterance, "hard to see" (duddasaṃ) means: it is called "hard to see" because it cannot be seen by those who have not accumulated the requisites of knowledge, due to its inherent depth and its extremely subtle and delicate nature. For this was said by the Blessed One: "Māgaṇḍiya, you do not have that noble eye of wisdom by which you might know health and see Nibbāna." (M. Ni. 2.218). It was also said elsewhere: "This state is hard to see, that is, the stilling of all formations (saṅkhāra)..." (Mahāva. 8, M. Ni. 1.281, 2.337).
356:
Craving is called 'nata' (bending) because it bends towards objects such as forms and towards existences such as the sensual realm, because it proceeds with the nature of inclining towards them, and because it causes beings to bend towards those objects and existences. Because that craving called 'nata' does not exist in this Nibbāna, it is called 'anata' (non-bending); this means Nibbāna. Some also read it as 'ananta' (endless); it means the Deathless (amata), which is the cessation that is without end because of its permanent nature and is without the nature of passing away. However, some teachers say the meaning of the word 'ananta' is 'immeasurable' (appamāṇa). In this context, by the word 'hard to see' (duddasa), He shows that it is not easy for beings to develop Nibbāna, which is without conditions, because they have been saturated for a long time with defilements such as greed which weaken wisdom; therefore, Nibbāna is to be attained with difficulty. By this statement, "The truth is not easily seen," He makes that same meaning clear. In that statement, 'truth' (sacca) is Nibbāna. That Nibbāna is called 'truth' (sacca) in the sense of being non-perverted, because it is not a nature that is non-existent by any means, but exists solely as ultimate reality. That Nibbāna is not easily seen, it is not to be seen with ease and comfort, because it is to be attained only with difficulty even by those who accumulate the requisites of merit and knowledge for a very long time. For this reason, it was said by the Blessed One: "I have attained it with difficulty." (Mahāva. 8, M. Ni. 1.281, 2.337).

"For one who knows and sees, craving has been penetrated; there is no impurity" means that for one who realizes that Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca) through the realization of making it manifest (sacchikiriyā-abhisamaya), it is penetrated (paṭividdha) by way of domain, function, and object, through the penetration of the object and the penetration of non-delusion. Just as the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca) is penetrated through the realization of full understanding (pariññā-abhisamaya) and the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca) is penetrated through the realization of development (bhāvanā-abhisamaya) without delusion, so too craving is penetrated through the realization of abandoning (pahāna-abhisamaya) without delusion. Thus, for one who knows and sees the Four Truths as they really are with the wisdom of the Noble Path, the craving that bends towards existences and so on no longer exists. In the absence of that craving, the entire round of defilements (kilesa-vaṭṭa) no longer exists, and from that, the rounds of kamma and its result (kamma-vipāka-vaṭṭa) simply cannot arise. In this way, the Blessed One proclaimed to those monks the power of the Great Deathless Nibbāna, which is the cause for the complete stilling of the suffering of the round. The rest is as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Second Sutta is finished.

## 3. The Commentary on the Third Sutta Connected with Nibbāna

In the third sutta, "Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter" (atha kho bhagavā etamatthaṃ viditvā) means: at that time, it is said, the Blessed One, having shown the danger of saṃsāra through many methods...
357:
On the day the Dhamma discourse connected with Nibbāna was delivered through the power of seeing and so forth, this thought arose to those monks: "This Saṃsāra has been declared by the Blessed One as having a cause through such factors as ignorance (avijjā) and so forth; however, no cause has been stated for Nibbāna, which is the cessation of that Saṃsāra. This Nibbāna is without a cause; if it is without a cause, how can it be obtained as a true reality and an ultimate sense?"

Then the Blessed One, knowing the meaning of the monks' reflection as stated, uttered this Udāna for the purpose of dispelling the doubt of those monks, and for the purpose of crushing the false views of those outside the Dispensation, such as the Lokāyatikas, who are wrongly established in the view that "Nibbāna is merely a matter of words; Nibbāna does not exist in the ultimate sense because its nature is not found." This Udāna demonstrates that the Great Deathless Nibbāna exists in the ultimate sense.

In that Udāna, all the terms—*ajāta* (unborn), *abhūta* (unbecome), *akata* (unmade), and *asaṅkhata* (unconditioned)—are synonyms of one another. Alternatively, it is *ajāta* because it is not born or produced by a combination of causes, known as the concurrence of conditions, like feelings (*vedanā*) and so forth. It is *abhūta* because it has not become, manifested, or arisen by itself without a cause. Because it is thus unborn (*ajāta*) and unbecome (*abhūta*), it is *akata* because it is not made by any cause whatsoever. The nature of being born, become, and made belongs only to conditioned things (*saṅkhata-dhamma*) consisting of mind and matter (*nāmarūpa*); to show that this does not belong to Nibbāna, which is of an unconditioned nature, it is called *asaṅkhata*.

Or conversely, that which is made by conditions coming together is called *saṅkhata*; Nibbāna is called *asaṅkhata* because it is not so made and is devoid of the characteristics of the conditioned. Even though the state of being produced by many causes is thus denied, there might be a doubt: "Could it be made by a single cause?" To show that "it is not made by any cause whatsoever," it is called *akata*. Even though it is without conditions, there might be a doubt: "Did it become or manifest by itself?" To prevent that, it is called *abhūta*. To show that "this unconditioned, unmade, and unbecome state of Nibbāna is due to its being of a non-arising nature in every respect," it is called *ajāta*.

Having thus understood the purpose of these four terms, it should be understood that the existence of Nibbāna in the ultimate sense is proclaimed by the words: "Monks, there is that Nibbāna." Here, the reason for the Blessed One addressing them as "Monks" while uttering the Udāna should be understood in the same manner as stated below.

Thus the Teacher, having said, "Monks, there is the unborn, the unbecome, the unmade, the unconditioned," and wishing to show the reason therein, said the words beginning with: "Monks, if this [unconditioned] were not..."
358:
