The summary of the meaning of those words (beginning with "No ce taṃ, bhikkhave") is as follows: Monks, if this unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*) of the nature of the unborn and so forth did not exist, then in this world, the escape—the complete cessation—of the conditioned (*saṅkhata*) known as the five aggregates of form and so forth, which are of the nature of the born and so forth, would not be known, would not be obtained, and would not occur. For the factors of the Noble Path, such as Right View, which proceed by making Nibbāna their object, eradicate the defilements without remainder. Therefore, in this Nibbāna, the escape, which is the non-occurrence and departure of all the suffering of the round (*vaṭṭa-dukkha*), is evident.

Having thus shown the existence of Nibbāna by way of the negative method (*vyatireka*), he now spoke the words beginning with "Yasmā ca kho" to show it by way of the positive method (*anvaya*) as well. That has the same meaning as already stated. In this context, the existence of the Nibbāna element in the ultimate sense has been taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One, who has compassion for the whole world, through many scriptural passages such as: "Unconditioned phenomena, unmade phenomena"; "Monks, there is that sphere where there is neither earth..."; "This state, too, is difficult to see, namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions"; "Monks, I will teach you the unconditioned and the path leading to the unconditioned"; and also by this sutta: "Monks, there is the unborn..."

Therefore, even for the wise who have not yet realized it for themselves, there is no hesitation or doubt regarding Nibbāna. However, there are persons of wisdom who must be led by others; for the purpose of dispelling their doubt, a logical investigation by way of determining the meaning is as follows: Just as the escape, which is of an opposite nature and free from those things, is evident for the higher sensual and form realms which are to be fully understood, so too there must be an escape which is of an opposite nature and free from all conditioned things that possess such a nature. That which is this escape (*nissaraṇa*) is the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*).

Furthermore, what more is there to say? Neither insight knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) nor conformity knowledge (*anuloma-ñāṇa*), which take conditioned things as their object, are able to abandon defilements by way of eradication (*samuccheda*). Similarly, the knowledge in the first jhāna and so forth, which takes conventional truth (*sammuti-sacca*) as its object, abandons defilements only by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*), not by way of eradication. Thus, since knowledge taking conditioned things as its object and knowledge taking conventional truth as its object are incapable of the abandonment of defilements by eradication, the Noble Path knowledge (*ariya-magga-ñāṇa*), which effects the abandonment of defilements by eradication, must have an object that is of a nature opposite to those two...
359:
The object of the Noble Path knowledge, which eradicates those defilements through the abandonment by cutting off (samuccheda-pahāna), should be the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata dhātu) (which is the opposite of the two types of conditioned things). Similarly, the statement "Monks, there is the unborn, the unbecome, the unmade, the unconditioned" is a statement that illuminates the existence of the state of Nibbāna in the ultimate sense (paramattha), and because it was spoken by the Blessed One, it has an unerring meaning. This is because whatever is spoken by the Blessed One has an unerring ultimate meaning, such as "All formations are impermanent, all formations are suffering, all phenomena are non-self." Likewise, the word "Nibbāna" in some contexts refers to the true ultimate reality, while in other places, it is merely a figure of speech (upacāra), just like the word "lion." Alternatively, the unconditioned element truly exists in the ultimate sense because it has a nature that is distinct and opposite from other conditioned things. It is just like the earth element (pathavī-dhātu) or feeling (vedanā). In these ways, through logical reasoning as well, it should be understood that the unconditioned element exists in the ultimate sense.

## The Commentary on the Third Sutta is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Fourth Sutta Related to Nibbāna

In the fourth sutta, "Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter" (atha kho bhagavā etamatthaṃ viditvā) means: At that time, it is said that when the Blessed One had given a Dhamma teaching related to Nibbāna in many ways through demonstration and so on, those bhikkhus thought: "The Blessed One has shown the extraordinary power of the element of the Great Deathless Nibbāna, illustrating its benefits mixed with many aspects and variations. However, the means of attainment has not yet been spoken. How should we practice to attain this Nibbāna?" Then the Blessed One, having understood in every way this matter, which was the aforementioned reflection of those bhikkhus, "this inspired utterance" (imaṃ udānaṃ) means: He uttered this inspired utterance which clarifies the attainment of Nibbāna through the total abandonment of craving by the Noble Path for a person who, through the power of craving, does not depend on anything, has a tranquil body and mind, and has entered the path of insight (vipassanā).

In that inspired utterance, "for one who is dependent, there is wavering" (nissitassa calitaṃ) means: for one who depends on formations such as form through craving and views, there is wavering, which is the agitation of craving and views, thinking "This is mine, this is my self." For a person who has not abandoned craving and views, when pleasant feelings and so on arise, being unable to dwell overcoming them, there is the wavering, trembling, and slipping of the mental continuum from the occurrence of wholesome states due to the grasping of craving and views, such as "My feeling, I feel," and so on.
360:
...or it means "it occurs." "For one who is independent, there is no wavering" means: for one who, practicing the path of purification (visuddhipatipadā), suppresses craving and views through serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), and dwells contemplating formations by way of impermanence and so on; because he does not depend on those craving and views, there is no aforementioned wavering, slipping, or intense agitation, because the cause has been well suppressed.

"When there is no wavering" means: just as when there is no aforementioned wavering, the grasping of craving and views does not occur, so too (peace occurs) for one who strives in insight that has entered the process (vīthi). "Tranquility" (passaddhi) refers to the two kinds of tranquility that calm the defilements that cause the distress of body and mind which arise together with the insight mind. "When there is tranquility, there is no inclination" means: when there is tranquility endowed with the distinction of preceding and following, one develops concentration (samādhi) which is the basis of blameless happiness, and by making that concentration balanced with wisdom, one joins serenity and insight in tandem (yuganaddha). For one who exhausts the defilements through the sequence of the paths, craving, which receives the name "inclination" (nati) because of its bending towards the sense-sphere existence and so on, does not exist at all at the moment of the Path of Arahantship. It means it does not arise because it has been brought to the state of non-arising.

"When there is no inclination" means: because craving has been well abandoned by the Path of Arahantship, there is no obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna) of attachment or longing for the sake of existence and so on. "There is no coming and going" means: there is no coming to this world by way of rebirth (paṭisandhi), and no going from here to the next world by way of death (cuti); the future existence does not occur. "When there is no coming and going" means: when there is no coming and going in the manner described. "There is no passing away and reappearing" means: the repeated passing away and reappearing does not happen, does not occur. Indeed, when the round of defilements (kilesavaṭṭa) is absent, the round of kamma (kammavaṭṭa) is surely cut off; when that round of kamma is cut off, how can the round of result (vipākavaṭṭa) arise? Therefore, He said: "When there is no passing away and reappearing, there is neither here nor beyond," and so on. Whatever needs to be said regarding those words has already been stated in detail below in the Bāhiya Sutta. Therefore, the meaning should be understood in the same way as stated in that Bāhiya Sutta.

In this way, the Blessed One, in this sutta as well, demonstrates to those bhikkhus the power and majesty of the Great Deathless Nibbāna, which is the cause for the total cessation of the suffering of the round of rebirths, through right practice.

## The Commentary on the Fourth Sutta is finished.
361:
## 5. Commentary on the Cunda Sutta

In the fifth sutta, the term 'Mallesu' refers to the country named Malla. 'Mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena' means together with a great Sangha of bhikkhus, great in terms of both noble qualities and numerical strength. That Sangha of bhikkhus was great because they were endowed with special virtues such as morality (sīla); for even the lowest-ranking bhikkhu among them was a Sotāpanna (Stream-enterer). They were also great due to being countless in number. From the day the Buddha relinquished his life-force (āyusaṅkhāra), the bhikkhus who arrived from various places did not depart. 'Cundassa' refers to the person of this name. 'Kammāraputtassa' means the son of a goldsmith. That Cunda was a wealthy householder who became a Sotāpanna upon his first meeting with the Blessed One. In his mango grove, he prepared a Gandhakuṭi (Fragrant Chamber) suitable for the Blessed One’s residence, as well as night quarters, day quarters, assembly halls, pavilions, and walkways for the Sangha of bhikkhus. Having built a monastery surrounded by a wall and equipped with a gateway, he offered it to the Sangha headed by the Buddha. Referring to that monastery, it is said: "At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Pāvā, in the mango grove of Cunda the smith's son."

'Patiyādāpetvā' means having prepared or arranged. In the Mahā-Aṭṭhakathā, it is stated: "Sūkaramaddava is the soft and succulent meat of a pig." However, some teachers say: "Sūkaramaddava is not pork, but soft bamboo shoots trampled by pigs." Others say: "It is a type of mushroom that grows in a place trampled by pigs." Still others say: "Sūkaramaddava is a type of elixir (rasāyana)." It is said that Cunda the smith's son, having heard that "The Blessed One will attain Parinibbāna today," offered it with the wish that "By consuming this alms-food, may the Blessed One's life-span be further prolonged and sustained."

'Tena maṃ parivisa' means serve Me with that alms-food. Why did the Blessed One speak thus? Out of compassion for others. This reason is already explained in the Pāḷi text. It also shows that it was appropriate to speak thus because the alms-food he brought was unsuitable for others to consume. Into that sūkaramaddava alms-food, deities from the four great islands and their two thousand surrounding small islands infused divine essence (ojā). Therefore, no one else could properly digest it. To make this fact known and to free Cunda from the blame of others, the Teacher uttered a lion's roar (sīhanāda), saying: "Cunda, I do not see anyone else [who could digest it]..." and so forth. If others were to criticize, saying, "He did not give the leftovers of the food he ate to the bhikkhus or other people, but had it buried in a pit and destroyed," the Buddha spoke thus to ensure there would be no opportunity for such accusations and to free him from the blame of others.
362:
In those terms such as 'Sadevake', 'Sadevaka' means together with devas. 'Samāraka' means together with Māra. 'Sabrahmaka' means together with Brahmā. 'Sassamaṇabrāhmaṇī' means together with recluses and brahmins. 'Pajā' means generation, so called because of being born in various ways. 'Sadevamanussā' means together with devas and humans. In that world with its devas... in the world with its devas and humans. In that context, by the word 'Sadevaka', the five heavens of the sensual realm (kāmāvacara) are included. By the word 'Samāraka', the sixth heaven of the sensual realm is included. By the word 'Sabrahmaka', the Brahma realms such as the Brahmakāyika are included. By the word 'Sassamaṇabrāhmaṇī', both the recluses and brahmins who are hostile enemies of the Dispensation, as well as the true recluses and brahmins who have calmed or abandoned evil, are included. By the word 'Pajā', the world of beings (sattaloka) is included. By the word 'Sadevamanussā', conventional devas and the remaining humans are included. Thus, it should be understood that in this context, the world of beings is encompassed through three terms by way of the world of locations (okāsaloka), and through two terms by way of the generation of beings (pajā).

Another method: By the word 'Sadevaka', the formless realm (arūpāvacara) is included. By the word 'Samāraka', the six heavens of the sensual realm are included. By the word 'Sabrahmaka', the form realm (rūpāvacara) of Brahmā is included. By the word 'Sassamaṇabrāhmaṇī', the human world together with conventional devas by way of the four assemblies, or the rest of the world of beings, is included.

'Bhuttāvissa' means to one who has eaten. 'Kharo' means harsh or severe (pain). 'Ābādho' means a discordant (disordered) disease. 'Pabāḷhā' means strong or acute (pains). 'Māraṇantikā' means ending in death, or pains capable of bringing one near to death. 'Sato sampajāno adhivāsesi' means he endured it by establishing mindfulness well and discerning with wisdom. 'Avihaññamāno' means he endured it without being distressed, without tossing and turning like one who is unobservant of the Dhamma, as if he were not being oppressed, as if there were no suffering. In fact, those pains had already arisen for the Blessed One in Veḷuva village. However, because they were suppressed by the power of meditative attainment (samāpatti), they did not recur until the day of Parinibbāna, as they were dispelled daily through samāpatti. On that day, however, wishing to attain Parinibbāna, he did not enter samāpatti, thinking: "Even for the Buddhas who possess the strength of a billion elephants, whose bodies are like diamond, and who have accumulated the requisites of merit for an immeasurable time, such pains still occur as long as existence (bhava) remains; what then to say of others?" This was to inspire spiritual urgency (saṃvega) in beings. Therefore, the pains arose severely. 'Āyāma' means "Come, let us go."

The verses beginning with 'Cundassa bhattaṃ bhuñjitvā' were placed there later by the reciters of the Dhamma (dhamma-saṅgāhakas). Among those verses, 'Bhuttassa ca sūkaramaddavena' means that the pain arose while consuming the alms-food mixed with pork; it did not arise because of the consumption. Had it arisen before consuming it, the pain would have been extremely severe. However, because he consumed the soft food, the pain was mitigated and lessened. For that very reason, he was able to travel on foot.
363: Because he had eaten soft and oily food, the pain was slight; for that reason alone, he was able to go on foot. In this way, the 'lion's roar' he uttered—'I do not see anyone except the Tathāgata who could rightly digest that food when eaten'—was shown to be meaningful. For Buddhas, there is no such thing as a roar without cause. Because he consumed that food, it did not cause any disorder in the Blessed One; rather, it calmed the disorder arising from karma that had gained an opportunity, and because it was slight, it produced strength in his body. With that strength, he fulfilled the three purposes to be mentioned. Therefore, that consumed food was indeed rightly digested. Because the pains ended in death, they were unperceived and not apparent. ## "Viriccamāno" "Viriccamāno" means having a continuous purging of blood. "Avoca" means he spoke thus for the sake of attaining Parinibbāna in the place he desired. Why did the Blessed One go to Kusinārā while suffering from such a disease? Was it not possible to attain Parinibbāna elsewhere? It is not that it was impossible to attain Parinibbāna in any other place. However, he thought thus: "When I reach Kusinārā, there will be the occasion for the preaching of the Mahāsudassana Sutta. Through that discourse, I will preach, adorned in two recitations (bhāṇavāra), the splendor I once enjoyed in the human world, which was similar to the splendor to be enjoyed in the celestial realm. Having heard that discourse, many people will realize that merit should be performed. The wanderer Subhadda will also approach me, ask questions, and at the conclusion of the answers, he will be established in the Refuges, ordain, and having received higher ordination and developed meditation, he will attain Arahantship while I am still alive, becoming my last disciple. If I attain Parinibbāna elsewhere, there will be a great conflict over the relics; blood will flow like a river. But if I attain Parinibbāna in Kusinārā, the Brahmin Dona will settle that dispute and distribute the relics." Seeing these three reasons, the Blessed One went to Kusinārā with great effort. ## "Iṅgha" "Iṅgha" is an indeclinable in the sense of exhortation. "Kilantosmi" means "I am tired." By that word, he shows only the great strength of the aforementioned pains. Although the Blessed One could go on foot at that time by his own power, for others, the pains were so sharp, harsh, and piercing that they would not even be able to take a single step. For that reason, he said, "I will sit down." ## "Idāni" "Idāni" means "now." "Luḷitaṃ" means disturbed, as if trampled. "Āvilaṃ" means turbid. "Acchodakā" means having clear water. "Sātodakā" means having sweet water.
364:
Sītodakā means having cool water. Setodakā means being free from mud. Although water is naturally white in color, it may take on other colors due to the influence of the soil, mud, and so on. The Kakudhā River also flows with a white appearance because it has pure, clean sand. Therefore, it is called "Setodakā."

Supatitthā means having good landing places (ghats). Ramaṇīyā means being delightful because of the pleasant nature of the ground and because it is endowed with the aforementioned qualities of water.

In the statement, "Cunda, I am weary, I will lie down," the physical strength of the Blessed One is as follows: among the ten breeds of elephants—Kāḷāvaka, Gaṅgeyya, Paṇḍara, Tamba, Piṅgala, Gandha, Maṅgala, Hema, Uposatha, and Chaddanta—the strength of ten ordinary elephants known as Kāḷāvaka is equal to the strength of one Gaṅgeyya elephant. By this tenfold multiplication, His physical strength was equal to the strength of one thousand crore (ten billion) ordinary elephants. All that strength, from the time after His meal on that day, had become exhausted like water poured into a bowl. While traveling the distance of three gāvutas between the city of Pāvā and the city of Kusinārā, He rested at twenty-five places, and making a great effort, He reached Kusinārā at sunset. Thus, wishing to show the meaning that "that which is called disease comes by crushing all health," and speaking words that cause a sense of urgency (saṃvega) to the world of devas and humans, He said, "Cunda, I am weary, I will lie down."

Regarding the term Sīha-seyyā (the lion's posture), there are four types of lying down: Kāmabhogī-seyyā, Peta-seyyā, Tathāgata-seyyā, and Sīha-seyyā. Among these, "Monks, for the most part, those who enjoy sensual pleasures lie on their left side"—this is Kāmabhogī-seyyā. "Monks, for the most part, petas (hungry ghosts) lie flat on their backs"—this is Peta-seyyā. The Fourth Jhāna is Tathāgata-seyyā. "Monks, the lion, the king of beasts, lies on his right side"—this is Sīha-seyyā. This lying on the right side is called the noble posture because it is a posture of great power and majesty. Therefore, it is said, "He lay down on His right side in the lion's posture."

"Foot on foot" means placing the left foot upon the right foot. Accādhāya means placing it beyond the ankle. If the ankles and knees were to strike against each other repeatedly, pain...
365:
...would arise, and the lying down would not be comfortable. However, when placed beyond the other foot in such a manner that they do not strike each other, pain does not arise, and the lying down is comfortable. Therefore, the Blessed One lay down in this manner.

These verses beginning with "Gantvāna Buddho" were later inserted by the Elders who performed the Dhamma Recitation (Dhammasaṅgāhaka). In those verses, "Nadikam" refers to the river. "Appaṭimo loke" means the Buddha who is peerless in this world together with its devas. "Hatvā ca pivitvā cudatārī" means that He bathed to cool His body, drank the drinking water, and ascended from the river. It is said that at that time, while the Blessed One was bathing, the fish and turtles in the river, the water, the forest groves on both banks, and the entire area of the ground shone brilliantly like the color of gold. "Purakkhato" means that because He is superior to and more noble than all beings distinguished by special qualities, He is worthy of reverence and was thus honored, respected, and placed at the forefront by the world of devas and humans. "Bhikkhugaṇassa majjhe" means in the midst of the assembly of monks. At that time, the monks, knowing that the Blessed One's pain was very intense, followed Him closely, surrounding Him on all sides. "Satthā" (Teacher) is so called because He admonishes beings with the benefits of the present life, the benefits of the future life, and the ultimate benefit which is unerring. "Pavattā Bhagavā idha dhamme" means that the Blessed One, endowed with the six glories, set in motion the teachings such as virtue (sīla) in this Dispensation, or it means He is the one who set in motion the eighty-four thousand units of the Dhamma. "Ambavana" refers to the mango grove on the bank of that river. "Āmantayi Cundakaṃ" means that at that moment, the Venerable Ānanda had stayed behind to wring out his bathing robe, and only the Elder Cundaka was nearby; therefore, the Blessed One addressed that Elder Cundaka. "Pamukhe nisīdi" means that he sat in front of the Blessed One as an act of service, thinking, "What will the Teacher command?" At this point, the Treasurer of the Dhamma, the Venerable Ānanda, arrived. When he arrived, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda.

"Upadaheyya" means it might cause, implying that there might be someone who could cause remorse. "Alābhā" refers to not obtaining the benefits of giving that others obtain when they give. "Dulladdhaṃ" means that the human state, though obtained through special merit, is poorly obtained. "Yassa te" means of you. One might cause remorse by saying, "Who knows whether the meal was undercooked or overcooked? What kind of final almsfood did the Tathāgata eat before passing into Parinibbāna? Surely, that which was given by Cunda must have been just anything (of poor quality)." "Lābhā" refers to the benefits of giving to be obtained in the present life and the future life. "Suladdhaṃ" means that your human state is well-obtained. "Sammukhā" means hearing directly from the presence of the Buddha, and not by hearsay or through a lineage of tradition. "Metam" should be resolved as "me etaṃ" or "mayā etaṃ" (this by me). "Dveme" should be resolved as "dve ime" (these two). "Samasamaphalā" means having equal fruit and result in every respect.
366:
There might be an objection: "Having eaten the alms-food given by Sujātā, the Tathāgata attained Enlightenment; that was a gift given when defilements had not yet been abandoned. But this gift of Cunda was given when defilements were already extinct. Why are these two of equal fruit?" They are of equal fruit because of the equality of the Parinibbāna, the equality of the attainments (samāpatti), and the equality of the recollection. Having eaten the alms-food given by Sujātā, the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna through the Sa-upādisesa nibbāna-dhātu (the extinction of defilements). Having eaten the alms-food given by Cunda, he attained Parinibbāna through the Anupādisesa nibbāna-dhātu (the extinction of the aggregates). Thus, they are of equal fruit because of the equality of the Parinibbāna. On the day he attained Enlightenment, he entered into two million four hundred thousand koti attainments which are the cause for the Supreme Path; on the day he attained Parinibbāna, he also entered into all those same attainments. Thus, they are of equal fruit because of the equality of the attainments. This was said by the Blessed One: "Having partaken of whose alms-food, he dwells having entered into the incomparable and immeasurable concentration of mind (samādhi), for that person there is an immeasurable flow of merit, a flow of wholesome states," and so on. 

Sujātā also later heard: "That person was not a tree-deity; he was indeed the Bodhisatta. Having partaken of that alms-food, he attained the incomparable Supreme Enlightenment. With that alms-food alone, he was able to sustain himself for seven weeks." Upon hearing this, powerful joy and gladness (pīti-somanassa) arose in Sujātā as she repeatedly recollected, "What a great gain for me!" Cunda also later heard: "I have given the last alms-food. I have obtained the pinnacle of the Dhamma. Having partaken of my alms-food, the Teacher attained Parinibbāna through the Anupādisesa nibbāna-dhātu, which he himself had long desired." Upon hearing this, powerful joy and gladness arose in Cunda as he repeatedly recollected, "What a great gain for me!" Thus, it should be understood that both these gifts of alms-food are of equal fruit because of the equality of the recollection.

"Āyusaṃvattanika" means the benefit that conduces to long life. "Upacita" means the benefit that is accumulated or produced. "Yasasaṃvattanika" means the benefit that conduces to having many followers. "Ādhipateyyasaṃvattanika" means the benefit that conduces to the state of being a supreme leader.

"Having known this matter" means having known in every respect these three meanings: the greatness of the fruit of this gift, the fact that he himself is the incomparable recipient of gifts due to qualities such as virtue, and the attainment of Anupādā Parinibbāna. Having known this, he uttered this Udāna (Inspired Utterance) which illustrates that meaning.
367:
In that verse, 'Dadatō puññaṃ pavaḍḍhati' means that for the person who gives, merit consisting of giving accumulates due to the fulfillment of the mind and the fulfillment of the noble recipient; it means the primary fruit becomes greater and the secondary benefits become more numerous. Alternatively, 'Dadatō puññaṃ pavaḍḍhati' means that because the person who relinquishes the objects of donation repeatedly exercises the volition of relinquishment, they gradually become free from offenses in all respects, protect extremely pure virtue, and are able to develop tranquility and insight. Therefore, for that person, the threefold merit increases greatly through the power of giving and so forth—this is how the meaning should be understood here.

'Saṃyamatō' means for one who well-guards the three doors of body, speech, and mind through the restraint of virtue, and who stands in self-control. 'Veraṃ na cīyati' means that the fivefold enmity does not increase. Or, because virtue is characterized by non-hatred, one who possesses extremely pure virtue and guards themselves through body, speech, and mind does not create enmity with anyone due to their abundance of patience; how could there be an accumulation of enmity in them? Therefore, for such a person who practices restraint, enmity does not accumulate because of that restraint.

'Kusalō ca jahāti pāpakaṃ' means that the wise one, endowed with wisdom and established in extremely pure virtue, takes a meditation subject suitable for themselves from among the thirty-eight objects, fulfills the jhānas consisting of access and absorption, and abandons unwholesome states such as base sensual desire through the abandonment by suppression. That person, making that very jhāna the basis, contemplates the cessation and vanishing of conditioned phenomena, performs the work of insight, and after exerting effort in insight, abandons the base unwholesome states without remainder through the Noble Path by the abandonment by eradication.

'Rāgadōsamōhakkhayā sa nibbutō' means that such a person, having abandoned base unwholesome states, becomes extinguished through the extinction of defilements without remainder (kilesa-nibbāna) due to the destruction of lust and so forth, and thereafter through the extinction of the aggregates (khandha-nibbāna). In this way, the Blessed One, based on Cunda's fulfillment of the gift and his own fulfillment as a worthy recipient, uttered this inspired utterance released by the force of joy.

## The Commentary on the Fifth Sutta is finished.

## 6. Pāṭaligāmiyasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the sixth sutta, 'Magadhēsu' means in the kingdom of Magadha. 'Mahatā' means here also with a great Saṅgha of monks, great both in terms of the greatness of their attributes and in terms of their number being an undefined quantity. 'Pāṭaligāmō' is the name of a village in the kingdom of Magadha. It is said that on the day that village was being founded, at the site where the village was being demarcated, two or three Pāṭali (trumpet flower) sprouts broke through from the earth. Therefore, they called it 'Pāṭaligāma'. 'Avasari' means he arrived at that Pāṭali village. At what time did the Blessed One arrive at Pāṭali village? According to the method to be mentioned below, after having a stupa built for the General of the Dhamma, the Great Elder, in Sāvatthī, he departed from there and while staying in Rājagaha...
368:
...they broke through and emerged from the earth. For that reason, they called that village 'Pāṭaligāma'. 'Tadavasari' means he arrived at or reached that Pāṭali village. When did the Blessed One reach Pāṭali village? As stated below, after having a stupa built for the General of the Dhamma in Sāvatthī, he departed from there and, while staying in Rājagaha, also had a stupa built for the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. Departing from there and staying at Ambalaṭṭhikā, he wandered through the countryside in a leisurely manner, staying for one night in various places, and while favoring the world of beings, he gradually reached Pāṭali village.

'Pāṭaligāmiyā' refers to the lay followers living in Pāṭali village. It is said that upon their first sight of the Blessed One, some were established in the refuges, some in the precepts, and some in both the refuges and the precepts. Therefore, they are called 'lay followers' (upāsakas). 'Approached where the Blessed One was' means that in Pāṭali village, the men (officials) of King Ajātasattu and the Licchavī kings used to come from time to time, evict the householders from their homes, and stay for a month or half a month. Therefore, the people living in Pāṭali village, being constantly oppressed, thought, 'This will be a place for these officials to stay when they come,' and they had a large hall built in the center of the town, sufficient for everyone to stay without crowding each other: one side for storing the property of the rulers, one side for living quarters, one side for travelers and wayfarers, one side for the poor and destitute, and one side for the sick. The name of that hall was 'Āvasathāgāra'.

That hall reached completion on that very day. Those people went there and, having looked from the gateway at that hall which was well-finished and well-decorated with handiwork, plasterwork, and painting, resembling a celestial mansion, they thought, 'This Āvasathāgāra is exceedingly delightful and magnificent. If someone were to use it first, who would it be that would lead to our welfare and happiness for a long time?' At that very moment, they heard, 'The Blessed One has reached that village.' Hearing this, they became filled with joy and happiness, thinking, 'Even if we had to go and invite the Blessed One, we should do so; but now the Blessed One has arrived at our place of residence by himself. Today, we will have the Blessed One stay here and have him use it first along with the Saṅgha of monks. When the Saṅgha of monks arrives, the Tipitaka, the Word of the Buddha, will also surely arrive. We will have the Teacher speak words of blessing and deliver a Dhamma talk. Thus, after the Triple Gem has used it first, it will later be for our use and the use of others. Doing this will be for our...'
369:
Having resolved that "This will be for our welfare and happiness for a long time," they approached the Blessed One for that very purpose. Having approached, they said, "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept our rest-house."

"They approached where the rest-house was" means that although the rest-house had been completed that very day and was well-prepared and cleaned like a celestial mansion, it had not yet been furnished in a manner suitable for the Buddha. Thinking, "The Buddhas are those who delight in the forest and have forest-dwelling inclinations; forest dwellings alone are suitable for monks. We shall furnish it only after knowing the Blessed One's preference, whether he will stay inside the village or not," they approached the Blessed One. Now, having learned the Blessed One's preference and wishing to furnish it accordingly, they approached where the rest-house was. "Having spread the rest-house with all-over spreading" means making it so that spreads are laid out in all places. First, considering that "Cow dung is appropriate for all auspicious occasions," they had even the floor made of lime plaster smeared with fresh cow dung. When it was dry, so that footprints would not appear where stepped upon, they smeared it with four kinds of perfumes. Then, they spread mats of various colors on top, and over those, they had all the necessary areas covered with various colored spreads, starting from large carpets to elephant-back rugs and so forth. Therefore, it is said, "Having spread the rest-house with all-over spreading."

In the middle of the seats, first, leaning against the auspicious pillar, they prepared a seat worthy of the Blessed One. On that seat, they spread soft and delightful coverings and placed a beautiful pillow with red borders at both ends. Above, they hung a canopy adorned with gold and silver stars and decorated it with garlands of perfumes and flowers. They had a floral net made in the surrounding area of twelve cubits and enclosed a space of about thirty cubits with curtains. Leaning against the western wall, they arranged couches, chairs with backrests, beds, and stools for the Saṅgha of monks, covering them with pure white spreads. On the eastern side of the hall, they prepared suitable seats for themselves. Referring to such an arrangement, it is said, "Having prepared the seats."

"Water pot" refers to a large-bellied water jar. So that the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks could wash their hands and feet and rinse their faces as they pleased, they filled jars at various places with water the color of emerald. To scent it, they added various flowers and perfumed powders, covered them with banana leaves, and set them down. Therefore, it is said, "Having set down a water pot."
370:
"Having lit the oil lamps" means lighting oil lamps in bowls made of gold, silver, etc., held in the hands of figures such as those from the Yona country or the Cīna country, which were on lampstands made of silver, gold, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "They approached where the Blessed One was," those lay followers of Pāṭaligāma did not only clean the rest-house for guests; they also had all the village streets cleaned, raised banners, and placed full jars and banana trees at the doors of houses. They made the entire village glitter with garlands of lamps, like a cluster of stars appearing here and there. They had a drum beaten, announcing: "Nurse the suckling infants, feed the young children quickly and put them to sleep, do not make loud noises; today, for this whole night, the Blessed One will stay within the village. Buddhas desire silence." Then, carrying lampstands themselves, they approached where the Blessed One was.

Then the Blessed One, having dressed, taking his bowl and robes, went to the rest-house together with the Saṅgha of monks. When those donors announced the time, saying, "Venerable Sir, it is now time for the Blessed One to depart," the Blessed One, having properly arranged his lower robe to cover the three circles—like cutting a lotus flower with scissors—put on his double-layered robe which was as red as a coral tree flower soaked in lac-dye. Having fastened his waistband, which shone like a flash of lightning, as if binding a bunch of lotuses with a golden chain; and as if covering an elephant's forehead with a red woolen cloth; as if draping a coral net over a golden pillar a hundred cubits high; as if covering a great golden stūpa with a red woolen mantle; as if veiling the full moon moving in the sky with a great red cloud; as if pouring well-cooked lac-dye on the peak of a golden mountain; as if encircling the peak of Mount Cittakūṭa with a net of lightning; causing the entire universe, Mount Sineru, Mount Yugandhara, and the great earth to tremble, he donned his noble rag-robe, red and having the color of a held banyan sprout. He emerged from his beautiful pavilion like a maned lion coming out of a forest thicket, like the full moon rising from the peak of Mount Udaya, and like the young sun.

Then, from the Blessed One's body, various rays emerged like flashes of lightning from between rain clouds, making the surrounding trees appear as if golden liquid had been poured over their leaves, flowers, fruits, and branches. At that very moment, the great Saṅgha of monks, taking their own bowls and robes, surrounded the Blessed One. And those monks stood surrounding the Blessed One.
371:
The monks were of such a nature: they were of few wishes, contented, secluded, unmingled with the crowd, energetic, speakers of advice, patient of speech, reprovers of faults, censurers of evil, endowed with virtue, endowed with concentration, endowed with wisdom, endowed with liberation, and endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation. Surrounded by those monks, the Blessed One shone like a great mass of gold wrapped in a red woolen blanket, like the full moon surrounded by stars, like a golden boat in the midst of a red lotus forest, and like a golden palace surrounded by coral railings. The Great Elders, headed by Mahākassapa, wearing rag-robes the color of rain clouds, surrounded him like great elephants clad in jeweled armor. These elders were those who had vomited out lust, destroyed defilements, untangled the tangle of defilements, severed the bonds, and were unattached to families or groups.

Thus the Blessed One, himself free from lust among those free from lust, himself free from hatred among those free from hatred, himself free from delusion among those free from delusion, himself free from craving among those free from craving, himself free from defilements among those free from defilements, himself having realized the Four Noble Truths among the Great Elders who followed in his realization, was surrounded [by them] like a lotus filament surrounded by petals, like a pericarp surrounded by filaments, like the Chaddanta elephant king surrounded by eight thousand elephants, like the Dhataraṭṭha swan king surrounded by ninety thousand swans, like a Cakkavatti king surrounded by his army, like Sakka, the king of gods, surrounded by the host of deities, like Hārita Mahābrahmā surrounded by the host of Brahmas, and like the full moon surrounded by the host of stars. With incomparable Buddha-guise and immeasurable Buddha-grace, he set out on the road to Pāṭaligāma.

Then, from the front of the Blessed One’s body, dense golden Buddha-rays issued forth and spread to a distance of about eighty cubits. Likewise, from the back of his body, from the right side, and from the left side, dense golden Buddha-rays issued forth and spread to a distance of about eighty cubits. Starting from the top of his head, from all the curls of his hair, dense black Buddha-rays, the color of a peacock’s neck, issued forth and spread eighty cubits into the sky. From the soles of his feet, coral-colored rays issued forth and spread eighty cubits into the dense earth. From his teeth, from the white portions of his eyes, and from the parts of his nails free from flesh, dense pure white Buddha-rays issued forth and spread to a distance of about eighty cubits. From the junction of the red and yellow colors, madder-colored rays issued forth and spread to a distance of about eighty cubits. From his entire body, brilliant rays issued forth. Thus, in all directions within eighty cubits, the six-colored Buddha-rays, shining, vibrating, and racing, issued forth like great flames of lamps leaping into the sky from golden lampstands, or like a great rain cloud covering the four continents...
372: (The rays of light) spread in all directions like streaks of lightning emerging from a bank of clouds. Because of those rays, all directions shone beautifully, as if strewn with golden campaka flowers, as if poured with streams of liquid gold from a golden pot, as if wrapped in outspread golden cloth, as if covered with the pollen of Butea, Bauhinia, and Kanikara flowers blown by the Veramba winds, and as if smeared all around with fine vermilion powder. The Blessed One's body, glowing all around with the eighty minor marks and the fathom-wide radiance, and adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, was as beautiful as the sky shining with bright stars, free from impurities such as clouds and mist; as beautiful as a forest of blooming lotuses; and as beautiful as a Pāricchattaka tree a hundred yojanas in height, fully in bloom. He shone as if overwhelming with his own glory the glory of thirty-two suns, thirty-two moons, thirty-two Universal Monarchs, thirty-two Sakkas, and thirty-two Great Brahmas arranged in order. This was because he was adorned with the thirty perfections, namely, the ten perfections, the ten higher perfections, and the ten ultimate perfections, which he had fully practiced. The generosity (dāna) he had given, the virtue (sīla) he had observed, and the meritorious deeds he had performed for four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons seemed to have gathered together in this final existence, and finding no room to ripen, they appeared as if crowded. It was like the time when goods for a thousand boats are loaded onto a single boat, or when goods for a thousand carts are loaded onto a single cart, or like the time when twenty-five rivers meet simultaneously at a river mouth. Even though he was shining with such Buddha-glory, thousands of torches were carried before the Blessed One. Likewise, from behind and from the left and right sides, flowers such as jasmine, great jasmine, red lotus, blue lotus, and others, as well as fragrant powders of various colors like blue and yellow, were scattered like showers of rain released from a great cloud covering the four continents. The sounds of the five-fold musical instruments and the sounds of praise extolling the virtues of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha filled all directions, sounding as if they were direct verbal conversations. The eyes of devas, garudas, nagas, yakkhas, and humans received delight as if drinking the nectar of immortality (Amata). At this point, it is appropriate to pause and praise his manner of walking with thousands of verses. Here, I shall speak only in brief. ## The Blessed One, the Leader of the World, endowed with all physical perfections, walked making the earth tremble but without harming any living beings. The Blessed One, the noblest of men, the most excellent of bipeds, endowed with glory and majesty, walked gracefully; when he first placed his foot down in the Sakyan kingdom, the soft soles of that Great Buddha touched the ground evenly. No dust adhered to his feet. When the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, walked, the insentient earth rose in low places and became level in high places. When the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, walked, all stones and pebbles...
373: ...stones, pebbles, potsherds, stumps, and thorns moved away from the path. Endowed with all physical perfections, the Leader of the World thus walked, making the earth tremble without harming any living beings. The noblest of men, endowed with glory and majesty, the most excellent of bipeds, walked gracefully, lifting his right foot first. As the Great Buddha walked, his soft soles touched the ground evenly, and no dust adhered to them. When the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, walked, the insentient earth rose in low places and became level in high places. When the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, walked, all stones, pebbles, potsherds, stumps, and thorns moved away from the path. He lifted his feet neither too far nor placed them too near; he proceeded without his knees or ankles knocking against each other. The Sage (Muni), endowed with perfect conduct and a concentrated mind, walked neither too fast nor too slow. The Blessed One did not walk looking up, down, sideways, or towards the main or intermediate directions; he looked only a yoke's length ahead. The Conqueror (Jina) shone in his gait, walking like a noble elephant; the Supreme One of the world walked beautifully, bringing joy to devas and humans alike. Shining like a king of bulls, walking gracefully like a king of lions, the Most Excellent Buddha approached the village, bringing delight to many beings. This time is known as the time for praise. At such a time, in praising the physical appearance or the virtues of the Blessed One, the capacity of the Dhamma preacher is the only measure; one should speak as much as possible through prose or verses. It should not be said, "It is poorly spoken," or "He has plunged into a place that is not a landing-place." For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, possess immeasurable virtues; even Buddhas themselves are unable to describe their virtues exhaustively. Even if they were to praise them for an entire aeon, they could not reach the end, let alone other beings. To the village of Pāṭali, thus adorned with all this splendor...
374:
The Blessed One, being worshipped by the multitude of people with devoted hearts using flowers, scents, incense, and powders, entered the guesthouse. 

Therefore, it is said (in the Pali): "Then the Blessed One, having dressed and taking his bowl and robes, approached the guesthouse together with the community of monks."

"Having washed his feet": Although dust and dirt never cling to the Blessed One's feet, he washes them out of a desire for the lay followers' increase in merit and to set an example for others to follow. Furthermore, what is called the "body born of grasping" (upādinnaka-sarīra) needs to be cooled; for this purpose, the Blessed One performs acts such as bathing and washing his feet.

"With the Blessed One in front": This means placing the Blessed One at the head. There, the Blessed One sat in the midst of the monks and lay followers. Having bathed with scented water, dried with a fine cloth (dukūla), rubbed with natural cinnabar (jātihingulaka), and wrapped in a red blanket, he shone exceedingly like a solid red-gold statue placed on a pedestal.

In this regard, the following is the traditional sequence of praise by the ancient teachers:

Having gone to the circular pavilion, with a gait like that of a noble elephant,
The Foremost of the World, illuminating with his radiance, sat upon the noble seat.

Sitting there, the Charioteer of men to be tamed,
The God above gods, endowed with the marks of a hundred merits,
Shines in the midst of the Buddha's seat,
Like a golden ornament upon a crimson rug.

Like an ornament of Jambu-river gold placed on a crimson rug,
He shines, free from stain, like the Vairocana gem.

Like a great Sal tree in full bloom, like the adorned King of Mountains (Meru),
Resembling a golden pillar, he is like a red Kokanada lotus.

Like a blazing lamp-stand, like a flame upon a mountain peak,
Like the Parijata tree of the gods in full bloom, he shines.
375: "He addressed the lay followers of Pāṭaligāma": Since many of those lay followers were established in virtue, he addressed them to preach the Dhamma, starting with "Five, O householders," first showing the danger of failing in virtue and then the benefits of being endowed with virtue. In that passage, "dussīlo" (immoral) refers to one without virtue. "Sīlavipanno" (one who has failed in virtue) refers to one whose virtue is ruined and whose restraint is broken. Here, the term "dussīlo" expresses the person's state of lacking virtue. That lack of virtue is of two kinds: either by not undertaking the precepts or by the breaking of undertaken precepts. Of these two, the former is not as blameworthy as the latter; the second is much more blameworthy. To show the lack of virtue, which is the cause of the intended danger, through a person-centered (puggala-adhiṭṭhāna) teaching, he said "sīlavipanno." By this, he shows the meaning of the term "dussīlo." "Pamādādhikaraṇaṃ" means due to the cause of negligence. Although this sutta comes by way of householders, it is also applicable to monks. For a householder, if he is negligent through acts such as killing while earning a living through crafts, farming, trade, or cattle-herding, he cannot complete those tasks in time, and then his work is ruined. Furthermore, if he commits acts such as killing during a time when slaughter is prohibited, he meets with great loss of wealth due to state punishment. An immoral monk, due to negligence, also meets with loss—loss of virtue, loss of the Buddha's word, loss of jhāna, and loss of the sevenfold Noble Wealth. "Pāpako kittisaddo" (a bad reputation) means for a householder, a bad report spreads in the midst of the assembly: "This person born in such-and-such a family is immoral, of evil conduct; he has abandoned this world and the next; he does not give even a ticket-meal." For a monk, a bad report spreads: "This monk named so-and-so, having gone forth in the Teacher's Dispensation, could not guard his virtue, could not learn the Buddha's word, lives by practicing medicine and so on, and is possessed of the six kinds of disrespect." "Avisārado" (not confident) means a householder must approach a large gathering of people with fear, thinking, "Will someone know of my deed? If so, will they blame me or report me to the royal family?" He sits down dejected, with drooping shoulders and downcast face, unable to speak with confidence. A monk also must approach a large gathering of the Saṅgha with fear, thinking, "Will someone know of my deed? If so, will they prohibit me from the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā, and having removed me from the monkhood, expel me?" Being [unable to be] confident...
376:
...is unable to speak. Some people, though immoral, behave as if they are virtuous; such a person also becomes dejected within their own disposition. 'He dies confused' means that for an immoral person, while lying on their deathbed, the immoral deeds they have undertaken and performed appear in their mind's eye. Opening their eyes, they see this world; closing their eyes, they see the next world. For them, the four states of deprivation appear according to their own kamma, as if being pierced by a hundred swords or being burned by the heat of flames. That person dies wailing, 'Stop it! Stop it!' Therefore, it is said, 'He dies confused.'

'The breaking up of the body' means the relinquishing of the grasped aggregates (upādinnakkhandha). 'After death' means the taking up of new aggregates immediately following that. Alternatively, 'the breaking up of the body' means the cessation of the life faculty (jīvitindriya), and 'after death' means after the death-consciousness (cuti).

All terms such as apāya are synonyms for hell (niraya). It is called apāya because it is devoid of 'aya' (merit), which is the cause of heaven and liberation, or because there is an absence of the arrival of happiness. It is called duggati because it is the destination of suffering, or because it is a destination produced by corrupt kamma due to an abundance of hatred. It is called vinipāta because evildoers fall into it helplessly, or because they fall into it while their limbs and organs are being destroyed. It is called niraya because there is no 'aya' (benefit) known as pleasure.

Alternatively, by the term apāya, the animal realm is indicated. The animal realm is called apāya because it is removed from the happy destinations (sugati), but it is not called duggati because great beings like Naga kings can be born there. By the term duggati, the ghost realm (peta-visaya) is indicated. It is called both apāya and duggati because it is removed from happy destinations and is a destination of suffering; however, it is not called vinipāta because they do not fall into ruin like the asuras, and because there are ghosts of great power (mahiddhika). By the term vinipāta, the host of asuras is indicated. It is called both apāya and duggati for the reasons mentioned above, and it is also called vinipāta because they have fallen away from all heights of prosperity. By the term niraya, various hells such as Avīci are indicated. 'Is reborn' means to be produced through rebirth.

The discourse on the benefits (āniśaṃsa) should be understood in the opposite way to what was stated above. Here is the distinction: Sīlavā (virtuous) refers to one who is virtuous by way of undertaking the precepts. Sīlasampanno (endowed with virtue) refers to one who is endowed with virtue by making it pure and complete.
377:
One is virtuous by way of undertaking the precepts. One is called 'endowed with virtue' (sīlasampanno) by making it pure and complete. 'Mass of wealth' (bhogakkhandha) means a heap of riches. In the phrase 'happy destination, heavenly world' (sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ), the term 'happy destination' (sugati) also includes the human realm, while the term 'heaven' (sagga) refers only to the celestial realms. In that context, it is called sugati because it is a good destination. It is called sagga because it is exceedingly sublime due to sense objects such as forms. All of it is called loka (world) because of the sense of crumbling and dissolving.

'To the lay followers of Pāṭaligāma... with a Dhamma talk late into the night' means preaching with other Dhamma talks outside the Pali text, as well as with a talk of appreciation for the rest-house (āvāsathānumodana). At that time, because King Ajātasattu was building the city of Pāṭaliputta at that Pāṭaligāma, he brought householders endowed with virtuous conduct from other villages, towns, districts, and royal capitals, and settled them there after providing them with houses, fields, wealth, grain, clothing, and protection. Therefore, those lay followers of Pāṭaligāma, seeing the benefits, were especially respectful of virtue. Since virtue is the foundation of all qualities, the Blessed One first revealed the benefits of virtue to them. Then, like bringing down the celestial Ganges, like drawing out the essence of the earth, like shaking a great Jambu tree by its top, or like pressing a honey-comb a league wide with a machine to provide the sweet taste, he preached a miscellaneous Dhamma talk that brings welfare and happiness to the lay followers of Pāṭaligāma, saying:

'Householders, the gift of a dwelling (āvāsadāna) is a great merit. Your dwelling has been used by me; it has been used by the Saṅgha of monks. When it is used by me and the Saṅgha of monks, it is also used by the Dhamma Jewel. When it is thus used by the Three Jewels, the result is immeasurable. Furthermore, when the gift of a dwelling is given, it is as if all gifts have been given. The benefit of building and offering even a leaf-hut on the ground or a pavilion of branches for the sake of the Saṅgha cannot be measured. By the power of the gift of a dwelling, even when being reborn in a state of existence, there is no such thing as living in a cramped and crowded womb; the mother's womb for such a person is not narrow but spacious, like a chamber twelve cubits wide.' Thus, he preached many diverse and wonderful Dhamma talks through various methods, and said:

'It wards off cold and heat,
And also wild beasts,
Reptiles and mosquitoes,
And the rains in the cold season.

'It also wards off the terrible wind and sun
When they arise.
(A dwelling is given) for the sake of shelter and comfort,
For the sake of meditation and for insight.'
378:
“The Buddha praised the donation of a monastery to the Saṅgha as supreme. Therefore, a wise man, seeing his own benefit, should have pleasant monasteries built. In those monasteries, he should have many learned persons reside. To those persons, he should donate almsfood, drink, clothing, and lodgings.

He should donate with a clear mind to those who practice uprightly. Those persons will preach to that donor of the monastery the Dhamma that dispels all suffering. Having understood that Dhamma in this Dispensation, that donor of the monastery, with taints exhausted, attains Parinibbāna.”

In this way, saying that there is great benefit in this donation of a dwelling, he preached the discourse on the benefits of donating a dwelling (āvāsadāna-ānisaṃsa-kathā) for more than a watch and a half throughout the night. Among those teachings, only these verses are included in the compilation (saṅgaha); the miscellaneous Dhamma teachings, however, do not enter the compilation. The words beginning with “sandassetvā” have the meanings already mentioned.

“Abhikkantā” means that two watches have passed. “Yassa dāni kālaṃ maññatha” means “Know the time for your departure; it is time for you to go; go.” Why did the Blessed One dismiss them? Out of compassion. If they were to spend the time sitting in that rest house for all three watches of the night, illness might arise in their bodies; also, it is proper for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus to have the opportunity for sleeping and sitting in the early dawn. Thus, out of compassion for both parties, he dismissed them.

“Suññāgāraṃ”: There was no such thing as a separate secluded room in that rest house. Therefore, it is said that the lay followers had a side of that very rest house partitioned with a cloth curtain, had a proper couch prepared, spread a proper bedspread on that couch, and above it, tied a canopy adorned with gold stars, silver stars, and garlands of fragrant flowers, and placed an oil lamp. They did this thinking, “May the Blessed One, after rising from the preaching seat and wishing to rest a little, lie down here. In this way, if this rest house of ours is used by the Blessed One in all four postures, it will be for our long-term welfare and happiness.” The Teacher, also intending that very purpose, had his double robe (saṅghāṭi) spread there and took the lion’s posture (sīhaseyya). With reference to that, it is said, “He entered the empty room (suññāgāraṃ).”

In that rest house, starting from the place for washing feet up to the preaching seat, by walking there, the act of walking (gamana) was accomplished. Reaching the preaching seat and standing for a moment is the act of standing (ṭhāna) there. By the Blessed One sitting on the preaching seat for two watches, the act of sitting (nisajjā) was accomplished. Having dismissed the lay followers...
379:
...descending from the preaching seat, he took the lion’s posture in the aforementioned place. In this way, that place was used by the Blessed One in all four postures.

“Sunidhavassakārā” refers to two brahmins named Sunidha and Vassakāra. “Magadhamahāmattā” refers to the chief ministers of the King of Magadha, or they are called “Mahāmattas” because they were endowed with great sovereign power in the country of Magadha. “Pāṭaligāme nagaraṃ māpenti” means they were building a city in the area known as Pāṭaligāma. “Vajjīnaṃ paṭibāhāya” means for the purpose of cutting off the revenue routes of the Licchavi kings. “Sahassasahasseva” means in groups of a thousand each. “Vatthūni” refers to house sites. “Cittāni namanti nivesanāni māpetuṃ” means the deities incline the minds of the site-readers to build the houses and dwellings of the king and his chief ministers. Those site-readers, by the power of their craft, know at a depth of about thirty cubits underground, “This place is the haunt of nagas; this place is the haunt of yakkhas; this place is the haunt of spirits; in this place there is a stone or a stump.” At that time, they recite their craft’s spells and build the towns and villages as if they were consulting with the deities.

Or else, the deities possess the bodies of those site-readers and incline their minds to build dwellings in various places. Those deities, having struck stakes at the four corners and merely demarcated the house site, then depart. Deities with faith do so for the dwellings of faithful families; deities without faith do so for the dwellings of unfaithful families.

For what reason do they do so? Faithful deities have this thought: “When people build dwellings in this place, they will first invite the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and have them recite auspicious discourses. Then we shall get to see the virtuous ones, hear Dhamma talks, hear the answering of questions, and hear the discourse of appreciation (anumodanā). The people, having given gifts, will also share the portion of merit with us.” Unfaithful deities also do so in order to see the behavior and hear the words of those devoid of faith, according to their own desires.

“Tāvatiṃsehi”: For example, based on one wise person in a family, or one learned bhikkhu in a monastery, the fame spreads that “the people in such-and-such a family are wise” or “the bhikkhus in such-and-such a monastery are learned.” In the same way, based on Sakka, the king of devas, and Vissakamma, the son of a deva, the fame spread that “the Tāvatiṃsa devas are wise.” Therefore, the Blessed One said, “Tāvatiṃsehi.”
380:
With the words beginning with "Seyyathāpi," it is shown that the ministers Sunidha and Vassakāra founded the city as if they were consulting with and building it together with the Tāvatiṃsa devas.

Ananda, "yāvatā ariyaṃ āyatanaṃ" refers to as far as there is a place where noble persons gather. "Yāvatā vaṇippatho" refers to as far as there is a place for buying and selling the goods brought by merchants in heaps, or a place where merchants reside. "Idaṃ agganagaraṃ" means that among those places where noble ones gather and merchants trade, this city will be the chief, the greatest, and the foremost. "Puṭabhedanaṃ" means a place for opening bundles of goods, a place for unpacking merchandise. It means that even goods not obtainable in the whole of Jambudīpa will be obtained here, and goods that cannot be sold elsewhere will be sold here; therefore, they will break open their bundles here. Regarding taxes, five hundred thousand will be collected there daily: four hundred thousand at the four gates and one hundred thousand at the assembly hall. This shows the collection of such taxes.

In the words beginning with "aggito vā," the word "vā" expresses the sense of inclusion (samuccaya). It means it will be destroyed by fire, by water, or by internal dissension. One part of the city will be destroyed by fire, which they will be unable to extinguish. One part the Ganges River will wash away. One part will be destroyed through mutual dissension among the people caused by slanderous speech, saying to one what another did not say, and to another what this one did not say. Having spoken thus, the Blessed One went to the bank of the Ganges at dawn, washed his face, and sat down waiting for the time to go for alms.

The ministers Sunidha and Vassakāra thought: "Our King is an attendant of the Samaṇa Gotama. When we return, he will ask, 'Did the Teacher go to Pāṭaligāma? Did you approach him or not?' If we say, 'We approached him,' he will ask, 'Did you invite him for a meal or not?' If we say, 'We did not invite him,' he will blame and rebuke us. Furthermore, we are building this city in a place where none was built before. Wherever the Samaṇa Gotama goes, unlucky beings depart. Therefore, we will have the Blessed One recite a blessing for the city." Thinking thus, they approached the Blessed One and invited him for a meal. Therefore, it is said in the Pāḷi: "Atha kho sunidhavassakārā," and so on.
381:
The King is an attendant of the Samaṇa Gotama. When we return, he will ask, "Did the Teacher go to Pāṭaligāma? Did you approach that Blessed One?" If we answer, "We approached him," he will ask again, "Did you invite him for a meal?" If we say, "We did not invite him," he will blame and oppress us. We are also founding this city in a place where none was built before. Wherever the Samaṇa Gotama arrives, malevolent beings depart. We will have the Blessed One recite a blessing for the city. Thinking thus, they approached the Blessed One and invited him for a meal. Therefore, it is said in the Pāḷi: "Atha kho sunidhavassakārā," and so on.

"Pubbaṇhasamayaṃ" means in the morning time. "Nivāsetvā" means dressing (the lower robe) in the manner of entering a village and tying the belt. "Pattacīvaramādāya" means putting on the robe and taking the bowl in hand.

"Sīlavantettha" refers to those who possess virtue in their own dwelling place here in Pāṭaliputta. "Saññate" refers to those who are restrained in body, speech, and mind. "Tāsaṃ dakkhiṇamādise" means that when offering the four requisites to the Sangha, one should dedicate the merit to those house-guarding deities; one should share the portion of merit.

"Pūjitā pūjayanti" means that the deities, thinking, "These people are not our relatives, yet they share the portion of merit with us in this way," provide well-arranged protection; they protect them well. "Mānitā mānayanti" means that the deities, honored by the performance of bali offerings from time to time, think, "These people are not our relatives, yet they perform bali offerings for us every four, five, or six months," and thus they honor them and remove any dangers that have arisen. "Tato naṃ" refers to that wise man. "Orasaṃ" means like a mother who cherishes her own breast-born son, striving to remove any dangers that have arisen; in the same way, they (the deities) have compassion for him. "Bhadrāni passati" means seeing auspicious things.

"Anumoditvā" means having given a Dhamma talk to them to make them rejoice in the merit acquired by those virtuous ones. Sunidha and Vassakāra, having heard the Blessed One's words, "One should dedicate the merit to the deities who are there," shared the portion of merit with the deities. The gate of the city through which the Blessed One exited came to be known as the Gotama Gate. However, because he did not descend to cross the Ganges, it did not come to be known as the Gotama Ferry.

"Pūrā" means full of water. "Samatittikā" means overflowing with water, level with the banks. "Kākapeyyā" means having water that can be drunk by crows standing on the bank. By both these terms, he shows the state of being full to the level of both banks. "Uḷumpaṃ" is a raft made by joining timbers and driving in pegs to cross to the other side. "Kullaṃ" is a raft made by binding bamboo stalks and the like with creepers and such.

"Etam-atthaṃ viditvā" means knowing the inability of the great multitude to cross even the water of the Ganges, and knowing the extreme depth and width for himself and the community of monks.
382:
Having known in every aspect the state of being established after crossing the great ocean of Saṃsāra, he uttered this inspired utterance (Udāna) explaining that meaning.

In that Udāna verse, "aṇṇavaṃ" is the name for a place of water that is, at the very least, one yojana in depth and extent. The word "saraṃ" refers here to a river because it flows. The intended meaning is this: Those Noble Ones who cross the extremely deep and wide ocean of Saṃsāra and the river of craving, they do so by constructing the bridge known as the Noble Path (Ariya Magga). Without touching the mud and swamps, they cross over the low-lying areas filled with water. These ordinary people, however, desiring to cross only a small amount of water, prepare only a raft and undergo the labor of binding a raft. "Tiṇṇā medhāvino janā" means that because they are endowed with the wisdom known as the knowledge of the Noble Path, the Buddhas and the disciples (sāvakas), who are called the wise (medhāvī), have crossed over even without a raft and stand on the other shore.

## The Commentary on the Sixth Sutta is finished.

## 7. Dvidhāpatha Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, "addhānamaggappaṭipanno" means one who is traveling on a long journey known as addhāna. "Nāgasamālena" means together with the Elder of this name. "Pacchāsamaṇena" means this Elder was the Buddha's attendant at that time. Therefore, the Buddha traveled taking that Elder as his attendant monk. Indeed, during the first twenty years of the Buddha's enlightenment (paṭhamabodhi), the attendants were not permanent; after that, until his parinibbāna, the Venerable Ānanda attended to him like a shadow for twenty-five years. This Elder Nagasamāla, however, served during the period when attendants were not permanent. Therefore, it is said, "with the Venerable Nagasamāla as the attendant monk." "Dvidhāpathaṃ" refers to a road that has become forked. It is also read as "dvedhāpathaṃ." The Venerable Nagasamāla, because he had previously been familiar with that place, said, "Venerable Sir, this is the path," referring to its straightness.

At that time, the Buddha, knowing that the path was dangerous (saparissaya) and wishing to go by another road, said, "Nagasamāla, this is the path." If he had said "it is dangerous," the Elder might have disbelieved and said, "Blessed One, there is no danger there," and such disbelief and speech would lead to his harm and suffering for a long time. Therefore, without saying "it is dangerous," for up to three times...
383:
Intending that this road was the straight one, he said, "Venerable Sir, this is the path." At that time, the Blessed One, knowing the dangerous nature of that path for the Venerable Nagasamāla and wishing to go by a different path, said, "Nagasamāla, this is the path." Even if told it was dangerous, the Elder would not have believed and would have said, "Venerable Sir, there is no danger on that path." Such disbelief and speech would have led to the Elder's harm and suffering for a long time. Therefore, without saying "it is dangerous," the Buddha said three times, "This is the wrong path; I will go by this one."

On the fourth time, thinking, "The Blessed One does not wish to go by this path, yet this is the straight path; I will give the Blessed One his bowl and robes and go by this path," he did not dare to hand over the bowl and robes directly and instead placed them on the ground. Driven by karma that brings about imminent suffering, he disregarded the Buddha's words and departed. Referring to this, it is said: "Then the Venerable Nagasamāla, having deposited the Blessed One's bowl and robes right there on the ground, departed." In that passage, "the Blessed One's bowl and robes" refers to the bowl and robes of the Blessed One that were in his hands. "Right there" means he placed them on the ground on that very road and left. The intention was: "Venerable Sir, here are your bowl and robes; if you wish, take them; I desire to go only by the path I prefer." The Blessed One then took his bowl and robes himself and proceeded along the path he intended.

"Robbers came out in the middle of the way" means that at that time, it is said, five hundred men who were fierce, blood-stained, and outlaws had entered the forest and were making a living by robbery, staying in the forest near the road thinking, "By being a danger, we will cut off the King's revenue route." When those robbers saw the Elder traveling along that road, they became angry, saying, "This ascetic is coming by this road; he is using a path that should not be used; he does not know of our presence; come, let us make him know," and they rushed out from the thickets. They suddenly threw the Elder to the ground, beat and kicked him with their hands and feet, broke his clay bowl, and tore his robes into pieces. Because he was a renunciant, they said, "We will not kill him; from now on, know the danger of this road," and they released him. Referring to this, it is stated in the Pāḷi: "Then, of the Venerable Nagasamāla... (pe) ...they tore."

The Blessed One, knowing, "This Nagasamāla who went by that road has been oppressed by robbers and will now come seeking me," traveled a little further, stepped off the road, and sat at the foot of a certain tree. The Venerable Nagasamāla returned, following the same path the Teacher had taken, and seeing the Blessed One at the foot of that tree, he approached, paid homage, and reported everything that had happened. Referring to this, it is stated in the Pāḷi: "Then the Venerable Nagasamāla... (pe) ...and they tore the outer robe (saṅghāṭi)."

"Having known this matter" means knowing that the Venerable Nagasamāla had gone on the unsafe path by disregarding his words, and that he himself had gone on the safe path, he uttered this inspired utterance (Udāna) illuminating that meaning. The meaning of that Udāna verse should be understood thus: "Living together" means practicing together, staying in one group; this text...
384:
In that (verse), 'saha caranti' means practicing together, living together. This phrase (ekato vasanti) is a synonym for that very term (saha caranti); it means living together. 'missō aññajanena vedagū': He is called 'vedagū' because he has reached (attained) the knowledge of the Noble Path of the Four Truths, known as 'veda' because it is to be known; or because he has reached the further shore of all knowable things (ñeyyadhamma). One is called 'añña' (other) because he does not know his own benefit or harm; it means an ignorant fool. He is 'mixed' (missa) with that 'añña' person merely by the act of wandering together. 'vidvā pajahāti pāpakaṃ': The wise one, knowing through that state of being a 'vedagū', abandons evil that brings suffering to himself; or he abandons an evil, ignoble person (akalyāṇapuggala).

How? It is like 'koñco khīrapakovā ninnagaṃ'. When milk mixed with water is brought near, the crane is called a 'milk-drinker' because it drinks only the milk, excluding the water. Just as it abandons the water called 'ninnaga' (flowing downwards), so too the wise person, even when together with unwise persons in standing, sitting, etc., abandons them through his conduct; he never mixes (in heart) with them.

## The Commentary on the Seventh Sutta is finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Visākhā Sutta

In the eighth sutta, 'Visākhā Migāramātā's granddaughter had passed away' means the young daughter of the son of the great lay devotee Visākhā had died. That young girl was accomplished in conduct and had great faith in the Dispensation. She diligently performed the services (veyyāvacca) for the monks and nuns who came to the house of the great lay devotee Visākhā, both before and after the meal. She acted according to the wishes of her grandmother, Visākhā. Therefore, when Visākhā went out of the house, she would go only after entrusting all household affairs to that young girl. She was also beautiful and pleasing to look at. Thus, she was especially dear and beloved to Visākhā. She passed away, overcome by illness. Therefore, it is said: 'Now at that time, Visākhā Migāramātā's granddaughter, who was dear and beloved, had passed away.' Then, the great lay devotee, unable to restrain the grief caused by her death, being pained and dejected, after performing the funeral rites, approached the Blessed One, thinking, 'Perhaps I might find relief for my mind when I go to the presence of the Teacher.' Therefore, it is said: 'Then Visākhā Migāramātā...' and so on. Therein, 'divā divassa' means during the day, at the time of midday.
385:
The Blessed One, knowing Visākhā's delight in the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa), spoke the words beginning with 'Would you, Visākhā...' for the purpose of thinning out her grief by a skillful means. Therein, 'yāvatikā' means as many as. At that time, it is said that seventy million people lived in Sāvatthī. Referring to that population, the Blessed One asked, 'Visākhā, how many people in Sāvatthī die every day?' Visākhā replied, 'Venerable Sir, even ten die (every day),' and so on. Therein, 'tīṇi' means three people. Or, this 'tīṇi' itself is the original reading. 'avivittā' means not empty (constantly occurring).

Then the Blessed One, wishing to make his intention clear, said, 'Visākhā, would you ever be with clothes not wet or hair not wet?' This shows: 'If it were so, would you not always be one with wet clothes and wet hair because of descending into the water for the funeral rites of deceased children and so on, being overcome by grief at all times?' Hearing this, the lay devotee, struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega), rejected it saying, 'Not so, Venerable Sir.' Then, wishing to inform the Teacher of how her mind had turned away from the regret caused by dear objects, she said, 'Venerable Sir, I have had enough of so many children and grandchildren.'

Then the Blessed One, wishing to teach the Dhamma to her, saying, 'This suffering has its root in dear objects; as many as there are dear objects, so many are the sufferings. Therefore, one who desires happiness and loathes suffering should detach the mind from dear objects in every way,' spoke the words beginning with 'Visākhā, those for whom there are a hundred dear things, for them there are a hundred sufferings.' Therein, 'sataṃ piyāni' means a hundred objects to be loved. Some also read 'sataṃ piyaṃ'. Here, since numbers from one to ten emphasize the things numbered (saṅkhyeyya), the Pali text appears as 'yesaṃ dasa piyāni, dasa tesaṃ dukkhāni' and so on. Some teachers read 'yesaṃ dasa piyānaṃ, dasa nesaṃ dukkhānaṃ', but that reading is not good. Since numbers from twenty to a hundred also emphasize the things numbered, taking that emphasis on the things numbered even there, the Pali text appears as 'Visākhā, those for whom there are a hundred dear things, for them there are a hundred sufferings' and so on. In all the Pali passages, the reading should be 'yesaṃ ekaṃ piyaṃ, ekaṃ tesaṃ dukkhaṃ' (for those who have one dear thing, for them there is one suffering), and it should not be 'dukkhassa'. In this way, the Blessed One's teaching has a single flavor and a single intention. Therefore, the Pali text should be understood according to the method mentioned.
386:
Having understood this matter—meaning that mental and physical suffering such as sorrow and lamentation have a dear object as their cause and sign; that they exist when a dear object exists, and do not exist when it does not—having understood this matter in all its aspects, he uttered this inspired utterance that clarifies that meaning.
