The meaning of that inspired utterance is as follows: Whatever sorrows of various kinds, whether mild or moderate, characterized by the mental burning of a fool who is burning within, being afflicted by the loss of relatives, wealth, health, virtue, or view; or whatever lamentations characterized by verbal wailing produced by the outburst of sorrow in one afflicted by those very losses; or whatever pains characterized by bodily oppression in one whose body is struck by undesirable tangibles; or furthermore, grief (domanassa) and despair (upāyāsa) and so forth, which are included by the word 'vā' (or) to encompass meanings not explicitly mentioned—these are seen and found in this world of beings in many forms and various ways due to the diversity of their bases. All these arise, are produced, come into being, and are generated depending on, based on, and having as their condition a being or a formation (saṅkhāra) that is dear and of a dear nature. However, when that aforementioned dear object is absent, or when the desire and lust (chanda-rāga) that creates the state of being dear is abandoned, these sufferings never occur. For it has been said: "From the dear, sorrow is born... from affection, sorrow is born," and so forth (Dhp. 212-213). Likewise, it is said: "Quarrels, disputes, lamentations, and sorrows, along with stinginess, have their origin in the dear" (Sn. 869). Here, in the phrase "paridevitā vā dukkhā vā," it should be understood that there is a change of gender (liṅga-vipallāsa), or that the case endings have been elided where it should have been said "paridevitāni vā dukkhāni vā."

Therefore, those for whom sorrows and so forth originating from the dear do not exist are indeed the happy ones, the sorrowless ones. Who are they? They are those who have no dear thing anywhere in the world. They are the Noble Ones (Ariyas) who, because they are entirely free from lust, have no dear thing or affection in the world of beings or the world of formations, such as "son," "brother," "sister," or "wife." Even in the world of formations, they have no dear thing or affection such as "this is mine; through this, I obtain or will obtain such happiness." Therefore, one who desires the sorrowless and dustless state should not make anything dear anywhere in the world. Since the happy ones are sorrowless, and because they are sorrowless, they have no affection for any object. Therefore, one who has the wholesome desire (kusalacchanda) to attain the state of Arahatship or Nibbāna—called 'sorrowless' (asoka) because of the absence of the aforementioned sorrow, and 'dustless' (viraja) because of the removal of the dust of lust and so forth—should not make or produce affection for things such as visible forms in the world, or even for the states of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). For it has been said: "Monks, even [good] states (dhamma) are to be abandoned by you, how much more so the wrong states (adhamma)" (M. i. 240).

The Commentary on the Eighth Sutta is finished.

Commentary on the Ninth Sutta (Dabba Sutta). "Āyasmā" is a term of endearment. "Dabba" is the name of that Elder. "Mallaputta" means he was the son of a Malla king. That venerable one had made an aspiration at the feet of the Buddha Padumuttara and had accumulated a store of merit for a hundred thousand aeons. In the time of our Buddha, he was born in the clan of the Malla kings...
387:
One who desires the state of Arahatship, which is called 'dustless' (viraja) because it is free from the dust of lust and so forth; or Nibbāna, which has acquired the names 'sorrowless' (asoka) and 'dustless' (viraja) because it is the cause for the non-existence of sorrow and the dust of lust and so forth—such a person, having the desire produced by the power of wholesome desire to act (kattukamyatā-kusala-chanda), should not make or produce affection or attachment for things such as visible forms in the world, or even for the states of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). For this is true: "Monks, even wholesome states (dhamma) are to be abandoned, how much more so unwholesome states (adhamma)," as the Blessed One has said.

## The Commentary on the Eighth Sutta is finished.

## 9. Commentary on the First Dabba Sutta

In the ninth sutta, the word "Āyasmā" is a term of endearment. "Dabba" is the name of that Elder, and "Mallaputta" means the son of a Malla king. That venerable one had made an aspiration at the feet of the Buddha Padumuttara and had accumulated a store of merit for a hundred thousand aeons. In the time of our Blessed One, he was conceived in the womb of Devikā, the chief queen of a Malla king. Because of his previous meritorious deeds (adhikāra), at the age of only seven years from birth, he approached his parents and requested ordination. His parents consented, thinking, "Let him first train in the conduct of a monk; if he does not find delight in it, he will return right here."

That youth Dabba approached the Teacher and requested ordination. The Teacher, seeing his possession of the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya), granted him ordination. Because of the advice given at the time of his ordination, the three worlds appeared to him like a blazing fire. He established insight and attained Arahatship at the very end of the hair-shaving ceremony (khuragge). He attained everything that a disciple should attain, such as the three knowledges (tisso vijjā), the four analytical insights (catasso paṭisambhidā), the six higher powers (chaḷabhiññā), and the nine supramundane states (nava lokuttara-dhamma), and became one of the eighty Great Disciples. This is true, for that venerable one said: "I realized Arahatship at the age of seven from birth; whatever is to be attained by a disciple, all that has been reached by me" (Pārā. 380).

Regarding "approached where the Blessed One was": the reason is that one day, Venerable Dabba, after wandering for alms in Rājagaha and returning from his alms-round after his meal, performed his duties to the Blessed One, went to his day-quarters, took water from a water-jar, washed his feet, cooled his body, spread out his sitting cloth (leather skin), sat down, and entered meditative attainment for a determined period. Or, having emerged from the attainment at the determined time, he reviewed his life-formations (āyu-saṅkhāra). It appeared to Venerable Dabba that his life-formations would be exhausted in a few moments. Then Venerable Dabba thought: "It is not fitting for me to attain final passing away (parinibbāna) in this very sitting posture without informing the Blessed One, the Teacher of gods and men, and without letting my fellow practitioners know. I shall approach the Blessed One, ask for permission, perform my duties to the Blessed One, and in order to demonstrate the state of being released from the round of the dispensation..."
388:
Having cooled his body and spread out a leather mat, he sat down, determined a time limit, and entered into meditative attainment (samāpatti). Then, the Venerable Dabba emerged from that attainment at the determined time and contemplated his own life-formations (āyusaṅkhāra). He saw that his life-formations would be exhausted in just a few moments.

He then thought: "It is not proper for me to attain Parinibbāna while sitting here as I am, without informing the Blessed One and without letting my fellow practitioners know. What if I were to approach the Blessed One, ask permission for Parinibbāna, perform duties for the Blessed One, and then, to demonstrate the liberating nature of the Dispensation (Sāsana) by manifesting my psychic power, sit in the air, enter the fire element (tejodhātu), and attain Parinibbāna? If I do this, those who lack faith and devotion in me will gain faith, and that will lead to their long-term welfare and happiness." Having thought thus, the Venerable Dabba approached the Blessed One and did everything exactly as planned. Therefore, it is said: "Then the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta approached the Blessed One," and so forth.

In that text, "parinibbānakālo me" means: "O Blessed One, the time for my Parinibbāna by way of the Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu) has arrived. I wish to attain Parinibbāna after informing the Blessed One of this."

However, some teachers say: "The Elder was neither old nor ill, yet he asked the Blessed One for permission to attain Parinibbāna. What was the reason? 'The Mettiya and Bhummajaka monks previously accused me of a groundless Pārājika offense. Even though that dispute was settled, they still continue to revile me. Believing their words, other worldlings (puthujjana) also show me disrespect and contempt. What is the use of carrying this heavy burden of suffering to no purpose? Therefore, I shall attain Parinibbāna right now.' It was with this resolution that he asked the Blessed One." 

That statement is without reason. For those whose taints are exhausted (arahants) do not think of, strive for, or exert themselves toward Parinibbāna out of fear of others' blame and so forth when their life-formations are not yet exhausted. Nor do they remain for a long time for the sake of others' praise and so forth. Rather, they simply await the exhaustion of their own life-formations in accordance with their natural course. As it is said:

"I do not long for death, I do not long for life;
I await my time, like a hireling waiting for his wages."

The Blessed One also, having looked at the Elder's life-formations and knowing they were exhausted, said: "Dabba, you may do now what you think is timely (for Parinibbāna)."
389:
"Vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā" means having ascended into the sky and going into the air. Because it is used with the prefix 'abhi', this is an accusative case (upayogavacana), but the meaning should be understood in the sense of the locative case (bhummavasena). To the question of what he did after ascending into the sky, it is said: "Sitting cross-legged in the air, in the firmament," and so forth. In that passage, "entering the fire element" (tejodhātuṃ samāpajjitvā) means entering the fourth jhāna attainment associated with the fire kasina (tejokasiṇa).

Indeed, at that time, the Elder paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him three times, and standing at a respectful distance, said: "Blessed One, for a hundred thousand aeons, while living with you in various births and performing meritorious deeds, I did so aiming for this very goal. That goal has reached its culmination today. This is my final sight of you." Among the worldling monks, Stream-enterers (sotāpanna), and Once-returners (sakadāgāmi) present there, some felt great spiritual urgency (saṃvega), while some were moved to tears. Then, the Blessed One, knowing the Elder's intention, said: "Therefore, Dabba, show a psychic miracle to me and to the Saṅgha of monks."

At that very moment, the entire Saṅgha of monks assembled. Then the Venerable Dabba, by the method described as "being one, he becomes many," and so forth, displayed all the miracles common to disciples. He then paid homage to the Blessed One again, ascended into the sky, created earth in the sky, and sat there cross-legged. Having performed the preliminary work (parikamma) for the fire kasina attainment, he entered the attainment, emerged from it, contemplated his body, re-entered the attainment, and having resolved upon the fire element that would consume the body, he attained Parinibbāna. Simultaneously with his resolution, his entire body was set ablaze with fire. In an instant, that fire, like the fire at the end of an aeon, consumed everything by the power of his resolution, leaving behind not even a trace of the formations, not even ash or soot, and then extinguished. Therefore, it is said: "Then the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta," and so forth. In that context, "emerging, he attained Parinibbāna" means emerging from the psychic consciousness (iddhicitta) and attaining Parinibbāna with the life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅgacitta).

"Jhāyamānassa" means burning. "Ḍayhamānassa" is a synonym for the same. Alternatively, "jhāyamānassa" refers to the moment when flames are present, while "ḍayhamānassa" refers to the moment of glowing embers without flames. "Chārikā" means ash. "Masī" means soot (charcoal). "Na paññāyittha" means was not seen; the meaning is that by the power of resolution, everything disappeared in an instant. But why did the Elder display the psychic miracle of superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma)? Did the Blessed One not forbid the performing of psychic miracles? This should not be questioned. For the prohibition was only against performing miracles in the presence of laypeople. That prohibition also, by the power of creation...
390:
Is it prohibited? Because performing miracles in the presence of laypeople is prohibited, this matter should not be questioned. Furthermore, that prohibition applies to miracles performed through the power of transformation (vikubbana), not to those performed through the power of resolve (adhiṭṭhāna) like this. This venerable one, however, displayed the miracle only because he was commanded by the Lord of Dhamma (the Buddha).

'Knowing this significance' means knowing in every aspect this final passing away without clinging (anupādā-parinibbāna) of the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta, he uttered this inspired utterance that clarifies that meaning.

In that inspired utterance, 'the body broke up' means the physical body (rūpakāya) produced by the four causes, consisting of the primary elements and derived matter, broke up without remainder, was consumed, disappeared, and reached the state of non-arising. 'Perception ceased' means all perceptions, such as perception of forms, etc., which range over objects like the base of forms, etc., ceased through the cessation that leaves no link to rebirth. 'All feelings have become cool' means all feelings, such as resultant (vipāka) feelings and functional (kiriya) feelings, have become cool because there is no longer even a slight distress of feeling, as they have ceased through the cessation that leaves no link to rebirth. Wholesome and unwholesome feelings, however, had already reached cessation at the moment of the fruit of Arahantship. Some also read 'sītirahimsu,' which means they became tranquil and ceased. 'Formations were stilled' means all mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), such as contact (phassa), etc., consisting of resultants and functionals, were especially stilled because they ceased through the cessation that leaves no link to rebirth. 'Consciousness has come to an end' means all consciousness, consisting of resultants and functionals, has come to an end, destruction, and annihilation through the cessation that leaves no link to rebirth.

Thus, because the five aggregates of the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta had already ceased without remainder regarding defilements, kamma-formations, and clinging, the Blessed One, based on the fact of his cessation through the cessation that leaves no link to rebirth—like a fire whose fuel is exhausted—uttered this inspired utterance with an outpouring of joy.

## The Commentary on the Ninth Sutta is finished.

## 10. Commentary on the Second Dabba Sutta

In the tenth sutta, 'Then the Blessed One addressed the monks' means that after the Blessed One had stayed in Rājagaha as long as he liked, while wandering through the countryside, he gradually reached Sāvatthī and stayed in the Jeta Grove. He addressed them to make the final passing away of the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta manifest to those monks who had not witnessed it, and also to inspire great affection for the Elder Dabba in those worldling (puthujjana) monks who lacked respect for the Elder due to the false accusations made by the monks Mettiya and Bhummazaka.
391:
The Blessed One addressed the monks so that the worldling monks, who lacked respect for the Elder Dabba due to the false and baseless accusations made by the monks Mettiya and Bhummazaka, might develop great appreciation and honor for that Elder. In that passage, 'tatra' is merely a particle used to introduce the speech. 'Kho' is an emphatic particle (avadhāraṇa). By the word 'tatra,' the significance of the words 'the Blessed One addressed the monks' is clarified. By the word 'kho,' it shows that the Blessed One indeed addressed them, and that there was no obstacle to his addressing them. Alternatively, 'tatra' means in that monastery. 'Kho' is an ornamental particle (vacanālaṅkāra). 'Āmantesi' means he spoke. Why did the Blessed One address only the monks? Because they are the seniors, the best, are close by, are always present, and are especially suitable recipients for the Dhamma teaching. 

'Bhikkhavo' (Monks) shows the manner of addressing them, and 'Bhadante' (Venerable Sir) is the respectful reply of the monks who were addressed to the Teacher. In that context, by saying 'Bhikkhavo,' the Blessed One addresses those monks. By saying 'Bhadante,' those monks reply. Furthermore, by this word 'Bhikkhavo,' which is preceded by and based on a gentle heart pervaded by great compassion, he turns those monks away from meditation on a subject (kammaṭṭhāna) and reflection on the Dhamma, etc., and makes them face him. By the word 'Bhadante,' which expresses great regard, appreciation, and respect for the Teacher, those monks announce their desire to listen and their respectful state of accepting the advice. 'Bhagavato paccassosum' means those monks listened to the words of the Blessed One; they generated a desire to hear. 'Etadavoca' means the Blessed One spoke the entire sutta discourse that is about to be recited. The meaning of the words beginning with 'Dabbassa, bhikkhave, Mallaputtassa' is just as stated in the preceding sutta. In 'etam-atthaṃ' and so on, there is nothing new; it should be understood in the same way as stated in the preceding sutta.

In the verses: 'ayoghanahatassa' means struck with an iron sledgehammer or an iron mallet used for striking iron. Some teachers, however, explain 'ayoghanahatassa' as 'struck upon a solid iron mass.' Here, the word 'eva' is merely a particle. 'Jalato jātavedaso' means of the blazing fire. Here, the genitive case is used in the sense of disregard (anādara). 'Anupubbūpasantassa' means gradually stilled, extinguished, or ceased. 'Yathā na ñāyate gatī' means just as the destination of that fire is not known. This is what is meant: of the blazing fire struck by a large iron sledgehammer, mallet, etc., or of one situated in a bronze vessel, etc., similarly...
392:
Just as when a red-hot iron bar, whether placed on an anvil or in a bronze vessel, is struck with a heavy hammer, or likewise when a sound that has arisen gradually subsides and reaches complete cessation, its destination cannot be known in any of the ten directions because it has ceased without rebirth due to the cessation of its causes; in the same way, those who are 'Rightly Liberated' (Sammāvimutta) because they have been well-liberated from the four types of clinging and the taints (āsavas) by the Noble Path preceded by liberation by substitution of opposites (tadaṅgavimutti) and liberation by suppression (vikkhambhanavimutti), and because of that liberation, they have crossed over and stand beyond the flood of sensual desire (kāmogha), known as the bond of sensuality, and the remaining floods such as the flood of existence (bhavogha); having well-stilled all the agitations of defilements and being unshakable by the storms of the volitional formations of defilements, they have reached the bliss of the stilling of all formations known as Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna). The destination (gati) of such Arahants cannot be designated as 'such and such a destination' among the destinations of devas, humans, and so forth, because there is no such designation possible and it cannot be found. Just like the aforementioned fire, the Arahant has gone to a state that cannot be designated; this is the meaning to be understood.

## The Explanation of the Tenth Sutta is finished.

## The Explanation of the Pāṭaligāmiya Chapter is also finished.
393:
## Concluding Remarks
In this sequence of words: The Great Buddha, who has no attachment to existence, who is well-liberated, who is honored by devas and dānavas, who has cut the continuity of craving, who inspires joy and sense of urgency, who always delights in the gift of the True Dhamma, and who leads to the destruction of clinging, uttered these inspired utterances (udānas) in various places.

The Elder Dhamma-collectors, who brought all those inspired utterances together and performed the rehearsal, compiled them into the text named 'Udāna'.

In order to clarify the meaning of that Udāna text, relying on the method of the ancient commentaries, I have undertaken this commentary (atthavaṇṇanā).

Because it explains the ultimate meanings in the Sutta discourses as is appropriate, it is named 'Paramatthadīpanī' (Elucidator of the Ultimate Meaning).

This commentary, which contains clear decisions and is equal in extent to thirty-four recitation sections (bhāṇavāras) of the Pali text, has now reached completion.

By the power of the merit I have gained through composing this commentary, may all beings enter the Dispensation of the Lord of the World and experience the taste of liberation through pure practices such as virtue (sīla).

May the Dispensation of the Fully Enlightened One endure long in the world. May all living beings always have reverence for that Dispensation.

May the rain-god send down rain in due season. May the Great King, the lord of the earth, delighting in the True Dhamma, rule the world only in accordance with the Dhamma.

## The Commentary on the Udāna, composed by the Teacher, Elder Dhammapāla, who resided at the Badaratittha Monastery, is finished.
